- Then U_x V_x F = x⟨x⟩F.
- This also matches the paper's own W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ (p. 317), since V_x = W_x∘π1^*.

With ψ(f,g) = π1^*f + V_x g, the corrected relation gives U_x ψ(f,g) = ψ(T_x f + x⟨x⟩g, −f/x). That is exactly the printed matrix A. Its characteristic polynomial is det(X−A) = X^2 − T_x X + ⟨x⟩, as the proof's (A−α_x)(A−β_x) ≡ 0 needs. The printed relation would instead give the (1,2) entry ⟨x⟩ and the polynomial X^2 − T_x X + ⟨x⟩/x. So the printed matrix agrees with the corrected relation, not with the printed one.

A(f,0)^T = (T_x f, −f/x)^T, so the printed −f does not match the printed matrix either. Since x is a prime different from p, x is a unit in O. So −f/x is non-zero exactly when f is, and the argument goes through unchanged.

This has nothing to do with the 47 known bracket errors. I tried to defend the printed relation and could not.

(1) The paper's own conventions (§3.2.3, pp. 316–317) give a factor x:
- x T_x = tr(π1)∘φ12∘π2^*, and x U_x is defined the same way. So U_x g(E,α,C) = (1/x) Σ_{D≠C} φ_D^* g(E/D, φ_Dα, (C+D)/D).
- V_x = φ12∘π2^*.
- The paper itself says each of the x terms equals x⟨x⟩f, and then divides by 1/x. That gives x⟨x⟩f, not ⟨x⟩f. The step "[x]^* acts on ω by x" is the paper's own; weight 1 has no other normalization that would absorb the factor.

(2) A second check, using only identities the paper itself proves:
- The claim on p. 320, (1/x)π1^*∘tr(π1)∘W_x = U_x + (1/x)W_x, is a true operator identity. Directly, Σ_D φ_D^* g(E/D, φ_Dα, E[x]/D) = xU_x g + W_x g, since C+D = E[x].
- The paper has V_x = W_x∘π1^* (p. 320), W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ (p. 317) and tr(π1)∘π1^* = x+1.
- So U_xV_x = (1/x)π1^* tr(π1) W_x^2 π1^* − (1/x)W_x^2 π1^* = ⟨x⟩(x+1)π1^* − ⟨x⟩π1^* = x⟨x⟩π1^*.

(3) Tate-curve check at the cusp (Tate(q), α_can, μ_x): V_xF = x⟨x⟩F(q^x) and U_x(Σ b_n q^n) = Σ b_{nx}q^n, so U_xV_xF = x⟨x⟩F.

(4) The only partial defence: in Lemma 3.5, x ≡ 1 mod p, so x ≡ 1 mod m_∅ and the missing factor makes no difference mod m_∅. But the display claims an exact equality of maps over O, which is false.

Consequences:
- The very next display, A = (T_x, x⟨x⟩; −1/x, 0), is exactly what the corrected relation gives. With ψ(f,g) = π1^*f + V_xg, we get U_xψ(f,g) = ψ(T_xf + x⟨x⟩g, −f/x).
- A has characteristic polynomial X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩. The printed relation would give X^2 − T_xX + x^{-1}⟨x⟩ instead.
- So A, the Hensel step, and the V[m]=0 part are all consistent with the corrected relation. The V[m]=0 part uses only the first relation and W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩.
- Lemma 3.6's proof (p. 321) needs exactly X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩ when x ≢ 1 mod p: "T acts via T_{∅,m∅}[X]/(X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩)". It gets this from A, not from the misprinted relation.
- Later arguments that say "as in Lemma 3.5" do not rely on the misprinted relation: p. 331 (§3.5, U_p; states the quadratic relation directly), p. 350 (Thm 3.30(1); cites W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ and the p. 320 claim), p. 376 (H^1 analogue).
- The vector entry −f contradicts the printed A, whose (2,1) entry is −1/x. It should be −f/x. Since x ≠ p, x is a unit in O, so "non-zero whenever f is" still holds.

I classify both as misprints rather than errors: the intended values are fixed by the paper's own computation and by the next display. Nothing downstream is affected, and both stated results (Lemmas 3.5 and 3.6) stand.

issues.correction: Replace "by length considerations" with "comparing lengths of ϖ^m-torsion submodules for every m". Write M = H^0(X,ω_{K/O})_{m∅}, A = (Im ψ)_m = ker(U_x − α̃_x) and B = ker(U_x − β̃_x), so that A ⊕ B = (Im ψ)_{m∅} ≅ M². Since X is flat over O, M[ϖ] = H^0(X,ω_k)_{m∅} is finite, so each M[ϖ^m] has finite length. The injections restrict to M[ϖ^m] ↪ A[ϖ^m] and M[ϖ^m] ↪ B[ϖ^m], and A[ϖ^m] ⊕ B[ϖ^m] ≅ M[ϖ^m]². So ℓ(A[ϖ^m]) + ℓ(B[ϖ^m]) = 2ℓ(M[ϖ^m]) with each term at least ℓ(M[ϖ^m]), which forces both restricted maps to be isomorphisms. A and B are ϖ-power torsion, so taking the union over m gives the result. An equivalent route works on Pontryagin duals: compare O-ranks first, then the lengths of the torsion submodules. The candidate's proposed correction is right; the ϖ^m-torsion version is the minimal one.
issues.reason:
I checked the page image. The printed sentence justifies the isomorphism by length. But M = H^0(X,ω_{K/O})_{m∅} ≅ (H^0(X,ω)⊗K/O)_{m∅} ⊕ (finite torsion) is a cofinitely generated O-module. It has infinite length whenever there are characteristic-zero weight-one forms at m∅, and those are exactly the cases the paper cares about (for example, dihedral forms). In those cases "ℓ(A)+ℓ(B)=2ℓ(M), ℓ(A),ℓ(B) ≥ ℓ(M)" is ∞ = ∞ and proves nothing. The argument works literally only when H^0(X,ω_K)_{m∅} = 0.

Defence I tried: the paper has no convention that makes "length" meaningful here. It introduces Pontryagin duality only afterwards, before Lemma 3.7, and grepping the paper finds no corank or length convention. So the justification as printed does not apply.

The conclusion is still true, and the fix takes one line (details in the correction field). The rest of the setup holds: ψ is injective on the m∅-part because ψ^∨∘ψ is an isomorphism, α̃_x − β̃_x is a unit, and (U_x − β̃_x)∘π_1^* lands in (Im ψ)_m. Since the statement of Lemma 3.5 is correct, Lemma 3.6, Theorem 3.30(1), Lemma 5.8 and the patching arguments that use it are unaffected. §3.5 (p. ~333) reuses the argument with finite coefficients O/ϖ^m, where lengths are finite, so the printed wording is valid there. This is a minor, routine imprecision rather than a real hole. It counts as a gap under PROTOCOL §18 because the stated reason does not apply as written.

issues.printed: p. 320 (PDF p. 24), proof of Lemma 3.5 (§3.2.4): "We claim that (1/x)(π1^* ∘ tr(π1) ∘ W_x) = U_x + (1/x)W_x. To see this, we will rewrite the relation π1^* ∘ T_x = U_x ∘ π1^* + (1/x)V_x that we established earlier. Since π2 = π1 ∘ w_x, we have that T_x = (1/x) tr(π1) ∘ W_x ∘ π1^* and V_x = W_x ∘ π1^*. The earlier relation can thus be written: (1/x)π1^* ∘ tr(π1) ∘ W_x ∘ π1^* = U_x ∘ π1^* + (1/x)W_x ∘ π1^*. Since π1^* is fully faithful, the claim follows." Reused on p. 350 (PDF p. 54), proof of Theorem 3.30, item (1): "such that W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ and (1/x)π1^* ∘ tr(π1) ∘ W_x = U_x + (1/x)W_x." The arXiv v2 has the same sentence ("Since π1 is fully faithful, the claim follows.", cg-v2.txt line 905).
issues.reason:
I transcribed both passages from the page images (PDF pp. 24 and 54). The deduction as printed is invalid. The displayed relation is an identity of maps H^0(X,ω) → H^0(X_0(x),ω) of the form A∘π1^* = B∘π1^*. Cancelling π1^* on the right to get A = B would need π1^* to be surjective (an epimorphism). "Fully faithful" is meaningless for a linear map, and injectivity does not help. π1^* is not surjective: the proof itself shows that H^0(X,ω)^2_{m∅} (the image of ψ = (π1^*, φ12∘π2^*)) is a direct factor of H^0(X_0(x),ω)_{m∅}. Even read as the pullback functor on sheaves, π1^* is not fully faithful for a finite flat map of degree x+1. The claim is needed exactly off the image of π1^*. It is applied to f ∈ V[m], where V = ker ψ^∨ is a complement to Im ψ, and property (3), tr(π1)W_x f = 0, is turned into −xU_x f = W_x f. So the printed argument leaves a gap. I redid the moduli computation using the paper's own conventions: W_x on p. 315, U_x on X_0(x) from §3.2.3 and p. 319 (where the sum over D ≠ C_x is identified with U_x∘π1^*), and T_x = (1/x)tr(π1)∘W_x∘π1^*. It gives π1^* tr(π1) W_x = xU_x + W_x on all of H^0(X_0(x),ω), so the claim is true and the candidate's correction is right. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not address it. On 'affects': Lemma 3.5 and Theorem 3.30 remain true, and every later use of the identity (Thm 3.30(1) via G-invariants of the level-V operator) goes through once the claim is proved directly. No stated result is affected. But the printed proof of Lemma 3.5 (and of the corresponding step of Theorem 3.30(1)) does not establish its intermediate claim. Under PROTOCOL §18, where 'nothing' means the mathematics is right as intended, I classify this as 'the proof' rather than 'nothing'. 'nothing' is defensible only if one counts the one-line computation as what the authors intended. I checked the page images for p. 318, p. 319, p. 320 and p. 350, and for arXiv v2 p. 18.

Why the defence fails:
- The displayed relation is an identity of maps H^0(X,ω) → H^0(X_0(x),ω) of the form A∘π1^* = B∘π1^*, with A, B endomorphisms of H^0(X_0(x),ω).
- Cancelling π1^* on the right needs π1^* to be surjective. "Fully faithful" does not apply to a linear map. Reading π1^* as the pullback functor on sheaves does not help either: the operators are composed with π1^*, not obtained by applying π1^* to morphisms, and pullback along a finite flat map of degree x+1 is not full anyway.
- π1^* is not surjective. The proof itself makes Im ψ ⊇ Im π1^* a proper direct factor with complement V = ker ψ^∨.
- The claim is needed exactly off Im π1^*. It is applied to f ∈ V[m] to turn property (3), tr(π1)W_x f = 0, into −xU_x f = W_x f. Adding the V_x relation only gives the identity on Im ψ, and x-new forms are not generated by old ones.
- No charitable reading or nearby statement supplies the step. The printed inference is invalid.

The claim itself is true. By the moduli computation above, π1^* tr(π1) W_x = xU_x + W_x holds on the whole space. Consistency checks:
1. On π1^*f it reduces to the paper's xπ1^*T_x = xU_xπ1^* + V_x.
2. On V_x f both sides give x(x+1)⟨x⟩π1^*f. This uses W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ and U_x∘V_x = x·π1^*⟨x⟩. That value of U_x∘V_x is the one in the matrix A on p. 319 (upper-right entry x⟨x⟩), not the printed "U_x∘V_x = π1^*⟨x⟩", which is the separate candidates H-part1a-1 / X-K2-2.
3. On x-newforms it says W_x = −xU_x. This agrees with the classical a_x = −λ_x x^{k/2−1}, since here W_x = x^{k/2}·w_classical.

The downstream steps are then fine: x²U_x²f = W_x²f = x⟨x⟩f gives xα_x² = α_xβ_x, so α_x ≡ β_x mod m, a contradiction. Theorem 3.30(1) takes the identity on X_{V_0(x)} to X_{U_0(x)} via G-invariants, and the same direct computation works at that level. This is not one of the 47 bracket defects, and the 2022 Correction does not address it.

Affects: Lemma 3.5 and Theorem 3.30 remain true. The printed proof, though, does not establish its intermediate claim, and the repair is a new (short) computation, not a clear-context slip. So I set 'the proof', not 'nothing'.

The paper itself calls the Pontryagin dual 'third quadrant', i.e. E^{−i,−j}, which is what you get by negating the first quadrant. Negating the second quadrant would give the fourth. So 'second' is inconsistent with the paper's own next sentence and with the standard Hochschild–Serre sequence (Milne III.2.20). Nothing in the argument uses the quadrant label.

issues.locator: §3.3, Remark 3.10, footnote 3, published pp. 325–326 (PDF pp. 29–30). The two sheaves printed as ω^2 (in the "naïvely … vanish" sentence and in the displayed H^0(X_H(13)_{F_3}, ω^2) = H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2)^{Z/3Z}) should be ω^2(−∞). arXiv v2 has the same text (cg-v2.txt ll. 1104–1113). arXiv v1 does not have this footnote or example; its only footnote at that point is a different one about representability when p = 3.
issues.printed: Footnote 3 (to Remark 3.10), p. 325 continued on p. 326: "Here is a somewhat different example: let H ⊂ (Z/13Z)^× denote the group of squares; there is a finite étale map X_1(13) → X_H(13) with Galois group Z/3Z (viewing X_H(13) as a stack). The underlying scheme of X_H(13) is isomorphic over O (for p ≠ 13) to the projective line, and hence, naïvely, one would expect H^0(X_H(13), ω^2) to vanish. However, as noted by Serre [34,35], there exists a Galois representation ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(F_3) with N(ρ̄) = 13, k(ρ̄) = 2, and ε(ρ̄) quadratic. (The representation ρ̄ is induced from Q(√−3)). The original conjecture 3.2.4_? of [36] asserts that ρ̄ gives rise to a mod-3 modular form on X_H(13). However, considering X_H(13) as a stack, one finds, for p = 3, that the group H^0(X_H(13)_{F_3}, ω^2) = H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2)^{Z/3Z} is indeed non-zero, even though the scheme underlying X_H(13) has genus zero."
issues.correction: Replace ω^2 with ω^2(−∞) in all three places. The footnote should read: "one would expect H^0(X_H(13), ω^2(−∞)) to vanish" and "H^0(X_H(13)_{F_3}, ω^2(−∞)) = H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2(−∞))^{Z/3Z} is indeed non-zero". An equivalent fix is to localize at the maximal ideal m of ρ̄. The (−∞) version is the minimal correction because it matches the genus-zero heuristic, since Ω^1 ≅ ω^2(−∞).
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the rendered pages (PDF 29–30). I then redid the mathematics for Γ_H(13) with H = the squares {1,3,4,9,10,12}, which contains −1.
(1) Invariants. [PSL_2(Z):Γ_H(13)] = 28. The d with d^2 ≡ −1 are 5 and 8, and neither is a square, so there are no order-2 elliptic points. The d with d^2 − d + 1 ≡ 0 are 4 and 10, both squares, so there are 4 order-3 elliptic points. There are 4 cusps. The genus is 1 + 28/12 − 4/3 − 4/2 = 0, which agrees with the paper. So dim M_2(Γ_H(13)) = g + #cusps − 1 = 3 and dim S_2 = 0.
(2) Characteristic 0. In characteristic 0, H^0(X_H(13), ω^2) is 3-dimensional. It is M_2(Γ_0(13)) plus the two Eisenstein series with the quadratic character; S_2(13, χ_quad) = 0. The "naïve" expectation that it vanishes is therefore wrong, even for the coarse scheme. On the stack, deg ω^2 = 14/3. Its pushforward to the coarse P^1 has degree 14/3 − 4·(2/3) = 2, so it is O(2) with 3 sections. The pushforward of ω^2(−∞) has degree −2, so it is Ω^1_{P^1} and has no sections. Only the cuspidal version matches "P^1, hence vanishes" and "genus zero".
(3) Characteristic 3. Mod 3, the printed claim "H^0(X_H(13)_{F_3}, ω^2) is indeed non-zero" is true but trivial. It contains the reduction of (E_2(z) − 13E_2(13z))/(−12) = 1 + 2Σσ(n)q^n − 26Σσ(n)q^{13n}, which has constant term 1 mod 3. So the "However … even though genus zero" contrast shows nothing as printed.
(4) The corrected statement holds. Let f be the weight-2 newform on Γ_1(13) whose character ε has order 6. For d ∈ H, the operator ⟨d⟩ multiplies f by ε(d) ∈ μ_3, and μ_3 ≡ 1 mod (√−3). So f mod (√−3) is a non-zero Z/3Z-invariant element of H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2(−∞)). This is Serre's ρ̄.
Classification. The slip is the omitted "(−∞)". Nothing false is asserted as a mathematical fact: the final non-vanishing is true, and the false claim is labelled a naïve expectation. The intended meaning is clear from "genus zero", from Serre's cuspidal example, and from the paper's own Ω^1 ≅ ω^2(−∞). So I classify it as a misprint, not the "error" the reader proposed. It is a genuine mistake either way. It is a side remark in a footnote, so it affects nothing. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors fixed by the 2022 Correction. 1. The paper's own conventions rule out the charitable reading. The paper always separates ω^n from ω^n(−∞) (e.g. §3.2, and Lemma 3.7 with dim H^0(ω(−∞))_m against dim H^0(ω)_m). It identifies Ω^1 with ω^{⊗2}(−∞) by Kodaira–Spencer (p. 314 of the text). Remark 3.10 itself says H^0(X_R, ω^k) is the space of Katz modular forms, which includes non-cuspidal forms. So H^0(X_H(13), ω^2) means M_2(Γ_H(13)).

2. M_2(Γ_H(13)) is 3-dimensional in characteristic 0. The characters trivial on the squares are 1 and (·/13), and both are even. This gives three Eisenstein series: E_2(z) − 13E_2(13z), E_2^{1,χ} and E_2^{χ,1}. The count matches dim M_2 = g + c − 1 = 0 + 4 − 1 = 3. The stack degree gives the same answer: deg ω^2 = 14/3 on X_H(13), and its pushforward to P^1 has degree 14/3 − 4·(2/3) = 2, so h^0 = 3. Reducing an integral lattice injects into H^0 over F_3 (use 0 → L → L → L/3 → 0), so these forms are also non-zero mod 3.
   - So the printed "naive" expectation fails already over Q.
   - The printed "indeed non-zero" is true but trivially so, and has nothing to do with genus zero.
   - The word "naïvely" cannot rescue the text: the closing contrast ("even though the scheme underlying X_H(13) has genus zero") only has content for cusp forms.

3. With ω^2(−∞) both claims are right.
   - Genus is 0: g = 1 + 28/12 − ν_2/4 − ν_3/3 − 4/2 = 0. Here ν_2 = 0, because the roots ±5 of x^2 + 1 mod 13 are non-squares. ν_3 = 4, because the roots 3 and 9 of x^2 + x + 1 are squares. There are 4 cusps. Riemann–Hurwitz for X_1(13) (genus 2) → P^1 checks out: 2 = 3·(−2) + 4·2.
   - Hence S_2(Γ_H(13)) = 0 over C. Equivalently, the pushforward of ω^2(−∞) is O(−2).
   - Mod 3: take the newform in S_2(Γ_1(13)), whose character has order 6. Modulo (√−3) its character is congruent to (·/13), so it is fixed by H/±1 ≅ Z/3Z. It therefore gives a non-zero class in H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2(−∞))^{Z/3Z}. This is exactly Serre's ρ̄, and it is the stacky mod-3 phenomenon the footnote is describing.

4. Classification. The intended meaning (weight-2 cusp forms, the Ω^1 heuristic) is clear from context and the paper's conventions. The fix is a mechanical insertion of (−∞). So I classify it as a misprint rather than the candidate's "error". "Error" is still defensible, because the heuristic as literally printed is false.

5. Consequences. Footnote 3 is purely illustrative. Nothing later in the paper uses footnote 3 or X_H(13); the only other hits for "(13)" are inside the footnote itself. The main text avoids stacks altogether by adding Γ_1(q)-level. So affects = nothing.

issues.locator: §3.3, the continuation of Remark 3.10 (the "fix" paragraph choosing an auxiliary prime q), published p. 326 (PDF p. 30), lines 9–11 of the page. arXiv v2 has the same sentence (cg-v2.txt l. 1079–1080). arXiv v1 does not have this sentence: its footnote 1 in §3 only says the prime's existence is "guaranteed by the Chebotarev density theorem".
issues.printed: First, we claim that the Chebotarev density theorem guarantees the existence of such primes. Since det(ρ̄) is unramified at p, the fixed field of ker(ρ̄) does not contain Q(ζ_p) (note that p ≠ 2). Hence, we may find infinitely many primes q such that the fixed field of ker(ρ̄) splits completely and q ≢ 1 mod p; such primes satisfy the required hypothesis.
issues.correction: Replace 'det(ρ̄)' with 'ρ̄': 'Since ρ̄ is unramified at p, the fixed field of ker(ρ̄) is unramified at p, so it does not contain Q(ζ_p), which is ramified at p because p ≠ 2.' The minimal fix is to delete 'det( )'. Both readers' proposed corrections are right.
issues.reason:
The next sentence needs Q(ζ_p) ⊄ L, where L is the fixed field of ker ρ̄. Only then is there a σ with ρ̄(σ) = 1 and χ_p(σ) ≠ 1, which is what gives primes q that split in L with q ≢ 1 mod p. The paper gets this from "det(ρ̄) unramified at p", and that implication is false in general.

Counterexample (checked by hand), p = 3:
- Setup: take K = Q(√−3) = Q(ζ_3) and 𝔮 | 7 (7 splits in K). Let ψ be the quadratic character of (O_K/(√−3)𝔮)^× = F_3^× × F_7^× given by (sign) × (Legendre symbol).
- ψ is trivial on O_K^× = μ_6:
  - ψ(−1) = (−1)·(−1/7) = (−1)(−1) = 1.
  - ζ_3 ≡ 1 mod √−3, and ζ_3 mod 𝔮 has order 3, so it is a square in F_7^×. Hence ψ(ζ_3) = 1.
  - Since h_K = 1, ψ is a ray class character of conductor (√−3)𝔮.
- ρ̄ is absolutely irreducible and odd. Set ρ̄ = Ind_K^Q ψ : G_Q → GL_2(F_3). It is absolutely irreducible because ψ^σ has conductor (√−3)𝔮̄, so ψ^σ ≠ ψ.
- det ρ̄ is unramified at 3. We have det ρ̄ = η_K · (ψ∘V). As a Dirichlet character, ψ∘V(ℓ) = ψ((ℓ)) = (ℓ/3)(ℓ/7), and η_K = (·/3). So det ρ̄ = (·/7), the character of Q(√−7). It is unramified at 3 and odd, since (−1/7) = −1.
- L contains Q(ζ_3). Every element of G_Q \ G_K acts antidiagonally, so it is never the identity. Hence ker ρ̄ ⊂ G_K, and L ⊇ K = Q(ζ_3).

So the stated reason does not give the conclusion. (For comparison, the footnote on the same page mentions Serre's mod-3 example, which is also induced from Q(√−3).)

The conclusion is still true in the paper's setting. Section 3.1 assumes ρ̄|G_p is unramified, so L is unramified at p and cannot contain Q(ζ_p), which is totally ramified of degree p − 1 > 1. The fix swaps det(ρ̄) for ρ̄, i.e. it uses a hypothesis already in force. The mistake is therefore an inadequate justification, not a false statement. Nothing downstream changes.

On the kind: I file this as a gap because the step is asserted with a reason that does not prove it. X-K3-10's "misprint" is also defensible, since the intended reason (ρ̄ unramified at p) is clear from §3.1. WHY THE PRINTED STEP FAILS: in general, knowing that det(ρ̄) is unramified at p does not stop Q(ζ_p) from lying inside L, the fixed field of ker ρ̄. Whether Q(ζ_p) ⊂ L depends on whether ω mod p factors through Gal(L/Q), which can have abelian quotients much larger than the one cut out by det. I checked the reader's counterexample and it holds. Take p = 3, K = Q(√−3), and 7 = 𝔮𝔮̄ (7 splits because −3 ≡ 2² mod 7). Let ψ be the order-2 character of conductor (√−3)𝔮 given by sign on F_3^× times the Legendre symbol on F_7^×.
- ψ is trivial on O_K^× = μ_6: ψ(−1) = (−1)(−1) = 1, and ψ(ζ_3) = 1, because ζ_3 ≡ 1 mod √−3 and an element of order 3 in F_7^× is a square.
- ψ ≠ ψ^c because their conductors differ. So ρ̄ = Ind_K^Q ψ : G_Q → GL_2(F_3) is odd and absolutely irreducible.
- det ρ̄ = η_K·ψ|_{A_Q^×}. On Z_3^× both factors are the character Z_3^× → F_3^× → ±1: for η_K because local norms from Q_3(√−3) are ≡ 1 mod 3. So det ρ̄ is unramified at 3.
- ker ρ̄ ⊂ G_K, so L ⊃ K = Q(ζ_3).
An even simpler example is ω ⊕ ω^{-1}. So 'since det(ρ̄) is unramified' does not justify the claim as written.

DEFENCE: The conclusion itself is true throughout §3. The standing hypothesis of §3.1 (p. 310) is 'Let us suppose that ρ̄|G_p is unramified', and every §3 result assumes it (Cor. 1.5(3), Cor. 1.6). Then L is unramified at p, while Q(ζ_p)/Q is totally ramified at p of degree p − 1 > 1. The parenthetical '(note that p ≠ 2)' is exactly what this ramification argument needs, which is why the intended reason is clear. det(ρ̄) alone would be enough only when Gal(L/Q)^ab is cut out by det, for example when the image contains SL_2(F_p) with p ≥ 3. That is not assumed. The counterexample's ρ̄ is ramified at 3, so it lies outside the paper's setting and does not touch the conclusion.

The rest of the step is fine. If q splits completely in L, then ρ̄(Frob_q) = 1 and the eigenvalue ratio is 1. If also q ≢ 1 mod p, then 1 ≠ q^{±1} mod p. Chebotarev applies because Q(ζ_p) ⊄ L. The printed passage is a slip in the cited reason: it names a true but insufficient consequence (det unramified) instead of the hypothesis actually needed (ρ̄ unramified). It is not a false conclusion.

issues.locator: §3.3: the paragraph before Theorem 3.11 (published p. 326), Theorem 3.11 (local statement at primes x|Q, p. 327) and Remark 3.12 (p. 327); PDF pages 30–31. arXiv v2 has the same wording (cg-v2.txt around lines 1092–1119). In arXiv v1 the result is Theorem 3.8, which has no local statement at x|Q and no Remark 3.12 sentence.
issues.printed: p. 326: "Let Q be as in Sect. 3.2. For each x ∈ Q, assume that the polynomial X² − T_x X + ⟨x⟩ has distinct roots in T_∅/m_∅ = k and choose a root α_x ∈ k of this polynomial. Let m denote the maximal ideal of T generated by m_∅ and U_x − α_x for x ∈ Q." Theorem 3.11 (Local–Global Compatibility), continued on p. 327: "... For a prime x|Q, the restriction of ρ′_Q to D_x is conjugate to a direct sum of residually unramified characters ξ ⊕ ⟨det(ρ̄)⟩|_{D_x} ξ^{−1} where ξ̄(Frob_x) ≡ α_x mod m, and such that the restriction of ξ to I_x and hence via local class field theory to Z_x^× ⊗ Z_p = Δ_x is compatible in the usual way with the diamond operators in T_m." Remark 3.12 (p. 327): "The assumptions on x|Q imply that ρ̄|_{D_x} is p-distinguished and, because there are no local extensions, totally split. Hence the required information is preserved under congruences, and one is reduced once more to higher weight, where this statement is known."
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis x ≡ 1 mod p for every x|Q. This is the Taylor–Wiles condition. It is assumed in Lemma 3.5 and Proposition 3.3, and it is assumed explicitly in the paper's own analogues of this statement: Conjecture A (3) on p. 374 ("N(v) ≡ 1 mod p") and Lemma 5.8 on p. 376. Alternatively, require α_x/β_x ≢ x^{±1} in k, the hypothesis of Lemma 3.6 and of the auxiliary prime q on p. 326. Under either hypothesis every deformation of ρ̄|_{D_x} is a direct sum of characters, and Remark 3.12's argument goes through. Under the ratio condition with x ≢ 1 mod p, those characters are even unramified. The existence of ρ_Q and the claim that ρ′_Q is minimal outside Q need no change, because Definition 3.1 puts no condition at x ∈ Q.
issues.reason:
1. What the hypotheses allow. "Q as in Sect. 3.2" means only a squarefree Q prime to Np (§3.2.1, p. 312). Theorem 3.11 adds one condition: the roots α_x, β_x must be distinct. Nothing forces x ≡ 1 mod p. The paper itself separates the cases: Lemma 3.5 assumes x ≡ 1 mod p, and Lemma 3.6 assumes the ratio of the roots is not x^{±1}.

2. The local computation. Take ρ̄|G_x = χ₁ ⊕ χ₂, both unramified, and let ψ = χ₁/χ₂ with ψ(Frob) = c ≠ 1. The coefficients have order p, so any cocycle factors through tame inertia: σ with φσφ^{−1} = σ^x. Write a = f(σ) and b = f(φ). Applying f to the relation gives b + c·a = x·a + b, so (c − x)a = 0. The coboundaries fill out b because c ≠ 1. Hence dim H¹(G_{Q_x}, ψ) = 1 exactly when c = x in k, and 0 otherwise. The Euler characteristic formula agrees: h¹ = h⁰ + h²(ψ) = 0 + h⁰(ψ^{−1}ε̄) = 1 when ψ = ε̄|G_x. The nonzero class is the Kummer extension Q_x(x^{1/p}).
   - If x ≢ 1 mod p and α_x/β_x = x^{±1}, then ρ̄|D_x has nonsplit, ramified, Steinberg-type deformations. So the step "because there are no local extensions, totally split" fails.
   - If x ≡ 1 mod p, then ε̄|G_x = 1 ≠ ψ and H¹ = 0, as the paper intends.

3. The bad case occurs for every ρ̄. ρ̄ is unramified at p, and every nontrivial subfield of Q(ζ_p) is ramified at p. So the field cut out by ρ̄ is linearly disjoint from Q(ζ_p). By Chebotarev there are infinitely many primes x ∤ Np with ρ̄(Frob_x) conjugate to ρ̄(complex conjugation) (eigenvalues 1 and −1, distinct since p is odd) and x ≡ −1 mod p. These x satisfy every hypothesis of Theorem 3.11. Their eigenvalue ratio is −1 ≡ x ≡ x^{−1}, so the ratio is x^{±1} for either choice of α_x.

4. The reduction to higher weight fails too. Remark 3.12 sends the x|Q statement to higher weight, "where this statement is known". In weight n, when the ratio is x^{±1}, T_{n,m} can contain level-raised forms that are Steinberg at x. For those, ρ|D_x is ramified and not a direct sum of characters, so the higher-weight statement is false there. Sections 3.4–3.7 prove only the statement at p ("the main difficulty ... is showing that the Galois representation is unramified at p"). The Correction (Invent. Math. 227, 2022) deals only with the 47 bracket errors.

So in its stated generality the local claim at x|Q has no valid proof. I have not shown that the weight-one conclusion is actually false, so I classify this as a gap rather than an error.

5. Scope. The paper applies Theorem 3.11 only with Q = 1 and Q = Q_N, where x ≡ 1 mod p^N (§3.8). The main modularity results are therefore unaffected. The auxiliary prime q in the "fix" before Theorem 3.11 goes into the level N, not into Q, and it has ratio ≠ q^{±1} anyway. The defence fails.

(1) "Q as in Sect. 3.2" only requires Q to be squarefree and prime to Np (p. 312). The only extra assumption made before Theorem 3.11 is that the roots are distinct. The condition x ≡ 1 mod p is not a standing assumption. On p. 311 it is only a local "Suppose", and Lemma 3.5 states it again as an explicit hypothesis while Lemma 3.6 explicitly drops it. So the printed theorem covers primes x ≢ 1 mod p.

(2) Take such an x, and write χ1, χ2 for the unramified characters of ρ̄|_{G_x} with Frob_x-eigenvalues α_x, β_x (distinct). Suppose ψ = χ1/χ2 has ψ(Frob_x) = x = ε̄(Frob_x), that is, ψ = ε̄. Then:
- h^0(G_x, ψ) = 0, since ε̄|_{G_x} ≠ 1.
- h^2(G_x, ψ) = h^0(G_x, ε̄ψ^{-1}) = 1, by local Tate duality.
- The local Euler characteristic formula (for x ≠ p) gives h^1(G_x, ψ) = 1.
The nonzero class is ramified; it is the Kummer class of x. It gives a lift [[χ1, εc],[0, χ2]] of ρ̄|_{D_x} to k[ε] that is not split, and it is ramified on inertia. No sum of residually unramified characters can match it: when x ≢ 1 mod p we have Δ_x = 0, so such characters are unramified. So "there are no local extensions" in Remark 3.12 is false in this case.

(3) The paper itself says so on the same page, p. 326. It needs "ratio … neither q nor q^{-1}" for the auxiliary prime q ≢ 1 mod p precisely to exclude deformations "which are ramified and Steinberg (unipotent on inertia)".

(4) Remark 3.12's reduction to higher weight also fails. The level-raising condition in weight n ≡ 1 mod (p−1) is (α − xβ)(β − xα) ≡ 0, the same as in Lemma 3.6. For the root α_x with β_x = xα_x, the algebra T_{n,m} can contain ordinary forms that are Steinberg at x, and then ρ_n|_{D_x} is not a sum of characters. So "this statement is known" in higher weight is not available.

(5) §§3.4–3.7 treat only the prime p and never x|Q. The local assertion at x|Q is therefore unproved in the printed generality. Whether it is actually false in weight one would need new-at-x torsion classes, which the paper does not decide; this is why the finding is classed as a gap rather than an error.

(6) Consequences:
- Theorem 3.11 is used in §3.8 only with Q = 1 and with Q = Q_N from Proposition 3.3, where x ≡ 1 mod p^N. There the local splitting holds: ψ ≠ 1 = ε̄|_{G_x}, so H^1 vanishes in both directions.
- The §3.9 analogue (p. 353, item (4)) leaves out the local statement at x|Q altogether.
- The later analogues (Conjecture A, p. 374; Lemma 5.8, p. 376) state N(v) ≡ 1 mod p explicitly.
So Theorem 3.26, Theorem 1.4 and the paper's other main results are unaffected. Only Theorem 3.11 itself is stated more generally than the paper proves.

issues.reason:
I redid the computation. In weight 1, T_p f = U f + V(⟨p⟩f) on q-expansions. In weight n mod ϖ^m, U_p = U on q-expansions (as the paper says, because p^{n−1} ≡ 0), and φ is the identity on q-expansions. So W f = V⟨p⟩f = ⟨p⟩V_p f, which matches the paper's "ψ = (φ, ⟨p⟩V_p)". This gives two relations: U_p∘φ = φ∘T_p − W and U_p∘W = φ∘⟨p⟩ (since UV = id). Hence U_p ψ(f,g) = φT_p f − Wf + φ(⟨p⟩g) = ψ(T_p f + ⟨p⟩g, −f).

The column matrix of this action is (T_p ⟨p⟩; −1 0) and the row matrix is (T_p −1; ⟨p⟩ 0). Neither equals the printed (T_p 1; −⟨p⟩ 0).

Lemma 3.5 fixes the convention. Its U_x∘π1* = π1*∘T_x − (1/x)V_x together with U_x V_x = x⟨x⟩π1* gives U_xψ(f,g) = ψ(T_x f + x⟨x⟩g, −f/x). That equals A·(f;g), so the paper uses the column convention.

Under the column convention, the printed matrix is the one for the pair (φ, V_p): U_p V_p g = φ g and U_p φ f = φT_p f − ⟨p⟩V_p f. It is not the matrix for the stated ψ = (φ, ⟨p⟩V_p). I checked the page images: the published version and arXiv v2 print the same matrix. This has nothing to do with the 47 bracket errors.

Consequences: none. The correct and printed matrices both have trace T_p and determinant ⟨p⟩, and their entries commute, so Cayley–Hamilton still gives U_p + ⟨p⟩U_p^{−1} = diag(T_p, T_p). U_p is still invertible because the determinant ⟨p⟩ is a unit, and Tr = T_p is all that §3.5 uses. In Lemma 3.16, A·M + B = 0 with the correct M = (T_p ⟨p⟩; −1 0) has lower-left entry −A = 0, so A = 0 and then B = 0. The lemma's conclusion, and everything downstream (Lemma 3.17 and the rest of the proof of Theorem 3.11), is unchanged. The matrix appears nowhere else.

Side observation, not part of this item: on pp. 318–319, Lemma 3.5 states "U_x∘V_x = π1*∘⟨x⟩". Its own computation, and the matrix A, give x⟨x⟩ instead. This may be a separate missing factor of x.

issues.reason:
The printed text is confirmed on page images PDF pp. 33, 41 and 42. arXiv v2 has the same sentence (cg-v2.txt l.1236).

Setup (p. 329). T_n acts on the whole space H^0(X_1(Q), ω^n_O), which is level prime to p; T̃_n = T_n[U_p], where U_p means T_p in weight n. The ideals of T̃_n above m correspond to the reductions of U_p mod m. On p. 328 the paper itself says these can be "α, β, or 0" in higher weight. The injectivity claim ignores the possible third maximal ideal (m, U_p).

That ideal occurs for the weights actually used. I redid the computation:
- Take a non-zero mod-p form f in H^0(X_1(Q), ω_k)[m]. It exists because m is a maximal ideal of the weight-one Hecke algebra.
- h = θ^{p−1}f has weight 1+(p−1)(p+1) = p^2. For ℓ ∤ NQp, T_ℓ θ = ℓ θ T_ℓ, and since ℓ^{p−1} ≡ ℓ^{p^2−p} ≡ 1 mod p, h has the same T_ℓ eigenvalues as f. U_xθ = xθU_x gives U_x eigenvalue x^{p−1}α_x = α_x, and diamond operators commute with θ.
- In weight ≥ 2, T_p ≡ U_p on q-expansions mod p. Since a_{pn}(h) = (pn)^{p−1}a_{pn}(f) = 0, T_p h = 0.
- h ≠ 0: θ^{p−1}f = 0 would force θf = 0, and Katz's result (also used by the paper on p. 328) says θ has no kernel in weight 1.
- Multiplying by a power of the Hasse invariant gives weight n for any n ≥ p^2 with n ≡ 1 mod (p−1). The proof needs A ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m for every m, which forces (p−1)p^{j} | n−1 with j growing, so n ≥ p^2 once m is large.
- Base change for n > 1 (p. 329) plus Deligne–Serre then give a characteristic-zero eigenform g in H^0(X_1(Q), ω^n_O)_m with a_p(g) ≡ 0.

At level prime to p, the eigensystem away from NQp fixes the newform, and T_p is a scalar on the whole old space. So no form in the α-part (eigenvalue ≡ α, a unit) has g's eigensystem, or a Galois conjugate of it. Let e ∈ T_{n,m}⊗K be the idempotent for that orbit. Then ϖ^k e is a non-zero element of T_{n,m} that acts as 0 on H^0_{m̃_α}, where T̃_{n,m̃_α} acts faithfully. So the map is not injective when α = β.

Where it is used: in §3.7 (α = β, scalar case), the phrases "(and hence to T_{n,m}) factors through R^†", the R^†-algebra structure in Lemma 3.24, and the quotient T̃_{n,m̃}/T_{n,m} in Def. 3.25 all need T_{n,m} ⊂ T̃_{n,m̃}. Read literally, these fail: the non-ordinary factors do not factor through the ordinary-type ring R^†. With T_{n,m} replaced by its image, each step works:
- The map to the image factors through R^† because the image injects into T̃.
- T̃_{n,m̃} = image[U_p].
- T_m/I_m is a quotient of the image, as in §3.5 ("T_m/I_m is the corresponding quotient of T_{n,m_α}").

So the proposed correction is right and the damage is local. Minor locator note: Lemma 3.24 is stated on p. 337; the quoted proof sentence is on p. 338. I checked the printed text on page images (PDF pp. 32–34, 36–37, 41–42).

**The paper's own setup (p. 329).**
- T_n is generated by T_n^an and the U_x. It is defined as a subalgebra of End_O(H^0(X_1(Q), ω^n_O)), so it acts on the whole space. It is not restricted to the ordinary part.
- T̃_n = T_n[U_p], where U_p means T_p in weight n and the level is prime to p.
- T̃_{n,m} is the product of the localisations of T̃_n at the maximal ideals above m. Those ideals are m̃_α, m̃_β and, possibly, (m, U_p). On p. 328 the paper itself says U_p mod m can be "α, β, or 0".
- So when α = β, the map T_{n,m} → T̃_{n,m̃} is injective exactly when (m, U_p) does not occur. No defence from the paper's conventions or a charitable reading avoids this; the p. 330 display confirms that T_{n,m} is meant to embed into the product over ordinary eigenforms.

**(m, U_p) does occur for the weights used.**
1. Take 0 ≠ f ∈ H^0(X_1(Q), ω_k)[m], and set h = A_Hasse^j·θ^{p−1}f, which has weight n.
2. The q-expansion of h is Σ_{p∤r} a_r(f) q^r.
3. h ≠ 0: Katz's theorem, cited by the paper on p. 328, says θ is injective in weight 1. So a_r(f) ≠ 0 for some r prime to p.
4. Hecke eigenvalues of h:
   - T_ℓ (ℓ ∤ NQp): the same as for f, using ℓ^{n−1} ≡ 1 mod p.
   - U_x (x | Q): α_x.
   - Diamond operators: they commute with θ.
   - U_p: in weight ≥ 2, T_p acts as U_p on q-expansions mod p, so U_p h = 0.
5. This needs n ≡ p^2 mod (p−1), which holds, and n ≥ p^2. For m > 2e the condition ε^{n−1} ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m forces (p−1)p^2 | n−1, so n ≥ p^2.
6. By base change for n > 1 (p. 329), (m, U_p) is a maximal ideal of T̃_n. The factor T̃_{n,(m,U_p)} is a nonzero finite flat O-algebra, so it has a point in characteristic zero: an eigenform g with a_p(g) in the maximal ideal.

**The map has a kernel.**
- The level is prime to p. By strong multiplicity one, the T_n^an-eigensystem of g determines a newform g_0. T_p acts on the whole g_0-oldspace as the scalar a_p(g_0), which is a non-unit, and this stays true for Galois conjugates.
- So no eigensystem occurring in the m̃ part, where U_p ≡ α is a unit, agrees with g's.
- Let e ∈ T_{n,m}⊗K be the idempotent for the eigensystems of the (m, U_p) part. For suitable k, ϖ^k·e is a nonzero element of T_{n,m} that acts as 0 on the m̃ part, where T̃_{n,m̃} acts faithfully.
- Hence the map is not injective, and the p. 330 inclusion fails for α = β.

**What uses the false claim.**
- Proof of Lemma 3.24, "(and hence to T_{n,m}) factors through R^†": false for the full T_{n,m}. Non-ordinary points with 0 < v(a_p) < n−1 have irreducible local representations at p, so they are not points of R^†.
- Lemma 3.24 itself needs an R^†-algebra structure on T_{n,m}, and Definition 3.25 with the next paragraph ((T_{n,m}⊗_{R^†}R̃^†)/T_{n,m} ≃ T_{n,m}⊗_{R^†}R̃^†/R^†) needs the same.

**With T_{n,m} replaced by its image T′ ⊂ T̃_{n,m̃} ⊂ ∏E_i, every step holds.**
- R^† is the image of R^univ in R̃^†, so R^univ → T′ factors through R^†.
- T̃_{n,m̃} = T′[U_p].
- The Definition 3.25 computation works for T′.
- In §3.6 only the image of T_{n,m} and ⊗_{T_{n,m}}T̃_{n,m̃} are used, and T_m/I_m is a quotient of T′.
- ρ_{n,α} exists over T′, and over the full T_{n,m} by standard results as well.

**Consequences.** Nothing outside §§3.4–3.7 uses the claim, and Theorem 3.11 (weight one, T_m) and everything after it are unaffected. So a proof step fails as written but is repaired locally. That makes affects "the proof", not "nothing" as X-K3-1 has it.

issues.locator: §3.4, proof paragraph immediately after Theorem 3.14, published p. 330 (PDF p. 34), lines 3–5 of that paragraph. arXiv v2 has the same text in the same place ("(The choice of H ensures that for each prime x ≠ p, det(ρ_{n,α})|I_x has order prime to p.)"). arXiv v1 has it word for word too, after the analogous theorem (citing [CDT99, Lemma 5.1.1]).
issues.printed: This follows from the choice of N and H together with the local Langlands correspondence and results of Diamond–Taylor and Carayol (see [15, Lemma 5.1.1]). (The choice of H ensures that for each prime x ≠ p, det(ρ_{n,α})|I_x has order prime to p).
issues.correction: "(The choice of H ensures that for each prime x ∤ pQ, det(ρ_{n,α})|I_x has order prime to p.)" The only case with content is x | N; for x ∤ NQp the character is unramified. The claim must leave out x | Q. For x ∈ Q with x ≡ 1 mod p, det(ρ_{n,α})|I_x is, by local class field theory, the diamond (nebentypus) character of (Z/xZ)^×. After localising at m̃ this character has p-power order, and in general that order is not 1.
issues.reason:
Setup (§3.2.1, §3.3): X_1(Q) is X_1(NQ) divided by H, where H is the p-Sylow subgroup of (Z/NZ)^× only. So T_n contains diamond operators ⟨a⟩ for every a in (Z/NQZ)^×, and (Z/QZ)^× is not quotiented out. By §3.4(b), det ρ_{n,α}(Frob_ℓ) = ℓ^{n−1}⟨ℓ⟩ for ℓ ∤ pNQ. By Chebotarev, det ρ_{n,α} = ε^{n−1}·χ, where χ is the character ⟨·⟩ of Gal(Q(ζ_{NQ})/Q) = (Z/NQZ)^×. For x | Q, ε is trivial on I_x, and I_x maps onto the (Z/xZ)^× factor. So det ρ_{n,α}(I_x) = {⟨a⟩ : a ≡ 1 mod NQ/x}, the image of the diamond operators at x.

This image is not of order prime to p when x ≡ 1 mod p. Let Δ be the p-part of (Z/xZ)^×. X_Δ(Q) → X_0(Q) is étale Galois with group Δ (§3.2.3). For n ≥ 3, H^1(ω^n) vanishes on these curves: by Serre duality it is dual to H^0(ω^{2−n}(−∞)), and deg ω > 0. So RΓ(X_Δ(Q), ω^n_O) is a perfect O[Δ]-complex concentrated in degree 0. Hence H^0(X_Δ(Q), ω^n_O) is projective, so free, over the local ring O[Δ]. So is its direct summand cut out by localising at m and applying the Δ-equivariant ordinary projector. That summand is nonzero: its Δ-coinvariants are the weight-n ordinary forms at level X_0(Q) for m̃_α, which contain the Hasse-invariant lifts of the weight-one form. In the proof n is large, since n − 1 is highly divisible.

So Δ acts faithfully on H^0(X_Δ(Q), ω^n)_{m̃_α}, a Hecke-stable submodule of H^0(X_1(Q), ω^n)_{m̃_α}. The image of I_x in T_{n,m_α}^× therefore contains elements of order p. The printed claim is false for such x.

These primes do occur: Theorem 3.11, proved in §§3.4–3.7 with ρ_{n,α}, is applied in §3.8 with Q = Q_N, where x ≡ 1 mod p^N (Prop. 3.3). Theorem 3.11 itself makes ξ|I_x realise the diamond operators, and §3.8 uses the O[Δ_N]-action on H_N.

No harm is done. Theorem 3.14 only concerns Definition 3.1(2), which is vacuous at x ∈ Q, and 3.1(4), at x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄), i.e. x | N. There, (Z/NZ)^×/H has order prime to p, so the claim is true. The later use on p. 332 is stated only as "ν := ⟨det ρ̄⟩ det(ρ_{Q,m})^{-1} is thus unramified outside Q", which shows the authors do not rely on the claim at x | Q. The fix is to restrict the quantifier to x | N. One could call it a misprint, since "choice of H" signals x | N, but as printed it is a false assertion about ramification at x | Q. Defence tried: H ⊂ (Z/NZ)^× is the p-part of (Z/N(ρ̄)Z)^×, and X_1(Q) is the quotient of X_1(NQ) by H alone (§3.2.1, §3.3). T̃_{n,m̃} is built from forms on X_1(Q) and contains the diamond operators ⟨a⟩ for all (a, NQ) = 1 (p. 329). By (b), det ρ_{n,α}(Frob_ℓ) = ℓ^{n−1}⟨ℓ⟩, so det ρ_{n,α} = ε^{n−1}·(diamond character).

- **x | N:** ε is unramified at x. The diamond character on I_x factors through (Z/x^aZ)^× ⊂ (Z/NZ)^×, whose p-part lies in H and acts trivially. So the order is prime to p and the claim holds here.
- **x ∤ NQp:** the character is unramified, so the claim holds trivially.
- **x | Q:** H places no condition on (Z/QZ)^×. Since m ∋ ⟨ℓ⟩ − det ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) and det ρ̄ is unramified at Q, ⟨a⟩ ≡ 1 mod m for a ∈ (Z/QZ)^×. So after localisation det|I_x has p-power order, the opposite of the claim. It is nontrivial in general: Theorem 3.11 itself says ξ|I_x realises the diamond operators through Z_x^× ⊗ Z_p = Δ_x, and §3.8 applies the result with Q = Q_N, x ≡ 1 mod p^N, where Δ_{Q_N} acts nontrivially. That action is the whole Taylor–Wiles mechanism: O[Δ_Q] → R_Q through χ_{α_x}|I_x. In weight n ≥ 2, Hecke modules of Taylor–Wiles type are free over O[Δ_Q], so there are eigenforms whose nebentypus at x has order p.

So the literal statement "for each prime x ≠ p" is false. The paper's own text shows that the intended range is x ∉ Q:
- Theorem 3.14 only asserts conditions (2) and (4) of Definition 3.1, and both concern primes outside Q.
- The only use of the claim, on p. 332 (and reused through "as in Case 3.5" in §3.6–3.7 and in §3.9 item (4)), concludes that ν = ⟨det ρ̄⟩det(ρ_{Q,m})^{-1} is "unramified outside Q". It needs the claim only at x | N.

Classification: this is a false statement, so I call it an error. It is borderline misprint, since the intended quantifier range is clear from "the choice of H" and from the p. 332 use. The proposed correction is right; "x ∤ pQ" is minimal, and "x | N" is equivalent in content. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.locator: §3.4, Lemma 3.15 (4), p. 330 (published version)
issues.printed: Lemma 3.15 (p. 330, PDF p. 34): "Suppose that ρ̄(Frob_p) is not a scalar. Then there exists an exact sequence of T̃_{n,m̃}[G_p]-modules 0 → A → B → C → 0 such that: (1) A and C are free T̃_{n,m̃}-modules of rank one. (2) The sequence splits B ≃ A ⊕ C as a sequence of T̃_{n,m̃}-modules. (3) The action of G_p on C factors through G_{F_p} = G_p/I_p, and Frobenius acts via the operator U_p ∈ T̃_{n,m̃}. (4) The action of G_p on A is unramified and is via the character ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩ U_p^{−1})." The proof ends on p. 331: "it follows that G_p acts on A ⊗ Q via ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩U_p^{−1}). Since T̃_{n,m̃} is O-flat, the action of G_p on A itself is given by the same formula, proving the lemma." The accepted arXiv v2 (line 1287 of cg-v2.txt) has the same wording.
issues.correction: The minimal fix deletes "is unramified and": "(4) The action of G_p on A is via the character ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩U_p^{−1})." Here λ is the unramified character from (c). That is the v1 wording with λ restored, and it is exactly what the proof establishes. The unramifiedness the later argument needs holds only modulo ϖ^m, and only for the special n chosen on p. 327 ("n − 1 sufficiently divisible ... to ensure that ε^{n−1} ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m"). For that n, A ⊗ T_m/I_m is unramified with Frob_p acting by ⟨p⟩U_p^{−1}. That could be added as a remark, but it is not part of the lemma as stated for general weight n ≥ 2. Both candidate corrections (X-K3-2, H-part1a-6) are right. Neither rewrite changes any later argument.
issues.reason:
I checked this against the page images of PDF pp. 33–36. The claim about A in the printed lemma is false:
- By the notation section (p. 300), ε: G_F → Z_p^× is the p-adic cyclotomic character.
- §3.4 works in weight n ≥ 2, and property (c) on p. 329 puts ε^{n−1}λ(φ(⟨p⟩)/φ(U_p)) in the upper-left (sub) position. The printed statement and proof then identify that character as the action on A.
- B = T̃²_{n,m̃} is a module over the full Hecke algebra, not a mod-ϖ^m quotient. T̃_{n,m̃} is O-flat and nonzero: the proof itself says it is O-flat, and it is a localisation at a maximal ideal of a subalgebra of End_O(H^0(X_1(Q), ω^n_O)).
- Take σ ∈ I_p with ε(σ) = 1+p. Since n−1 ≥ 1, ε^{n−1}(σ) = (1+p)^{n−1} ≠ 1 in Z_p ⊂ T̃_{n,m̃}, and λ(·)(σ) = 1. So σ acts on the free rank-one module A by a scalar ≠ 1, and A is ramified.
- The proof only establishes the formula. It never argues that A is unramified.

Nothing later depends on the false clause. Lemma 3.15 is cited only twice:
- §3.5 (p. 332) passes to T_m/I_m[U_p], using "as below, that ε^{n−1} is trivial modulo ϖ^m" (p. 331), where ⟨p⟩U_p^{−1} = β̃, to get the form (λ(β̃) *; 0 λ(α̃)).
- §3.6 (p. 334) uses only that C is unramified ("L is a quotient of C, which is by construction unramified").
No other text in the paper uses "unramified and is via".

Classification: I call it an "error" rather than a "misprint" because it is a false mathematical assertion, not a slip in an index or sign. "Misprint" is also defensible, since the intended content (the character formula) is clear from (c) and from the proof. Of the three allowed values, "a stated result" is the literal answer: the statement of Lemma 3.15 itself is wrong as printed. The effect is confined to that clause, and no later result depends on it. Theorem 3.11 and everything downstream are unaffected. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction, which concerns only brackets, does not fix it. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED.
(i) Conventions. ε is the p-adic cyclotomic character G_F → Z_p^× (Notation, p. 300). §3.4 works in weight n ≥ 2 (p. 329: "Note that since n > 1"). T̃_{n,m̃} is O-flat and nonzero: the proof says it is O-flat, and it embeds in ∏E_i (p. 330). So no convention makes ε^{n−1} trivial on I_p inside T̃_{n,m̃}.
(ii) Reading "unramified" as applying only to λ is not faithful. The text says "The action of G_p on A is unramified and is via ...".
(iii) The clause contradicts the lemma's own clauses (1)–(3) together with (b), without using (c):
- By (b), det ρ̃_{n,α}(Frob_x) = x^{n−1}⟨x⟩. So det = ε^{n−1}·(diamond character), and the diamond character is unramified at p because p ∤ NQ.
- By (2)–(3), I_p acts trivially on C. So σ ∈ I_p acts on the free rank-one module A by det(σ) = ε^{n−1}(σ).
- ε(I_p) = Z_p^×. Take σ with ε(σ) = 1+p. Then (1+p)^{n−1} − 1 has p-adic valuation 1 + v_p(n−1) < ∞, so it is nonzero in Z_p ⊂ T̃_{n,m̃}.
- Hence I_p acts nontrivially on A, and the claim "unramified" is false for every n ≥ 2.
(iv) The proof never argues unramifiedness. It proves only the formula ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩U_p^{−1}), so the clause is an unsupported and false addition. The v1 text (without "unramified") shows it was added in revision, most likely with "unramified mod ϖ^m" in mind.

CONSEQUENCES. Lemma 3.15 is cited only twice (grep of the full text; images of pp. 331–334 checked):
(a) §3.5, p. 332: "By Lemma 3.15, we may write ρ̃_{Q,m}|G_p ≅ (λ(β̃) *; 0 λ(α̃))".
- This works on the quotient T_m/I_m[U_p], where ϖ^m = 0 and ⟨p⟩U_p^{−1} = β̃.
- It needs only the corrected formula together with ε^{n−1} ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m.
- The paper states that fact explicitly just before (p. 331: "(We use here, as below, that ε^{n−1} is trivial modulo ϖ^m)"), and it is guaranteed by the choice of n on p. 327.
(b) §3.6, p. 334 uses only C ("L is a quotient of C, which is by construction unramified"), i.e. clause (3).
§3.7 does not use the lemma. So Theorem 3.11 and everything downstream are unaffected; the defect is confined to the one clause.

CLASSIFICATION. I classify it as an error: a false mathematical assertion in a lemma statement, which is more than a typographic slip in an index, sign or name. "Misprint" is defensible, since the intended content (the formula of (c)) is clear from (c) and from the proof. The literal value of affects is "a stated result": Lemma 3.15(4) as printed is false. No later result depends on the false part.

issues.locator: §3.6 (Proof of Theorem 3.11, case 2), Lemma 3.16 (Doubling), published p. 332 (PDF p. 36). arXiv v2 (p. 27) has word-for-word the same lead-in and statement. arXiv v1 has it as Lemma 3.12, p. 19, where it is different: there is no "Without any assumption" clause, and the lemma comes after "Let us now assume that α = β is a generalized eigenvalue of ρ̄(Frob_p), and furthermore that ρ̄(Frob_p) is non-scalar." So v1 is correct within its scope. The clause that goes too far was added in v2 and kept in the published version.
issues.printed: [§3.6, lead-in] "We will assume below that α = β is a generalized eigenvalue of ρ̄(Frob_p), and furthermore that ρ̄(Frob_p) is non-scalar. However, we first prove the lemma below." [Statement] "Lemma 3.16 (Doubling) Without any assumption on ρ̄(Frob_p), the action of T̃_{n,m̃} on ψ(H^0(X_1(Q), ω_{O/ϖ^m})^2_m) factors through a quotient isomorphic to T_m/I_m[T_p][X]/(X^2 − T_pX + ⟨p⟩), where U_p acts by X."
issues.correction: The first clause should read "Suppose α = β, whether or not ρ̄(Frob_p) is scalar". With that change the statement and proof are correct and cover every use. An equally minimal alternative keeps the words "without any assumption" and replaces T̃_{n,m̃} by the semilocal ring T̃_n ⊗_{T_n} T_{n,m}. The matrix argument in the proof proves exactly this version, verbatim. When α ≠ β this semilocal ring acts through T_m/I_m[T_p][X]/(X^2 − T_pX + ⟨p⟩) ≅ T_m/I_m[T_p] × T_m/I_m[T_p]. The local ring T̃_{n,m̃_α} acts on the m̃_α-part of Im ψ through T_m/I_m[T_p] alone, with U_p = α̃ (as in §3.5). The candidate's correction is correct and minimal.
issues.reason:
The notation: on p. 330 the paper fixes an eigenvalue α and writes m̃ = m̃_α, for any α, not only α = β. Read literally, "without any assumption on ρ̄(Frob_p)" includes the case α ≠ β, and the lead-in "However, we first prove the lemma below" supports that reading.

The case α ≠ β:
- A = T_m/I_m[T_p] is a finite local ring, and the reduction of X^2 − T_pX + ⟨p⟩ is (X−α)(X−β) (p. 328: ⟨p⟩ ≡ αβ, and T_p − α − β lies in the maximal ideal). The two roots are distinct, so Hensel's lemma gives (X−α̃)(X−β̃) with α̃−β̃ a unit, exactly as the paper argues in §3.5. By the Chinese remainder theorem the displayed ring is A × A. That ring is not local (unless the m-part is 0), and it has twice the length of A.
- A nonzero quotient of the local ring T̃_{n,m̃_α} is local, so it cannot be isomorphic to A × A.
- Worse, ψ(H^0^2_m) splits as Im(ψ)_{m̃_α} ⊕ Im(ψ)_{m̃_β}, so it is not even a T̃_{n,m̃_α}-module. On the m̃_α-part, U_p = α̃, and §3.5 itself says that A[U_p] = A ⊂ End(Im(ψ)_{m̃_α}) is the quotient of T̃_{n,m̃_α}. That contradicts the lemma read literally.
- The proof hides the problem because it works with the matrix of U_p on all of Im ψ, not on the m̃_α-part. What it actually proves is the statement for T̃_n ⊗ T_{n,m}.

Defence tried: the lemma sits in §3.6, whose heading assumes α = β. The phrase "the action of T̃_{n,m̃} on ψ(…)_m" only makes sense when α = β. And v1 shows the phrase was added so that the lemma also covers the scalar case of §3.7. So the intended meaning is α = β, scalar or not, and in that case the statement is true: Im ψ_m is m̃-local and the proof is valid. The defence explains the intent, but it does not rescue the printed words, which explicitly drop every assumption on ρ̄(Frob_p). So this is a real overstatement of the lemma's scope, but a harmless one.

Consequences: Lemma 3.16 is cited in only two places. One is §3.6, p. 333 ("By Lemma 3.16, there is an isomorphism T_m/I_m[U_p] ≃ T_m/I_m ⊕ T_m/I_m"; α = β, non-scalar). The other is §3.7, after Definition 3.25, p. 339 ("by Lemma 3.16, this applies to the quotient … T_m/I_m[T_p][U_p]"; scalar, so α = β automatically). Case α ≠ β (§3.5) is handled separately by the Hensel splitting and never uses the lemma. Nothing later is affected. It could be filed as a misprint, since the intent can be recovered, but the words were deliberate and the literal statement is false, so "error" with affects = nothing fits best.

Proof of Lemma 3.24, pp. 337–338: "Recall that T̃_{n,m̃} = T_{n,m}[U_p]. Since U_p is given as an eigenvalue of Frobenius, T̃_{n,m̃} naturally has the structure of a R̃^univ-algebra. We claim that the map from R̃^univ to T̃_{n,m̃} factors through R̃^†. … By the construction of R̃^†, it follows that the map from R̃^univ to this product factors through via R̃^†. … and hence there exists a map T_{n,m} ⊗_{R^†} R̃^† → T̃_{n,m̃}, sending α ∈ R̃^† to U_p."
issues.correction: Before treating T̃_{n,m̃} as an R̃^{univ}-algebra (and so as an R̃^{univ,χ^{n−1}}-algebra), replace ρ̃_{n,α}|G_p by its twist ρ' = ρ̃_{n,α}|G_p ⊗ λ(c^{−1}). Here c ∈ T_{n,m}^× is the square root of ⟨p⟩ with c ≡ α mod m. It exists by Hensel's lemma: p is odd and ⟨p⟩ ≡ αβ = α² mod m (p. 328). Then ρ' reduces to the trivial representation, and it has det ρ' = ε^{n−1} = χ^{n−1}, because (p−1) | (n−1) (p. 327). Choose a framing. Because χ(φ_p) = 1, c^{−1}U_p is the root of the characteristic polynomial of ρ'(φ_p) that goes with the unramified quotient. So the map in Lemma 3.24 sends α ↦ c^{−1}U_p, not α ↦ U_p. Since c lies in T_{n,m}, R^† still maps into T_{n,m}, and the image still contains T_{n,m} and U_p. So Lemma 3.24, Definition 3.25, the inclusion 𝒥 ⊂ 𝒥^glob and the conclusion that the doubled quotient is unramified at p all hold as stated. The twist is unramified and does not change unramifiedness.
issues.reason:
I transcribed the printed text from PDF pages 33, 38, 41 and 42.

(1) The determinant does not match. By §3.4(b), the characteristic polynomial of ρ_{n,α}(Frob_x) is X² − T_x X + x^{n−1}⟨x⟩. By Chebotarev, det ρ̃_{n,α} = ε^{n−1}·(diamond character), so det ρ̃_{n,α}|G_p = ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩). The shape in §3.4(c) confirms this: the diagonal is ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩/U_p) and λ(U_p), and their product is ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩). Since (p−1) | (n−1), ε^{n−1} = χ^{n−1}. The printed text shows that the paper assumes (p−1) divides n−1 ("n − 1 is sufficiently divisible by powers of p (and (p − 1))"). So det = χ^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩). But R̃^{univ,χ^{n−1}}, and hence R̃^†, requires determinant exactly χ^{n−1}, as the generic-fibre shape (χ^{n−1}λ(α^{−1}), *; 0, λ(α)) in Theorem 3.19 shows.

(2) ⟨p⟩ ≠ 1 in the case where the theorem is used. For the Q_N used in §3.8, H_N is free over S_N = O[Δ_N]. So a nontrivial group element, such as the Δ_N-part of ⟨p⟩, is not a scalar in T. The image of p in Δ_N is nontrivial for a generic choice of Q_N. Separately, ρ̄|G_p = λ(ᾱ)⊕λ(ᾱ) is not trivial unless ᾱ = 1. So without a normalisation, the map from R̃^univ to T̃ does not exist, and it cannot factor through R̃^† either. It also cannot factor after the naive constant twist that only makes ρ̄ trivial.

(3) The only twist that works is T-valued, and it moves α. Let μ be a twist with μ ≡ ᾱ^{−1} and μ² = λ(⟨p⟩)^{−1}. Then μ|I_p takes values in 1+m and has order dividing 2, so μ|I_p = 1 because p is odd. Hence μ = λ(c^{−1}) with c² = ⟨p⟩ and c ≡ ᾱ, and c is unique by Hensel. After twisting, the unramified-quotient eigenvalue of φ_p is c^{−1}U_p. Here I use χ(φ_p) = 1, so ε^{n−1}(φ_p) = 1. The char poly X² − c^{−1}(U_p + ⟨p⟩U_p^{−1})X + 1 has root c^{−1}U_p, and I checked this through T̃ ↪ ∏E_i. So the printed "sending α ∈ R̃^† to U_p" is literally wrong unless c = 1.

(4) The proof can be repaired. c ∈ T_{n,m}, so the image of the map is unchanged. J^glob is still the annihilator of T̃/T. The twist is unramified, so the conclusion that the doubled quotient is unramified at p carries over to the untwisted ρ̃.

The paper does signal a twist ("trivial after twisting"), and experts would probably supply this. But the normalisation that fixes the determinant, which the fixed-determinant rings need, is never stated. The formula α ↦ U_p is incorrect under every twist that works. So this is a minor omission in the proof. It is not a false result. Defence tried: the parenthetical "(If ρ̄ is scalar, it is trivial after twisting)" could be read as allowing an unramified twist of the Hecke-side representation. But it deals only with making the residual representation trivial, and the determinant mismatch remains even when α = 1. By §3.4(b), det ρ̃_{n,α}(Frob_x) = x^{n−1}⟨x⟩, and (c) gives the diagonal characters ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩/U_p) and λ(U_p). So det ρ̃_{n,α}|G_p = ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩) with ⟨p⟩ ∈ T_{n,m}^×. The rings R̃^{univ,χ^{n−1}} and R̃^† (Thm 3.19) require determinant exactly χ^{n−1} = ε^{n−1}. In general ⟨p⟩ ≠ 1 in T: the Hecke algebra contains the diamond operators ⟨a⟩ for (a,NQ)=1, and the image of p in Δ_Q is typically nontrivial at the Taylor–Wiles levels Q_N where Theorem 3.11 is used in §3.8. When ⟨p⟩ ≠ 1, the untwisted representation is not a point of Spec R̃^{univ,χ^{n−1}}, so the literal claim "the map from R̃^univ to this product factors through via R̃^†" fails. It holds after twisting by the specific T_{n,m}-valued unramified character λ(c^{−1}), which the paper never names. Twisting only by a constant (Teichmüller) lift of α would leave the determinant ε^{n−1}λ(⟨p⟩α̃^{−2}) ≠ χ^{n−1}.

Checks on the proposed correction:
- c exists: X² − ⟨p⟩ has the simple root α mod m, since 2α is a unit.
- After the twist the diagonal is χ^{n−1}λ((U_p/c)^{−1}) and λ(U_p/c), matching Theorem 3.19(1) with α' = c^{−1}U_p.
- The image still contains T_{n,m} and U_p = c·α'.

Only (p−1)|(n−1) is needed for the determinant; χ(φ_p) = 1 is used for the eigenvalue pairing. The candidate cites both together, which is a harmless imprecision.

Downstream: the R^†-structure on T_{n,m} is used in Definition 3.25 and the end of §3.7 (proof of Thm 3.11, case 3). The final conclusion (unramified at p) does not change under an unramified twist. §4 (Thm 4.3) uses only the ring R^† and is not affected. This is a routine but unstated normalisation, so it is a gap in the proof. No stated result is wrong.

issues.printed: p. 339: "By Theorem 3.11, we deduce the existence of a surjective homomorphism R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}. Since T_{Q_N,m} acts on H_N, we get an induced action of R_∞ on H_N (via φ̃_N and the map R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m})." The only local statement at x in Theorem 3.11 (p. 327) is: "For a prime x|Q, the restriction of ρ'_Q to D_x is conjugate to a direct sum of residually unramified characters ξ ⊕ ⟨det(ρ̄)⟩|_{D_x} ξ^{-1} where ξ̄(Frob_x) ≡ α_x mod m, and such that the restriction of ξ to I_x and hence via local class field theory to Z_x^× ⊗ Z_p = Δ_x is compatible in the usual way with the diamond operators in T_m." (§3.2.4, p. 325: "Let T denote the O-algebra generated by these same operators together with U_x for x dividing Q.")
issues.correction: There are two minimal fixes. (i) Replace "surjective homomorphism R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}" with "homomorphism R_{Q_N} → T_{Q_N,m} whose image contains the diamond operators at Q_N". This is all the proof uses. (ii) Keep surjectivity and add the missing local-global compatibility at x|Q to Theorem 3.11. That statement says the unramified constituent ξη^{-1} of ρ_Q|_{D_x} sends Art_x(x) to U_x. Then U_x lies in the image of R_{Q_N}, which is generated by traces together with the local characters χ_{α_x}. The statement follows from the proof of Theorem 3.11 as given: ρ_{Q,m} is the pushforward of ρ_{n,α} along T_{n,m} → T_m/I_m. That map is equivariant for U_x (x ≠ p), and in weight n ≥ 2 the relation is the classical Carayol/Langlands compatibility. The candidate's correction is right.
issues.reason:
1. The printed page (p. 339) matches the quoted sentence. T_{Q_N} is the full algebra T of §3.2.4, which includes U_x for x | Q_N (p. 325).
2. R_{Q_N} is topologically generated by the traces of the universal deformation, because ρ̄ is absolutely irreducible. So its image in T_{Q_N,m} is the O-subalgebra (a closed submodule of a finite O-module) generated by the traces of ρ'_Q = ρ_Q ⊗ η. By Chebotarev, that is generated by the T_ℓ η(Frob_ℓ) with ℓ ∤ pNQ, together with the diamond operators, since η is diamond-valued. Surjectivity is therefore equivalent to U_x lying in the anaemic subalgebra of T_{Q_N,m}.
3. That can only come from local information at x. On the ramified-at-x part, where Δ_x acts nontrivially, the U_x eigenvalue is the value at Frobenius of the unramified constituent of ρ|D_x. This is Carayol's local–global compatibility, and traces at unramified primes do not recover it.
4. Theorem 3.11 as printed states only the residual congruence ξ̄(Frob_x) ≡ α_x mod m (the bar over ξ is confirmed at 300 dpi) and the compatibility of ξ|I_x with the diamond operators. It never relates U_x to ξ. So "By Theorem 3.11 ... surjective" does not follow from what is cited.
5. The authors do handle this explicitly in the analogous place in §5. Conjecture A(3) builds the full T_α-character, including the operator at a uniformiser, into ρ|D_v, and Lemma 5.6 then argues "the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces". Nothing like that appears in §3.
6. The claim is still true: local–global compatibility at x holds in higher weight, where x ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄|D_x is unramified with distinct eigenvalues. It passes to weight one because the Hasse-invariant map is Hecke-equivariant away from p modulo ϖ^m (Remark 3.12).
7. Surjectivity is never used afterwards. Proposition 2.3 needs only an R_∞ ⊗ S_N-module structure; (5a) uses the diamond compatibility, which is stated; (5b) needs only T^an-equivariance, since the R_Q-action factors through traces, and Lemma 3.5 provides it. The final conclusion uses R^min ↠ T_{∅,m∅}, where Q = 1 and there are no U_x.
So this is a genuine but minor gap: a step asserted with an insufficient citation. The mathematics is right as intended. Defence tried and fails. By §3.2.4, T_{Q_N} = T is generated over O by T_n, the diamond operators ⟨a⟩ and U_x for x|Q_N. So surjectivity needs U_x in the image of R_{Q_N}. From Theorem 3.11 as printed, the image contains the following. (a) Traces: tr ρ′_Q(Frob_ℓ) = T_ℓ·η(Frob_ℓ). (b) The values of ξ on D_x: the universal representation splits at x as χ_α ⊕ χ_β over R_{Q_N}, and ξ is the image of χ_α. (c) Hence the Δ_{Q_N} diamond operators, by the I_x compatibility. (d) Hence η, a p-power-order function of those diamond operators, and so every T_ℓ. U_x is not reached. On forms whose Δ_x-character is nontrivial, ρ_Q is ramified at x, so no trace of a Frobenius lift equals U_x. Theorem 3.11 fixes ξ(Frob_x) only mod m ("ξ̄(Frob_x) ≡ α_x mod m"), and the diamond compatibility is only for ξ|I_x. Nothing else in §3 closes the gap. Lemmas 3.5 and 3.6 get U_x from T^an by Hensel only at Γ_0(Q) level, where U_x² − T_xU_x + x⟨x⟩ = 0. A characteristic-0 argument (T^an determines the eigensystem) is not available either, because weight-one H^0 can have torsion that does not lift, which is the point of the paper. Remark 3.12's "the required information is preserved under congruences" covers only what the theorem states. §5 shows the authors knew the step is needed. Conjecture A(3) includes U_x = T_{π_x} in the local character φ, and Lemma 5.6 then argues explicitly "by Hensel's Lemma … the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces" before claiming R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m} in Thm 5.11. §3 has no such argument. So this is a step asserted without adequate proof, a gap. Consequences: surjectivity is never used. The R_∞-action on H_N only needs some homomorphism. Condition (5a), first part, needs the S_N (Δ_N-diamond) image inside the image of R_∞, which comes from the I_x compatibility in Thm 3.11. Its second part is argued from χ_{α_x}|I_x and R_{Q_N}/aug = R^min. (5b) and (5c) use Lemmas 3.5/3.7 and Prop. 3.8. The proof of Prop. 2.3 (p. 312) never uses surjectivity onto a Hecke algebra. Theorem 3.26's conclusion needs surjectivity only for Q = 1 (R^min ↠ T_∅,m∅), and T_∅ has no U_x. Theorem 3.30, which repeats this proof, and §4 add no dependence on it. The claim is also true, by standard local-global compatibility transported from weight n.

issues.locator: §3.8, argument after the deduction of Theorem 1.4 (rank one), p. 340 (same text in arXiv v2, p. 33)
issues.printed: We claim that U_x ∈ T_{∅,m_∅} for all x|N. This is a consequence of the assumption that N(ρ̄) = N as we now explain. Suppose that x‖N. Then the T^2_m-representation has a unique invariant T_m-line on which Frob_x acts by U_x, and so U_x ∈ T_m. On the other hand, if x^2|N, then U_x = 0 is also in T_m. Since we have also shown that T_p ∈ T_{∅,m_∅}, we may deduce this from the fact that q-expansion is completely determined by the Hecke eigenvalues T_x for all (x, N) = 1 and U_x for all x|N. (§3.8, p. 340 = PDF p. 44, checked on the rendered page. arXiv v2 has the same wording, and the 2022 Correction deals only with the brackets.)
issues.correction: Split the cases by whether ρ̄^{I_x} is zero, not by the exponent of x in N. (1) If ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0, it is a line. This always happens when x‖N. By the standing hypothesis of §3.1 it also happens whenever ρ̄|G_x is reducible, including cases with x²|N, e.g. ρ̄|G_x ≅ μ ⊕ μχ with χ wildly ramified. In this case the paper's own argument works: the minimal representation into GL_2(T_m) has a unique invariant T_m-line (Def. 3.1(4)) on which Frob_x acts by U_x, so U_x ∈ T_m. (2) If ρ̄^{I_x} = 0, which is equivalent to ρ̄|G_x being irreducible and forces x²|N, then U_x = 0. The conclusion U_x ∈ T_{∅,m∅} for all x|N still holds, and so does the rank-one claim. This correction is right and minimal: it changes only which condition labels the two cases.

Minimal deformations have det equal to the Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄, and their I_x-invariants are a rank-one direct summand when ρ̄|G_x is reducible. The conductor exponent at x is codim ρ̄^{I_x} + Swan. So x‖N does imply dim ρ̄^{I_x} = 1, but x^2|N does not imply ρ̄^{I_x} = 0: a 1-dimensional invariant space with a wild complementary character gives exponent ≥ 2. I redid the counterexample. Take p = 3, K = Q(i), and ψ a character of the ray class group mod 7O_K, which is (Z[i]/7)^×/μ_4 = F_49^×/μ_4 ≅ Z/12. Choose ψ faithful of order 12, so ψ̄ = ψ mod 3 has order 4. On F_49^×, ψ̄^c = ψ̄^7 = ψ̄^{-1} ≠ ψ̄, so ρ̄ = Ind ψ̄ is irreducible. It is odd (det(c) = χ_{-4}(c) = -1) and unramified at 3. It stays irreducible on G_{Q(ζ_3)}, since the inertia at 7 still separates ψ̄ from ψ̄^c. At 2, ψ̄ is unramified and K_2/Q_2 is totally ramified, so ρ̄|G_2 ≅ μ ⊕ μχ_{-4}: reducible, invariants 1-dimensional, and χ_{-4} is wild with Swan conductor 1, so the exponent is 2. At 7 (inert, and 7 ≡ 1 mod 3, so not vexing), ρ̄|I_7 = ψ̄ ⊕ ψ̄^{-1} with no invariants, exponent 2. Hence N(ρ̄) = 196, T(ρ̄) = ∅, and every standing hypothesis plus Assumption 3.9 holds. The nebentypus of θ_ψ is χ_{-4}·(n ↦ ψ((n))), and the second factor is cubic because F_7^× maps onto a subgroup of order 3 in F_49^×/μ_4. So it is not trivial on H. Twist by a cubic η mod 7 with η^2 = (ψ|_Z)^{-1}: this gives ψ' = ψ·(η∘N), a newform θ_{ψ'} of level 196 with nebentypus χ_{-4} (the Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄). It lies on X_1(196)/H and reduces to ρ̄, since η ≡ 1 mod 3. Its a_2 = ψ((1+i))η(2) is a root of unity. So U_2 acts on H^0(X,ω)_{m_∅}, and on the reduction in H^0(X,ω_k(-∞))[m_∅], by a unit, although 4|N. This agrees with Li's theorem: a newform with v_x(N) ≥ 2 has a_x ≠ 0 exactly when v_x(N) = v_x(cond ε), and here both equal 2. So the printed step 'x^2|N ⇒ U_x = 0' is false, not a slip of notation. The repair uses the paper's own invariant-line argument. With N(ρ_f) = N(ρ̄) and Swan conductors unchanged by reduction (wild inertia acts through an x-group, x ≠ p), the lift also has a 1-dimensional inertia-invariant line. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED.
- Setup (pp. 310, 325): N = N(ρ̄) is the prime-to-p Artin conductor, and X = X_1(N)/H with H the p-part of (Z/N)^×. The paper defines U_x only for x|Q, so U_x for x|N here must be the standard operator.
- §3.1 standing hypothesis: "if x ∈ S(ρ̄) and ρ̄|G_x is reducible, then ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ (0)". It forces ρ̄^{I_x} to be a line in the reducible case. It does not force x‖N, because the conductor exponent is codim ρ̄^{I_x} + Swan, and Swan is positive when the ramified character is wild. For x = 2 this is possible for every odd p, since χ_{-4} is ±1-valued.
- The paper's split is correct only in the tame case. Nothing nearby, including Assumption 3.9 (T(ρ̄) = ∅), excludes the wild case.

EXPLICIT COUNTEREXAMPLE (the F_49 facts were checked in python).
- Take p = 3, K = Q(i), and ψ' the order-4 character of the ray class group mod 7 of K, i.e. of F_49^×/μ_4 ≅ Z/12.
- Computed facts: ψ' is trivial on the units and on the image of Z, so it gives an order-4 ray class character. ψ'^c = ψ'^7 = ψ'^{-1} ≠ ψ'. ψ'^2 = χ_{-7}∘N. ψ'((1+i)) = −1 (a root of unity for any choice).
- ρ̄ = Ind_K^Q ψ̄' has these properties:
  - It is absolutely irreducible and odd, with det = χ_{-4}.
  - It is unramified at 3.
  - It stays irreducible over Q(ζ_3), since the quadratic fields in Q(i, √−7) do not include Q(√−3).
  - At 7 (7 ≡ 1 mod 3, so not vexing), ρ̄|G_7 is irreducible and ρ̄|I_7 = ψ̄' ⊕ ψ̄'^{-1}, so the exponent is 2.
  - At 2, ρ̄|G_2 ≅ μ ⊕ μχ_{-4}. This is reducible, with a 1-dimensional invariant line, and χ_{-4} is wild, so the exponent is 1 + 1 = 2.
- So N(ρ̄) = 196 and 4|N, and every hypothesis of §3.1, Assumption 3.9 and Theorem 1.4 holds.
- The theta series θ_{ψ'} is a weight-1 newform of level 196 with nebentypus χ_{-4}, which is trivial on H. It therefore lies in H^0(X,ω)_{m∅}. Its U_2-eigenvalue is a_2 = ψ'((1+i)) = −1, which is nonzero mod 3. So "x²|N ⇒ U_x = 0" is false.
- This agrees with Atkin–Lehner–Li: when v_x(N) ≥ 2, a_x ≠ 0 exactly when v_x(N) = v_x(cond ε). In the wild reducible case both equal a(χ).
- Reporter X-K4-0's local example (ρ̄|G_2 ≅ χ_{-4} ⊕ 1, 4‖N) is the same phenomenon. I agree with the earlier verdict on H-part1a-7.

'FINITE CASE' DEFENCE. The passage sits inside "In the finite case", but the step is justified only by N(ρ̄) = N. In a finite case with the same local type the claim still fails:
- Take a U_x-eigenform f in H^0(X,ω_k(−∞))[m∅]. Multiply by the Hasse invariant to get weight p, where H^1 vanishes.
- Lift by Deligne–Serre to a characteristic-0 eigenform g of weight p and level N. It is new, because N(ρ̄) | N(ρ_g) | N.
- Swan conductors are unchanged by reduction, so ρ_g^{I_x} is a line, and a_x(g) = its Frob_x-eigenvalue, which is a unit. So U_x f ≠ 0.

CONSEQUENCES.
- The passage is used only to prove the side claim, made in prose, that H_0(X,ω)_{m∅} has rank one over T_{∅,m∅} in the torsion ('finite') case.
- It is not part of any numbered statement. Theorem 1.4 asserts only R^min ≅ T_m and freeness, which come from Theorem 3.26.
- Theorem 4.8 does not use it. The §3.9.2 rank-one remark is only for the characteristic-0 case, via multiplicity one.
- With the corrected split, U_x ∈ T_{∅,m∅} still holds for every x|N, so the side claim survives. Only the proof step is wrong.

issues.locator: §3.8 (Modularity lifting), the paragraph after the deduction of Theorem 1.4 that proves 'H_0(X,ω)_{m∅} has rank one' in the finite case. Published p. 340 (PDF p. 44), checked on the rendered page. arXiv v2 has the same wording on p. 33 (rendered and checked). arXiv v1 (p. 30, §3.8) does not have the sentence: it says only 'Since we have shown that T_p ∈ T_{∅,m∅}, we may deduce this from the fact that q-expansion is completely determined by the Hecke eigenvalues T_x for all x.' So the U_x claim and its one-line justification were added in v2. The 2022 Correction deals only with the brackets.
issues.printed: We claim that U_x ∈ T_{∅,m_∅} for all x|N. This is a consequence of the assumption that N(ρ̄) = N as we now explain. Suppose that x‖N. Then the T^2_m-representation has a unique invariant T_m-line on which Frob_x acts by U_x, and so U_x ∈ T_m. On the other hand, if x^2|N, then U_x = 0 is also in T_m.
issues.correction: Justify local–global compatibility at x‖N for U_x. Let A ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m lift a power of the Hasse invariant. Multiplication by A embeds H^0(X, ω_{O/ϖ^m})_{m∅} injectively into H^0(X, ω^n_O)_{m∅}/ϖ^m. The embedding respects T_ℓ (ℓ ∤ Np), the diamond operators and U_x for x|N, because on q-expansions mod ϖ^m it is the identity and U_x acts by a_j ↦ a_{jx} in every weight. In weight n, every eigenform f in the m∅-part has level N with N(ρ̄) | N(ρ_f) | N, so f is new at x. This is where N(ρ̄) = N is really used. By Carayol, U_x f is the Frob_x-eigenvalue on the line ρ_f^{I_x}. The weight-n Hecke algebra T^an_{n,m∅} is O-flat and becomes a product of fields after inverting p (strong multiplicity one for newforms), and ρ_n^{I_x} is a rank-one direct summand. So the Frob_x-eigenvalue λ_x ∈ T^an_{n,m∅} on that summand equals U_x. Hence U_x ∈ T^an_{n,m∅}, and its image gives U_x ∈ T_m. The case m = 1 already gives what the rank-one argument needs. The candidate's correction is this argument and is correct. The one point it should state explicitly is the newness at x of every weight-n form, which gives both the reducedness it invokes and Carayol's formula.
issues.reason:
Defence attempted. Nothing in the paper supplies the Frobenius/U_x identification for x|N.
(1) Theorem 3.11 ('Local–Global Compatibility', p. 323) gives only three things: traces T_x for x ∤ pNQ, minimality outside Q, and the local shape at x|Q. For x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄), minimality (Definition 3.1(4)) says only that ρ^{I_x} is a rank-one direct summand. It says nothing about which element of T acts on it by Frob_x. So existence and uniqueness of the line are supplied, but 'Frob_x acts by U_x' is not.
(2) U_x for x|N is not even in the paper's Hecke algebras. T and T^an_n are generated by T_ℓ (ℓ ∤ NQp), the diamond operators, U_x for x|Q and U_p (pp. 314–315, 327). So Theorem 3.14 ([15, Lemma 5.1.1], Carayol) and the proof in §3.5 transfer only conditions (2) and (4) to weight one, not any U_x-compatibility.
(3) Remark 3.12 describes the Hasse-invariant congruence method only for x|Q. It is the right tool here, but the paper never applies it to x|N.
(4) In the 'finite case' (H_0(X, ω_K)_{m∅} = 0) there are no characteristic-0 weight-one forms, so compatibility must be proved for a torsion, possibly non-reduced T_m. The paper itself stresses that such local–global compatibility for weight-one Katz forms over Z_p-algebras 'is non-trivial, and requires us to prove' it (p. 298). So the one-line assertion is a step without proof or citation, which is a gap under PROTOCOL §18.
The assertion is nevertheless true, by the argument in the correction; I checked each step. One check was that I_x-invariants of the minimal ρ commute with base change here: when x‖N, ρ̄|I_x is either 1 ⊕ ψ with ψ of prime-to-p order or non-trivial unipotent, and in both cases the rank-one summand persists in quotients. So nothing false is asserted.
Consequences: the claim feeds only the unnumbered remark 'We also show that H_0(X,ω)_{m∅} has rank one as a T_{∅,m∅}-module' in the finite case. Theorem 1.4 as stated (R^min ≅ T_m and H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ)_m free, with no rank) does not use it. Corollary 1.5 does not use it, and nothing later cites it. The analogous remarks after Theorem 3.30 and after Theorem 5.11 claim rank one only when there are characteristic-0 forms. The companion sentence 'x^2|N ⇒ U_x = 0' is a separate error, recorded as X-K4-0 / H-part1a-7, and is not judged here.
