issues.locator: §5.2.1 (Arithmetic quotients), item (5)(b) in the definition of K_Q and L_Q, published p. 373 (PDF p. 77). It is read with the definition of Γ_p(v^c) (p. 372), deformation condition (6) P (p. 369), standing hypothesis (3)(c) (p. 369) and Conjecture A(2)(b) (p. 374). arXiv v2 §5.2.1 has the identical text. arXiv v1 §4.2.1 has the same item (5)(b), but with GL_2 in place of PGL_2 and an extra type Sc.
issues.printed:
(5) If v ∈ S(ρ̄), K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} is defined as follows:
(a) If ρ̄ is of type S at v, then K_{Q,v} = Γ_0(v).
(b) If ρ̄ is of type P, M or H at v, then K_{Q,v} = Γ_p(v^c), where c is the conductor of ρ̄|D_v.
[p. 372: Γ_0(v^c) = {g ∈ PGL_2(O_v) | g ≡ (1 *; 0 *) mod π_v^c}, Γ_p(v^c) = {g ∈ PGL_2(O_v) | g ≡ (1 *; 0 d) mod π_v^c, d has p− power order}. p. 369, condition (6): "P : If x ∈ S(ρ̄), and ρ̄|I_x ≃ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, then ρ|I_x ≃ ⟨ψ⟩ ⊕ ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}." p. 374, Conjecture A(2)(b): "If ρ̄|D_v is of type P, so that ρ̄|I_v ≅ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, then ρ|I_v ≅ ⟨ψ⟩ ⊕ ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}."]
issues.correction: At a type-P prime the level has to cut out the minimal inertial type ⟨ψ⟩ ⊕ ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}. With c equal to the Artin conductor 2a(ψ) of ρ̄|D_v, it does not. Γ_p(v^c) ⊂ Γ_0(v^c), and Γ_0(v^c) fixes the newvector of every π(χ'', χ''^{−1}) with a(χ'') ≤ a(ψ). This includes the non-minimal case χ''|O_v^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ, with ξ ≠ 1 of p-power order, which occurs exactly when p | N(v) − 1. When ψ² = 1, the level also contains the ⟨ψ⟩-twisted Steinberg lifts, and (when N(v) ≡ −1 mod p) depth-zero supercuspidal lifts; these are non-minimal and are congruent to ρ̄ under a level-raising condition on ρ̄(Frob_v). Proposed fix for ψ² ≠ 1: take c = a(ψ), the conductor of ψ, which is half the conductor of ρ̄|D_v at type-P primes. Then Γ_p(v^{a(ψ)}) sees π(χ, χ^{−1}) only with a(χ) ≤ a(ψ) and χ|O_v^× of prime-to-p order, so χ|O_v^× = ⟨ψ⟩^{±1}; this is the analogue of v1's level. For multiplicity one, also take the ⟨ψ⟩-isotypic part under Γ_0/Γ_1. The candidate's suggested fix is right in substance for ψ² ≠ 1. It does not cover ψ² = 1; there a twisted-spherical level is needed, namely the ⟨ψ⟩∘det-isotypic part of the PGL_2(O_v)-invariants. Theorem 1.3's Y_0(N) must change in the same way. Types M and H are fine as printed.
issues.reason:
1. The printed text matches the rendered page. Γ_p(v^c) ⊂ Γ_0(v^c), and Γ_0(v^c) is the image of K_0(π^c) in PGL_2.

2. For v ∤ p, a p-power-order character ξ of O_v^× factors through (O_v/π_v)^×, so a nontrivial one exists iff p | N(v) − 1. Put χ″|O^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ.
- If a(ψ) ≥ 2, then ⟨ψ⟩ξ agrees with ⟨ψ⟩ on 1 + π^{a−1}.
- If a(ψ) = 1, then ⟨ψ⟩ξ is still nontrivial, because the orders of ⟨ψ⟩ and ξ are coprime.
Either way a(⟨ψ⟩ξ) = a(ψ). So π″ = π(χ″, χ″^{−1}) is irreducible with trivial central character and conductor 2a(ψ) = c. By Casselman its newvector is K_0(π^c)-fixed, hence Γ_p(v^c)-fixed.

3. Mackey check (script at work/agents/K6-1-A/mackey.py). Take N(v) = 7, p = 3, ψ quadratic, so c = 2. Double cosets B(O)\GL_2(O)/K_0(7^n) have representatives (1 0; 7^i 1), and the character condition becomes a(χ) ≤ min(i, n − i). For both the minimal χ = ⟨ψ⟩ (order 2) and the non-minimal χ″ = ⟨ψ⟩ξ (order 6):
- n = 1: no coset contributes.
- n = 2: only i = 1 contributes.
So each has exactly a 1-dimensional space of K_0(v²)-fixed vectors.

4. π″ reduces to ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1} on I_v, and T_∅ has no operators at v, so π″ lies in the m∅-part. Moreover ⟨ψ⟩ξ ∉ {⟨ψ⟩, ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}}, because ξ ≠ 1 has p-power order while ⟨ψ⟩ has prime-to-p order. So π″ is excluded by condition (6).

5. Existence of such forms. Take r̄ over Q with trivial character and weight 2, ℓ ≡ 1 mod p split in F, and r̄|I_ℓ = ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}. Lifts of prescribed type exist (Diamond–Taylor 1994; Gee 2011); take a newform f with type ⟨ψ⟩ξ ⊕ (⟨ψ⟩ξ)^{−1} at ℓ and minimal elsewhere. Then BC_F(f) is a cohomological cuspidal π″ at level K_∅. At the Q̄_p-point of T_{∅,m∅} it defines, the specialisation of ρ_m has the traces of r_f|G_F. So it is r_f|G_F, and by Carayol r_f|I_v has the non-minimal type, contradicting A(2)(b). In that case R^min ≅ T_m (Theorem 1.3) fails too, and the theorem survives only because its hypothesis, Conjecture A, is false.

6. §3 avoids this by twisting (p. 310: ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0) together with X_H / U_x at level x^{c_x}, c_x = a(ψ). That route is unavailable in §5, where det = ε is fixed on PGL_2.

7. Types M and H are fine: with fixed determinant ε, a non-minimal lift at a type-M prime needs p | N(v) + 1, which is excluded. A separate case, not checked in detail: when ψ is quadratic, a twisted Steinberg St⊗χ (conductor c) also sits at Γ_0(v^c) whatever N(v) is.

I classify this as an error rather than the candidate's "gap": Conjecture A as formulated at this level is false in cases where π″ occurs. Defence attempts, none of which works:
(1) Γ_p(v^c) is contained in Γ_0(v^c) by definition. Take π'' = π(χ'', χ''^{−1}) with χ''|O^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ, where ξ ≠ 1 is tame of p-power order. Then π'' has trivial central character and conductor 2a(⟨ψ⟩ξ) = 2a(ψ) = c. By Casselman newform theory, K_0(ϖ^c) acts on the newvector through ω(d) = 1, so the newvector is Γ_0(v^c)-fixed and hence Γ_p(v^c)-fixed. The restriction "d has p-power order" therefore removes nothing here.
(2) Explicit check in the induced model: at PGL-level {a ≡ d, c ≡ 0 mod ϖ^n}, π(χ, χ^{−1}) has vectors on which K_0 acts by χ^{±1}(a/d), and only when a(χ) ≤ n. The p-power restriction does separate ⟨ψ⟩ from ⟨ψ⟩ξ at n = a(ψ), but not at n = 2a(ψ), where both have Γ_0-fixed newvectors. The paper's own §5.5 (p. 380) says the level was chosen as the X_H(N) analogue to exclude such twists. v1's GL_2 version (type 1 ⊕ ψ, c = a(ψ)) does exclude them. Nothing in the hypotheses rules out p | N(v) − 1 at type-P primes: (3)(c) and Theorem 1.3(4) only exclude N ≡ −1 for vexing primes.
(3) Consequence. π'' has I_v-type ⟨ψ⟩ξ ⊕ (⟨ψ⟩ξ)^{−1}, which fails condition (6). If π'' is cohomological at level K_∅ with residual representation ρ̄, it contributes to T_{∅,m} ⊗ Q̄_p. Then Conjecture A(2)(b) for Q = ∅ contradicts local–global compatibility at v, even up to semisimplification.
Such π'' exist. Take the base change to F, with ℓ split, of a classical weight-2 form on Γ_0(ℓ²) with ℓ ≡ 1 mod p and local type ⟨ψ⟩ξ that is congruent to a minimal form of type ⟨ψ⟩; Carayol and Diamond–Taylor give such congruences. So Conjecture A as stated is false for such ρ̄, and Theorems 5.11 and 1.3 are vacuous for them.
Theorem 1.2 is unaffected: semistable minimal ρ has only type-S primes. The proofs of 5.11 and 1.3 use the level only through Conjecture A, so the patching argument survives once the level is corrected. However, the conclusion of Theorem 1.3 as stated, R^min ≅ T_m on H_1(Y_0(N)), is false in these cases.
On kind: I classify this as an error (a wrong definition that makes a stated conjecture false), not a gap.

issues.printed: (4) If v|p, then K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = GL_2(𝒪_v) if ρ̄|D_v is finite flat. Otherwise, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = Γ_0(v).
issues.correction: (4) If v|p, then K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_2(𝒪_v) (equivalently, the image of GL_2(𝒪_v) in PGL_2(F_v)) if ρ̄|D_v is finite flat. Otherwise, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = Γ_0(v).
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered image of p. 373 (PDF p. 77). Item (4) of §5.2.1 does print "GL_2(𝒪_v)". On p. 372, §5.2 sets G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(2), and K_Q = ∏_v K_{Q,v} is described as an open compact subgroup of G(A) (the text says G(A); it should be G(A^∞)). So each K_{Q,v} has to be a compact open subgroup of PGL_2(F_v), and GL_2(𝒪_v) is literally not one. The rest of the definition is written for PGL_2 throughout:
- Item (3) on the same page uses PGL_2(𝒪_v).
- Γ_0(v^c), Γ_1(v^c) and Γ_p(v^c) on p. 372 are all defined as subsets of PGL_2(𝒪_v), and item (5) uses them.
- §5.5 ("The distinction between GL and PGL") explains why the paper deliberately works with PGL rather than GL.
- In the PGL(n) analogue in §9.1, the authors write "the image in PGL(𝒪_v) of {g ∈ GL_n(𝒪_v) | …}", which shows they distinguish the two groups when they mean the image.

The intended meaning is still clear. 𝒪_v is local, so Pic(𝒪_v) = 0 and PGL_2(𝒪_v) = GL_2(𝒪_v)/𝒪_v^×. That is the image of GL_2(𝒪_v) in PGL_2(F_v), the maximal compact subgroup that stabilises the lattice class [𝒪_v^2]. So the proposed correction to PGL_2(𝒪_v) is right, and it agrees with the finite-flat (unramified, maximal level at p) intent and with item (3) of §9.1 (PGL_n(𝒪_v) for v ∉ S ∪ Q, which includes v|p). The arXiv v2 text (§5.2.1) has the identical wording "GL2 (Ov)", so the slip was never corrected. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

Downstream: I searched the rest of the paper for K_{Q,v}, "maximal compact" and "hyperspecial", and found nothing that relies on the literal GL_2(𝒪_v). All later arguments use Y(K_Q) and Y(L_Q) with the evident maximal level at p. This is a purely notational slip with no mathematical consequence.

issues.locator: §5.3, Lemma 5.6 (statement and proof), published p. 375 (PDF p. 79); Conjecture A(3) runs from p. 374 to p. 375. arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2, §5.3, p. 58) has word-for-word the same text for Conjecture A(3) and Lemma 5.6. arXiv v1 does not contain this section.
issues.printed: Lemma 5.6 Assume Conjecture A. Assume that there exists a maximal ideal m of T_Q associated to ρ̄. Suppose that Q consists entirely of Taylor–Wiles primes. Then there exists a representation: ρ_Q : G_F → GL_2(T_{Q,m}) whose traces generate T_{Q,m} and such that ρ_Q is a minimal deformation of ρ̄ outside Q with cyclotomic determinant. Proof By Conjecture A, the representation ρ_Q := ρ_m to T_{Q,m} is such a representation. Moreover, assumption 3 above guarantees (by Hensel's Lemma) that the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces. [Conjecture A(3), same page: "... and so φ(Frob_v) mod m is well defined; assume that φ(Frob_v) ≢ ±1 mod m. Then ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}."]
issues.correction: Lemma 5.6 needs one more hypothesis: for each v ∈ Q, U_v = T_{π_v} ≢ ±1 mod m, which is the same as φ_v(Frob_v) ≢ ±1 mod m. One way to guarantee this is to take m ⊇ (m_∅, U_v − α_v) with α_v a root of X² − T_vX + 1 mod m_∅, as in Lemma 5.8 and Theorem 5.11. The proposed correction is right and minimal for the Hensel step. Conjecture A(3) also takes "the image of φ mod m is unramified" "by assumption". If that phrase is read as a hypothesis too, the lemma also needs the diamond operators at v to be trivial mod m. That holds in Theorem 5.11, where the diamond operators act through the p-group Δ_N. The rest of the lemma does not use (3): the minimality and cyclotomic-determinant parts need no change.
issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 374–375 and read them. Conjecture A(3) is conditional: it gives ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1} only after "assume that φ(Frob_v) ≢ ±1 mod m". Nothing else in Conjecture A mentions v ∈ Q: (1) covers λ outside S ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}, (2) covers S(ρ̄) and (4) covers v|p. Lemma 5.6 allows any maximal ideal m of T_Q associated to ρ̄. By Definition 5.5, "associated to ρ̄" only constrains T_λ for λ outside S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}. "Taylor–Wiles primes" (§5.1 and Prop. 5.2) only means N(x) ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄(Frob_x) has distinct eigenvalues, which is a condition on ρ̄ and not on m. So nothing ensures U_v mod m ≠ ±1. The proof uses the conclusion of (3) without checking its hypothesis. Without that conclusion, the operators T_α at Q are not linked to ρ_m at all, so "traces generate T_{Q,m}" is not justified. Hensel's lemma alone splits ρ|D_x into two characters, but it cannot identify either character with the Hecke character φ.

I also checked whether the paper excludes such m elsewhere. It does not. Lemma 5.8, like Lemma 3.5 (pp. 305–307), treats only the m containing U_x − α_x. The step showing V[m] = 0 gives x·U_x² = ⟨x⟩, i.e. γ² ≡ α_xβ_x ≡ 1 for the eigenvalue γ of U_x on V. That contradicts γ = α_x (since α_x ≠ β_x), but it is consistent with γ = ±1. So "new at x" torsion with U_x ≡ ±1 (Steinberg type) is not ruled out without local–global compatibility at x, which Conjecture A deliberately leaves out.

The minimality part of the conclusion and the cyclotomic determinant (from (1) plus Chebotarev) do not use (3). Lemma 5.6 is never cited later. Theorem 5.11 repeats the argument itself for m ∋ U_x − α_x, where α_x ≢ ±1, and its step (a) invokes (3) correctly. So the main results are unaffected, and only Lemma 5.6 as stated overreaches. A charitable reading ("there exists m" meaning a suitably chosen m) does not help, because the conclusion is about T_{Q,m} for the given m and no choice of U_x-eigenvalue is specified. Defence tried and failed. (i) The "Taylor–Wiles primes" hypothesis (Prop. 5.2: N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, ρ̄ unramified at v, ρ̄(Frob_v) has distinct eigenvalues) is a condition on ρ̄, not on U_v mod m. It would give U_v ≢ ±1 mod m only through the conclusion ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}. Then the eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v) are φ̄(Frob_v)^{±1}, which are distinct iff φ̄(Frob_v) ≠ ±1, because ε(Frob_v) = N(v) ≡ 1. But that conclusion is exactly what (3) withholds when φ(Frob_v) ≡ ±1, so the argument is circular. (ii) "Associated to ρ̄" (Def. before Conj. A) constrains only T_λ for λ ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}. (iii) Nothing else in Conjecture A controls U_v mod m. (1) gives ρ_m mod m ≅ ρ̄, but no statement ties φ(Frob_v) to the eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v) in the ±1 case. (iv) No nearby result supplies the step. Lemma 5.8 and the Ihara argument in the proof of Lemma 9.6 deal only with m ∋ U_x − α_x where U_x² − 1 is invertible. They do not show that H_1(Y_1(Q))_m = 0 when U_x ≡ ±1. For torsion classes, nothing rules out "new at x" classes with U_x ≡ ±1. Such classes would be excluded under full local–global compatibility (Steinberg at v would force equal eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v)), but Conjecture A does not assume that. (v) T_{Q,m} is generated by the T_λ, which are traces by (1), together with U_v and the diamond operators at v ∈ Q. The only route to putting U_v in the trace subalgebra is Hensel applied to ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}, using the fact that the roots φε(σ) and φ^{-1}(σ) are distinct mod m. So for an m with U_v ≡ ±1 mod m, "traces generate T_{Q,m}" is not proved. The rest of the lemma does not use (3). Minimality outside Q holds because R_Q (§5.1) puts no condition at x ∈ Q, and L_{Q,x} is the full H^1. The determinant is cyclotomic by (1) and Chebotarev. Consequences: the paper never cites Lemma 5.6 by number (grep finds only its own statement). Its content is re-derived in the proof of Theorem 5.11 ("Applying Conjecture A to T_{Q_N,m}, we deduce the existence of a surjective homomorphism R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}", together with step (5a) using part (3)). There m ⊇ (m_∅, U_x − α_x), and by Lemma 5.8, which step (b) invokes, α_x is a root of X² − T_xX + 1 whose two roots are distinct mod m_∅. Since α_xβ_x ≡ 1 and α_x ≢ β_x, we get α_x ≢ ±1, so (3) applies. Theorem 5.11, Theorem 1.3 and §9 (Conjecture B, with m = (m, U_x − α_x) stated explicitly) are therefore unaffected. Only Lemma 5.6, as stated for an arbitrary m, overreaches.

issues.locator: §5.3.1, Remark 5.7 (last sentence), published p. 375 (PDF p. 79). arXiv v2 Remark 5.7 has the same text. Remark 5.7 is not in v1.
issues.printed: However, this operator is only well defined up to a diamond operator ⟨α⟩, where α ∈ O_x^× ⊂ A_F^{∞,×}. On the other hand, by Conjecture A, the image of U_x modulo m is well defined, because the associated character φ is unramified.
issues.correction: ... the image of U_x modulo m is well defined, because the image of the associated character φ modulo m is unramified.
issues.reason: Conjecture A(3) (pp. 374–375) defines φ through F_v^× → T_{Q,m}^×, x ↦ T_x, and asserts only that 'the image of φ mod m is unramified, and so factors through F_v^×/O_v^× ≅ Z, and so φ(Frob_v) mod m is well defined'. On O_x^×, φ is given by the diamond operators ⟨α⟩. These act non-trivially in general on H_1(Y_1(Q),O), since Y_1(Q) → Y_0(Q) is Galois with group Δ_Q = ∏(O_F/x)^× (p. 376). So φ itself is ramified in general. If φ really were unramified, U_x would be well defined outright, not just modulo m, which contradicts the previous sentence of the remark. The intended meaning, 'φ mod m is unramified', is clear from Conjecture A(3). The slip changes nothing.

issues.locator: §5.3, Conjecture A(4), p. 375 (published version)
issues.printed: (4) If v|p, then ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary.
issues.correction: (4) If v|p and ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, then ρ|D_v is finite flat (that is, (ρ ⊗ T_{Q,m}/m^n)|D_v is finite flat for all n ≥ 1, as in §5.1 condition (3)); and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary. An equivalent phrasing is "If v|p, then ρ|D_v is finite flat if ρ̄|D_v is". Deleting the first bar alone would not fix it. An unconditional "ρ|D_v is finite flat" would force ρ̄|D_v to be finite flat, because finite flat representations are closed under quotients when e = 1 < p − 1 (Raynaud). That contradicts the allowed case where ρ̄ is ordinary but not finite flat.
issues.reason:
I checked the page images at 110 and 250 dpi. Conjecture A starts on p. 374 (PDF p. 78), and part (4) is at the top of p. 375 (PDF p. 79). It reads exactly: "(4) If v|p, then ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary." The first two ρ's have bars and the last one does not. arXiv v2 (p. 58, image checked) has the same text.

As printed, the first clause says something about the residual representation ρ̄ and nothing about ρ = ρ_m. Taken literally, it contradicts the paper's own setup:
- §5.1 hypothesis (2), p. 369: "ρ̄ is either ordinary or finite flat at v|p".
- Theorem 1.3(1): ρ̄ is "either finite flat or ordinary" at v|p.
- §5.2 level condition (4), p. 373: K_{Q,v} = GL2(O_v) "if ρ̄|D_v is finite flat. Otherwise … Γ0(v)".

So the printed conjecture would be false whenever ρ̄ is ordinary but not finite flat. When ρ̄|D_v is finite flat and not ordinary, it says nothing about ρ|D_v.

The conclusion that is missing is exactly what the proofs need. §5.1 deformation conditions (2) and (3), p. 369, require the reductions mod m^n to be finite flat or ordinary, and finite flat whenever ρ̄|G_v is finite flat. These conditions define R_Q and R^min. They are used in three places:
- Lemma 5.6, p. 375: "By Conjecture A, the representation ρ_Q := ρ_m … is such a representation", i.e. a minimal deformation.
- §5.4, p. 378: "Properties (1)–(4) of Conjecture A then imply that ρ_{m∅} gives rise to a homomorphism ϕ : R^min → T_{m∅}".
- §5.4, p. 379: the surjection R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}, which the proof of Theorem 5.11 uses. Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 are deduced from that result.

Under the printed wording, ρ_m need not satisfy condition (3), so ϕ is not justified. The intended meaning is clear, and the proofs work once (4) is corrected. So this is a misprint in the statement of an assumed conjecture that the proofs depend on. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

A side note on a separate issue: the pdftotext layer drops the ε in part (3). The image shows "ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}", which is correct as printed.

issues.locator: §5.3.1, proof of Lemma 5.9(1) (and hence (2)), p. 377 (published version)
issues.printed: Proof Consider part (1). By Nakayama’s Lemma, we reduce to the case when μ = k. Yet H_3(Y_0(Q), k) = 0 and the action of Hecke operators on H_0(Y_0(Q), k) (which preserve the connected components) is via the degree map, and this action is Eisenstein (in the sense that the only m in the support of H_0 are Eisenstein).  [§5.3, proof of Lemma 5.9, p. 377 = PDF p. 81; identical wording in arXiv v2, line ~3114 of cg-v2.txt]
issues.correction:
Replace "H_3(Y_0(Q), k) = 0" by the localized statement "H_3(Y_0(Q), k)_m = 0". That is all the Nakayama/dévissage step needs.

For p ≥ 5 the step holds as intended. A finite-order element of PGL_2(F) has order 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6, since ζ+ζ^{-1} ∈ F ∩ R = Q. So the lattices have no p-torsion, the orbifold homology with k-coefficients is the homology of a non-compact 3-dimensional quotient, and H_3 = 0 even before localizing.

For p = 3 the paper gives no argument, although §5.1 and Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 allow p = 3. Two fixes are possible:
(a) add the hypothesis p ≥ 5 to §5 and to Theorems 1.2 and 1.3; or
(b) prove that the 3-primary Farrell classes vanish after localizing at m. These classes are carried by order-3 subgroups, whose centralizers are rank-one tori coming from F(√−3). My unproved assessment is that their Hecke eigensystems are induced from F(ζ_3). The standing hypothesis that ρ̄|G_{F(ζ_3)} is absolutely irreducible would then exclude them.

Two corrections proposed earlier are not quite right:
- H-part1b-13 calls these classes "Eisenstein". That is inaccurate, and m being non-Eisenstein is probably not enough on its own.
- X-K6-10 suggests restricting to 3-torsion-free levels. That is not available in general, because the level is fixed by ρ̄ and by Γ_0(x) at Taylor–Wiles primes, where N(x) ≡ 1 mod 3.
issues.reason:
Checked on the page image of p. 377: the text is as quoted. The setting of §5 allows p = 3: §5.1 says "let p ≥ 3 be a prime that is unramified in F", and Thms 1.2 and 1.3 also take p ≥ 3. Remark 5.3 and §5.2.2 take (co)homology in the orbifold sense, i.e. group homology of the arithmetic lattices. Under that convention the step is false for p = 3 whenever a component lattice has 3-torsion. My own check of the candidate's example, F = Q(i) (3 is inert) and level PGL2(O_v) everywhere, so Γ = PGL2(Z[i]):
(i) g = [[0,−1],[1,1]] has order 3 in PGL2.
(ii) Its centralizer in Γ is Z[i][g]^×/Z[i]^× = Z[ζ12]^×/μ4 ≅ Z/3 × Z, because Q(ζ12) has unit rank 1.
(iii) h = [[0,1],[1,0]] conjugates g to g^{-1}.
(iv) Γ has 3-rank 1 and vcd = 3 − 1 = 2. By Brown's theorem, Ĥ^4(Γ,Z)_(3) contains Ĥ^4(C,Z)_(3)^{N/C} = H^4(Z/3,Z) = Z/3 ≠ 0. Aut(Z/3) acts trivially on H^4.
(v) By universal coefficients, H_3(Γ,Z)_(3) ≠ 0, so H_3(Γ,F_3) ≠ 0.
Independent cross-check: Fine's amalgam PSL2(Z[i]) = (S3 *_{Z/3} A4) *_{PSL2(Z)} (S3 *_{Z/2} D2) with Mayer–Vietoris gives dim H^3(PSL2(Z[i]),F_3) = 2. This matches Z/3 in integral degrees ≡ 0, 3 mod 4.
The failure does not depend on this particular example. Every allowed level has 3-torsion: Γ_0(x) for Taylor–Wiles x (N(x) ≡ 1 mod 3) and Γ_0(v) for v|3 contain conjugates of g, since g fixes a point of P^1(k_x). The candidate's p ≥ 5 claim and element-order list are also correct.
The localized statement Lemma 5.9(1) is probably still true under the paper's hypotheses, but the printed proof does not establish it for p = 3.
Dependencies: Lemma 5.9(2) uses the H_3 vanishing from (1). Prop. 5.10 uses 5.9(1) and (2), the latter to get H_2(Y_0(Q),O)_m free. Thm 5.11(c) uses Prop. 5.10. Thm 5.11(b) needs only the H_0 part, which is fine. Thm 1.3 follows from Thm 5.11. Remark 9.3 makes a related unproved claim ("may be verified directly" for GL(2)/F, F imaginary quadratic), but that is outside this item. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, ALL FAIL.
(i) Convention. Remark 5.3 (p. 372) says explicitly that for every K the cohomology of Y(K) is taken in the orbifold sense, i.e. as the cohomology of the arithmetic lattices. It adds that this can differ from the cohomology of the underlying space. The argument itself needs this convention: the Shapiro isomorphism H_1(Y_0(Q),O[Δ]) ≅ H_1(Y_Δ(Q),O) and the Hochschild–Serre sequences in Prop. 5.10 and Thm 5.11(b) hold for group homology. So H_3 cannot be read as homology of the coarse space.
(ii) Scope. §5.1 and Thms 1.2 and 1.3 take any p ≥ 3 unramified in F. So p = 3 is allowed for F = Q(i), Q(√−2), and so on.
(iii) 3-torsion is present. g = [[0,−1],[1,1]] ∈ SL_2(Z) has order 3 in every PGL_2(O_F). Its characteristic polynomial X²−X+1 splits mod x when N(x) ≡ 1 mod 3, which holds at every Taylor–Wiles prime for p = 3. So Γ_0(x) contains conjugates of g.
  Example: F = Q(i), p = 3, S(ρ̄) = ∅, ρ̄ finite flat at 3. Then Y = Y_0(∅) = PGL_2(Z[i])\H³.
(iv) H_3 ≠ 0 there. The lattice Γ = PGL_2(Z[i]) has vcd 2 and 3-rank 1. The centralizer of ⟨g⟩ is Z[ζ12]^×/Z[i]^× ≅ Z/3 × Z; mod torsion it is generated by 1−ζ12. Conjugation by h = [[0,1],[1,0]] acts as ζ12 ↦ ζ12^5, so N/C = Z/2 inverts both factors. It follows that Ĥ^n(N)_(3) = Z/3 for n ≡ 0, 3 mod 4.
  By Brown's p-rank-one theorem, H^4(Γ,Z)_(3) = Ĥ^4 ≠ 0. Hence H_3(Γ,Z)_(3) ≠ 0 and H_3(Γ,F_3) ≠ 0.

  The example is not special to Q(i). For any F, the relative automorphism of F(√−3)/F inverts norm-one units, so Ĥ^4 ⊇ Z/3 for every component lattice with 3-torsion.
(v) Nothing nearby supplies the missing step.
  - Remark 9.3 concerns only low degrees, via the congruence subgroup property.
  - §9 assumes the needed vanishing as Conjecture B(4)(a).
  - Footnote 3 in §3 on X_H(13) shows the authors knew stacky p = 3 classes exist; that class is induced from Q(√−3).

So the printed statement H_3(Y_0(Q),k) = 0 is false, not merely unproved. Under PROTOCOL §18 that is a step that fails, hence "error". The lemma itself is not shown false.

- Lemma 5.9(1) with i = 3 is left unproved.
- Lemma 5.9(2) is left unproved: its proof uses H_3(μ/ϖ)_m = 0.

- Thm 5.11(c) depends on Prop. 5.10.
- Thm 5.11(b) uses only the i = 0 vanishing (low-degree Hochschild–Serre terms) and is unaffected. X-K6-10 says (b) relies on the H_3 vanishing; that is slightly off.

I checked the page image of PDF p. 81 (published p. 377), and the text is printed as quoted. Lemma 5.9(2) is about homology: "If μ is p-torsion free, then H_2(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪 is p-torsion free." Its only use, in the proof of Prop. 5.10 on p. 378, is also about homology: H_2(Y_0(Q), O)_𝔪 must be O-free. So "cohomology" and the superscript H^2 are slips. Throughout §5.3 the paper writes H_i for homology and H^i for cohomology. Cohomology would also give the wrong sequence: H^1(μ/ϖ) → H^2(μ) → H^2(μ) (the second map multiplication by ϖ) says nothing about H^2[ϖ].

I redid the argument myself. Multiplication by ϖ commutes with the Hecke operators, and localizing at 𝔪 is exact. The homology long exact sequence of 0 → μ → μ → μ/ϖ → 0 (first map multiplication by ϖ) therefore gives, after localizing:
H_3(μ)_𝔪 → H_3(μ)_𝔪 (multiplication by ϖ) → H_3(μ/ϖ)_𝔪 → H_2(μ)_𝔪 → H_2(μ)_𝔪 (multiplication by ϖ).
Hence H_2(μ)_𝔪[ϖ] is the image of H_3(μ/ϖ)_𝔪. If only H_3(μ)_𝔪 = 0, we get H_2(μ)_𝔪[ϖ] ≅ H_3(μ/ϖ)_𝔪, which need not be zero. So the fact actually needed is H_3(Y_0(Q), μ/ϖ)_𝔪 = 0. Part (1) supplies it, because μ/ϖ is a finitely generated O[Δ]-module and part (1) holds for all such modules. Since H_2(μ)_𝔪 is a finitely generated O-module, having no ϖ-torsion means it is p-torsion free.

This is the paper's own pattern done slightly wrong. In the parallel Lemma 3.7(1) (p. 316) the authors correctly use the quotient coefficients: "H^2(X_Δ(Q), L_k) vanishes". Lemma 5.9's proof looks adapted from it, with the words "Taking cohomology" left in and the coefficients left as μ instead of μ/ϖ.

The candidate's correction is accurate. This is not one of the 47 known bracket errors: the "[ϖ]" here correctly means the ϖ-torsion, not a mangled ⟦ ⟧.

On 'affects': the statement of Lemma 5.9(2) is correct, and the corrected proof is immediate from part (1). Prop. 5.10 and §5.4 use only the statement, so nothing downstream is affected.

I rendered pp. 373-377 and read them. (a) §5.2.2 on p. 373 says: 'The Hecke operators act on H•(Y(K), O) but do not preserve the homology of the connected components. Take F = Q(√−5), whose class group is Z/2 = Cl/Cl^2, and p = 7. Let λ = (3, 1+√−5), which has norm 3 and is not principal because a^2 + 5b^2 = 3 has no solution. Assume ρ̄ is unramified at 3; the primes above 3 are not in Q, since Q consists of primes with N(v) ≡ 1 mod 7. We have L_Q ⊆ ∏ PGL_2(O_v), so det(L_Q) ⊆ Ô^×·(squares). Hence A surjects onto F^×\A^{∞,×}/(A^{∞,×})^2 Ô^× = Cl/Cl^2 = Z/2. The class of ϖ_λ maps to the nontrivial element there. So T_λ carries each component to one with a different determinant class: T_λ[C] = 4[C'] with C' ≠ C, because the transfer on H_0 has total degree [K : gKg^{-1} ∩ K] = N(λ)+1 = 4. The parenthetical claim is therefore false, and 'the action is via the degree map' is only true up to this permutation of components. (c) The conclusion still holds. H_0(Y_0(Q), k) = k[A] with p odd, so it decomposes into χ-eigenspaces, and T_λ acts on them by χ(λ^{±1})(1+N(λ)). This equals 2 mod p whenever λ splits completely in F(ζ_p)·(class field of A), an abelian extension of F. That is exactly the form required by Definition 5.5, so the support of H_0 is Eisenstein. The v1 wording, with its restrictive clause, already gave this argument. The published version and v2 added parentheses, which turned the clause into a false general assertion. I classify this as an error in one step of the proof whose conclusion is unaffected; since v1 shows what was intended, one could also argue it is a punctuation-level misprint. The printed parenthetical is false. G = Res_{F/Q} PGL_2, and F is an arbitrary imaginary quadratic field in which p ≥ 3 is unramified (§5.1). Every double-coset representative of K diag(α,1) K has determinant in α·det(K). So T_α translates components by the class of α in the component group F^×\A_F^{∞,×}/(A_F^{∞,×})^2 det(K), which the paper identifies in §5.2.2. That group surjects onto Cl(F)/Cl(F)^2, which is nontrivial for most F (for example Q(√−5)). Then T_λ for a non-principal λ swaps components. The paper itself says so three pages earlier (§5.2.2, p. 373): "The Hecke operators act on H•(Y(K), O) but do not preserve the homology of the connected components."

Defence: the intended meaning is clear, and the argument is complete under it. arXiv v1 has the same sentence without parentheses, as a restrictive clause: only the Hecke operators that preserve components are claimed to act by degree. That is true. It is also enough, because Def. 5.5 only asks that T_λ − 2 ∈ m for almost all λ splitting completely in some fixed abelian extension of F. For λ trivial in the component group, T_λ acts on each component's H_0 = k by its degree N(λ)+1. That equals 2 in k once N(λ) ≡ 1 mod p. So every m in the support of H_0 is Eisenstein, and since m ∩ T^an = m_∅ is non-Eisenstein, H_0(Y_0(Q),k)_m = 0. The parentheses were added in revision (v2 and published) and turned a restrictive qualifier into a false blanket assertion.

This is a slip whose intended meaning is clear from context (v1 and §5.2.2), so it is a misprint rather than an error. The candidate's statement of the fact is right, as is its fix via characters χ, but the minimal correction is simply the restrictive reading.

The remark and Theorem 1.3's clause "then μ = 1" are therefore correct only when every prime of S(ρ̄) has type S. (Theorem 1.2 only has type S primes and does not claim μ = 1 anyway.) Δ has prime-to-p order and commutes with T_∅, so H^Δ is a T_m-direct summand of the free module H, hence itself free. Its rank in characteristic 0 is ∏ dim π_v^{Γ_0(v^c)} = 1, and it is nonzero once H⊗Q ≠ 0. This restores "μ = 1" for the space Y_0(N) of literal Γ_0(N) level.

The group. In PGL_2, "g ≡ (1 *; 0 d)" only makes sense up to scalars. So Γ_p(v^c) is the set of g that are upper triangular mod π^c with d/a of p-power order. The map g ↦ d/a gives Γ_0(v^c)/Γ_p(v^c) ≅ (O_v/π^c)^×/Syl_p. Since π_v has trivial central character, π_v^{Γ_p} = ⊕_η π_v^{(K_0(v^c), η(d/a))}, where η runs over the characters of (O_v/π^c)^× of order prime to p.

The η-summand. Let η̃ be any extension of η to F_v^×. If v ∈ π_v transforms under K_0 by η(d/a), then as a vector of π_v⊗η̃ (central character η̃²) it transforms by η(d)². So the η-summand equals (π_v⊗η̃)^{K_1(v^c)}. By Casselman this has dimension max(0, c − a(π_v⊗η̃) + 1).

Tame η contribute. Let η be tame, of prime-to-p order. There are (N(v)−1)_{p'} such η.
- Types M/H: π_v is supercuspidal and a tame twist keeps the conductor, since the Swan conductor is unchanged and there are no inertia invariants. So a(π_v⊗η̃) = c.
- Type P: π_v = π(χ,χ^{-1}) with χ|O^× = ψ̃, and a(ψη) + a(ψ^{-1}η) ≤ 2a(ψ) = c.
Either way each such η contributes at least 1.

Brute-force check. I computed dim π^{K'} by Mackey double cosets on GL_2(Z/ℓ²) (script work/agents/k6v/ps.py).
- ℓ = 7, p = 3, ψ quadratic (a valid type P): dimension 4, as the formula predicts.
- ℓ = 7, p = 5, ψ of order 3: dimension 8, as predicted.
- The unramified test case also matches.

Global step. Localized at the non-Eisenstein m∅, H ⊗ Q̄ is the direct sum of the spaces π_f^{K_∅} ⊗ H^1(g,K;π_∞) over the π that contribute. Here m(π) = 1 and the (g,K) cohomology has dimension 1. Definition 5.4 builds T_∅ only from T_α with α trivial at S(ρ̄) ∪ {v|p}, so T_∅ acts on each π_f^K by a scalar. By strong multiplicity one, different π have different eigensystems. So T⊗Q̄ is a product of copies of Q̄, and freeness of rank μ forces μ = dim π_f^K ≥ (N(v)−1)_{p'}. For v ∤ 2 this is at least 2, because N(v)−1 is even and p is odd.

The extra vectors lie in the same π and have the same Hecke eigenvalues. Classically they correspond to the twists f⊗η: same level, nebentypus η². In §3 (GL(2)/Q, U_x with d of p-power order) and in v1 (GL(2)/F), the nebentypus is pinned instead, so no extra vectors arise there.

Hence the printed claim is false whenever S(ρ̄) has a P/M/H prime v ∤ 2 and H⊗Q ≠ 0. Theorem 1.3 inherits the error if "Y_0(N)" means the paper's Y, as the deduction "Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11" requires. If Y_0(N) is read literally as Γ_0(N) level, the μ = 1 clause can be rescued via the prime-to-p invariants, but that is not the argument the paper gives. (The separate issue that non-minimal type-P forms also appear at this level is candidate C-K6-1, not this one.) The defence fails.
(1) T_∅ is generated only by T_α with α trivial at Q ∪ S(ρ̄) ∪ {v|p} (Def. 5.4), and m_∅ involves only T_λ for λ ∉ S∪{v|p} (§5.4). T_α then acts on π_f^{K} = ⊗_w π_w^{K_w} by the characteristic function of K_λ g K_λ, which is a scalar on the whole space. So the T_∅-eigenspace of π in H_1(Y,K)_{m∅} has dimension dim π_f^{K_∅} · dim H^1(g,K;π_∞) = dim π_f^{K_∅}, and μ = dim π_f^{K_∅} (strong multiplicity one rules out any other π with the same eigenvalues).
(2) In PGL2, Γ_p(v^c) = {d/a ∈ Syl_p((O_v/π^c)^×)}, and Γ_0/Γ_p has prime-to-p order. Hence π_v^{Γ_p} = ⊕_η π_v^{(Γ_0, η(d/a))}, summed over characters η of prime-to-p order. Twisting by η̃ and conjugating by Atkin–Lehner, Casselman's theory gives dim of the η-summand = max(0, c − a(π_v⊗η̃^{-1}) + 1). With trivial central character, nothing forces η = 1. That is exactly what v1 had (GL2, central character in T) and v2 lost.
(3) For a minimal π_v, a(π_v) = c. For every tame η, a(π_v⊗η̃^{-1}) ≤ c:
- type P: a(χη̃^{-1}) + a(χ^{-1}η̃^{-1}) ≤ 2a(ψ) = c;
- types M and H: σ⊗η stays without inertia invariants and keeps its Swan conductor.
So each such η contributes at least 1, giving dim ≥ (N(v)−1)_{p'}, which is ≥ 2 for N(v) odd since p ≥ 3.
(4) I checked this numerically (principal series, computed as dim of K-invariants of Ind_{B(O)}^{GL2(O)}(ψ(a)ψ^{-1}(d)) by the character formula; script work/agents/K6-B/ps.py). Results:
- q=5, c=2, p=3, ψ of order 4: Γ_0-invariants 1, Γ_p-invariants 6;
- q=7, p=3, ψ quadratic: 1 and 4;
- q=13, p=3, ψ of order 4: Γ_p-invariants 6.
All three match the formula exactly.
(5) If H⊗Q ≠ 0, then under Theorem 5.11 every contributing π is a minimal lift, so μ ≥ 2 whenever there is a P/M/H prime with v ∤ 2. For H/M primes (not vexing), minimality is automatic, so Conjecture A is not contradicted and such cases can really occur.
Consequences: the remark is used only to deduce Theorem 1.3 ("From these remarks we see that Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11"). That deduction identifies H_1(Y_0(N),O)_m with H = H_1(Y,O)_{m∅} at Γ_p level, so the μ = 1 clause of Theorem 1.3 is false as the paper intends it. Nothing else in the paper uses μ = 1. The candidate's correction is right. Fix (b) above is a minimal alternative that keeps μ = 1.
Separate issue, not verified here and not part of this finding: at type P primes with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, the level Γ_p(v^c) already contains Γ_0(v^c)-newforms π(χ,χ^{-1}) with χ|O^× = ψε, ε of p-power order. These are non-minimal, which puts pressure on Conjecture A(2)(b) at this level.

issues.locator: §5.5 (informal sketch for GL), p. 381 (published version)
issues.printed: (§5.5 "The distinction between GL and PGL", p. 381, last paragraph) "splits. This imposes a further Chebotarev condition on the Taylor–Wiles primes x ∈ Q which corresponds to x splitting completely in a metabelian extension of F. Explicitly, if 𝔞 ∈ Cl_p(𝒪_F) has p-power order h, let 𝔞^h = (α). The necessary condition on x is that (assuming p is prime to the order of the unit group of F) that α^{(N(x)−1)/p} ≡ 1 mod x, or equivalently that x splits completely in F(α^{1/p}, ζ_p)." (displayed formula checked on the page image; the text is identical in arXiv v2, p. 63)
issues.correction: Replace p by h in both places: "α^{(N(x)−1)/h} ≡ 1 mod x, or equivalently that x splits completely in F(α^{1/h}, ζ_h)". This is needed for every 𝔞 ∈ Cl_p(𝒪_F), or equivalently for the generators 𝔞_i (of orders h_i) of a cyclic decomposition. In that case x splits completely in the metabelian compositum of the fields F(α_i^{1/h_i}, ζ_{h_i}). The formula needs h | N(x)−1. This holds for Taylor–Wiles primes, where N(x) ≡ 1 mod p^N and p^N ≥ h. With no divisibility assumption the condition is α^{(N(x)−1)/gcd(h, N(x)−1)} ≡ 1 mod x. The printed p-th-power condition is necessary but not sufficient when h > p. It gives the right answer only when Cl_p(𝒪_F) has exponent p, for example the Z/pZ case discussed earlier in the paragraph.
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the rendered page (PDF p. 85 = p. 381). I redid the computation. Assume p ∤ |O_F^×|, as the paper does. Then tensoring O_F^× → (O/x)^× → RCl(x) → Cl(O_F) → 0 with Z_p gives 0 → G → RCl_p(x) → Cl_p(O_F) → 0, where G = ((O/x)^×)_p is cyclic of order p^v, v = v_p(N(x)−1).

Take the lift ã = [𝔞] of 𝔞. Every lift has the form ãu with u ∈ G, and (ãu)^h = [α]·u^h. So a lift of order h exists iff the image of α lies in G^h. In a cyclic group of order N(x)−1 this is the same as α being an h-th power, i.e. α^{(N(x)−1)/h} ≡ 1 when h | N(x)−1. It is not p-th power residuosity.

Explicit counterexample to sufficiency: Cl_p = Z/p^2, v ≥ 2, and α ≡ g^p for a generator g of G. Then the printed condition holds, but E ≅ (Z × Z/p^v)/⟨(p^2, −p)⟩. The Smith normal form of [[p^2, −p], [0, p^v]] gives E ≅ Z/p × Z/p^{v+1}, which is not Z/p^2 × Z/p^v. So the map does not split. Applying the printed condition to every element of Cl_p does not help: an element b with b^p = 𝔞 gives the same α.

Interpretive caveat: read literally, "The necessary condition" is true as a necessary condition, and the stated equivalence with splitting in F(α^{1/p}, ζ_p) (given N(x) ≡ 1 mod p) is correct. But the sentence is introduced by "Explicitly" as the explicit form of the Chebotarev condition equivalent to splitting ("corresponds to x splitting completely in a metabelian extension"). As that, it is wrong for h > p. It looks like a slip from generalising the Z/pZ example: h is introduced but only used to define α.

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It sits in an informal, hedged sketch ("It seems that…") of an alternative GL approach that the authors explicitly do not pursue ("We ultimately decided, however, to impose the simplifying assumption that det(ρ) is cyclotomic"). No theorem, lemma or proof uses it. I checked the printed text on the rendered page (PDF p. 85).

Setup. Assume p ∤ |𝒪_F^×|, as the paper does. Tensoring 𝒪_F^× → (𝒪/x)^× → RCl(x) → Cl(𝒪_F) → 0 with Z_p gives 0 → G → RCl_p(x) → Cl_p(𝒪_F) → 0, where G = (𝒪/x)^× ⊗ Z_p is cyclic of order p^v, with v = v_p(N(x)−1).

Why h, not p. The class ã = [𝔞] lifts 𝔞, and every lift of 𝔞 has the form ãu with u ∈ G. Then (ãu)^h = ι(α)·u^h. So a lift of order h exists iff α ∈ G^h. For a set Q of primes the kernel is ∏G_x, so the condition is imposed prime by prime. Because Cl_p is a direct sum of cyclic groups, the map splits iff this holds for the generators. So the correct condition is that α is an h-th power mod x, not a p-th power.

Group-theoretic counterexample. Take Cl_p = Z/p², v ≥ 2 and α = g^p, with g a generator of G. Then RCl_p ≅ Z²/⟨(p², −p), (0, p^v)⟩. Its Smith normal form is Z/p × Z/p^{v+1}, which is not Z/p² × Z/p^v, so the map does not split.

Concrete counterexample (python, ex.py in my work dir).
- F = Q(√−199), 𝒪_F = Z[ω] with ω² − ω + 50 = 0, and Cl ≅ Z/9. Take p = 3, which is prime to |𝒪^×| = 2.
- 𝔭' = (2, ω−1) has order exactly 9, and 𝔭'^9 = (21+ω), since the norm of 21+ω is 512. So h = 9 and α = 21+ω.
- Take x | 487 with ω ≡ 185, so N(x)−1 = 2·3^5.
- Then α^{162} ≡ 1 mod x, so the printed condition holds and x splits completely in F(α^{1/3}, ζ_3).
- But α^{54} ≢ 1 mod x, so α is not a 9th power. Hence RCl_3(x) ≅ Z/3 × Z/3^6 does not split over Z/9.
- Primes over 829 and 1009 behave the same way.

Defence attempts.
(i) Read literally, "necessary condition" is true. But the sentence opens with "Explicitly", continues "or equivalently", and is presented as the explicit form of the Chebotarev condition that "corresponds to" splitting. As that it is wrong for h > p. If the authors had meant only a necessary condition, h would still be introduced solely to define α, so the context does not show which reading was intended.
(ii) The printed condition is exactly the splitting condition for the pushout extension by G/G^p. That corresponds to Taylor–Wiles data Δ_N with N = 1. The text, however, speaks of RCl_p(Q) = RCl(Q) ⊗ Z_p, and Taylor–Wiles needs N → ∞. For the pushout to G/G^{p^N} the condition is α ∈ G^{p^{min(k,N)}} (where h = p^k), which is the h-th-power condition once p^N ≥ h. So neither reading saves the printed claim.
(iii) Because p appears consistently twice, this looks like a generalisation of the Z/pZ example rather than a one-character typo, and the intended meaning is not clear from context. That makes it an error rather than a misprint.

Consequences. The passage is an informal, hedged sketch ("It seems that…") of a GL approach that the authors explicitly abandon ("We ultimately decided, however, to impose the simplifying assumption that det(ρ) is cyclotomic"). No theorem, lemma, remark or proof cites it. §8.2 uses RCl(Q)/p^n, but not this splitting condition. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.locator: Part 2, Theorem 5.16, hypothesis (6), p. 383 (PDF p. 87). arXiv v2 (p. 64) has identical text. arXiv v1 does not contain Part 2.
issues.printed: (6) If r is ramified at a prime x, then r|I_x is unipotent. Moreover, if, furthermore, r̄ is unramified at x, then N(x) ≡ 1 mod p.
issues.correction: (6) If r is ramified at a prime x ∤ p, then r|I_x is unipotent. Moreover, if r̄ is unramified at x, then N(x) ≡ 1 mod p. (Dropping the redundant "if, furthermore" is only stylistic.)
issues.reason:
Rendered PDF p. 87 at 130 and 250 dpi. The text matches word for word, and no restriction to x ∤ p appears. The paper's Notation section has no convention that x denotes a prime away from p.

Read literally, (6) contradicts (1) and (2) when n ≥ 2. By (1) and (2), r|G_v is crystalline with Hodge–Tate weights 0, …, n−1 at each v | p, so r is ramified at v (an unramified representation has all HT weights 0). (6) would then force r|I_v to be unipotent. That makes r^ss|I_v trivial, so r^ss|G_v is unramified and all its Hodge–Tate weights are 0. Sen weights are additive in extensions, so this contradicts weights 0, …, n−1. The theorem would therefore be vacuous for n ≥ 2.

The context shows that x ∤ p is intended:
(i) The remark right after the theorem (p. 384) says "If conditions 1, 2, and 3 are satisfied, then conditions 5 and 6 are satisfied after a solvable extension which is unramified at p". That is impossible at primes above p under the literal reading.
(ii) The setting of §8.5 (p. 406), from which Theorem 5.16 is deduced, says "For each v ∤ p, r̄|G_v has at worst unipotent ramification…".
(iii) The definition of semi-stable before Theorem 1.2 (p. 301) asks for unipotence only "for all finite v not dividing p".
(iv) In §10 the theorem is applied to crystalline r with distinct weights.

Not a bracket error. A separate issue is whether the N(x) ≡ 1 mod p clause matches §8.5, which requires N(v) ≡ 1 mod p where r̄ is ramified. That is candidate X-K10-10, not this one.

issues.locator: Part 2, Theorem 5.16, hypothesis (4), p. 383 (PDF p. 87). arXiv v2 (p. 64) has identical text ("[CHT08], Definition 2.5.1, r̄ is big"). arXiv v1 does not contain Part 2.
issues.printed: (4) In the terminology of [3], Definition 2.5.1, r̄ is big.
issues.correction: (4) In the terminology of [3], Definition 2.5.1, r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big.
issues.reason:
Rendered PDF p. 87 at 250 dpi. The text is exactly as printed above. [3] = CHT, whose Definition 2.5.1 defines bigness for a subgroup H ⊂ GL_n(k). The paper never defines "r̄ is big" (grep finds 'big' only at pp. 383, 410, 422, 425). The natural literal reading, r̄(G_F) big, is not the hypothesis the proof uses.

The theorem is said to "follow immediately from Theorem 9.19" (p. 384). §9.5 (p. 425) says "Theorem 5.16 follows from it immediately as a corollary". Theorem 9.19 is proved under the standing assumption "We assume also that r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big" (p. 425). It uses Proposition 8.5 (p. 410), "Assume that r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big", which follows CHT Prop. 2.5.9 and needs bigness over F(ζ_p).

Bigness of r̄(G_F) does not formally pass to the normal subgroup r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) of prime-to-p cyclic index, and the paper gives no argument that it does. The CHT conditions are not inherited in general: no p-power quotient; H^1(H, ad^0) = 0 (restriction only controls the H/H'-invariants); and condition (c) on irreducible submodules. Hypothesis (3) only says F(ad^0 r̄) ⊉ F(ζ_p); it does not make the intersection F(ad^0 r̄) ∩ F(ζ_p) trivial, so it does not close the gap.

issues.printed: Lemma 6.1 Let S be a Noetherian local ring. If N is an S-module with depth n, and 0 ≠ M ⊆ N, then dim(M) ≥ n. Proof Let 𝔭 be an associated prime of M (and hence of N). Then 𝔭 is the annihilator of some 0 ≠ m ∈ M, and it suffices to prove the result for M replaced by mS ⊂ M. On the other hand, for a Noetherian local ring, one has the inequality (see [69], Theorem 17.2) n = depth(N) ≤ min_{Ass(N)} dim S/𝔭 ≤ dim(M).
issues.correction: Assume N is finitely generated: "If N is a finitely generated (finite) S-module with depth n, and 0 ≠ M ⊆ N, then dim(M) ≥ n." Nothing else needs to change. This is the minimal fix, and it is exactly the hypothesis of the cited result, Matsumura Thm 17.2 (depth M ≤ dim A/p for p ∈ Ass M, where M is a finite module over a Noetherian local ring). With it the proof is complete as printed.
issues.reason:
I rendered PDF page 89 and the printed text is as quoted. The Notation section adds no convention that modules are finitely generated, and elsewhere the paper states that hypothesis explicitly (for example Lemma 5.9, "Let μ be a finitely generated O[Δ]-module"). The cited result, Matsumura Thm 17.2 (depth M ≤ dim A/𝔭 for 𝔭 ∈ Ass M), is stated for finite modules, and its proof needs Nakayama on Hom(A/𝔭, M).

Without finite generation the lemma is false under every standard definition of depth (Ext, Koszul, or regular sequence). My counterexample: S = k⟦x,y⟧ and N = S ⊕ k((x)), where y acts as 0 and x acts invertibly on k((x)).
(1) (x, y) is an N-regular sequence. x is injective on both summands. N/xN = k⟦y⟧ ⊕ 0, and y is regular on it. N/(x,y)N = k ≠ 0.
(2) Ext^i_S(k, k((x))) = 0 for all i, because x acts on it both as 0 (through k) and invertibly. So Ext^i_S(k, N) = Ext^i_S(k, S), which is nonzero first at i = 2. Hence depth N = 2 under either definition.
(3) Take M = S·(0,1) ≅ S/(y) ≅ k⟦x⟧, a nonzero cyclic submodule of N. Then dim M = 1 < 2 = depth N, which contradicts the lemma.

The reader's own example (S = k⟦x⟧, N = M = k((x))) gives depth ∞ only under the Ext definition. Under the regular-sequence definition its depth is 0, so the example above is the sturdier one. Note that here M is even finitely generated, so the finiteness is needed on N specifically.

I class this as an error (the statement as printed is false) rather than a gap. The intended fix is clear from the citation, and one could argue the hypothesis is implicit, since Matsumura defines depth only for finite modules. That is why I rate confidence medium, not high. No stated result is affected: the lemma is used only in Lemma 6.2, with N = K^m = P^m/Im(δ^{m−1}), a cokernel in a perfect complex and hence finitely generated. This is not one of the 47 bracket defects. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED. (a) The paper sets no convention that modules are finitely generated. The Notation (p. 306) only defines a perfect complex as a bounded complex of finitely generated projective modules. Elsewhere, whenever finiteness matters the paper says "finitely generated" explicitly, e.g. Thm 6.3's P∞ "of finitely generated S∞-modules". (b) The paper never defines depth. The strongest defence is that the textbook definitions (Matsumura §16; Bruns–Herzog 1.2) define depth only for finite modules. On that reading "an S-module with depth n" tacitly means a finite one, and the lemma holds. So the intended meaning is clear. But the printed hypothesis says only "an S-module", and depth is routinely used for arbitrary modules (via Ext, local cohomology or regular sequences). Under those definitions the literal statement is false.

ROBUST COUNTEREXAMPLE, which works under every standard definition of depth, including the regular-sequence definition with no ∞ convention. Take S = k⟦x,y⟧ and N = S ⊕ k((x)), where y acts as 0 on k((x)). Take M = 0 ⊕ k⟦x⟧, which is finitely generated, or M = 0 ⊕ k((x)).
- dim M = dim S/(y) = 1.
- depth N = 2. x, y is an N-regular sequence: x is injective on S and invertible on k((x)); N/xN = k⟦y⟧, on which y is regular; and N/(x,y)N = k ≠ 0.
- Ext check: Ext^i_S(k, k((x))) = 0 for all i, because x acts on it both as 0 (through k) and invertibly (through k((x))). Hence Ext^i_S(k, N) = Ext^i_S(k, S), which is first nonzero at i = 2.
So depth N = 2 > 1 = dim M. The reporter's own example (S = k⟦x⟧, N = M = k((x)), depth ∞ via Ext) also works, but it depends on the convention for depth; the example above does not. The proof's step "depth(N) ≤ min_{Ass N} dim S/p" is exactly where it fails, because Matsumura 17.2 needs N finite.

CONSEQUENCES. Lemma 6.1 is cited only once, in the proof of Lemma 6.2 (p. 385: "where the central inequality is Lemma 6.1"). There it is applied with N = K^m = P^m/Im(δ^{m−1}) and M = H^m(P) ≠ 0. K^m is a quotient of the finitely generated projective module P^m, since P is perfect, so it is finitely generated. Lemma 6.2 is then used in the proof of Thm 6.3 (p. 389) with the perfect complex P∞. All uses therefore satisfy the added hypothesis, and no stated result beyond the literal Lemma 6.1 is affected.

CLASSIFICATION. It is "error" rather than "gap": with N finite the proof is complete, and without it the statement is false. It could also be seen as a misprint-level omitted word, since the intended meaning is clear. Either way it affects nothing.

issues.locator: §6, Lemma 6.2 and proof, p. 385 (published version)
issues.printed: p. 385 (PDF p. 89): "Lemma 6.2 Let l0 ≥ 0 be an integer and let S be a Noetherian regular local ring of dimension n ≥ l0. Let P be a perfect complex of S-modules which is concentrated in degrees 0, . . . , l0. Then codim(H^*(P)) ≤ l0, and moreover, if equality occurs, then: (1) P is a projective resolution of H^{l0}(P), (2) H^{l0}(P) has depth n − l0 and has projective dimension l0." Proof: "Let δ^i : P^i → P^{i+1} denote the differential and let m ≤ l0 denote the smallest integer such that H^m(P) ≠ 0." (arXiv v2 has the same wording, cg-v2.txt l. 3400-3422.)
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis H^*(P) ≠ 0, i.e. P is not exact, to Lemma 6.2. This is the minimal correct fix. Requiring only "P ≠ 0" is not enough: P = [S →id S] in degrees 0, 1 is non-zero but exact. The same non-vanishing (H ≠ 0, or equivalently T ≠ 0) is also implicitly needed in Theorem 6.3(iii), Theorem 6.4(2) and Proposition 6.6. Every application in the paper satisfies it.
issues.reason:
The page image matches the quoted text. The paper never defines codim. It uses codim(M) = n − dim(M) in the proof, and dim(0) is −1 or −∞ under any standard convention. So codim(0) is at least n+1 > n ≥ l0. Taking codim as the height of Ann(M) gives ht(S) = +∞, the same result. Counterexamples: P = 0, or P = [S → S] by the identity in degrees 0 and 1 with l0 ≥ 1. Both are perfect and concentrated in degrees 0..l0, but H^*(P) = 0 has codimension > l0. The claimed inequality therefore fails. The proof starts by choosing the smallest m with H^m(P) ≠ 0, which silently assumes H^*(P) ≠ 0. Lemma 6.1, used as the central inequality, explicitly requires 0 ≠ M.

I redid the proof with the extra hypothesis and it goes through:
- H^i = 0 for i < m makes 0→P^0→…→P^m→K^m→0 exact, so pd K^m ≤ m.
- Since 0 ≠ H^m ⊆ K^m, Lemma 6.1 and Auslander–Buchsbaum give codim H^m ≤ n − depth K^m = pd K^m ≤ m.
- codim H^* ≤ codim H^m.
- In the equality case m = l0 and H^{l0} = P^{l0}/Im δ^{l0−1} = K^{l0}.
The proposed correction is therefore right and sufficient.

Downstream, Theorem 6.3 (p. 387) is the only use. There P∞^□ is minimal, since P∞^□ ⊗ k ≅ T has d = 0, and H^{l0}(P∞^□)/a ≅ H. So when H ≠ 0 its cohomology is non-zero and the lemma applies as intended. The degenerate case H = 0 forces T = 0 and P∞^□ = 0. In that case Theorem 6.3(iii) (depth of the zero module) and Theorem 6.4(2) (the zero module is not nearly faithful) also fail as literally stated. Those theorems likewise implicitly need H ≠ 0, and in the §9 applications H is a non-zero localized cohomology module. Main results are unaffected. This is a degenerate missing non-vanishing hypothesis in a stated lemma, not a substantive mathematical error. I looked for a defence and found none.
- The paper never defines codim. The proof uses codim(M) = n − dim(M).
- For M = 0, every standard convention gives dim(0) = −1 or −∞, so codim(0) ≥ n+1 > l0. Reading codim as the height of Ann(M) gives +∞, and the minimum of ht over an empty support is also +∞. No reading makes codim(0) ≤ l0.
- Counterexamples: P = 0, or P = [S →id S] in degrees 0, 1 (with l0 ≥ 1). Both are perfect and concentrated in degrees 0..l0, and H^*(P) = 0 violates the inequality. Conclusion (2) also fails, since depth(0) ≠ n − l0.
- The proof starts by choosing "the smallest m such that H^m(P) ≠ 0", and no such m exists. The authors did put "0 ≠ M" into Lemma 6.1 but left the analogous condition out of 6.2.

With H^*(P) ≠ 0 added, I re-checked the proof and it goes through:
- 0 → P^0 → … → P^m → K^m → 0 is exact, so pd K^m ≤ m.
- K^m ⊇ H^m ≠ 0, so Lemma 6.1 and Auslander–Buchsbaum give codim H^m ≤ pd K^m ≤ m ≤ l0, hence codim H^* ≤ codim H^m ≤ l0.
- In the equality case, l0 ≤ codim H^{l0} ≤ pd K^{l0} ≤ l0. This forces m = l0 and H^{l0} = K^{l0}, since P^{l0+1} = 0. Both (1) and (2) follow.

Consequences. Lemma 6.2 is used only in the proof of Theorem 6.3 (p. 389), and through it in Theorem 6.4 and Proposition 6.6, whose proof is "much the same".
- There P∞^□ ⊗ k ≅ T has zero differential, so P∞^□ is minimal. By Nakayama, a minimal exact bounded complex of free modules is 0.
- If H ≠ 0, then H^{l0}(P∞^□)/a ≅ H forces H^*(P∞^□) ≠ 0, and the lemma applies as intended.
- If H = 0, then H^*(P∞^□) = 0: otherwise the corrected lemma plus Nakayama would force H ≠ 0. So T = 0 and P∞ = 0. That degenerate data satisfies every hypothesis of 6.3, for example R∞ = O⟦x_1..x_{q+j−l0}⟧, H = 0, D_N = 0.
- In that degenerate case, 6.3(iii) ("depth of H^{l0}(P∞) = 1+j+q−l0") fails. So does 6.4(2), because the zero module is not nearly faithful: Ann = R is not nilpotent. The proof of 6.4 in fact asserts "Since H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ {0}" without justification.

In the §8–9 applications, T is the mod-ϖ cohomology localized at a maximal ideal m in its support, so T ≠ 0 and hence H ≠ 0. The main theorems are therefore unaffected. This is a missing non-degeneracy hypothesis, not a substantive flaw. It is still a literally false stated lemma, so "error" (a false statement and a failing step) fits better than "gap". It is not among the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not mention it.

(1) The printed (c) cannot hold for n > N. D_N is a complex of S_N/ϖ^N-modules, so ϖ^N kills it. A derived tensor product would not help either: its cohomology is still killed by ϖ^N. So (c) says ϖ^N kills H/ϖ^n for every n, i.e. ϖ^N H ⊂ ∩_n ϖ^n H. The compatibility clause gives the same thing, since the transition maps H/ϖ^{n+1} → H/ϖ^n would all be isomorphisms. Conclusions (ii) and (iv) make H ≅ H^{l0}(P∞^□)/𝔞 a finite module over the Noetherian local ring R∞. By Krull's intersection theorem ∩ ϖ^n H = 0, so ϖ^N H = 0; with N = 1, ϖH = 0.

(2) A minimal example shows this: take l0 = q = j = 0, R∞ = R = O, H = O, T = k, D_N = O/ϖ^N. Here (a), (b) and (d) hold, but (c) would need O/ϖ^N ≅ O/ϖ^n for all n, which fails for n > N. The expected conclusion (H free) is exactly what the corrected (c) gives.

(3) The application relies on the printed version holding. In the proof of Theorem 9.19 (pp. 426–427), D^1_N is the complex D̃_N/ϖ^N of S_N/ϖ^N-modules, and "its cohomology computes H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_m". Also H^1 = H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_m, which is not killed by ϖ in general: the proof itself uses that H^{l0}(P∞^{1,□}) is p-torsion free. Yet the text says "condition (c) is clear". That is true only for n ≤ N.

(4) The proof of Theorem 6.3 only uses n ≤ N. The level-N datum D_{M,N} uses ψ = the given isomorphism H^{l0}(D_M^□ ⊗ O/ϖ^N) ≃ H/ϖ^N with N ≤ M (p. 388). The datum definition only needs "each N ≥ n′ ≥ 1" (p. 387). Proposition 6.6 only needs n = 1. So the candidate's correction is sufficient, and it matches the application. Hypothesis (b)'s "each n ≥ 1" does no harm, because it only asks for compatible actions.

This is a genuine error in how the hypothesis is stated, not a bracket misprint. On 'affects': I disagree slightly with "a stated result". Theorem 6.3 and Prop. 6.6 are true as printed, just unusable, and no downstream statement is false. What is invalid as printed is the proof of Theorem 9.19 (and so the chain to Theorems 5.16/1.1), which checks a hypothesis that fails. The fix, weakening the hypothesis in the statements of Thm 6.3/Prop 6.6, repairs everything. I checked the rendered pp. 386–391 and 425–428 of the published PDF, the text of arXiv v2 (Theorem 6.3 and the proof of Theorem 9.19), and arXiv v1.

DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, ALL FAIL.
(i) The expression is well-defined for every n. The tensor product is over S_N, and the paper's own convention makes O/ϖ^n = S_0/ϖ^n a quotient of S_N for every n. So nothing in the notation limits n to n ≤ N.
(ii) Reading the tensor product as derived does not help. D_N is a complex of S_N/ϖ^N-modules, so multiplication by ϖ^N is zero on D_N, and hence on the cohomology of D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^n whether the tensor is termwise or derived. For n ≥ N, the termwise D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^n equals D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^N.
(iii) Take N = 1 in the printed (c). It gives ϖ(H/ϖ^n H) = 0 for all n, i.e. ϖH ⊂ ∩_n ϖ^n H. When H is finitely generated this intersection is 0 by Krull, so ϖH = 0. Finite generation is needed anyway: the conclusion H ≅ H^{l0}(P∞^□)/a forces it.
(iv) The simplest model case fails. Take l0 = q = j = 0, R∞ = R = O, H = O, T = k and D_N = O/ϖ^N. Then (1)–(3), (a), (b) and (d) hold, and the intended conclusion (H free) is true. But the printed (c) would need O/ϖ^{min(n,N)} ≅ O/ϖ^n for all n, which is false.

WHY IT MATTERS. The printed Theorem 6.3 and Prop 6.6 are not false: their proofs go through whenever the stronger hypothesis holds. But that hypothesis can never be met in the application. In the proof of Thm 9.19 (p. 427), D^1_N = D̃_N/ϖ^N, "whose cohomology computes H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_m", and H^1 = H^{q0}(Y,K/O)^∨_m, which is finite over O. By (iii), the printed (c) would force ϖH^1 = 0. Yet Theorem 9.19 concludes that H^1 is nearly faithful over R_S. Theorem 5.16 is deduced from this using the characteristic-0 point of R_S given by r, so ϖH^1 ≠ 0. The proof itself (p. 428) also uses p-torsion-freeness of H^{l0}(P∞^{1,□}). So "condition (c) is clear" is false as printed; it is true only for n ≤ N.

THE FIX SUFFICES. Every use involves only n ≤ N:
- D_{M,N} (p. 388) takes ψ to be the given isomorphism for D_M at n = N ≤ M.
- The patching datum (p. 387) records only "N ≥ n′ ≥ 1".
- The extra data and commuting square of Prop 6.6 use only n = 1 ≤ M.
- Hypothesis (b) also says "each n ≥ 1", but that is harmless there, because it only asks for compatible actions.

CLASSIFICATION. The intended range can be recovered from the patching-datum definition, so this is close to a misprint. I call it an error because it is not a one-character slip: the unbounded "n ≥ 1" is written deliberately in (b), (c), (d) and again in §9. As printed, the verification in Theorem 9.19 asserts a condition that fails.

AFFECTS: the proof. No stated result becomes false. Theorems 6.3 and 6.6 only get stronger under the fix, and their existing proofs support it. What fails is the proof of Thm 9.19, and through it the chain to Thms 5.16 and 1.1. The fix repairs it.

SEPARATE ISSUE, NOT PART OF THIS CANDIDATE. Thm 6.3(2) lets H be any R-module. ψ∞ comes from lim H/ϖ^{N_i}H, so it tacitly needs H to be finitely generated (and nonzero, for (iii)). For example, H = K with T = 0 and D_N = 0 satisfies all the hypotheses but not (iv). This is harmless in §9.

issues.correction:
Theorem 6.3(2) should read: "Let R be an object of C_O, and let H be a non-zero finite R-module." Under (3), being finitely generated over R is the same as being finite over O, which matches Prop. 2.3(1). The reason is that a finite R-module with H/ϖH finite-dimensional is ϖ-adically complete, so it is finite over O by complete Nakayama. Also, for H finite over O, H ≠ 0 holds exactly when H^{l0}(T) ≠ 0.
Theorem 6.3 itself and Theorem 6.4(1) need only finiteness. Non-vanishing is needed for 6.4(2), for 6.3(iii) under the usual convention depth(0) = ∞, and for the use of Lemma 6.2 in the proof. Alternatively, "H ≠ 0" can be added only in 6.4(2).
Theorem 6.4 and Prop. 6.6 inherit the corrected hypothesis.

Lemma 6.2's proof also assumes that some H^m(P) is non-zero.
Minor point: the proposed "equivalently T ≠ 0" works only through the theorem's own dimension argument. "H^{l0}(T) ≠ 0" is the cleaner equivalent.

- **Global convention?** There is none. The Notation section (p. 299) only fixes C_O and defines "perfect complex". Elsewhere the authors state finiteness when they need it: in Prop. 2.3(1) (p. 307), and they write "finitely generated" for P∞ in the conclusion.

- **Do (a)–(d) force it?** No. They only constrain H/ϖ^n.

**(A) Finiteness fails.**

- Theorem 6.4(1) applies, since O is p-torsion free and formally smooth with 0 variables. It would say that K is a free O-module, which is false.
- For l0 ≥ 1, take q = 0 and j = l0. Then 𝔞 = (z_1..z_j), and H^{l0}(P∞^□)/𝔞 is finite over O, so it again cannot be ≅ K. Taking H = O ⊕ K shows that the proof really produces the ϖ-adic completion of H, not H.

- R∞ is p-torsion free and R∞[1/p] = K is irreducible. So 6.4(2) says that 0 is a nearly faithful O-module.
- In Taylor's sense ([11]), nearly faithful means Ann is nilpotent. Here Ann_O(0) = O, so this is false.
- The proof on p. 390 itself uses "Since H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ {0}", and Lemma 6.2's proof needs some H^m(P) ≠ 0.

**Where the result is used.** Only in the outline of §8.1 (pp. 369–370) and in Theorem 9.19 (pp. 417–419), through Prop. 6.6 and Theorem 6.4(2) with i = 2 and conclusion (iv).

The readers' label "gap" also describes the proof step (𝔡_N and ψ∞), but the statement as printed is false.

The ⊗ is plain, with no hat. p. 387 (PDF p. 91), statement (ii): "There is an action of R∞⊗̂_O S∞^□ on H^{l0}(P∞^□) extending the action of S∞^□ ...". issues.correction: Read M^□ := M ⊗̂_O O^□, the completed tensor product. This equals ⊗_O whenever M is finitely generated over O, so it changes nothing for S_N, S_N/I, D_N or the finite-level P. In particular S∞^□ = O⟦(Z_p)^q, z_1,…,z_j⟧ and P∞^□ = P∞ ⊗_{S∞} S∞^□, which also fixes H^*(P∞^□). In §9, R^□_{S_Q} = R_{S_Q}⟦z_1,…,z_j⟧, as the paper itself writes on p. 426. The O[…] → O⟦…⟧ bracket is Correction item (10) and is not part of this finding. The candidate also proposes changing "R∞ ⊗̂_O S∞" on p. 387 to "R∞ ⊗̂_O S∞^□". That change is not needed: the maps on cohomology come from P → P′ by base change to O^□, so they are automatically O^□-linear. For these maps, being R∞⊗̂S∞-linear is therefore the same as being R∞⊗̂S∞^□-linear. The candidate's claim that "only S∞^□ is affected" is also incomplete, because P∞^□ and H^*(P∞^□) need the completed product too.
issues.reason:
The paper has no convention that ⊗ means the completed tensor product. The Notation section only defines C_O. The paper also writes ⊗̂ explicitly where it means the completion: in (ii) of this same theorem, in the proof, and in Lemma 4.2. Read literally, S∞^□ = O⟦x_1..x_q⟧ ⊗_O O⟦z_1..z_j⟧ is the algebraic tensor product. For q, j ≥ 1 this ring is not local.

Proof that it is not local:
- A = O⟦x⟧⊗_O O⟦z⟧ is O-flat, so it embeds in A⊗K = O⟦x⟧[1/p]⊗_K O⟦z⟧[1/p].
- That ring maps injectively to coefficient arrays K^{N^q×N^j}, and every element has a coefficient matrix of finite rank.
- The inverse of 1 − x_1z_1 in O⟦x,z⟧ is Σ(x_1z_1)^n. Its coefficient matrix contains an infinite identity block, so the inverse is not in A, and 1 − x_1z_1 is not a unit of A.
- But x_1z_1 lies in the maximal ideal ker(A → k). So the non-units of A do not form an ideal, and A is not local.

So, as printed, S∞^□ is not in C_O. It is not the Noetherian regular local ring that Lemma 6.2 requires ("let S be a Noetherian regular local ring"), and it has no "dim S∞^□ = 1+j+q". P∞ ⊗_O O^□ is likewise not the complete module whose cohomology carries the patched R∞-action.

The intended meaning is clear. The proof uses the completed ring throughout: "open ideal", ı in C_O, the dimension count, Lemma 6.2. On p. 427 the same notation is identified with R⟦z⟧. With the completed ring every step works as written. So this is a notational slip and should be classed as a misprint, not a gap: no step is missing an argument.

One part of the candidate is wrong. On p. 387, "isomorphisms of R∞⊗̂_O S∞-modules" is fine as printed. The induced map on the □-cohomology is (P → P') ⊗ id, which is automatically O^□-linear, so S∞-compatibility suffices. Rendered PDF pp. 90–93 (published pp. 386–389) and read the zoomed crops.

1) Read literally, the definition fails. Even after Correction item (10) (O^□ = O⟦z⟧), M^□ is defined with the plain ⊗_O. Take q = j = 1: S∞ ⊗_O O⟦z⟧ = O⟦T⟧ ⊗_O O⟦z⟧, which embeds in O⟦T,z⟧. Its image consists of power series whose coefficient matrix (c_{a,b}) has finite rank over K. In O⟦T,z⟧ the inverse of 1 − Tz is Σ T^n z^n, whose coefficient matrix is the identity and has infinite rank. So 1 − Tz is not a unit in the plain tensor product. Tz is not a unit either. Hence the ring is not local, so it is not in C_O and not a Noetherian regular local ring. Its Krull dimension is also not 1 + j + q.

2) The proof needs the completed ring at every step:
- "dim R∞ = dim S∞^□ − l0" needs dim S∞^□ = 1 + j + q.
- "By Lemma 6.2 (with S = S∞^□ and P = P∞^□)": Lemma 6.2 needs S Noetherian regular local.
- "since S∞^□ is formally smooth over O, we can and do choose a homomorphism ı: S∞^□ → R∞ in C_O".
- (ii) asks H^{l0}(P∞^□) to be a finite R∞-module carrying an action of R∞ ⊗̂ S∞^□. That action arises as an inverse limit, so it lives on P∞ ⊗̂ O^□, not on P∞ ⊗_O O^□. The latter is in general not complete.

3) Defence tried and rejected. One could argue the paper uses ⊗ to mean ⊗̂ by convention. It does not: it writes ⊗̂ explicitly elsewhere, e.g. Lemma 4.2's B ⊗̂_O C, R_loc, and R∞ ⊗̂_O S∞^□ in the same theorem. So the plain ⊗ is a genuine slip and is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

4) The intended meaning is nonetheless unambiguous from context: the dimension count, formal smoothness, the use of C_O, Lemma 6.2, and p. 426, where R_{S_{Q_N}}⟦z_1,…,z_j⟧ is identified with "R^□_{S_Q} in the notation of Proposition 6.3". With the completed product, every step of Thms 6.3 and 6.4, Prop 6.6 and Thm 9.19 goes through unchanged. So this is a misprint, not a gap, and it affects nothing.

5) The p. 387 wording is correct as printed (see correction).

issues.correction:
Restrict the third condition to ideals I for which O^□/I is O-flat. The simplest choice is I = (z_1^{a_1},…,z_j^{a_j}) with 1 ≤ a_i ≤ N, or even just I = (z_1^m,…,z_j^m) with 1 ≤ m ≤ N. Make this change both in the definition of a patching datum and in the check for D_{M,N}. With O^□/I free over O, the display holds, since B := O^□/(I+ϖ^{n′}) is then flat over A := O/ϖ^{n′}. The rest of the proof uses only these ideals:
- H^*(P_∞^□) = lim_i H^*(P_i^□ ⊗ S_∞^□/𝔟_{N_i}) uses I = (z^{N_i}).
- The transition maps compare (z^{N_{i+1}}) with (z^{N_i}).
- ψ, and conclusions (i)–(iv), use I = (z_1,…,z_j).
The restricted family is stable under "D mod N′", and the finiteness of patching data still holds. The statements of Theorem 6.3 and Proposition 6.6 are unchanged. H-part2-7's correction is right and minimal. X-K7-10's correction also works, but its extra finiteness objection is unfounded (see reason).
issues.reason:
I confirmed the printed text on the rendered page (p. 388); v2 is the same. Set Y = D_M ⊗_{S_M} S_{N′}/ϖ^{n′}, a bounded complex of free A-modules (A = O/ϖ^{n′}). Since n′ ≤ N and N′ ≤ N, the left side is H^i(Y ⊗_A B). Since O^□ is flat over O, the right side is H^i(Y) ⊗_A B. These two agree for all Y only when B is A-flat.

The reader's own example does NOT satisfy the theorem's hypotheses:
- D_M = (O/ϖ^M →ϖ O/ϖ^M →ϖ O/ϖ^M) is not a complex for M ≥ 3, because d∘d = ϖ^2 ≠ 0.
- With q = 0, j = 2, l0 = 2, condition (d) cannot hold. H^0 contains k⟦z_1,z_2⟧ faithfully, so the image of R_∞ would have dimension at least 2, but dim R_∞ = 1.
- The reader only checked condition (a).

Here is an example that satisfies all of (1)–(3) and (a)–(d):
- q = 0, j = 1, l0 = 1, so S_N = S_∞ = O.
- D_N = (O/ϖ^N →ϖ O/ϖ^N) and T = (k →0 k).
- R_∞ = k⟦z⟧, which has dimension 1 = 1+j+q−l0. It acts on H^*(D_M^□/ϖ^n) ≅ k⟦z⟧ in degrees 0 and 1 via z ↦ z.
- R = H = k, and φ_N sends z ↦ 0.
- (c) holds: H^1(D_N/ϖ^n) = k. (d) holds: S_M^□ and R_∞ have the same image, and the augmentation ideal (z) of S_N^□ and ker φ_N = (z) also have the same image.

Now take N ≥ 2, n′ = 2 and I = (ϖz, z^2). Then (z^N) ⊂ I ⊂ (z), and B = O⟦z⟧/(ϖz, z^2, ϖ^2) = A·1 ⊕ k·z.
- Left side: H^0 = ker(ϖ on B) = span(ϖ, z). Here z acts as 0.
- Right side: H^0(Y)⊗_A B = k⟦z⟧/I = k[z]/(z^2). Here z acts nontrivially.
The two sides are not isomorphic even as O^□-modules. The natural map ϖ⊗z ↦ ϖz = 0 is neither injective nor surjective.

So the proof cannot get the required R_∞-action on the left side from (b) for such I. In this example an action exists anyway, since R_∞ = S_∞^□/ϖ. So this is a flaw in the argument, not a counterexample to the claim, and it is fixed by restricting to monomial I.

I checked what the rest of the proof uses. The passage to H^*(P_∞^□), the transition maps, ψ, (d) and the use of Lemma 6.2 involve only I = (z_1^m,…,z_j^m), so no stated result depends on the general I. The reader's diagnosis, correction and "affects" are right; only their example needs replacing. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED. Put Y := D_M ⊗_{S_M} S_{N′}/ϖ^{n′}. It is a bounded complex of free A-modules, where A = O/ϖ^{n′}. Since N′ ≤ N and n′ ≤ N, the left side is H^i(Y ⊗_O O^□/I) = H^i(Y ⊗_A B), with B = O^□/(I+ϖ^{n′}). O^□ = O⟦z⟧ is O-flat, so the right side is H^i(Y) ⊗_O O^□/I = H^i(Y) ⊗_A B. These agree for all such Y exactly when Tor^A(H^*(Y), B) causes no trouble, for example when B is A-flat. That is not true for every I allowed in the text.

Other readings do not rescue the step:
- The display is a plain tensor of a cohomology module with O^□/I. No derived reading gives the left side.
- Hypothesis (b) gives R_∞-actions only on H^*(Y ⊗ O^□), with O^□ not reduced modulo I. These actions live on cohomology, not on the complex. So they do not induce an action on H^*((Y⊗O^□) ⊗^L_{O^□} O^□/I) when O^□/I is not flat.
- No nearby statement restricts I.
- In top degree l_0 the display does hold, by right exactness. But the proof needs every degree: it uses the dimension of H^*(P_∞^□) and then Lemma 6.2.

COUNTEREXAMPLE WITHIN THE HYPOTHESES. I checked this by hand; it is the example in H-part2-7's verdict.
- Take q = 0, j = 1, l_0 = 1. Then S_N = O and O^□ = O⟦z⟧.
- D_N = (O/ϖ^N →ϖ O/ϖ^N) and T = (k →0 k), R = H = k.
- R_∞ = k⟦z⟧, of Krull dimension 1 = 1+j+q−l_0. It acts on H^*(D_M^□/ϖ^n) ≅ k⟦z⟧ by z ↦ z. φ_N sends z to 0.
- Conditions (1)–(3) and (a)–(d) all hold.

Now take M ≥ N ≥ 2, n′ = 2, N′ = 0 and I = (ϖz, z^2). This I lies between (z^N) and (z). Then B = O⟦z⟧/(ϖz, z^2, ϖ^2) = A·1 ⊕ k·z.
- Left side: H^0 = ker(ϖ on B) = span(ϖ, z), and z acts as 0 on it.
- Right side: H^0(Y) ⊗ O^□/I = k[z]/(z^2), and z acts nontrivially.
The two sides are not isomorphic even as O^□-modules. The check with O = Z_3 is: 3(a + bz) = 3a in Z/9 ⊕ (Z/3)z.

X-K7-10's example I = (z^N, ϖz) has O^□/I ≅ O ⊕ k^{N−1}. It shows the same failure in general, but it was not checked against (a)–(d).

X-K7-10'S FINITENESS SUB-CLAIM IS WRONG. The groups depend only on I + ϖ^{n′}O^□, which contains (z_1^N,…,z_j^N, ϖ^N). So they correspond to ideals of the finite ring (O/ϖ^N)[z]/(z_i^N); k is finite by the paper's conventions. Two ideals I and I′ with the same I + ϖ^{n′} both map compatibly to I + I′, so they carry the same action. Hence the paper's claim of "finitely many patching data" is fine as it stands.

CONSEQUENCES. The false display is used only to check that D_{M,N} is a patching datum. After that, the proof uses only I = (z^{N_i}) and (z_1,…,z_j). So restricting to monomial or O-flat I repairs it with no change to any statement. The same applies to Proposition 6.6. Kind: an error, because the displayed identity is false for some admissible I. It is a local error with a routine fix, and it does not reach a stated result. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.correction: (iii) The R∞-depth of H^{l0}(P∞^□) is equal to 1 + j + q − l0 (= dim R∞).
issues.reason:
Rendered PDF pp. 90–94. In the statement, (i), (ii) and (iv) all concern P∞^□ and H^{l0}(P∞^□). Only (iii) prints P∞ without □. The proof (p. 389) proves depth_{S∞^□}(H^{l0}(P∞^□)) = dim S∞^□ − l0 = 1 + j + q − l0. The proof of Theorem 6.4 (p. 389) uses "Since depth_{R∞}(H^{l0}(P∞^□)) = dim R∞".

The printed statement is false whenever j > 0 and H ≠ 0. P∞^□ = P∞ ⊗_O O^□ with O^□ = O⟦z_1,…,z_j⟧ flat over O. Write M := H^{l0}(P∞^□). Then M = H^{l0}(P∞) ⊗_O O^□, z_1, …, z_j is an M-regular sequence, and H^{l0}(P∞) = M/(z_1,…,z_j)M. Here z_i acts through ι(z_i) ∈ R∞, so R∞ acts on the quotient. Hence depth_{R∞} H^{l0}(P∞) = (1 + j + q − l0) − j = 1 + q − l0. Also dim H^{l0}(P∞) ≤ dim R∞ − j. H is a nonzero quotient of H^{l0}(P∞) by (iv), so the printed value 1 + j + q − l0 cannot hold.

In the application (§9.5, p. 426), j = n²|T| − 1 > 0.

The p. 401 sentence ("the corresponding depth of H^{l0}(P∞) is also exactly l0 less than the classical case") is only a relative comparison. It holds for P∞ (1+q−l0 vs 1+q) as well as for P∞^□, so it is not an error. Not a bracket error.

As written, the two bullets are satisfied by the constant sequence (M_i, N_i) = (1, 1): 1 ≥ 1, and D_{1,1} mod 1 is D_{1,1} itself, since "D mod N'" for N' = N is the identity operation defined on p. 387–388.

With that sequence the rest of the proof fails:
- ϕ∞ = lim ϕ_i is just ϕ_1 : R∞ ↠ R/𝔡_1, not a surjection onto R.
- The transition maps P_{i+1} → P_{i+1}/(ϖ^{N_i} + 𝔞_{N_i}) ≅ P_i are isomorphisms, so P∞ = P_1. That is a complex of S∞/(𝔞_1 + ϖ) = S_1/ϖ-modules, so it is not a complex of projective S∞-modules.
- ψ∞ only gives H^{l0}(P∞^□)/𝔞 ≅ H/ϖH, not H.
- H^{l0}(P∞^□) is killed by ϖ and 𝔞_1, so its dimension is at most j. The depth claim (iii), 1 + j + q − l0, therefore fails as soon as q ≥ l0.

So the claim "Then P∞ is a perfect complex of S∞-modules … ϕ∞ : R∞ ↠ R" does not follow from the bullets as printed. The argument needs N_i → ∞, which the parallel proof of Proposition 2.3 gets from strict inequalities. The intent is obvious and the fix is one character, so this is a misprint rather than a real gap. It is not one of the 47 known ⟦ ⟧ bracket errors.

The statement of Theorem 6.3 is still true: the corrected choice of sequence exists by the same finiteness argument. Theorem 6.4 and the applications in §9 use only the statement, so nothing downstream is affected. Defence attempted and failed.
- Nothing on pp. 387–389 forces N_i → ∞. The patching-datum definition, the D mod N' operation, the definitions of ϕ∞, P∞ and ψ∞, and the rest of the proof never pass to a cofinal subsequence.
- The inverse-limit construction is used as if the levels grow, but that is never stated.
- The bullets as printed allow the constant sequence (M_i, N_i) = (1, 1). Here 1 ≥ 1, and D_{1,1} mod 1 = D_{1,1}, since D mod N' is defined for 1 ≤ N' ≤ N, which includes N' = N.

With that sequence the conclusions of the proof fail:
- ϕ∞ = ϕ_1 : R∞ ↠ R/𝔡_1, not a map onto R.
- Every transition map P_{i+1} → P_{i+1}/(ϖ^{N_i} + 𝔞_{N_i}) ≅ P_i is an isomorphism, so P∞ = P_1. That is a complex of S∞/(𝔞_1 + ϖ)-modules, not a perfect complex of S∞-modules resolving anything of the stated depth.
- ψ∞ only gives an isomorphism onto H/ϖH, not onto H.
- H^{l0}(P∞^□) is killed by ϖ, so the depth claim 1 + j + q − l0 is false once q + j ≥ l0 ≥ 1.

So the step "Then P∞ is a perfect complex of S∞-modules …" does not follow from the text as printed. It does follow once N_{i+1} > N_i.

The intended meaning is clear:
- the identical construction in Prop. 2.3 uses strict inequalities;
- the authors fixed exactly this slip in §2 between v1 and v2;
- the claimed existence is just as easy with strict inequalities.

So this is a misprint rather than an error or gap. It is not one of the 47 known ⟦ ⟧ bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not mention it.

Downstream, the construction is used by:
- the proof of Theorem 6.4 (p. 389), which uses ι and ψ∞ "as in the proof of Theorem 6.3";
- Prop. 6.6, whose proof is omitted as "much the same way as Theorem 6.3";
- §8.1 (p. 5303 of the text file region), which cites the depth information "deduced in the proof of Theorem 6.3".

With the corrected sequence all of these go through unchanged. No stated result changes, because the statements of 6.3, 6.4 and 6.6 remain true.

On 'affects': the protocol's gloss "nothing (the mathematics is right as intended)" could support "nothing", since the intended mathematics is right. I record "the proof" because the proof as printed does not establish the theorem until the inequality is fixed.

issues.reason:
Rendered PDF pp. 93–94. The proof (p. 390) argues only with P∞^□: "H^{l0}(P∞^□) is nearly faithful as an R∞-module if and only if each irreducible component of Spec(R∞[1/p]) lies in the support of H^{l0}(P∞^□)[1/p]. Part (3) follows immediately."

As printed, the hypothesis can never hold when j > 0 and M := H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ 0. H^{l0}(P∞) = M/(z)M with z_1 M-regular (see X-K7-6), so Supp H^{l0}(P∞) ⊂ Supp M ∩ V(ι(z_1)). A minimal prime 𝔭 of R∞ in Supp M is minimal in Supp M, hence lies in Ass M. So ι(z_1) ∉ 𝔭, because z_1 is a nonzerodivisor on M. Hence no irreducible component lies in Supp H^{l0}(P∞)[1/p]. The printed (3) is therefore vacuously true but useless in the case j = n²|T| − 1 > 0 of §9.5. The intended statement is the one the proof gives.

Later uses are unaffected: §9.5 applies Theorem 6.4 to H^{l0}(P∞^{2,□}) with R∞^2 irreducible, which is part (2). Not a bracket error.
