I checked the rendered PDF page 93 (p. 389), including a 250 dpi crop. Theorem 6.4(1) reads "If R∞ is formally smooth over 𝒪, so R ≃ 𝒪[x_1,…,x_{q+j−l_0}], then H is a free R-module." arXiv v2 (cg-v2.txt, line ~3594) has the same wording, with correct brackets: "so R ≃ O[[x1,…,xq+j−l0]]".

In Theorem 6.3 (p. 386), R∞ and R are separate objects. Hypothesis (1) says R∞ ∈ C_𝒪 has Krull dimension 1+j+q−l_0. Hypothesis (2) says R ∈ C_𝒪 is just some other ring, with an R-module H. Part (iv) on p. 387 gives a surjection φ∞ : R∞ ↠ R. So a formally smooth R∞ is 𝒪⟦x_1,…,x_{q+j−l_0}⟧, since a power series ring over 𝒪 in n variables has dimension 1+n. The proof starts with the correct hypothesis: "Proof Suppose first of all that R∞ ≃ 𝒪[x_1,…,x_{j+q−l_0}]."

As printed, the claim about R is false in general. The proof shows R = R∞/ı(𝔞)R∞, with ker(φ∞) = ı(𝔞)R∞, where 𝔞 is generated by q+j elements. There is also a direct contradiction with the setup. Hypothesis (3) of Thm 6.3 gives H/ϖ ≅ H^{l_0}(T), which is a finite-dimensional k-vector space. Suppose H ≠ 0 were free over R ≅ 𝒪⟦x_1,…,x_m⟧ with m = q+j−l_0 ≥ 1. Then H/ϖ would be free over k⟦x_1,…,x_m⟧ and so infinite-dimensional. So the printed statement only makes sense when q+j = l_0. In the applications R is a Hecke algebra that is finite over 𝒪. The "R" in the "so" clause must therefore be a slip for "R∞". This is not a bracket error; only the [ ] → ⟦ ⟧ part of this line is covered by the 2022 Correction.

Dependence: the text cites Theorem 6.4 only on p. 391 (the paragraph after Prop. 6.6) and on p. 428 (the §9 proof: "by Theorem 6.4 H^{l_0}(P∞^{2,□}) is nearly faithful as an R∞^2-module"). Both uses are of the nearly-faithful parts (2)/(3), not part (1). The proof of (1) already uses the correct hypothesis on R∞, and its conclusion (H free over R, with R = R∞/ı(𝔞)R∞) is correct.

issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 386–391 and 427–428 and checked them against the patching proof of Thm 6.3 (pp. 387–389).

1. The "same way as Theorem 6.3" proof: build a joint patching datum of level N from (φ^i, ψ^i, P^i) for i=1,2 plus the mod-ϖ isomorphism β, with D_{M,N} carrying β = α_{M,N}. Choose (M_i, N_i) with N_i → ∞ and take limits. The patched β_∞ on H^{l0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ is lim_i α_{M_i,N_i}. By right-exactness of top-degree cohomology, H^{l0}(P_∞)/(a+ϖ) is H^{l0}(D_{M_i}⊗_{S_{M_i}}O/ϖ). So β_∞ mod a equals α_{M_i,N_i}⊗_{S_{N_i}}O, and ψ^i_∞ mod ϖ is the (c) isomorphism of D_{M_i} with n=1.

2. The conclusion square therefore commutes exactly when ψ^2∘(α_{M_i,N_i}⊗O)∘(ψ^1)^{-1} = θ. The hypothesis only gives this for α_{M_i,0}, which never enters the patching because N_i → ∞. Nothing in the statement links α_{M,N} (N ≥ 1) with α_{M,0}. The third bullet only requires R_∞-linearity at each fixed (M,N). The authors state such compatibilities explicitly elsewhere: Thm 6.3 (b) says "compatible with the R_∞-actions" for N ≥ N', and (c) says "compatible for fixed N and varying n". So the omission here looks real, not a convention.

3. Explicit data where every hypothesis holds but the omitted argument gives a square that fails. Take q=1, j=0, l0=0 and R^i_∞ = O[[x,y]]/(y^2), which has dimension 2 = 1+j+q−l0. Take R^i = O, H^i = O^2 and T = k^2. Let D_N = (S_N/ϖ^N)^2 with x acting as [γ]−1 and y as ([γ]−1)·n, where n = [[0,1],[0,0]], and φ_N(x) = φ_N(y) = 0. Conditions (a)–(d) hold, with the same data for i=1,2. Take θ = Id and α_{M,0} = Id, so the square commutes. For N ≥ 1 take α_{M,N} = [[1,1],[0,1]]; this commutes with n, so it is R_∞⊗S_N-linear. The patched β_∞ then reduces to [[1,1],[0,1]] ≠ θ, and the square fails.

Here the literal existential conclusion still holds, because β = Id works. So I have not refuted the statement itself: it is a gap in the omitted proof, not a proven false statement. It does not affect Thm 9.19, where the needed compatibility holds by naturality. Defence attempted, and it fails.

(1) The omitted proof must patch θ as well as the rest. The conclusion needs one isomorphism Θ: H^{l0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ → H^{l0}(P^2_∞)/ϖ. This can only come from the level isomorphisms θ_{M,N}, which have to be added to the level-N patching datum of Theorem 6.3's proof (p. 391). Pigeonholing then picks pairs (M_i, N_i), and Θ is the limit of the θ_{M_i,N_i}. So Θ mod a is θ_{M_i,N_i} ⊗_{S_{N_i}} O.

(2) The vertical maps ψ^i_∞ mod ϖ are the n = 1 isomorphisms of hypothesis (c) for D_{M_i}. This uses (c)'s compatibility "for fixed N and varying n".

(3) The patched square therefore commutes exactly when β∘ψ^1 = ψ^2∘(θ_{M_i,N_i} mod a), where β: H^1/ϖ → H^2/ϖ. The hypothesis only gives this for θ_{M_i,0}. Nothing in the statement links θ_{M,N} to θ_{M,0}. Both are R_∞/ϖ-linear isomorphisms between the same two modules, so they differ by an arbitrary automorphism γ of H^1/ϖ as an R^1_∞/ϖ-module.

(4) The obvious repairs do not work in general. One could twist ψ^1_∞ by γ, but then γ must lift to an automorphism of H^1 as an integral R^1-module. One could twist Θ, but then γ must lift to an automorphism of H^{l0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ as an R_∞/ϖ-module. In general Aut_R(H) → Aut_{R/ϖ}(H/ϖ) and End_{R_∞}(M) → End(M/aM) are not surjective.

(5) A charitable reading does not help. Elsewhere the paper states such compatibilities explicitly: Theorem 6.3(b) covers N ≥ N' and n ≥ n', and (c) says "compatible for fixed N and varying n". Here the square is imposed only for "S_N/ϖ = O/ϖ", i.e. N = 0.

(6) Degenerate check: when q = j = l0 = 0 the conclusion holds trivially, since Θ := ψ^{2,-1}βψ^1 works. I have no counterexample to the statement as printed, so this is recorded as a gap, not an error.

Downstream use: the only use is the proof of Theorem 9.19 (pp. 426–427). There the level isomorphisms are the natural ones H^{l0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ) ≅ H^{l0}_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ), which exist because χ ≡ 1 mod ϖ. They are functorial in the covers, so they are compatible as N varies and reduce to the N = 0 isomorphism. The paper only says they "give rise to the commutative square required", but the added hypothesis does hold there. Theorem 9.19, and so the main theorems, are unaffected.

R = O[Δ] acts on X_Δ(Q) = X_K by right translation by δ ∈ K_0(Q), which normalizes K = K_Δ(Q). If KγK is the disjoint union of the cosets γ_i K, then r_δ^{-1} T_γ r_δ sends xK to the sum of the x δ^{-1}γ_i δ K. So conjugating T_γ by δ gives T_{δ^{-1}γδ}, which in general is a different operator. If T_γ does not commute with Δ on H_*(X_Δ(Q), A), then no R-linear chain map C → C can induce it. The lemma allows any γ ∈ G(A^{∞,p}), and that includes components at the places v ∈ Q (they do not divide p).

Counterexample inside the paper's own §9 setting, with n = 2. At v ∈ Q, K_{Q,v} is the Iwahori subgroup and L_{Q,v} is the kernel of the character [[a,b],[c,d]] ↦ d/a mod π_v. The Atkin–Lehner element w = [[0,1],[π_v,0]] satisfies w^{-1}[[a,b],[c,d]]w = [[d, c/π_v],[bπ_v, a]]. So w normalizes K_{Q,v} and L_{Q,v}, K w K = wK, and T_w is right translation by w (K' = K'' = K and tr = id in the paper's proof). Since w^{-1} diag(a,b) w = diag(b,a), we get T_w⟨t⟩ = ⟨t^{-1}⟩T_w. Because w² is central, T_w is invertible. If T_w were R-linear, then ⟨t⟩ = ⟨t^{-1}⟩, so ⟨t⟩² = 1. Δ has odd p-power order, so Δ would act trivially on H_*.

But Δ does act nontrivially. Classical check: q = 31, p = 5, Δ = Z/5. By the dimension formula, dim S_2(31, χ) = 8/3 − 2/3 − 1 = 1 for each of the 4 characters χ of order 5. As a consistency check, 2·2 + 4·1 + 8·2 = 24 = g(X_1(31)) − g(X_0(31)) = 26 − 2. So H_1(Y_Δ, O) ⊗ E has χ-isotypic pieces with χ ≠ 1, and Lemma 7.2 fails for γ = w (N = ∞, or N large). Adding auxiliary level at another prime to make the quotient neat changes nothing.

The step of the proof that fails is the implicit claim that C(X_K) → C(X_{K''}) → C(X_{K'}) → C(X_K) is a diagram "of complexes of R-modules". Δ need not act on X_{K'} or X_{K''}, and even when it does, the maps need not be equivariant. The same unjustified R-linearity occurs in §7.2, where the pullback to Y^γ is treated as a morphism in D^b(R).

The paper is aware that the condition matters: p. 395 requires P_x to "commute with the action of the diamond operators". All operators actually used satisfy the condition: diagonal g in §9.2 commutes with torus representatives of Δ. So no main theorem is affected. I class this as an error in the stated generality, not merely a gap, because the lemma as printed is false for some allowed γ. Defence attempted and failed. An R-linear chain map C → C induces an R-linear map on H_*(C) = H_*(X_Δ(Q), A), and the R-action there is the Δ-action by right translation, because the map C → C(X_Δ(Q)) of Lemma 7.1 is R-linear. So the lemma forces T_γ to commute with Δ. Lemma 7.2 is stated for every γ ∈ G(A^{∞,p}), and that is false.

Counterexample inside the paper's own §9 setting. Take n = 2, x ∈ Q, and γ = w = (0 1; π_x 0) at x, trivial elsewhere (x ∤ p, so w ∈ G(A^{∞,p})). A direct computation gives w (a b; πc d) w^{-1} = (d c; πb a). So w normalizes K_{Q,x} (the Iwahori) and L_{Q,x} = {d/a ≡ 1}, and it acts on Δ by δ ↦ δ^{-1}. Hence K' = K'' = K and T_w = w_* is right translation, with w_*∘r_δ = r_{δ^{-1}}∘w_*. Also w^2 = π·I, which is central, so T_w is invertible. R-linearity would then force r_{δ^2} = id on H_*(X_Δ(Q), O). For p odd, δ ↦ δ^2 is bijective on Δ = (Z/p^N)^q, so Δ would act trivially on H_*(X_Δ(Q), O). Taking transfer, dim H_*(X_Δ, K) = dim H_*(X_0, K). That is false in general. For example, with F = Q allowed by the general setting of §7.1, the Euler characteristic gives χ(X_Δ) = |Δ|·χ(X_0) ≠ χ(X_0). In any case, patching needs Δ to act nontrivially.

The failing step in the proof is the claim that T̃_γ is a map of complexes of R-modules. C(X_{K'}) and C(X_{K''}) carry no Δ-action. Computed out, T̃_γ(σ) = Σ_{hK ⊂ KγK} σ·h. This commutes with r_δ exactly when δKγK = KγKδ, which is the candidate's condition. Under that condition the rest of the proof (Tag 08FQ over R) is fine.

The authors evidently meant only operators that commute with Δ: p. 394 says "In practice, the Hecke algebra T will be of the form T^an[U_x : x ∈ Q]", and p. 395 says "a projector P_x which commutes with the action of the diamond operators". The intro to §7.2 on p. 395 speaks of "'good' Hecke operators … together with certain operators at the primes in Q". §7.2 (pp. 398–400) has the same unrestricted γ, and its "element of the right hand side" in D^b(R) likewise needs Δ-equivariance.

Downstream uses:
- Lemma 7.3, Lemma 7.4 and the choice of T on pp. 394–395 use only operators that satisfy the condition.
- §9 (p. 425: "By Conjecture B and the results of Sect. 7.1") uses T_{Q,ψ}, which is generated by diagonal g (Def. 9.1), so the condition holds there.
- §7.2 feeds no stated theorem.

So Lemma 7.2 is false as stated and needs the added hypothesis. No later theorem changes.

II.5 Lemma 1], there exists a perfect complex of R-modules C together with a quasi-isomorphism C → C(X_Δ(Q)) of complexes of R-modules. (Mumford only guarantees that the final term of the complex is flat, but since R is local, this final term is also free). Earlier on the same page: "Recall that by a perfect complex of R-modules, we mean a bounded complex of finite free R-modules. If Y is a topological space, we let C(Y) denote the complex of O-valued singular chains on Y." The wording in arXiv v2 (p. 71) is identical.
issues.correction:
The singular chain complex C(X_Δ(Q)) is not bounded. It is non-zero in every homological degree i ≥ 0, so it is bounded only below homologically (bounded above cohomologically). Mumford's Lemma 1 therefore does not apply to it as the paper claims. The minimal repair adds finite-dimensionality, which is available in the §7 setting ("covering space X_Δ(Q) → X_0(Q) of manifolds").

Route (a), which makes Lemma 1 unnecessary: Δ acts freely on the Borel–Serre compactification, a compact manifold with boundary. It is Δ-equivariantly homotopy equivalent to a copy of itself inside X_Δ(Q), obtained by removing a collar. Lift a finite triangulation of the quotient. The simplicial chains then form a bounded complex C of finite free R-modules, with a Δ-equivariant quasi-isomorphism C → C(X_Δ(Q)).

Route (b): use dim X_0(Q) = d. Then H_i(C(X_Δ(Q)) ⊗_R M) = H_i(X_0(Q), local system M) = 0 for i > d and every R-module M. So the truncation τ_{≤d}C(X_Δ(Q)) is a bounded complex of flat modules with finitely generated homology. Apply Lemma 1 to it. The resulting map P → τ_{≤d}C lifts to P → C(X_Δ(Q)) because P is a bounded complex of projectives.

In the next sentence, replace "bounded" by "bounded below (homologically)". Mumford's Lemma 2 still holds for such complexes by its mapping-cone proof: an exact complex of flat modules that is bounded above cohomologically has flat cycle modules. The finite generation of H_*(X_Δ(Q), O) is also needed and is not stated; it is standard via Borel–Serre.

The "since R is local" remark needs no change. The §7 introduction (p. 391) fixes Δ = (Z/p^N Z)^q, and in any case a finitely generated flat R-module is projective. That is perfect in the sense of the Notation on p. 306.

Rendered p. 393 and transcribed the passage above. The diagram is the triangle C --T̃_γ--> C(X_K) <--s-- C, described as a diagram "of complexes of R-modules", so "commute" literally means s∘T_γ = T̃_γ on the nose.
(1) The cited reference only gives homotopy. Stacks Tag 08FQ (Lemma 21.44.7, strictly perfect complexes) ends with "a dotted arrow ... making the diagram commute up to homotopy". Perfectness of C makes Hom^•(C,C) → Hom^•(C,C(X_K)) a quasi-isomorphism, which lifts cycles only up to boundaries (homotopy). It does not lift them strictly.
(2) The strict claim is false in general. Over any ring R, take P = R in degree 0 and M with M_1 = R, M_0 = R², d(a) = (a,0). Let s(1) = (0,1), which is a quasi-isomorphism since the cokernel is contractible. Let f(1) = (1,0), which is a chain map. Then s∘g = (0,g(1)) ≠ (1,0) for every g : P → P, so no strict lift exists, although f = d∘h ≃ 0 = s∘0. A strict lift would need, e.g., a surjective quasi-isomorphism, and s cannot be surjective: C is finite free while C(X_K) is free on uncountably many simplices.
(3) The strict claim also fails for some C that is "as in Lemma 7.1". Given any valid (C,s), add the contractible summand R --id--> R in degrees 1,0. Send its generators to a path σ from x to y and to y − x, extended R-linearly. The result is still a perfect complex with a quasi-isomorphism. For generic points x, y, the degree-0 chain T̃_γ(y − x) is supported on Hecke translates of x and y that lie outside the finite support of s(C_0) + R(y−x). So T̃_γ∘s does not factor through s.
Classification: the lemma's statement (the action on homology lifts to a chain map C → C) is true. The homotopy-commutative lift proves it, and later uses (polynomials in the T_γ, Lemma 7.3) need only an endomorphism of C inducing T_γ on homology. The missing "up to homotopy" is a slip whose intended meaning is clear from the cited Tag 08FQ, which states it. I therefore class it as a misprint (wording slip) with affects = nothing, rather than a substantive error. 1) The cited source gives only the weaker statement. Stacks Tag 08FQ is Lemma 21.44.7 (Cohomology on Sites, 'Strictly perfect complexes'). Its conclusion is a dotted arrow 'making the diagram commute up to homotopy', and the proof works in the homotopy category. So the paper's own citation supports only commutativity up to homotopy.

2) Strict commutativity is false in general. Toy example: C = R in degree 0; D_1 = R, D_0 = R⊕R with d(x) = (0,x); q(r) = (r,0), which is a quasi-isomorphism; f(r) = (0,r), which is a chain map. No g : C → C has q∘g = f, since f(C) is not contained in q(C). A strict lift needs something like a surjective quasi-isomorphism. Here q : C → C(X_K) goes from a finitely generated complex into singular chains, which are free of huge rank, so it is never surjective.

3) Strictness also fails for some C that Lemma 7.1 allows, and Lemma 7.2 is stated for any such C. Take any (C, q). Add the contractible summand R e_1 → R e_0 (d e_1 = e_0), sending e_1 to a singular 1-simplex σ and e_0 to ∂σ. This is still perfect with a quasi-isomorphism to C(X_K). Choose σ generic, away from the finite support of q(C_1), its Δ-translates, and the points fixed by the correspondence. Then T̃_γ(σ) is a nonzero positive combination of simplices, none of them in q(C_1) + Rσ, so no strict lift exists (for T_γ not the trivial correspondence).

Defence considered. The paper has no convention that diagrams of complexes commute up to homotopy. The diagram is explicitly one 'of complexes of R-modules', while §7.2 is careful to say 'in D^b(R)'. So as printed the sentence overstates, though the intent (up to homotopy) is clear from the citation. This could also be classed as a misprint.

Consequences. Lemma 7.2 itself only asks for a chain map lifting the action on homology, and the homotopy version gives exactly that. What uses the lift: expressing T ∈ T as a (not necessarily commutative) polynomial in the lifted T_γ; Lemma 7.3 (H_*(lim T^n C) = lim T^n H_*(C) by exactness); Lemma 7.4; the D at the end of §7.1 (H_n(D ⊗ O/ϖ^N) ≅ H_n(X_Δ(Q), O/ϖ^N)_m and so on); and §9's use of 'Sect. 7.1' (p. 431). All of these only need the induced maps on homology of C ⊗ A, and those are the same for homotopic maps. Nothing needs q∘T_γ = T̃_γ∘q on the nose, or the lifts to commute with one another. So no stated result is affected.

issues.reason:
I checked the page image and the v2 text. As printed, the lemma defines l_0 through the integral groups lim_→ T^n H^*(C), where C is the integral chain complex from Lemma 7.1. The paper uses "range/length l_0" to mean degrees q_0..q_0+l_0, so length means max − min.

The first part of the lemma, which is correct (the minimal-complex / Nakayama argument), forces dim D_n/𝔪_R = dim H_n(C_T ⊗ k). So D_n ≠ 0 whenever the mod-𝔪 homology is non-zero in degree n. Universal coefficients give 0 → H_n(C)⊗k → H_n(C⊗k) → Tor_1(H_{n-1}(C),k) → 0, so torsion in the top integral degree produces mod-ϖ homology one degree higher.

Counterexample (redone): take R = O (Δ trivial, which is of p-power order), T = 1, and C = [O --ϖ--> O] in degrees 1, 0. Then H_1(C) = 0 and H_0(C) = O/ϖ, so the integral range is 0. But C⊗k = [k --0--> k] has H_1 = H_0 = k. Any D as in the lemma must have rank 1 in degrees 1 and 0, so its length is 1 > 0.

A geometric instance: a Bianchi manifold with a non-Eisenstein 𝔪 such that H_1(X,O)_𝔪 is non-zero torsion. Then H_2(X,O)_𝔪 = 0, by Poincaré duality, vanishing boundary cohomology at 𝔪, and torsion-freeness of H^1. But H_2(X,k)_𝔪 ⊇ Tor(H_1,k) ≠ 0. The proof's claim that Mumford gives K "bounded of length l_0" fails for the same reason: any perfect complex quasi-isomorphic to C_T contains the minimal one as a summand.

"d on D" is a slip for "d on K", since D is only produced at the end of the induction.

Downstream: the bullets after the lemma on p. 395 use only the first part ("D_n ≠ 0 iff H_n(X_0(Q),k)_𝔪 ≠ 0"). §9.5 (p. 425) gets "D_N concentrated in degrees q_0,…,q_0+l_0" from Conjecture B(4)(a), which is stated with O/ϖ^m coefficients (reducible to k by dévissage, p. 413). So the main theorems are unaffected. Only the "Moreover" clause of Lemma 7.4 and its proof are wrong. The Correction (Invent. Math. 227) fixes brackets only, so this is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS
(1) The paper's convention, from the intro ("concentrated in l_0+1 consecutive degrees", "range of length l_0") and §9.5 ("q_0,...,q_0+l_0"), is that length = max − min. Counting terms instead makes no difference: the counterexample below fails under both conventions. It survives only if l_0 counts degrees while length(D) is max − min, and nothing in the paper supports mixing them like that.
(2) Standing hypothesis. §7 opens by saying that the cohomology localised at 𝔪 "is assumed to vanish outside a range of length l_0". Conjecture B(4)(a) is stated with O/ϖ^m coefficients, reducing to k by dévissage (p. 413). If that were the hypothesis, the lemma would be true. But the lemma defines l_0 itself, through the integral groups lim_→ T^n H^*(C). Here C is the O[Δ]-perfect complex of Lemma 7.1, quasi-isomorphic to C(X_Δ(Q)), so these are integral groups. They do not control the mod-𝔪 range.
(3) Reading H^* as cohomology of the dual complex does not help either (see below).

WHY THE PRINTED STATEMENT IS FALSE
The first part of the lemma is correct (minimal complex plus Nakayama). It gives D_n ≠ 0 exactly when H_n(C_T ⊗ k) ≠ 0. Universal coefficients give 0 → H_n(C_T)⊗k → H_n(C_T⊗k) → Tor_1(H_{n-1}(C_T),k) → 0, so torsion in the top integral degree creates mod-ϖ homology one degree higher.
- Abstract example: R = O (Δ trivial), T = 1, C = [O --ϖ--> O] in degrees 1, 0. The integral homology is O/ϖ in degree 0 only (range 0). But C⊗k has k in degrees 1 and 0, so every D satisfying the first part has length 1.
- Geometric example (Bianchi): Q empty, 𝔪 non-Eisenstein, H_1(X,O)_𝔪 non-zero torsion with no characteristic-zero classes at 𝔪 (the torsion phenomenon the paper is built around). Then H_0(X,O)_𝔪 = 0. Also H_2(X,O)_𝔪 = 0: it is torsion-free because X is homotopy equivalent to a 2-complex, and rationally it is H^1_c = H^1 at 𝔪, which is 0. So the integral homology sits in degree 1 only (range 0). But H_2(X,k)_𝔪 ⊇ Tor(H_1,k) ≠ 0, so length(D) = 1.
- Cohomology reading: with cohomology (or the dual complex), the torsion moves to degree 2 alone, so the range is again 0.
- General bound: over the depth-1 ring O[Δ], the bottom degree of D equals the bottom degree of H(C_T). Above the top homology degree, the complex is a finite free resolution of a submodule of a free module, which is free by Auslander–Buchsbaum. So length(D) ≤ l_0 + 1, and this is sharp.
- The proof's first sentence fails too: Mumford's Lemma 1 bounds K by the degree range of the complex it starts from, not by its homology. Any perfect complex quasi-isomorphic to C_T contains the minimal D as a direct summand, so no such K of length l_0 exists in the examples above.

CONSEQUENCES
- The bullets right after the lemma (p. 395) use only the first part ("D_n ≠ 0 iff H_n(X_0(Q),k)_𝔪 ≠ 0").
- §7.2 (the coherent case) does not use the "Moreover" clause.
- The only later use is §9.5 (p. 425): "By Conjecture B and the results of Sect. 7.1, there exists a perfect complex D̃_N ... concentrated in degrees q_0,...,q_0+l_0". That conclusion is true, because Conjecture B(4)(a) gives mod-ϖ vanishing, and together with the first part of Lemma 7.4 this yields the corrected clause. The main theorems are therefore unaffected. Only the "Moreover" clause of Lemma 7.4 and the corresponding proof step are wrong.

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors: the Correction (Invent. Math. 227) fixes brackets only.

VERDICT ON THE PROPOSED CORRECTIONS
Both are right and minimal. The X-K7-18 wording is good. H-part2-9 adds the correct "d on D → d on K" fix. I classify this as an error rather than a misprint because both the printed statement and a proof step fail.

issues.locator: §7.2, p. 395 (published version)
issues.printed: §7.2 "The Coherent case", p. 395 (PDF p. 99): "We will be given an automorphic vector bundle ℰ on Y (in the case of a toroidal compactification, this will either be a canonical or subcanonical extension) which pulls back to a bundle also denoted by ℰ on X." Earlier in the same paragraph: "We will have an étale map Y = X_Δ(Q) → X = X_0(Q) with Galois group Δ, a finite abelian p-group." arXiv v2 §7.2 has the same wording ("automorphic vector bundle E on Y ... which pulls back to a bundle also denoted by E on X").
issues.correction: "We will be given an automorphic vector bundle ℰ on X (in the case of a toroidal compactification, this will either be a canonical or subcanonical extension) which pulls back to a bundle also denoted by ℰ on Y." An equivalent fix keeps "ℰ on Y" and says "which is the pullback of a bundle also denoted by ℰ on X".
issues.reason:
This is a genuine swap of X and Y. The only map in the setup is f : Y = X_Δ(Q) → X = X_0(Q). On p. 397 (PDF p. 101) the paper restates it as "f : Y → X is an étale map of smooth proper O-schemes". Pullback along f therefore goes from bundles on X to bundles on Y, so a bundle on Y cannot "pull back to" a bundle on X. The rest of the paper uses ℰ the corrected way:
(i) On p. 398 (PDF p. 102) the paper sets ℱ = ℰ^* ⊗_{O_X} ω_X, "a coherent sheaf of O_X-modules". For this to make sense, ℰ has to live on X.
(ii) The Čech complex D computes H^i(Y, f^*ℱ). The paper then says its dual computes H_i(Y, ℰ⊗O/ϖ^n) := H^i(Y, ℰ^*⊗_{O_Y} ω_Y ⊗ O/ϖ^n)^∨. Here ℰ on Y means f^*ℰ.
(iii) On p. 398 the Verdier-duality line reads H^{d-i}(Y, Hom_{O_Y}(f^*ℱ, ω_Y)_A) = H^{d-i}(Y, (f^*ℰ)_A). This explicitly treats ℰ on Y as the pullback f^*ℰ.
I redid the computation. Since f is étale, f^*Ω^1_X ≅ Ω^1_Y, so f^*ω_X ≅ ω_Y. Hence f^*ℱ ≅ (f^*ℰ)^* ⊗ ω_Y, and because f^*ℰ is locally free, Hom(f^*ℱ, ω_Y) ≅ f^*ℰ. Both the corrected sentence and the identification f^*ℱ = ℰ^*⊗ω_Y on Y are consistent. The slip is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. The same text appears in arXiv v2, so it is an authors' slip, not a typesetting defect.

issues.locator: §7.2 "The Coherent case", the expository paragraph after the definition of coherent homology H_i(Y, 𝓔 ⊗ 𝒪/ϖ^n) := H^i(Y, 𝓔^* ⊗ ω_Y ⊗ 𝒪/ϖ^n)^∨, published p. 396 (PDF p. 100), lines 7–10 of the page. arXiv v2 has the same text word for word ("... non-zero homology group of highest degree with coefficients in O, namely H_{q0+l0}(X, O)_m"). The passage is not in arXiv v1, which has no Part 2/§7.
issues.printed: In Betti cohomology, the groups H^{q_0}(X, 𝓔/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 may be identified with the non-zero homology group of highest degree with coefficients in 𝒪, namely H_{q_0+l_0}(X, 𝒪)_𝔪. This identification is essentially a consequence of Poincaré duality (the manifolds X have boundary, but the ideals 𝔪 are chosen specifically so that the cohomology of the boundary becomes trivial after localization at 𝔪).
issues.correction: Minimal fix: "... may be identified with the non-zero cohomology group of highest degree with coefficients in 𝒪, namely H^{q_0+l_0}(X, 𝒪)_𝔪". This means changing "homology" to "cohomology" and the subscript to a superscript. It keeps the justification "consequence of Poincaré duality, with the boundary killed by localization", because H^{q_0}(X,E/𝒪)^∨ ≅ H_c^{d−q_0}(X,𝒪) = H_c^{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪) and H_c ≅ H after localization at 𝔪 (with d = 2q_0+l_0). An equivalent fix is "the homology group of lowest degree, H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)", which follows from universal coefficients alone, up to the paper's usual loose 𝔪/𝔪* bookkeeping. The unrelated E/𝓔 font slip in the same sentence is a separate issue.
issues.reason:
Setting (§8/§9): dim_R X = 2q_0 + l_0. After localising at 𝔪, the cohomology is concentrated in [q_0, q_0+l_0] (assumption (4)(a) of §9), and boundary cohomology dies, so H^*_c(X)_𝔪 = H^*(X)_𝔪.
(i) K/𝒪 is divisible, hence injective over 𝒪, so universal coefficients give H^{q_0}(X, K/𝒪) = Hom(H_{q_0}(X,𝒪), K/𝒪). Therefore H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪. The paper says the same on p. 376 (proof of Lemma 5.8): "H^1(Y, K/𝒪) = H_1(Y,𝒪)^∨". Poincaré–Lefschetz duality then identifies H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 with H^{2q_0+l_0-q_0}_c(X,𝒪)_𝔪 = H^{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪. That is cohomology of highest degree, not homology.
(ii) The printed group is torsion-free. By Poincaré–Lefschetz duality, H_{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 ≅ H^{q_0}_c(X,𝒪)_𝔪 = H^{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪. Its ϖ-torsion is the image of H^{q_0-1}(X,k)_𝔪 = 0, so it is torsion-free. It is the 𝒪-dual of H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪, not that module itself.
(iii) The paper's own Part 1 contradicts the printed identification. Take the Bianchi case q_0 = l_0 = 1, d = 3. Lemma 5.9(2) (p. 376, checked on the rendered page) says "If μ is p-torsion free, then H_2(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪 is p-torsion free." But the module that patches there is H^1(K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 = H_1(Y_Δ(Q),𝒪)_𝔪, which can have torsion; torsion classes are the point of the paper. Suppose H_1(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 is finite and non-zero. Then H_2(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 ≅ Hom(H_1(Y,𝒪)_𝔪, 𝒪) = 0, while H^1(Y,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 = H_1(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 ≠ 0. So the printed group is zero, and even the words "non-zero" fail.
(iv) Unlocalised toy check: for the lens space L(p,1), H^1(L, Q_p/Z_p)^∨ ≅ Z/p ≅ H_1(L, Z_p) ≅ H^2(L, Z_p), but H_2(L, Z_p) = 0.
No reading rescues the printed text. Borel–Moore H_{q_0+l_0} ≅ H^{q_0} is also torsion-free, and reading H_i as H^i(K/𝒪)^∨ would make the identification tautological and of degree q_0, not "a consequence of Poincaré duality".
The statement is false as printed. It sits in a motivational remark, though. Nothing later uses it: §9 works directly with H^{q_0}(Y,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 (e.g. Thm 9.19). So no proof or result is affected. Defence attempted and failed. (1) Universal coefficients: since K/𝒪 is injective, H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪) = Hom(H_{q_0}(X,𝒪), K/𝒪), so H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 (degree q_0, not q_0+l_0). The paper says the same on p. 376 (proof of Lemma 5.8): "H^1(Y,K/𝒪) = H_1(Y,𝒪)^∨". Its own convention in §7.2 also gives degree q_0: it defines homology as H_i := (H^i of the dual with torsion coefficients)^∨, so the dual of lowest-degree cohomology is lowest-degree homology. (2) Poincaré–Pontryagin duality gives H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)^∨ ≅ H_c^{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪) ≅_𝔪 H^{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪, which is cohomology, not homology. The only charitable reading that uses homology of degree q_0+l_0 drops the ∨ and keeps K/𝒪 coefficients: H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)_𝔪 ≅ H_{q_0+l_0}(X,K/𝒪)_𝔪. That is not what is printed. (3) The printed identification is false exactly where it matters. H_{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 is ϖ-torsion free, because its ϖ-torsion is the image of H_{q_0+l_0+1}(X,k)_𝔪 = 0. The paper proves this itself for Bianchi manifolds in Lemma 5.9(2): H_2(Y_0(Q),μ)_𝔪 is p-torsion free, where q_0 = l_0 = 1. By contrast, H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 carries the torsion classes the paper is about. Take a Bianchi 𝔪 supported only on torsion. Then H_1(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 is finite and non-zero, while H_2(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 is torsion free of rank dim H_1(Y,K)_𝔪 = 0, so H_2(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 = 0. The printed statement would therefore force the patched module to vanish. The ranks over K do agree (by Poincaré duality and universal coefficients), so the claim fails only on torsion. A toy check without localization: for the lens space L(p,1), H^1(Q_p/Z_p)^∨ ≅ Z/p ≅ H^2(Z_p), but H_2(Z_p) = 0. The statement is correct only when l_0 = 0. It is not a single-character slip: both the words "homology ... of highest degree" and the formula H_{q_0+l_0} say the same wrong thing, so I classify it as an error rather than a misprint. Consequences: the passage is expository. It only motivates the name "coherent homology", and nothing later cites it. Every place the paper actually uses this module agrees with the correction. §5 patches H_1(Y_0(Q),𝒪[Δ])_𝔪 (degree q_0). §9 patches H = H^{q_0}(Y,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 (Theorem 9.19 and its proof, pp. 425–427), using complexes D_N whose homology in degrees q_0..q_0+l_0 is the homology of Y. Remark 9.2 refers to the cohomology module H_ψ^{q_0+l_0}(Y_1(Q),𝒪), matching the proposed fix. The 2022 Correction covers only the bracket errors, and this is not one of them.

issues.locator: §7.2, pp. 399–400 (published version)
issues.printed:
• the duality isomorphism
    RHom(O_{Y^γ_A}, ω_{Y^γ_A}[d]) --∼--> A[0].
(§7.2 "The Coherent case", p. 400 = PDF p. 104. It is the third bullet in the definition of T̃_γ, after "the pullback under π_1^* ⊗ (φ ∘ π_2^*)" and "the composition morphism". The arrow is printed with a tilde over it. The v2 text, cg-v2.txt line ~4017, is identical.)
issues.correction: Minimal fix, p. 400: "the trace (duality) morphism tr : RHom(O_{Y^γ_A}, ω_{Y^γ_A}[d]) = RΓ(Y^γ_A, ω_{Y^γ_A})[d] → A[0]", dropping the ∼ and the word "isomorphism". This is the counit Rπ_*π^!A → A of Grothendieck duality for the smooth proper map Y^γ_A → Spec A of relative dimension d. Equivalently, it is the composite of the canonical map K → H^0(K)[0], for K = RΓ(ω)[d] ∈ D^{[−d,0]}, with the trace H^d(Y^γ_A, ω_A) → A. Minimal fix, p. 399: "tr denotes the trace map H^d(Y^γ, (ω_{Y^γ})_A) → A". That map is an isomorphism only when Y^γ has geometrically connected fibres over O. Only a morphism is used in either place.
issues.reason:
Checked on the rendered page. The paper's own conventions make RHom a complex, not a Hom group. On p. 399, "Rπ_*(G) = RHom(O_{Y_A}, G)" is an object of D^b(R). Verdier duality is stated as an identity of complexes, RHom(RHom(O_{Y_A}, G), A[0]) = RHom(G, ω_{Y_A}[d]). The composition morphism in the preceding bullet uses ⊗^L of such complexes. So RHom(O_{Y^γ_A}, ω_{Y^γ_A}[d]) = RΓ(Y^γ_A, ω_A)[d], and I recomputed its cohomology: H^j of this complex is H^{j+d}(Y^γ_A, ω_A) for −d ≤ j ≤ 0.

Here Y^γ is smooth and proper over O of relative dimension d (p. 398), and ω is the top exterior power of Ω^1. By Serre duality, the map to A[0] can only be a quasi-isomorphism if H^i(Y^γ_A, ω_A) = 0 for all i < d, i.e. H^j(O) = 0 for j ≥ 1. This fails in general. Take the modular-curve instance of the setting, with d = 1 and genus g ≥ 1, which holds at the large levels in use once Taylor–Wiles primes are added. Then H^{-1} = H^0(Y^γ_A, ω_A) ≅ A^g ≠ 0. More generally, H^{-d} = H^0(Y^γ_A, ω_A), and this is typically nonzero for positive-dimensional Shimura varieties. So the ∼ and the word "isomorphism" are wrong; only a morphism exists. The candidate's correction and its degree computation (H^{i−d} = H^i(Y^γ_A, ω) for 0 ≤ i ≤ d) are correct.

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. A side remark, outside this candidate: the "trace isomorphism H^d(Y^γ, (ω)_A) → A" on p. 399 also assumes Y^γ is geometrically connected. I checked this on the rendered pages 399–400. I tried to defend the text, and none of the defences works.

(1) The paper's own conventions make RHom a complex. On p. 399 the paper writes "Rπ_*(G) = RHom(O_{Y_A}, G)" as an object of D^b(R). Verdier duality there is an identity of complexes. The preceding bullet takes ⊗^L of such RHom's. So RHom(O_{Y^γ_A}, ω[d]) = RΓ(Y^γ_A, ω_A)[d], and its cohomology in degree j is H^{j+d}(Y^γ_A, ω_A) for −d ≤ j ≤ 0. For a quasi-isomorphism with A[0], all of H^i(Y^γ_A, ω_A) for i < d would have to vanish. By Serre duality over the Gorenstein Artinian ring A = O/ϖ^n, H^i(ω_A) = Hom_A(H^{d−i}(Y^γ_A, O), A). So we would need H^j(Y^γ_A, O) = 0 for j ≥ 1, and also H^0 = A.

This fails in the paper's own motivating case: Y^γ is a modular curve (d = 1) at Taylor–Wiles level, of genus g ≥ 1. There H^{−1} = H^0(Y^γ_A, Ω^1) ≅ A^g ≠ 0, the weight-2 cusp forms. More generally H^{−d} = H^0(ω_A), and this is nonzero for positive-dimensional Shimura varieties of large level. The statement is also false for d = 0 whenever there is more than one point.

(2) Reading it as H^0 only, i.e. as the isomorphism Ext^d(O, ω) ≅ A, is ruled out. The paper treats RHom as a complex in the same paragraph, and the target is written A[0] with a tilde.

(3) Reading it as the genuine duality isomorphism RHom(O, π^!A) ≅ RHom_A(Rπ_*O, A) does not help. That has a different target. One reaches A[0] only by composing with restriction along the unit A → Rπ_*O, and that composite is not an isomorphism.

(4) The p. 399 claim is conditionally true. H^d(Y^γ_A, ω_A) = Hom_A(H^0(Y^γ_A, O), A), so it equals A exactly when the fibres are geometrically connected. That holds for X_1(N)-type modular curves, where det(L^γ) is surjective. It fails in the stated generality: "Shimura varieties associated to some reductive group G over a number field F", e.g. Hilbert modular varieties with several geometric components. There the trace is the sum map A^c → A.

So the text is genuinely wrong. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not mention it.

Consequences: every place where the paper uses the passage needs only a morphism. T̃_γ is defined as a composite of morphisms landing in Hom(RHom(O,G) ⊗^L RHom(G, ω[d]), A[0]). The claim that "T̃_γ induces the Hecke operator T_γ defined above" needs only that H^0 of the last arrow is the trace H^d(ω_A) → A used on p. 399. That holds for the trace morphism. The lift to C_n^∨ via Tag 08FQ and the localisation lim T^m C_n do not use invertibility. Perfect Serre/Verdier duality is needed only on Y, not on Y^γ, and it holds with the trace map without any connectedness hypothesis. §7.2 is also not used by any later theorem. The introduction (p. 300) says the Coherent case is confined to "constructing suitable complexes (see Sect. 7.2)". The weight-one results of §3 use their own modular-curve arguments, and "Sect. 7" is otherwise cited only through §7.1 (in §9). So the proposed correction is right and minimal. I classify it as an error, not a misprint: it is a false mathematical assertion, stated twice (in words and by the tilde), not a typographical slip. It affects nothing.

The candidate's correction for (c) is right but does not mention X_Q.
issues.reason: I rendered pp. 402–404 and cropped them at high resolution; all three printed items match exactly, and arXiv v2 p. 78 is the same. (a) The Greenberg–Wiles formula compares H^1_L(F, M) with H^1_{L^*}(F, M^*). For M = F_p, M^* = μ_p. The sentence just before the display calls the dual Selmer group H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p), and items (1)–(3) and the conclusion dim H^1_L(F, F_p) − dim H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p) = −(r_1 + r_2 − 1) all use μ_p. So the F_p in the denominator is a slip. With μ_p, the arithmetic works out: +1 from the H^0 term (ζ_p ∉ F), −(r_1 + r_2) from the infinite places, and 0 from v|p. (b) F has characteristic 0, so H^1_fppf(F, μ_p) = H^1(G_F, μ_p) = F^×/F^{×p}. That is the whole group, not something that 'sits inside' it, as the next sentence says. The dual Selmer group is the set of classes that are unramified or flat at every place. That is H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p), which sits in the exact sequence 0 → O_F^×/p → H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p) → Cl(F)[p] → 0 given on p. 402. (c) U_Q is a subgroup of the finite ideles, obtained from U by changing O_v^× at v ∈ Q. So the printed Y_Q is not the level-Q analogue of Y = F^×\A_F^×/UK_∞, even though the text says Y = Y_0(Q) and Y_Q = Y_1(Q). The fibres of Y_Q are then described as components of the cokernel of O_F^× → R^{×r_1} × C^{×r_2}/K_∞, which is (S^1)^{r_1+r_2−1} × R, and that description divides by K_∞. I redid the dimension count. Without K_∞, the identity component R_{>0}^{r_1} × (C^×)^{r_2} modulo units and A^0_∞ has dimension r_1 + 2r_2 − 1. With K_∞ it has dimension r_1 + r_2 − 1 = ℓ_0, which is what the text uses. None of these is one of the 47 known bracket errors. None is correct under the paper's own conventions, since the paper itself writes the correct forms nearby.

issues.locator: §8.2, p. 402 (last paragraph) (published version)
issues.printed: We can, in fact, deduce this equality directly by computing both terms via class field theory. The first group has dimension dim Cl(F)/p. For the second, recall that for v|p the group L_v^* is one-dimensional and is dual to the unramified classes in H^1(F_v, F_p). This dual consists of classes which are finite flat. So we are interested in H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p), which sits in the exact sequence: 0 → O_F^×/O_F^{×p} → H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p) → Cl(F)[p] → 0
issues.correction: Minimal fix: "recall that for v|p the group L_v^* ⊂ H^1(F_v, μ_p) = F_v^×/F_v^{×p} is the annihilator, under local Tate duality, of the one-dimensional space L_v of unramified classes in H^1(F_v, F_p). So L_v^* has codimension one, and the quotient H^1(F_v, μ_p)/L_v^* is dual to L_v. This annihilator is O_v^×/O_v^{×p}, which consists of the finite flat classes." The dimension of L_v^* is [F_v:Q_p] + dim H^0(F_v, μ_p). That equals 1 only when F_v = Q_p (p is odd because ζ_p ∉ F).
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered PDF page 106 (= p. 402, §8.2) at 200 dpi, and the sentence is printed as quoted. The arXiv v2 text (line 4115) is the same. The paper does not define L^* in §8.2. It is the dual Selmer condition in the Greenberg–Wiles formula displayed just above, and §8.3 writes L^⊥ for the same object. So L_v^* is the Tate annihilator of L_v.

I redid the computation. Kummer theory gives H^1(F_v, μ_p) = F_v^×/F_v^{×p}. By the local Euler characteristic formula, with h^2(μ_p) = h^0(F_p) = 1, this has dimension [F_v:Q_p] + 1 + h^0(F_v, μ_p). Here L_v is the unramified line, so dim L_v = 1 = h^0(F_v, F_p), and its annihilator has dimension [F_v:Q_p] + h^0(F_v, μ_p). Concretely, the Tate pairing sends (a, χ) to χ(rec(a)). Unramified characters kill exactly the classes with v(a) ≡ 0 mod p, so L_v^* = O_v^×/O_v^{×p}. Since O_v^× ≅ k_v^× × μ_{p^∞}(F_v) × Z_p^{[F_v:Q_p]}, the dimension agrees.

This is 1 only if F_v = Q_p and ζ_p ∉ Q_p. F is an arbitrary number field of signature (r1, r2), so the claim "L_v^* is one-dimensional" is false in general. For example, take F real quadratic with p inert, so F_v is unramified quadratic over Q_p and dim L_v^* = 2. The assumption ζ_p ∉ F does not force ζ_p ∉ F_v: for p = 3 and F = Q(√6), Q_3(√6) = Q_3(√−3). That is why the H^0(F_v, μ_p) term in the candidate's formula is needed. "Dual to the unramified classes" is also loose, since L_v^* is the annihilator of L_v, not dual to it. The authors probably had F_v = Q_p in mind, or meant the quotient H^1/L_v^*.

The candidate's correction and dimension formula are right. The slip changes nothing. The following sentence ("This dual consists of classes which are finite flat") is true, because H^1_fppf(O_v, μ_p) = O_v^×/O_v^{×p}. The direct computation uses only that identification plus the fppf sequence and Dirichlet's unit theorem, which give dim Cl(F)/p − (r1 + r2 − 1) − dim Cl(F)[p] = −(r1 + r2 − 1). The Greenberg–Wiles computation in item (3) uses dim L_v = 1, not dim L_v^*. §8.2 is an explicitly heuristic illustration ("ultimately somewhat circular"), and no later result uses dim L_v^*.

A separate small typo sits in the Greenberg–Wiles display on the same page: the denominator reads H^1_{L^*}(F, F_p) where the text around it has H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p). It is outside this item. I rendered PDF pp. 105–108 (published pp. 401–404) and confirmed the printed text.

Defence attempts, all failed:
(a) Notation. §8.2 never defines L^*. It is the dual Selmer condition in the Greenberg–Wiles formula displayed just above, and §8.3 writes the same object as L^⊥ (p. 408ff., e.g. Prop. 8.5). So the only faithful reading of L_v^* is the Tate annihilator of L_v. No other convention in the paper makes "one-dimensional" true.
(b) Direct computation. H^1(F_v, μ_p) = F_v^×/F_v^{×p}, which has dimension [F_v:Q_p] + 1 + h^0(F_v, μ_p) by the local Euler characteristic formula. The pairing of a with an unramified χ is χ(Frob)^{v(a)}, so L_v^⊥ = O_v^× F_v^{×p}/F_v^{×p} ≅ O_v^×/O_v^{×p}. Its dimension is [F_v:Q_p] + h^0(F_v, μ_p), since O_v^× ≅ (prime-to-p part) × μ_{p^∞}(F_v) × Z_p^{[F_v:Q_p]}.
(c) Is it one-dimensional anyway? Only when F_v = Q_p. The hypothesis ζ_p ∉ F forces p odd, because −1 ∈ F. Nothing restricts F to have its p-adic completions equal to Q_p: §8.2 takes "an arbitrary number field F". Counterexamples: F = Q(√2), p = 3 (inert, F_v = Q_9, dim L_v^* = 2). F = Q(√6), p = 3 (F_v = Q_3(√−3) contains ζ_3, dim L_v^* = 3).
(d) The phrase "is dual to the unramified classes" is also wrong. L_v^* is orthogonal to L_v, not dual to it. The object that is one-dimensional and dual to L_v is the quotient H^1(F_v, μ_p)/L_v^*. The authors apparently merged "the quotient by L_v^* is dual to the 1-dim L_v" into "L_v^* is 1-dim and dual to L_v", or had F_v = Q_p in mind. The sentence is a false mathematical assertion, not a typographical slip, so I class it as an error. It is harmless.

Consequences: none. The very next sentence, "This dual consists of classes which are finite flat", is correct: L_v^* = O_v^×/O_v^{×p} = H^1_fppf(O_v, μ_p). With the unramified condition at v∤p (and H^1(R, ·) = 0 for p odd), this gives H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p) = H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p). From there the fppf sequence and Dirichlet's unit theorem (ζ_p ∉ F) give dim Cl(F)/p − (r1 + r2 − 1) − dim Cl(F)[p] = −(r1 + r2 − 1). This matches the Greenberg–Wiles count, whose item (3) uses only dim L_v = dim H^0(F_v, F_p) = 1. The later use on p. 404 ("the dual Selmer group, which is H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p) = H^1_fppf(F, μ_p)", choosing |Q| = dim H^1_{L^*}) needs only this identification, never dim L_v^*. §8.2 is explicitly a heuristic illustration ("ultimately somewhat circular"), and no numbered result depends on it.

Both candidates' corrections (H-part2-13, X-K8-1) are right. X-K8-1's wording ("codimension one; quotient dual to L_v; L_v^* = image of O_v^×/p, dim [F_v:Q_p] + h^0(μ_p)") is the most accurate minimal repair. The earlier verdict on H-part2-13 is consistent with this.

Unrelated minor slips on the same pages, outside this item: the Greenberg–Wiles display has denominator H^1_{L^*}(F, F_p) where μ_p is meant, and p. 404 writes H^1_fppf(F, μ_p) where O_F is meant.

issues.reason: J_F is not defined anywhere in the paper; this display is its only occurrence in both versions. In its standard meaning, the idele group (Cassels–Fröhlich), J_F/F^× is the idele class group C_F. The quotient by UK_∞ is missing, and that quotient is not trivial: UK_∞ is compact and meets F^× in at most a finite group, so its image in C_F is a large compact subgroup, and C_F ≠ F^×\A_F^×/UK_∞. If J_F instead meant the group of fractional ideals, J_F/F^× would be the finite class group, which is also wrong: the text says the components of Y are (S^1)^{r_1+r_2-1}×R. The object actually used is the second expression, as Y_Q = F^×\A_F^×/U_Q and X_Q show. The intended meaning is clear.

issues.locator: §8.2 "Modularity of one-dimensional representations", published p. 403 (PDF p. 107), last paragraph and the display Z_p[RCl(Q)/p^n]; "by class field theory" continues at the top of p. 404. arXiv v2 has the same wording (v2 p. 79). arXiv v1 does not contain this passage.
issues.printed: "What, geometrically, is X_Q? The component group is the maximal quotient of the ray class group of conductor Q and exponent p^n. [...] Let us examine the cohomology of X_Q. In degree zero, the cohomology is  Z_p[RCl(Q)/p^n],  by class field theory." (The definitions just above it: X_Q := F^×\A_F^×/U_Q A^0_∞, where "for v ∈ Q with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p^n, one replaces O_v^× by O_v^{×p^n}, the unique subgroup of index p^n".)
issues.correction: π_0(X_Q) = F^×\A_F^×/U_Q(F⊗R)^{×,0}. This is the narrow ray class group RCl(Q) of conductor ∏_{v∈Q} v modulo the image of ∏_{v∈Q}(O_v^×)^{p^n}. Equivalently, it is the largest quotient of RCl(Q) in which the image of each O_v^× (v ∈ Q) has exponent dividing p^n. So it is an extension of Cl^+(F) by Δ_Q modulo the image of the totally positive units. It is not RCl(Q)/p^n·RCl(Q). In degree zero, H^0(X_Q, Z_p) = Z_p[π_0(X_Q)]. After localising at m (trivial r̄) this becomes Z_p[π_0(X_Q)⊗Z_p]. The candidate's correction says the same thing and is right; the minimal fix is to replace "the maximal quotient … and exponent p^n" and "RCl(Q)/p^n" with this quotient.
issues.reason:
1. Page 403 (PDF p. 107) was rendered and read, and the text was transcribed above. v2 has the same text. The passage is not one of the 47 bracket errors: the Correction lists none in §8.2, and a group ring of a finite group rightly uses single brackets.

2. The component group, computed directly. U_Q is open, so the image of (F⊗R)^{×,0} is open and connected. Hence π_0(X_Q) = A_F^×/F^× U_Q (F⊗R)^{×,0}. The quotient map U_Q → U induces a surjection π_0(X_Q) → A^×/F^×U(F⊗R)^{×,0} = Cl^+(F). So for every Q, the exponent of π_0(X_Q) is a multiple of the exponent of Cl^+(F). It cannot be a group of exponent p^n (in particular not RCl(Q)/p^n) when Cl(F) has an element whose order does not divide p^n.

3. Explicit counterexample, computed. I wrote a Python composition of binary quadratic forms (…/work/agents/xk84A/cl.py). It gives h(−199) = 9 with exponent 9, so Cl(Q(√−199)) ≅ Z/9. Take F = Q(√−199), p = 3, n = 1; ζ_3 ∉ F, and l_0 = 0. For Q = ∅, X = F^×\A^×/U C^× is the 9-point space Cl(F) ≅ Z/9. Then H^0(X, Z_3)_m = Z_3[Z/9]. The paper's formula instead gives Z_3[Cl/3] = Z_3[Z/3]. The rank over Z_3 is 9, not 3. For nonempty Q the group still surjects onto Z/9, so the claim fails for every Q. Prime-to-p examples also break the unlocalised statement: for Q(√−23) with p = 5, the component group has order 3, while its maximal exponent-5 quotient is trivial.

4. The paper contradicts itself. At the end of §8.2 it concludes R^unr ≃ Z_p[Cl(O_F) ⊗ Z_p]. That is the full p-part of the class group, not Cl/p^n, and it is what the correct π_0(X) gives at Q = ∅. At Q = ∅ the printed formula would even depend on n, which is absurd.

5. Charitable reading. "And exponent p^n" might be meant to describe the local ramification at Q, cut to exponent p^n. Under that reading the group is right. But the notation RCl(Q)/p^n literally means RCl(Q) modulo p^n-th powers, and "maximal quotient ... of exponent p^n" naturally means the same thing. As printed, the statement is false.

6. Impact. §8.2 is a heuristic sketch. The later steps do not use the exponent claim: Hecke operators act through [π_v], R_Q → T_{Q,m} is a surjection, and the final isomorphism uses the correct group. So nothing downstream is affected. 1. What the definitions give. Since A_∞^0K_∞ is connected, π_0(X_Q) = A_F^×/F^×U_Q(F⊗R)^{×,0}. Here U_{Q,v} = (O_v^×)^{p^n} has index p^n, and the quotient is taken only at the places v ∈ Q. So π_0 = RCl^+(Q)/⟨image of ∏(k_v^×)^{p^n}⟩, which sits in 0 → Δ_Q/(image of units) → π_0 → Cl^+(F) → 0. The printed text says instead that π_0 is the maximal exponent-p^n quotient, and writes H^0 = Z_p[RCl(Q)/p^n].

2. Defences I tried.
(a) Reading "exponent p^n" as "inertia of exponent p^n". This would make the words true, but the grammar does not support it: "maximal quotient of G" needs a qualifier, and the displayed "RCl(Q)/p^n" can only mean G/p^nG.
(b) Localising at m. This removes the prime-to-p part, so it answers the candidate's example with h=3, p=5 only up to localisation.
(c) Taking n large. This answers the objection "Cl_p has exponent > p^n".
Neither (b) nor (c) saves the statement. The Taylor–Wiles condition in §8.2 itself forces RCl_p(Q) → Cl_p to be non-split, and then the p-parts differ as well.

Explicit example, with every hypothesis of §8.2 satisfied:
- F = Q(√−23), h = 3, p = 3, n = 1. ζ_3 ∉ F and ℓ_0 = 0.
- The dual Selmer group is H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_3) ≅ Cl[3], spanned by α = (3+√−23)/2, where 𝔭_2^3 = (α) (norm 8).
- Take Q = {v}, v | 13. Then N(v) = 13 ≡ 1 mod 3, and α ≡ 10 mod v is not a cube (computed: 10^4 ≢ 1 mod 13). So v is exactly the kind of Taylor–Wiles prime §8.2 asks for.
- The sequence ±1 → k_v^× → RCl(v) → Cl → 0 gives |RCl(v)| = 12·3/2 = 18.
- The cube of a lift of [𝔭_2] is the image of α, which generates (k_v^×/±1)_3. So RCl(v)_3 ≅ Z/9.
- U_Q contains (k_v^×)^3, which has order 4 and trivial 3-part, and its image in k_v^×/±1 has order 2. So π_0(X_Q) ≅ Z/9: X_Q has 9 components.
- Therefore H^0(X_Q, Z_3) = H^0_m = Z_3[Z/9]. The printed formula gives Z_3[RCl(v)/3] = Z_3[Z/3].
- On the Galois side, R_Q = Z_3[Z/9], which matches the correct answer, not the printed one.
The same failure occurs for every n: with Cl_p = Z/p and a Taylor–Wiles prime, π_0⊗Z_p = Z/p^{n+1} while RCl(Q)/p^n = Z/p^n. With Q = ∅ the printed formula does not even make sense, since n plays no role there. Note also that Remark 5.11 (p. 381) says this non-splitting happens.

3. Consequences. §8.2 is an explicitly heuristic, "somewhat circular" illustration. Remark 5.12 cites it only as "some indication". No lemma, theorem or proof uses RCl(Q)/p^n: the only other occurrence is [π_v] ∈ RCl(Q) on the next line. The section's final conclusion, R^unr ≃ Z_p[Cl(O_F)⊗Z_p], is stated correctly and agrees with the correct π_0 (for Q = ∅, π_0 = Cl^+ and p is odd), not with the printed formula. So the mistake affects nothing.

4. Classification. This is a false mathematical claim rather than a typographic slip, so it is an error; calling it a misprint would be a borderline reading. The candidate's own counterexamples are valid as unlocalised statements. The example above shows the statement fails even after localisation and even for large n.

issues.printed: p. 404: "primes which exactly annihilate the dual Selmer group, which is H^1_{L*}(F, μ_p) = H^1_fppf(F, μ_p). This group sits inside H^1(F, μ_p) = F^×/F^{×p}, by Hilbert's Theorem 90 in the classical version."
issues.correction: H^1_{L*}(F, μ_p) = H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p).
issues.reason: Over the field F of characteristic 0, μ_p is étale. So H^1_fppf(F, μ_p) = H^1(F, μ_p) = F^×/F^{×p}, which is infinite and is the whole group, not something that "sits inside" it. The dual Selmer group is cut out by the conditions L*_v. At finite v∤p these are the unramified (unit) classes, and at v|p they are the annihilator of the unramified classes, i.e. O_v^×/O_v^{×p}, the finite flat classes. This is {x ∈ F^×/F^{×p} : v(x) ≡ 0 mod p for all v}, which equals H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p). The paper itself says this on p. 402: "So we are interested in H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p), which sits in the exact sequence 0 → O_F^×/O_F^{×p} → H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p) → Cl(F)[p] → 0". So O_F was meant, and the slip is clear from context.

issues.locator: §8.4 "The invariant l_0", published p. 406 (PDF p. 110): the paragraph defining "odd" and the two displays that follow, ending with equation (1). arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2, §8.4, pp. 80–81) has word-for-word the same text. arXiv v1 has no GL(n)/§8 material. Prop. 8.5(4) (p. 410) uses the result through "The last property then follows from Proposition 8.4, equation (1)…" (p. 411).
issues.printed: Let V be a representation of G_F of dimension n over a field of characteristic different from 2, and assume that the action of G_{F_v} is *odd* for each v|∞. Explicitly, this is the trivial condition for complex places, and for real places v|∞ says that the action of complex conjugation c_v ∈ G_{F_v} satisfies Trace(c_v) ∈ {−1, 0, 1}. Then, via an elementary calculation, one has: Σ_{v|∞} dim H^0(F_v, ad^0(V)) = { r_1((n^2+1)/2 − 1) + r_2(n^2 − 1), n odd; r_1(n^2/2 − 1) + r_2(n^2 − 1), n even. } Thus, in both cases we see that: Σ_{v|∞} dim H^0(F_v, ad^0(V)) = [F : Q] n(n−1)/2 + l_0.   (1)
issues.correction: Change "satisfies Trace(c_v) ∈ {−1, 0, 1}" to "has ±1-eigenspaces whose dimensions differ by at most 1". This is equivalent to Trace(c_v) ∈ {−1,0,1} only in characteristic 0 or in characteristic ℓ > n+1 (n even), resp. ℓ > n (n odd). Alternatively, keep the trace criterion and restrict V to those characteristics. Under the §8.5 standing assumption p > n, the only bad case is n even with p = n+1. Optionally, the proof of Prop. 8.5(4) can cite the inequality Σ_{v|∞} h^0(F_v, ad^0 V) ≥ [F:Q]n(n−1)/2 + l_0, which holds for every V with no parity hypothesis, in place of equation (1).
issues.reason:
I rendered PDF p. 110 and transcribed the text as above. Setup: c_v^2 = 1 and char ≠ 2, so c_v is diagonalisable with eigenspace dimensions a, b (a + b = n). Its centraliser in ad has dimension a^2 + b^2 and contains elements of trace 1. Hence dim H^0(F_v, ad^0 V) = a^2 + b^2 − 1 = (n^2 + d^2)/2 − 1, where d = a − b. The printed formula is the case |d| ≤ 1. In characteristic ℓ, however, Trace(c_v) = d mod ℓ.

Counterexample (within the printed hypotheses): F = Q, n = 2, coefficient field F_3, V with c acting trivially. Then Trace(c) = 2 = −1 in F_3, so V counts as "odd". But dim H^0(R, ad^0 V) = dim ad^0 = 3, while the display gives r_1(n^2/2 − 1) = 1. Also l_0 = r_1(n−2)/2 = 0, so the right side of (1) is 1·1 + 0 = 1 ≠ 3.

A Python sweep over n ≤ 14 and primes ℓ < 40 confirms that the trace criterion fails exactly when ℓ ≤ n + 1 (n even) or ℓ ≤ n (n odd). With p > n, the failures are (n, p) = (2,3), (4,5), (6,7), (10,11), (12,13), … The case matters for the paper: §8.5 imposes "r̄|_{G_v} is odd" on r̄ : G_F → GL_n(k) with p > n. For example, n = 4, p = 5, r̄(c_v) = ±I has trace ±4 ≡ ∓1 mod 5. It is also compatible with the determinant, since ε^{6}(c_v) = 1. So r̄ meets the printed hypothesis, but (1) fails for it (15 versus 7 per real place).

How far it reaches: Theorem 5.16(5) defines oddness for O-valued (characteristic-0) representations, where the trace criterion is correct. Its residual r̄ then has the same eigenspace dimensions, so the main theorems are unaffected. The proof of Prop. 8.5(4) invokes (1), but it only needs Σ h^0 ≥ [F:Q]n(n−1)/2 + l_0. That inequality holds for every involution, since (n^2 + d^2)/2 − 1 is smallest at |d| ≤ 1. A larger h^0 only lowers the variable count, and a quotient of a power series ring in fewer variables is a quotient of one in more. So Prop. 8.5(4) remains true. The false statement is confined to the displayed formula and equation (1) (and the "Explicitly…" gloss) in small characteristic. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Suppose c_v has ±1-eigenspaces of dimensions a and b, with a + b = n. Then dim H^0(F_v, ad^0 V) = a² + b² − 1 in any characteristic other than 2, and Trace(c_v) = a − b computed in the field. In characteristic ℓ the trace condition only forces a − b ≡ −1, 0, 1 (mod ℓ).

Counterexample: take F = Q, n = 2, ℓ = 3 and V trivial, so c = I. Then Trace = 2 = −1 in F_3, so V is "odd" as printed. But Σ dim H^0 = 3, while the display gives r_1(n²/2 − 1) = 1, and (1) gives [F:Q]·1 + l_0 = 1 + 0 = 1.

This also happens inside §8.5's setting: n = 4, p = 5, F = Q, r̄(c) = ±I. The trace is ±4 = ∓1 in F_5, and det = 1 = ε(c)^6 matches ξ = ε^6. Here Σ h^0 = 15, but (1) gives 7.

A brute-force check over n ≤ 12 and primes ℓ < 40 shows the trace criterion fails exactly when ℓ ≤ n+1 (n even) or ℓ ≤ n (n odd). So the candidate's description is right.

Defence attempted:
- The only earlier definition of "odd" (p. 383) is for O-valued representations. There the trace is the integer a − b, and the criterion is correct.
- For a field of characteristic ℓ, the "Explicitly…" sentence is the only definition given. The text explicitly allows any characteristic other than 2, so the literal claim is false. Reading "Trace" as the integer a − b is not supported by the text.

Consequences (checked on the page images):
- Equation (1) is used only in the proof of Prop. 8.5(4). The variable count there is h^1_{L,T} + Σ_T h^0(ad) − h^0(ad) = q + |T| − 1 − Σ_{v|∞} h^0(ad^0 r̄), using Prop. 8.4.
- For every V, a² + b² ≥ its value when |a − b| ≤ 1. So Σ_{v|∞} h^0(F_v, ad^0 V) ≥ [F:Q]n(n−1)/2 + l_0 always, and the true count is at most the stated g.
- A quotient of R_loc⟦x_1..x_m⟧ with m ≤ g is also a quotient of R_loc⟦x_1..x_g⟧. So Prop. 8.5(4) is true as stated, with or without oddness.
- Thm 9.19 uses Prop. 8.5 only to choose surjections R^i_∞ = R_loc⟦x_1..x_g⟧ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}}. Their dimensions come from Lemma 8.2, so it is unaffected.
- Thm 5.16(5) assumes the O-valued r is odd, which forces r̄ to have balanced eigenspaces (p odd), so equation (1) holds there.

So the reach is limited to the display and equation (1) themselves. No numbered statement is affected. The mathematics is right with the intended notion of "odd", and the correction above is the minimal fix.

issues.reason:
Printed text confirmed from the page images. The cited sources do not give flatness. [11] is Taylor, IHES 108. I checked Prop. 3.1 in the author copy (…/agents/k8check/twugkfin.txt). It says only: Spec R^loc/I^χ is irreducible, its generic point has characteristic 0, and it has dimension n^2+1; for R^loc/I^{(1,…,1)}, all components have dimension n^2+1 and characteristic-0 generic points. Its proof shows only (R^loc/I^χ)_red is O-flat. Only the separate Steinberg quotient is "by definition flat over O". [76, Lemma 3.3] is BLGHT, CY II (…/k8check/cy2fin.txt). Its part 3 assumes O-flat inputs, and parts 5 and 7 are about minimal primes.

The statement is also false. Take n ≥ 2, p > n, v ∈ R with r̄|G_v trivial and q = N(v) ≡ 1 mod p; this is the intended Ihara-avoidance setting. Let Φ = ρ(φ_v) and Σ = ρ(σ_v) be the universal matrices over R^1_v, with φσφ^{-1} = σ^q in the tame quotient. Put N = log Σ; this is fine since (Σ−1)^n = 0 by Cayley–Hamilton and n < p. Then ΦNΦ^{-1} = qN. Taking traces, tr(ΦN) = q·tr(ΦN), so (q−1)·tr(ΦN) = 0. For n = 2 simply N = Σ−1, S² = 0 and Σ^q = 1+qS.

Now tr(ΦN) ≠ 0. Take B = O⟦u⟧[Y]/(Y², (q−1)Y) with c = ξ(φ_v) ≡ 1. Set Φ = diag(1+u, c/(1+u), 1, …) and Σ = diag(1+Y, 1−Y, 1, …), with σ_v^a ↦ diag(1+aY, 1−aY, …). This is a valid framed lift of determinant ξ. It reduces to 1, commutes, and Σ^q = Σ because (q−1)Y = 0. Every inertia element has characteristic polynomial (X−1)^2 − a²Y² = (X−1)^2 (times (X−1)^{n−2}). So there is a map R^1_v → B, and tr(ΦN) maps to ((1+u) − c/(1+u))·Y ≠ 0. This is because B ⊃ (O/(q−1))⟦u⟧·Y and the u-coefficient 1+c ≡ 2 is a unit.

So R^1_v has non-zero p-power torsion. The same holds for R^1_loc, via R^1_v → R^1_loc → B ⊗_O O' using O'-points of the other factors. Hence Lemma 8.2(1) fails for R^1_loc. For comparison, at points where Φ is regular semisimple the local ring is smooth ⊗ O[Y]/(Y², (q−1)Y), the same phenomenon.

The candidate is therefore genuine, and stronger than a gap: the claim is false. Downstream, only characteristic-0 minimal primes are used, so Theorem 9.19 stands after the repair. The cited sources give only characteristic-0 generic points, never p-torsion-freeness. I checked this in the texts. Taylor [11, Prop. 3.1] states: for distinct χ, Spec R^loc_v/I^χ is irreducible with generic point of characteristic zero; for (1,…,1), all components have dimension n^2+1 with characteristic-zero generic points. Its proof shows only that "(R^loc_v/I^χ)_red is flat over O". The only ring that is O-flat "by definition" is the separately saturated Steinberg quotient. BLGHT [76, Lemma 3.3](3) proves A⊗̂B is O-flat only for O-flat inputs. BLGHT's own use of the lemma for Taylor's ring R^{2T}_{χ,∞} derives irreducibility, dimensions and characteristic-0 generic points, never flatness. Taylor's main argument (p. 36) also asserts only these.

The claim is in fact false for R^1_loc. Take r̄|G_v trivial and q = N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. This is exactly the setting of [11, §3], so the citation applies, and N(v) ≡ 1 mod p is already required for v ∈ R. Take n = 2 and write Φ = ρ(φ_v), Σ = 1 + S = ρ(σ_v). The condition char Σ = (X−1)^2 gives tr S = det S = 0, so S^2 = 0 by Cayley–Hamilton and Σ^q = 1 + qS. The tame relation ΦΣΦ^{-1} = Σ^q then gives ΦS = qSΦ. Taking traces, (1−q)·tr(ΦS) = 0 in R_v^1, where 1−q = p^s·unit with s ≥ 1.

Now tr(ΦS) ≠ 0 in R_v^1. The lift Φ = diag(1+X, δ/(1+X)) (δ = ξ(φ_v)) and Σ = diag(1+α, 1−α), valued in A = O⟦X⟧[α]/(α^2, (q−1)α), is a valid point of R_v^1:
- Σ^q = Σ, since (q−1)α = 0;
- every inertia element acts by diag(1+mα, 1−mα), which has characteristic polynomial (X−1)^2 and determinant 1;
- det Φ = δ.
Under this point, tr(ΦS) maps to α((1+X) − δ/(1+X)). That is non-zero in (O/(q−1))⟦X⟧·α, and even modulo ϖ.

For general n with p > n, the same argument works with N = log Σ (so ΦN = qNΦ) and Σ = diag(1+α, 1−α, 1, …, 1). Since the other factors have O'-points, the p-torsion survives in R^1_loc = (⊗̂R_w)⊗̂(⊗̂R_v^1) and in R^1_∞. So (1) fails for R^1_loc whenever R ≠ ∅ in the cited setting, and even more so in the non-trivial cases raised in X-K8-12.

Defence attempt: read R_v^1 as the O-flat closure. That fails too. The torsion element is non-zero mod ϖ, so the flat closure's special fibre is a proper quotient of R_v^1/ϖ = R_v^χ/ϖ, and Noetherian rings are Hopfian, so (2) would then fail. §8.5.2 also makes the rings represent CHT-style deformation problems, which is the naive, non-saturated reading. For comparison, for n = 2 and trivial r̄ I checked that R_v^χ is O-flat: it is O⟦α,β,γ,u,y,z⟧ modulo the 2×2 minors and α^2+βγ−e, a hypersurface in an O-flat determinantal CM ring. So the defect is specific to R^1.

Consequences: Prop. 6.6 and Thm 6.3 need only dim R_∞ = 1+q+j−l_0, not torsion-freeness. The R^1 step (p. 428) explicitly uses only "all such primes have characteristic 0" plus [11, Lemma 2.2(2)]. The only place torsion-freeness enters is Theorem 6.4 for R^2_∞. There [11, Lemma 2.3] with Theorem 6.3(iii) and Lemma 8.2(3) gives near-faithfulness directly; the last paragraph of Theorem 6.4's proof is exactly this. So Theorem 9.19 survives with a local rerouting. Lemma 8.2(1) itself, a stated result, is false for R^1_loc. p-torsion-freeness of R^χ_loc for n ≥ 3 is unverified but not needed.

issues.reason:
I rendered PDF p. 111 and the printed text matches the candidate. Nothing in the Notation section restricts 'character' to finite order.

Counterexample: take n = 2 and p ≥ 3, and let v ∈ R. R may contain any prime with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, so it can be nonempty. Since v ∤ p, the maximal pro-p quotient of I_v is Z_p(1), and Frobenius acts on it by t ↦ t^{q_v}. Let t be a generator. Define the continuous character χ_1 : I_v → Z_p(1) → 1 + pZ_p by t ↦ 1 + p, and set χ_2 = χ_1^{-1}. These are distinct characters with trivial product, so they are admissible as printed.

Now take a Q̄_p-point ρ of R_v^{χ_v}, choose σ ∈ I_v mapping to t, and let φ be a Frobenius lift. Then φσφ^{-1} ∈ I_v, and ρ(φσφ^{-1}) is conjugate to ρ(σ), so the two have the same characteristic polynomial. The defining condition then forces {x, x^{-1}} = {x^{c}, x^{-c}}, where x = 1 + p and c = q_v^{±1}, depending on which way Frobenius is normalized. But x has infinite order in Z_p^×, so this needs c = ±1, which is impossible because q_v ≥ 2. As a sanity check with p = 3 and q_v = 7: 4^7 = 16384 is neither 4 nor 4^{-1}. So R_v^{χ_v}[1/p] = 0.

On the other hand, R_v^{χ_v} is not zero. Since r̄ is at worst unipotently ramified at v and det r̄ = ξ̄, r̄|_{G_v} is a k-point: its characteristic polynomial (X−1)^2 equals ∏(X − χ̄_i). Hence p^N R_v^{χ_v} = 0 for some N, with R_v^{χ_v} ≠ 0. The completed tensor product R^χ_loc is then killed by p^N and still surjects onto k. So it is nonzero and not p-torsion free, and Lemma 8.2(1) is false for this admissible choice.

The alternative reading, where R_v^{χ_v} is the maximal O-flat quotient, fails too. Then R_v^{χ_v} = 0, so R^χ_loc = 0, which breaks the dimension claim in (1) and also (2), because R^1_loc/ϖ ≠ 0.

Finite order is not enough on its own either. If p^2 ∤ q_v − 1, an order-p^2 character of I_v fails in the same way. The Frobenius-invariance supplied by ψ ∘ Art^{-1} is exactly what is missing.

The proof's citation, [11, Prop. 3.1] (Taylor), concerns characters of the residue field (via Art) and does not cover the printed generality. The main theorems are unaffected, since §9 only uses characters of k_v^× via Art (p. 413: 'ψ_v = χ_v'). But Lemma 8.2 as stated is false under the printed hypothesis. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The literal statement is false.

1. **Only certain characters of I_v can occur for a characteristic-zero lift.**
   - A continuous χ : I_v → 1 + m_O factors through the pro-p quotient Z_p(1) of tame inertia (v ∤ p). Write u_i = χ_{v,i}(t) for a generator t.
   - For a lift ρ over a finite extension of Q_p, ρ(φtφ^{-1}) = ρ(t^{q_v}) is conjugate to ρ(t). So the multiset {u_i^{q_v}} must equal {u_i}.
   - Hence some power u_i^{q_v^m − 1} = 1, so each u_i is a root of unity. For n = 2 and χ_2 = χ_1^{-1}, the condition forces u^{q_v − 1} = 1, i.e. χ factors through the p-part of k_v^×.
   - Counterexample: I_v ↠ Z_p(1) ≅ Z_p → 1 + pZ_p, t ↦ (1+p)^t, of infinite order. It is continuous, into 1 + m_O, distinct from its inverse, and the product is trivial, so it meets every printed condition.
   - Finite order is not enough either. With p = 3 and q_v = 7, the order-9 characters satisfy all printed conditions but are not Frobenius-stable. A script (work/agents/lensB-K8-11/chk.py) confirms the stable ones are exactly those with a(q_v − 1) ≡ 0 mod N.

2. **Lemma 8.2 then fails.** For such χ_v, R_v^{χ_v} has no Q̄_p-points, so R_v^{χ_v}[1/p] = 0 and the ring is killed by some p^N. It is still non-zero, because r̄|_{G_v} is a k-point: its inertia has characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^n, and ∏(X − χ_{v,i}(σ)) ≡ (X − 1)^n mod m_O. So R^χ_loc is non-zero and p-power torsion, and Lemma 8.2(1) ("p-torsion free and equidimensional of dimension …") fails. If R^χ_v is instead defined as the p-torsion-free closure of its Q̄_p-points, it is 0, and parts (1) and (2) fail anyway.

**Defence considered.** The notation section (p. 297) defines I_v ⊂ G_v as the full inertia group. So "characters of I_v" cannot faithfully be read as characters of the inertia of G_v^{ab}. The intended meaning can be recovered, but only from elsewhere:
- the proof of Lemma 8.2 cites [76, Lemma 3.3] and [11, Prop. 3.1], which are stated for characters of O_K^× via Art;
- §9.1 fixes ψ_v on (k_v^×)^n/(k_v^×);
- Conjecture B(3) uses ψ_{v,i}(Art_v^{-1}(σ)), and p. 415 identifies "ψ_v = χ_v".

So the defence fails for the statement as printed, but it shows the intended mathematics is correct.

**What depends on it.**
- Lemma 8.2 is used in Proposition 8.4/8.5 (R^χ_{S_Q}-type rings over R^χ_loc) and in the proof of Theorem 9.19 (pp. 425–427). There R^2_∞ = R^χ_loc⟦x_1..x_g⟧ is asserted p-torsion free, equidimensional and irreducible "by Lemma 8.2", and R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ.
- Theorem 9.19 also uses "the local system associated to our choice of characters χ = (χ_v)", which only makes sense for characters of Iw(v)/Iw_1(v) ≅ (k_v^×)^n/k_v^×. So the χ_v actually used are of the corrected form.

**Classification.** Main results unaffected; Lemma 8.2 needs a corrected hypothesis. I record this as an error in the hypothesis of a stated result. A reviewer could reasonably downgrade it to misprint/nothing, since §9 fixes the intended meaning.

**Side remark, not part of this candidate.** [11, Prop. 3.1] and Allen et al. §6.2.15 assume r̄|_{G_v} is trivial, while §8.5 only assumes unipotent ramification with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p.

So (1) should be weakened to that unless flatness is proved separately. This weaker form is all that the proofs of Theorem 6.4 and Theorem 9.19 actually use. Because §8.5 requires R to contain every prime where r̄ ramifies, the triviality hypothesis cannot simply be added. Theorem 9.19/5.16 must instead do one of two things: (a) split R into primes where r̄|G_v is trivial, which get Taylor's R^1/R^χ, and the remaining primes, which get minimal or fixed-type local conditions whose rings are shown to be suitable (for example formally smooth when r̄|I_v is regular unipotent); or (b) first make r̄|G_v trivial at the primes of R by a solvable base change. issues.correction: Minimal fix: "For example, if det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2} (as under Theorem 5.16(7)), we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}." General choice: ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}·[χ̄], where χ̄ := det(r̄)·ε̄^{−n(n−1)/2} and [·] is the Teichmüller lift into W(k)^× ⊂ O^×. This works because χ̄ is unramified at every finite place. At v∤p, unipotent ramification makes det(r̄)|_{I_v} = 1. So [χ̄] is unramified at all finite places, and ξ lifts det(r̄) and meets both inertia conditions. The correction proposed in the candidate is therefore correct.

I rendered p. 407 and read the text there; it matches arXiv v2 exactly. The §8.5 hypotheses on r̄ are: absolutely irreducible; Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1] at v|p; at worst unipotent ramification at v∤p, with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p where r̄ ramifies; odd at the real places. None of these fixes det(r̄). They only force det(r̄)|_{I_v} to be ε̄^{n(n−1)/2} at v|p and trivial at v∤p. So det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}·χ̄, where χ̄ is unramified at every finite place, and χ̄ need not be trivial.

The hypotheses are unchanged by twisting with an everywhere-unramified character η: G_F → k^× (whose order is automatically prime to p):
- Fontaine–Laffaille-ness and the weights survive an unramified twist.
- r̄|_{I_v} is unchanged, so unipotence holds and the set of ramified primes is the same.
- At a real place, Trace(c_v) only changes by the sign η(c_v) = ±1, so it stays in {−1,0,1}.
- Absolute irreducibility is preserved.
But det(r̄⊗η) = det(r̄)·η^n.

Concrete instance: F = Q(√−47) (class number 5), n = 2, p = 3, r̄ = E[3]|_{G_F} with E = 11a1.
- 3 splits in F, so it is unramified.
- E has good reduction at 3, which gives Fontaine–Laffaille weights [0,1] ⊂ [0,p−2].
- E has split multiplicative reduction at 11 with ord_11(Δ) = 5, so r̄ is unipotently ramified at 11. Also 11 is inert in F (since (−47/11) = −1), so N(v) = 121 ≡ 1 mod 3.
- r̄ is irreducible: 2 splits in F, and Frob_2 has characteristic polynomial X²−X−1, which is irreducible mod 3. (Absolute irreducibility follows from Serre's result that ρ_ℓ is surjective for 11a1 when ℓ ≠ 5. I did not recheck that here.)
- det r̄ = ω, the mod-3 cyclotomic character.
Now twist by a character η of order 5 of the class group, with values in F_81. Then r̄⊗η satisfies every §8.5 hypothesis, and det = ω·η² ≠ ω. So ξ = ε does not reduce to det(r̄⊗η), and the "for example" fails.

I call this an error with no downstream effect. A suitable ξ always exists (the Teichmüller-twisted choice above). The paper only applies §8.5 when det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}: Theorem 5.16(7) assumes det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2}, and §9.5 assumes r̄ ≅ r̄_m for PGL_n cohomology. So in that setting the example is valid and the results are untouched. The slip is the missing hypothesis in a general setup that deliberately allows any ξ lifting det(r̄). I looked for a defence and found none that covers §8.5 as stated. §8.5 assumes only: absolute irreducibility, Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0..n−1] at v|p, at most unipotent ramification (with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p if ramified) at v∤p, and oddness at real places. Nothing in §8 (§§8.1–8.4 included) fixes det(r̄). Those hypotheses force only that χ̄ = det(r̄)ε̄^{−n(n−1)/2} is unramified at every finite place, and such a χ̄ can be nontrivial when F has nontrivial narrow class group.

Explicit failure: take any r̄ satisfying §8.5 and an everywhere-unramified character η: G_F → k^× with η^n ≠ 1 (order necessarily prime to p). Then r̄⊗η still satisfies every §8.5 hypothesis. The unramified twist keeps it Fontaine–Laffaille with the same weights and keeps the ramification unipotent on the same primes. Trace(c_v) only changes sign, so it stays in {−1,0,1}. Irreducibility is kept. But det(r̄⊗η) = det(r̄)·η^n, so det(r̄) and det(r̄⊗η) cannot both equal ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}. For n odd, a character that is unramified at all finite places but nontrivial at a real place already works. The claim does hold automatically over F = Q, where such a χ̄ must be trivial, but the paper allows an arbitrary number field F.

So "we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}" is false as stated: that ξ meets both inertia conditions but need not lift det(r̄).

Why it is harmless: §8.5.1 and §8.5.2 (R_v, R_v^1, R_v^{χ_v}, the data S_Q) and Conjecture B / Theorem 9.19 all use only "a fixed ξ with the listed properties", never the specific example. The only route to a stated result is Theorem 5.16 ("follows immediately from Theorem 9.19"). There hypothesis (7) says det(r) = ε^{n(n−1)/2}, so det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2} and the example choice is valid. The PGL(n) automorphic side (§9, G = Res PGL(n)) also forces the determinant of r_m to be a fixed cyclotomic power, so in the application ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2} is the choice actually needed.

In short, this is an illustrative remark with a missing hypothesis. It is false in the generality of §8.5, but the mathematics is right as intended and in every place it is used.

Let σ be a generator there. Then ρ(σ) = diag((1+εa)·1_{s}, (1+εb)·1_{ψ}) with (n−1)a + b = 0, because det = ξ is unramified at v. Since ρ(σ) is block-scalar it commutes with ρ(Frob_v), so the relation Frob σ Frob^{-1} = σ^q forces (q−1)a = 0 in k.

Case q ≢ 1 mod p: then a = b = 0, so every lift of type D_v is unramified. Conversely every unramified lift is of type D_v, because the 1-dimensional generalized eigenspace lifts by Hensel's lemma. Hence L_v = H^1_ur(G_v, ad^0 r̄), and for the procyclic quotient G_v/I_v, dim H^1_ur = h^0. So the difference is 0, not 1. Check with n = 2: let Frobenius have eigenvalues α ≠ β and suppose q ≢ 1 mod p. Then h^0 = 1. Also Hom(G_v, k) = Hom(F_v^×, k) has no ramified part, because k_v^× ⊗ F_p = 0. So L_v = H^1_ur has dimension 1 and the difference is 0.

Case q ≡ 1 mod p: the framed tangent space with fixed determinant has dimension (n^2−1) + 1 = n^2. It equals dim L_v + (n^2 − 1 − h^0), so dim L_v − h^0 = 1, as the paper claims.

Defence considered: the sentence "Q will consist of Taylor–Wiles primes" and the heuristic of §8.2, where a Taylor–Wiles prime has N(v) ≡ 1 mod p^n, show what the authors meant. Against this, the formal hypotheses in §8.5.1 ("Let Q denote a finite set of primes ... disjoint from R ∪ S_p"; "For each v ∈ Q, we assume that: •...") leave the congruence out. Prop. 8.5 then lists "(3) N_{F/Q}(v) ≡ 1 mod p^N" as a separate property, so the paper itself does not treat the congruence as automatic. The analogous passages in §3 and §5 do state "Suppose that x ≡ 1 mod p". So the printed claim is a genuinely missing hypothesis. The meaning is recoverable from context, which puts it on the border between error and misprint.

Consequences: Prop. 8.4 is stated for general Q and keeps the term Σ_{v∈Q}(dim L_v − h^0) unevaluated, so it does not use the claim. The only use is the last line of the proof of Prop. 8.5: "the fact that dim_k L_v − h^0(G_v, ad^0 r̄) = 1 if v ∈ Q". There Q satisfies (3), N(v) ≡ 1 mod p^N, so the equality holds. The exact sequence with the map φ ↦ tr(e_v φ(Frob_v)) in the same proof also relies on (3). The later uses (§9.4.2, §10, the condition "r_m|G_v is of type D_v") involve only Taylor–Wiles sets Q_N from Prop. 8.5. No stated result is affected.

The proof of Prop. 8.5, p. 411, has "0 → H^1_{ℒ(Q)^⊥,T}(G_F, ad^0 r̄(1)) → H^1_{ℒ^⊥,T}(G_F, ad^0 r̄(1)) → ⊕_{v∈Q} k".

issues.reason: Only the ℒ(Q)-groups are defined (p. 409). Prop. 8.4 is about R^{□_T}_{𝒮_Q}, and its formula (2) contains Σ_{v∈Q}(dim_k L_v − h^0(G_v, ad^0 r̄)), which is the Euler-characteristic contribution of the Selmer conditions L_v at v ∈ Q. With the Q = ∅ group (classes over G_{F,S}) formula (2) would be false for Q ≠ ∅. The paper itself uses the bare subscript for the Q = ∅ group: Prop. 8.5 asks for q ≥ h^1_{ℒ^⊥,T}, and its proof puts H^1_{ℒ(Q)^⊥,T} and H^1_{ℒ^⊥,T} side by side in one exact sequence. That proof then applies Prop. 8.4 with the Q-groups (using H^1_{ℒ(Q)^⊥,T} = 0 and dim_k L_v − h^0 = 1 for v ∈ Q) to get Prop. 8.5(4). So the intended reading is clear and the argument goes through with it. It is a dropped '(Q)', not a bracket error.
