issues.locator: §9.2, definition of T(g), p. 412 (same in v2) (published version)
issues.printed: H_{•,ψ}(Y(K), O) → H_{•,ψ}(Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K_Q), O) → H_{•,ψ}(Y(K ∩ g^{−1}Kg), O) → H_{•,ψ}(Y(K), O),   [displayed in §9.2 'Hecke operators', bottom of p. 412 (PDF p. 116), after 'For K ⊂ G(A^∞) a compact open subgroup of the form K_Q or L_Q, the Hecke operator T(g) is defined on the homology modules H_{•,ψ}(Y(K), O) by considering the composition:'; the sentence continuing on p. 413 reads: 'the first map coming from the corestriction map, the second coming from the map Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K, O) → Y(K ∩ g^{−1}Kg, O) induced by right multiplication by g on G(A)']
issues.correction: In the second term, read H_{•,ψ}(Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K), O) instead of H_{•,ψ}(Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K_Q), O). This matches the next sentence on p. 413 ('Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K, O) → Y(K ∩ g^{−1}Kg, O)') and the same definition in §5.2.2, p. 373, which prints H_•(Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K), O). arXiv v2 (§9.0.2) has the same misprint, 'Y(gKg−1 ∩ KQ)'.
issues.reason: I rendered p. 412 at 300 dpi. The printed subscript really is K_Q, but the very next sentence (p. 413) uses gKg^{−1} ∩ K, and so does §5.2.2 (p. 373, checked on the page image). The paper allows K = K_Q or K = L_Q. When K = K_Q the two groups are the same. When K = L_Q, the corestriction H(Y(K)) → H(Y(K')) only makes sense if K' ⊂ K. Also, right multiplication by g sends level H to level g^{−1}Hg. For H = gKg^{−1} ∩ K_Q that level is K ∩ g^{−1}K_Q g, not the printed K ∩ g^{−1}Kg. For the composition to hold together, H has to be gKg^{−1} ∩ K. I checked by hand that the printed group can fail to lie in L_Q. Take v ∈ Q and let g_v be the permutation matrix w that swaps e1 and e2. Take x ∈ L_{Q,v} with x ≡ (a 0 *; 0 b *; 0 0 C) mod π_v, normalised so that b·det C/a^{n−1} ≡ 1. Then wxw^{−1} lies in K_{Q,v}, and the character K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^× takes the value a·det C/b^{n−1} = (a/b)^n on it, which need not be 1. So in general the printed group is not a subgroup of K = L_Q, and the printed diagram does not make sense. This is a genuine inconsistency and not one of the 47 known ⟦ ⟧ bracket errors. It is harmless, though. At places outside Q, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v}. For the diagonal g actually used (g = diag(α,…,α,1,…,1) for T_{α,k} and for the T_α at places in Q in Def. 9.1), conjugating by g leaves the (1,1) entry and the determinant of the lower (n−1)×(n−1) block unchanged. So gL_Qg^{−1} ∩ K_Q already lies in L_Q, and the printed and corrected groups coincide. The candidate's reason is correct in substance, though loosely worded.

issues.printed: p. 412 (PDF p. 116), §9.1, items (2)–(3): "(2) If v ∈ Q, L_{Q,v} ⊂ K_{Q,v} is the normal subgroup with quotient group k_v^×. Explicitly, K_{Q,v} = ( 1 ∗ ; 0 GL_{N−1}(O_v) ) mod π_v, L_{Q,v} = ( 1 ∗ ; 0 SL_{N−1}(O_v) ) mod π_v. (3) If v ∉ S_Q K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v). (4) If v ∈ R, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = the Iwahori Iw(v) subgroup ofPGL_n(O_v) associated to the upper triangular unipotent subgroup." Item (1), on p. 411, reads: "If v ∈ Q, K_{Q,v} is the image in PGL(O_v) of {g ∈ GL_n(O_v) | g stabilizes ℓ mod π_v} where ℓ is a fixed line in k_v^n." The arXiv v2 §9.0.1, p. 85, prints the same text: GL_{N−1}, SL_{N−1}, and "(3) If v ∉ S_Q K_{Q,v} = ...".
issues.correction: In (2), write GL_{n−1}(O_v) and SL_{n−1}(O_v) instead of GL_{N−1} and SL_{N−1}. In (3), write "If v ∉ Q ∪ R, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v)". Equivalently, keep "v ∉ S_Q" and add "if v | p, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v)" (hyperspecial, since p is unramified in F). The comma after S_Q is also missing.
issues.reason: I checked the rendered pages 411–412 (PDF pp. 115–116) and v2 p. 85. (a) The matrices are n×n. Item (1) takes g ∈ GL_n(O_v) and K_{Q,v} ⊂ PGL_n(O_v). A line-stabilizer mod π_v is of the form (a ∗; 0 D) with D ∈ GL_{n−1}(k_v), and dividing by the scalar a normalizes the corner entry to 1 in PGL. The map (a ∗; 0 D) ↦ det D / a^{n−1} is well defined modulo scalars and maps onto k_v^×. Its kernel is the (1 ∗; 0 SL_{n−1}) form, which matches "quotient group k_v^×". No N is defined at this point in §9. The letter N appears later only as the Taylor–Wiles index (Q_N, Δ_N = (Z/p^N Z)^q) and in norms N(x). So GL_{N−1} and SL_{N−1} are misprints for GL_{n−1} and SL_{n−1}. (b) §9 opens with "Let S = S_p ∪ R and S_Q = S ∪ Q be as in Sect. 8", and §8.5 defines S = S_p ∪ R and S_Q = S ∪ Q. Items (1)–(2) cover v ∈ Q, (3) covers v ∉ S_Q and (4) covers v ∈ R, so K_{Q,v} and L_{Q,v} are never defined for v | p. The authors' own GL_2 version in §5 lists v | p separately: "(3) If v is not in S(ρ) ∪ {v| p} ∪ Q, then K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_2(O_v). (4) If v| p, then ...". The setting fixes the intended level at p as hyperspecial PGL_n(O_v): p > n unramified in F, trivial coefficients, and Conjecture B(1) predicting Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1] at v | p. The proposed correction is therefore right. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It affects nothing: nothing later in §9 refers back to the level at p or uses N in this role, and all subsequent statements (Conjecture B, the Hecke algebra definitions, the patching argument) are correct under the evident intended definition. The (3) part is strictly an omission (gap-like) rather than a typo, but it is fixed trivially and unambiguously.

issues.printed: (3) If v ∉ S_Q K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v).   [context, p. 411: "Let S = S_p ∪ R and S_Q = S ∪ Q be as in Sect. 8." (1),(2) are "If v ∈ Q, ..."; (4) is "If v ∈ R, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = the Iwahori Iw(v) subgroup ofPGL_n(O_v) associated to the upper triangular unipotent subgroup."]
issues.correction: "(3) If v ∉ R ∪ Q, then K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v)." Equivalently, keep (3) and add "If v | p, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v)." This is the hyperspecial level at p, which makes sense because p is unramified in F. Only the index set changes (and a missing comma is added), so this is the minimal fix. Both readers' corrections (X-K9-3, C-K8-4) agree with this. I record it as a misprint, not the "gap" in C-K8-4: no proof step is missing, the definition just leaves out one case, and the intended value is clear from context.
issues.reason:
Sect. 8.5 (p. 409) defines S_p as the set of primes of F above p, R as disjoint from S_p, and Q as disjoint from R ∪ S_p. It sets S = S_p ⊔ R and S_Q = S ⊔ Q, and §9 says this notation carries over. In §9.1, conditions (1) and (2) cover v ∈ Q, (4) covers v ∈ R, and (3) covers v ∉ S_Q. So a prime v | p (v ∈ S_p) falls under none of the four conditions, and K_{Q,v}, L_{Q,v} are never defined there. The definitions of K_Q, L_Q, and therefore of Y = Y(K_∅), Y_0(Q), Y_1(Q), are incomplete as printed.

I searched the rest of §9 (Hecke operators, Conjecture B, Lemma 9.6, §9.4–9.5, Thm 9.16, Thm 9.19) and none of it fixes the level at p. By contrast, §5.2.1(4) on p. 330 does state the level at v | p explicitly for the GL_2 case.

The intended meaning is clear from context:
- p > n and p is unramified in F, so PGL_n(O_v) is hyperspecial.
- Conjecture B(1) and the local rings R_v are Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0, …, n−1], i.e. crystalline of trivial weight, which matches hyperspecial (spherical) level at p.
- The coefficients are trivial (O or O(ψ), with ψ supported on R).

So "v ∉ S_Q" is a slip for "v ∉ R ∪ Q". This is a misprint rather than a gap: it is an incomplete definition, not an unproved step. The minor typography on the same page (the missing comma after S_Q, "GL_{N−1}" in (2), "PGL(O_v)" in (1)) is separate and not part of this candidate. None of this is one of the 47 bracket errors. As printed, a place v | p is covered by none of the four conditions. §8.5 defines R as a finite set of primes "disjoint from S_p" and Q as disjoint from R ∪ S_p, so S_Q = S_p ⊔ R ⊔ Q. Conditions (1) and (2) cover v ∈ Q, (4) covers v ∈ R, and (3) excludes every v ∈ S_Q, including S_p. So the factor K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} at v | p is never specified, yet Y = Y(K_∅), Y_0(Q) and Y_1(Q) all need it.

Defence attempts that fail:
(a) §9 cannot be using a different S_Q. The §9 preamble explicitly takes S_Q = S_p ∪ R ∪ Q from §8, and Definition 9.1 uses "α which are units at primes in S_Q", which excludes the Hecke operators at p. That only makes sense if S_Q contains S_p.
(b) Reading "such that" as allowing any level at p does not rescue the text. Conjecture B(1) asserts that r_m|G_v is Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1] for v | p. At deeper level at p, for example Iwahori, the Hecke algebra would also see semistable, non-crystalline lifts, and (1) would fail. The patching in Theorem 9.19 likewise uses the Fontaine–Laffaille rings R_v of Lemma 8.2 at v | p.
(c) No later passage in §9 fixes the level at p. Lemma 9.6 talks only of "congruence subgroups commensurable with PGL2(O_F)", and §9.5 just uses Y = Y(K_∅).

The intended level (hyperspecial at p) is clear from context:
- Conjecture B(1).
- Theorem 5.16: (1)–(2) crystalline with Hodge–Tate weights 0,…,n−1 and p unramified in F; (8a) "good reduction at all v | p"; (8b) Serre-modular of minimal level N(r̄), which is prime to p.
- The parallel published §5.2.1(3)–(4) and arXiv v1 §4.2.1, which both give the level at v | p explicitly. Presumably the p-clause was lost when that template was rewritten as the S_Q-based (3).

issues.locator: §9.2, Definition 9.1, p. 413, against the construction of T(g) on p. 412 (PDF pp. 116–117). arXiv v2 §9.0.2 and Definition 9.1 (v2 p. 85) have the same text. Not in arXiv v1.
issues.printed: p. 412 (PDF p. 116), §9.2: "We recall the construction of the Hecke operators. Let g ∈ G(A^∞) be an invertible matrix trivial at each place v ∈ R. For K ⊂ G(A^∞) a compact open subgroup of the form K_Q or L_Q, the Hecke operator T(g) is defined on the homology modules H_{•,ψ}(Y(K), 𝒪) by considering the composition: ...". p. 413 (PDF p. 117): "For α ∈ A_F^{∞,×}, we define the Hecke operator T_{α,k} by taking g = diag(α, α, ..., 1, ..., 1) consisting of k copies of α and n − k copies of 1. ... Definition 9.1 Let T^an_{Q,ψ} denote the subring of End ⊕_{k,n} H^k_ψ(Y_1(Q), 𝒪/ϖ^n) generated by Hecke endomorphisms T_{α,k} for all k ≤ n and all α which are units at primes in S_Q. Let T_{Q,ψ} denote the 𝒪-algebra generated by the same operators with T_α for α non-trivial at places in Q."
issues.correction: "... and all α which are units at the primes in S_p ∪ Q and equal to 1 at the primes in R". This is consistent with the construction of T(g) and with the next paragraph's 'α is 1 for each component dividing the level'. Alternatively, extend the construction to g_v ∈ Iw(v) by letting g_v act on 𝒪(ψ) through ψ_v. The other reading ('trivial at primes in S_Q', as in Definition 5.4) is not a misprint fix: it would remove the diamond operators at Q from T^an_{Q,ψ}, which is the substantive question in the related gap (C-K9-0 / H-part2-18).
issues.reason: R ⊂ S_Q. The construction of T(g) on p. 412 is stated only for g trivial at each v ∈ R. That restriction is needed because on the ψ-twisted local system the operator depends on the representative g, not just the double coset. If α_v ∈ 𝒪_v^× with α_v ≠ 1 at some v ∈ R, then g_v = diag(α_v, ..., α_v, 1, ..., 1) is a non-trivial element of Iw(v), and it maps non-trivially to Iw(v)/Iw_1(v) ≅ (k_v^×)^n/k_v^×. So T_{α,k} is not covered by the stated construction, and Definition 9.1 as printed refers to operators the paper has not defined. The mismatch is harmless. With the natural extension (right translation by g_v is a deck transformation of Ỹ → Y and acts on 𝒪(ψ) by ψ_v(g_v)^{±1}), such a T_{α,k} is a unit scalar in 1 + 𝔪_𝒪 times T_{α',k}, where α' has v-component 1. So the 𝒪-algebra generated is unchanged. At v|p a unit α_v gives g_v ∈ PGL_n(𝒪_v), which is harmless. At v ∈ Q a unit α_v gives the diamond operators through K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^×. The printed 'units' includes these deliberately or not; the minimal correction keeps them, as printed. Whether they should be in T^an is the separate gap about local–global compatibility at Q, and it does not affect this verdict. It is not a bracket error.

issues.locator: §9.2, p. 413 (definition of T_{a,k}) together with §9.3, Conjecture B, p. 414 (characteristic polynomial) (published version)
issues.printed: p. 413 (§9.2, just after Definition 9.1): "If 𝔞 ⊆ O_F is an ideal prime to the level, we may define the Hecke operator T_{𝔞,k} as (1/N_{F/Q}(𝔞)^k)T_{α,k} where α ∈ A_F^{×,∞} is any element which represents the ideal 𝔞 and such that α is 1 for each component dividing the level." p. 414 (§9.3, Conjecture B): "... if λ ∉ S_Q is a prime of F, then r̄_𝔪 is unramified at λ, and the characteristic polynomial of r̄_𝔪(Frob_λ) is X^n − T_{λ,1}X^{n−1} + ··· + (−1)^i N_{F/Q}(λ)^{i(i−1)/2} T_{λ,i} X^{n−i} + ··· + (−1)^n N_{F/Q}(λ)^{n(n−1)/2} T_{λ,n}, in T^an_{Q,ψ}/𝔪[X]." arXiv v2 has identical wording (v2 p. 86, §9.1).
issues.correction: Define T_{𝔞,k} := T_{α,k}, i.e. drop the factor 1/N_{F/Q}(𝔞)^k. This is the §5 convention: Definition 5.4 has "T_𝔞 as T_α" and Conjecture A(1) has X^2 − T_λX + N(λ). With it, the Conjecture B polynomial becomes the standard one. An equivalent fix is to keep the normalisation and change the i-th coefficient to (−1)^i N(λ)^{i(i+1)/2} T_{λ,i}, which gives the same polynomial. Either change is a one-symbol fix. After it, det r_𝔪 = ε^{n(n−1)/2}, as ξ (§8.5), Theorem 5.16(7) and §5.5 ("PGL ... forcing the determinant to be cyclotomic") require. Nothing else in §9 needs to change.
issues.reason:
I checked this against the page images (PDF pp. 116–118 = pp. 412–414) and the text. It holds.
(1) §9 takes G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) (p. 411). T_{α,k} is the double coset operator for g = diag(α,…,α,1,…,1) with k copies of α, and k = n is allowed (Definition 9.1). For k = n, g is scalar, so it is the identity in PGL_n and T_{α,n} = id. Under the printed normalisation T_{λ,n} = N(λ)^{−n}. The constant term (−1)^n N^{n(n−1)/2} T_{λ,n} then gives det r̄_𝔪(Frob_λ) = N(λ)^{n(n−1)/2−n}.
(2) Frob_v is the arithmetic Frobenius (Notation, p. 306), so det r̄_𝔪 = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2−n} by Chebotarev.
(3) §8.5 fixes r̄ as Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1]. It also fixes ξ lifting det r̄, with ξ|I_v = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for v|p and ξ|I_v = 1 for v∤p. Theorem 5.16(7) has det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2}. Conjecture B supposes r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄ and concludes that r_𝔪 is a deformation of type S_Q, so it has determinant ξ. §9.5 assumes a maximal ideal 𝔪 with r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄. Together these force ω^{−n} = 1 on I_v for v|p. Since p is unramified in F, that means (p−1) | n. With p > n this happens only when p = n+1. So for p ≥ n+2, the printed Conjecture B, part 1, rules out every 𝔪 with r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄.
(4) Independent check. The un-normalised T_{α,k} acts on constant classes by its degree, the q-binomial [n,k]_q. I verified numerically that q^{i(i−1)/2}[n,i]_q = e_i(1,q,…,q^{n−1}). So without the factor, the formula gives 1⊕ε⊕…⊕ε^{n−1}, which has weights 0,…,n−1 and determinant ε^{n(n−1)/2}, as the paper's conventions require. With the factor, every root is multiplied by N^{−1}, so the formula describes r⊗ε^{−1}. For n = 2 it gives X^2 − (T_α/N)X + N^{−1}, which contradicts Conjecture A for the same T_α. For n ≥ 3 the determinant is wrong whichever sign or Frobenius convention is used. Lemma 9.6 also uses the un-normalised T_x (roots α_x, β_x with α_xβ_x = N(x)).
Two small problems with the candidate's reasoning:
- The mod-𝔪 contradiction needs p ≥ n+2, not just p > n. When p = n+1 one needs 𝔪-adic or characteristic-zero information instead.
- Printed B is not literally self-contradictory. Its part-3 hypothesis (and §9.5's standing assumption) simply cannot be met, so Theorem 9.19 becomes vacuous. The proof of 5.16 also fails: by the standard normalisation, the 𝔪 coming from π_0 would give r̄⊗ε̄^{−1}, not r̄.
Theorem 1.1 applies 5.16 to Sym^{2n−1} in dimension 2n with large p, so it is affected. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. I checked the page images: PDF pp. 115–118, pp. 77–79 and 87–88, and v2 p. 86.

Defences tried, and why each fails:
(a) Is T_{α,n} = id? Yes. §9 takes G = Res_{F/Q}PGL(n) (p. 411), and for k = n the matrix g = diag(α,…,α) is scalar, hence trivial in PGL_n. So under the printed normalisation T_{λ,n} = N(λ)^{−n}. The constant term then says det r̄_𝔪(Frob_λ) = N(λ)^{n(n−1)/2−n} = N(λ)^{n(n−3)/2} for every λ ∉ S_Q. This does not depend on how T_{α,k} is read for k < n: using α^{-1} just swaps T_k with T_{n−k}, and the determinant is unchanged.
(b) Frobenius convention. The Notation on p. 306 says Frob_v is the arithmetic Frobenius. Chebotarev then gives det r̄_𝔪 = ω^{n(n−3)/2}. Using the geometric Frobenius instead gives ε^{−n(n−3)/2}. That agrees with ε^{n(n−1)/2} on inertia only if ε^{n(n−2)} = 1, so it helps only when n = 2. The paper uses the arithmetic Frobenius anyway: Conjecture A has X^2 − T_λX + N(λ), and Lemma 5.6 has cyclotomic determinant.
(c) The paper's own T(g), defined by corestriction, then translation, then pushforward, acts on constant classes by its degree, the q-binomial [n,k]_q. I checked numerically (q = 5, 7, 9; n = 2..5) that q^{i(i−1)/2}[n,i]_q = e_i(1,q,…,q^{n−1}). So the unnormalised operators give 1⊕ε⊕…⊕ε^{n−1}, as intended. The printed normalised operators give roots q^{−1},1,…,q^{n−2}, which is r⊗ε^{−1}. No convention in the paper supplies the factor N^{−k}. Lemma 9.6 itself uses the unnormalised T_x: φ^∨∘φ = [[N(x)+1, T_x],[T_x, N(x)+1]] with α_xβ_x ≡ N(x).

Consequences. Conjecture B assumes r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄. Here det r̄ = ξ̄ with ξ|I_v = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for v | p, and p is unramified, so ω(I_v) = F_p^×. The printed text would therefore force (p−1) | n, which for p > n means p = n+1. So for p ≥ n+2 no 𝔪 satisfies r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄. Parts (1)–(5) of B become vacuous, and the standing assumption of §9.5 (p. 425, "a maximal ideal 𝔪 of T with r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄") can never hold. When p = n+1, part (1) (Fontaine–Laffaille weights [0..n−1]) fails at any characteristic-0 point instead, because of the ε^{−1} twist.

The deduction "Theorem 5.16 follows immediately from Theorem 9.19" also breaks. The 𝔪 attached to π_0 in hypothesis (8a) would, under the printed normalisation, have r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄⊗ω^{−1}, not r̄. And with B vacuous, 5.16 would claim far more than is proved. Theorem 1.1 applies 5.16 to Sym^{2n−1} (dimension 2n) at large p, so it inherits the problem.

Unaffected: Conjecture B(5) and Lemma 9.6. They only involve Taylor–Wiles primes, where N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, and the projectors lim Q_x(V_x)^{k!} do not change when V_x is scaled by a unit ≡ 1.

Remark on the kind: the intended normalisation is recoverable from §5, so some would call this a slip. But the printed definition, which introduces a deliberate normalisation, makes the hypothesis of 5.16/9.19 unsatisfiable. The correction is right and minimal. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.locator: §9.3, Conjecture B, p. 414, and the sentence after (5), p. 415 ('In this case, we obtain a surjection R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,m}'); used in §9.5, p. 427 ('Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B') (published version)
issues.printed: p. 414 (PDF p. 118), Conjecture B: "(2) If v ∈ Q, then r_𝔪|_{G_v} is a lifting of type 𝒟_v where 𝒟_v is the local deformation problem specified in Sect. 8.5.1." p. 427 (PDF p. 131), proof of Theorem 9.19: "Thus condition (b) of Proposition 6.3 is satisfied for both sets of patching data. Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B, while condition (c) is clear." (Both passages read the same in arXiv v2.)
issues.correction:
Add to Conjecture B a local–global compatibility clause at the Taylor–Wiles primes. This is the GL(n) analogue of Conjecture A(3), where T_α uses g = diag(α,1). Proposed clause: for v ∈ Q and α ∈ O_v^×, the operator T_{α,1} acts on H^*_ψ(Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^m)_𝔪 as the scalar by which r_𝔪(Art_v(α)) acts on the lift ψ_v of the line ψ̄_v. Here Art is normalised as in (3), with the transpose/inverse when one passes to the dual/homology side (𝔪*).

Why this is the right form: identify K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} with k_v^× by g ↦ det(B)·a^{1−n}, where g ≡ [[a,*],[0,B]]. Then diag(α^{(k)},1^{(n−k)}) has class α^{k−n}, and T_{α,1} has class α^{1−n}. Since p > n, the T_{α,1} run over the whole p-part of Δ_Q. So the clause fixes the diamond action of S_N = O[Δ_N]; equivalently, a diamond operator acts by the inertial scalar on s_v. With the clause, R_{𝒮_Q} → T is a map of O[Δ_Q]-algebras. The diamond operators lie in the image of R_{𝒮_Q}, so the p. 415 surjection holds even though T^an contains them. The augmentation ideal maps into the image of ker(R_{𝒮_Q} → R_𝒮), which gives both halves of Theorem 6.3(d). A relation "diamond = inertial character to a fixed power prime to p" would do just as well; this is all that is needed.

Alternative for Definition 9.1: read "units" as "trivial" at Q, as in Def. 5.4. That saves the p. 415 surjection but not (d); the clause is still needed.

Comments on the reporters' versions. X-K10-9's form (T_{α,1} ↔ ψ_v∘Art_v) is correct, but its cross-reference "p. 378" should be pp. 374–375. C-K9-0's phrase "ψ_x∘Art_x ... should match the Hecke action of the T_{α,k}" holds only for k = 1. Under the expected compatibility, T_{α,k} with α ∈ O_v^× acts by (ψ_v∘Art_v)^{(n−k)/(n−1)}, and T_{α,n} = 1. H-part2-18's "diamond character, or its inverse" is right only for a suitable choice of the unspecified isomorphism K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^×.
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the page images and it matches the quote.

1. What Theorem 6.3(d) asks for (p. 386, checked on the image). "the image of S_M^□ in End_O(H^*(D_M^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ^n)) is contained in the image of R_∞ and moreover, the image of the augmentation ideal of S_N^□ ... is contained in the image of ker(φ_N)." In §9.5, S_N = O[Δ_N] acts through the deck group of Y_{Δ_N}(Q) → Y_0(Q). That group is a quotient of K_Q/L_Q ≅ ∏ k_x^×, so S_N acts by diamond operators. R_∞ acts through R_{S_Q} → Hecke. The map φ_N sends R_∞ onto R_S, and ker(R_{S_Q} → R_S) is generated by the condition that inertia at Q acts trivially.

2. What Conjecture B gives at v ∈ Q. Only (2): r_𝔪|_{G_v} has type 𝒟_v. In §8.5.1 (p. 408), 𝒟_v is purely Galois-theoretic: "I_v acts via (possibly different) scalars on s_v and ψ_v". Clauses (1) and (3)–(5) are about v|p, v ∈ R, vanishing, and Y_0(Q) respectively. None of them ties the inertial scalars at v ∈ Q to the diamond operators. r_𝔪 is determined by Frobenius at λ ∉ S_Q, so its inertial character at v is a well-defined object. Saying that this character equals the diamond character is extra local–global content. Without it, nothing stops r_𝔪 from being unramified at v while ⟨δ⟩ ≠ 1. The second half of (d) then fails, and so can the first half. Conclusion (iv) of Theorem 6.3, which is used to finish the proof of Thm 9.19, needs the second half.

3. The paper's own GL_2 argument uses exactly this input. Conjecture A(3) (pp. 374–375) is local–global compatibility at Q. The proof of Lemma 5.6 says "assumption 3 above guarantees ... that the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces". On p. 380 the authors write: "The image of S_N ... is contained in the image of R_∞ by Conjecture A, because it is given by the image of the diamond operators. The second part of condition (5a) follows from Conjecture A part (3)". Conjecture B has no counterpart to A(3).

4. The claimed surjection R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,𝔪}. As printed, Definition 9.1 allows α that are only units at primes in S_Q. For α ∈ O_x^× with x ∈ Q, diag(α^{(k)}, 1^{(n−k)}) lies in K_{Q,x}. By my computation it acts on Y_1(Q) as a diamond operator (class α^{k−n}). So T^an contains the diamond operators, and surjectivity from the trace algebra again needs the missing compatibility. If "units" was meant to be "trivial", as in Def. 5.4, then the first half of (d) needs it instead.

5. Independent corroboration. Khare–Thorne, "Potential automorphy and the Leopoldt conjecture" (arXiv 1409.7007), which uses the Calegari–Geraghty method, builds this into its setup. It defines D_v^TW so that "C_i|_{I_{F_v}} agrees, on composition with the Artin map, with the ith canonical character" of Δ_v, makes R_{S_Q} an O[Δ_Q]-algebra, and puts the requirement in a separate Conjecture 6.27. Its Remark 6.28 calls that conjecture "a form of local-global compatibility ... at the places of S_p ∪ Q".

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The O[(Z_p)^q] on p. 427 is one of those and is a separate matter.

On "affects": the proof of Theorem 9.19 has a gap. Theorems 5.16 and 1.1 are deduced from it assuming Conjecture B, so their hypothesis must be strengthened by the clause above for the proof to go through. Nothing shows the conditional statements are false, so "the proof" is the right classification. Defence attempts. None of them works.

(a) The other clauses of Conjecture B. Clause (1) concerns v|p. Clause (3) gives inertia compatibility only at v ∈ R, with fixed O-valued Iwahori characters. Clause (4) is about vanishing. Clause (5) concerns only Y_0(Q), where the diamond operators act trivially. Clause (2) says only that the lift has type 𝒟_v, which is a purely Galois-side condition: "I_v acts via (possibly different) scalars" (p. 408). Nothing ties those scalars to the deck group Δ_Q of Y_1(Q) → Y_0(Q). r_𝔪 is pinned down by its Frobenius traces at λ ∉ S_Q, so its inertial scalar at v ∈ Q is a definite object. Saying that it equals the diamond character is an extra assertion, and Conjecture B does not make it. In particular, clauses (1)–(5) do not rule out r_𝔪 being unramified at v while a diamond operator ⟨δ⟩ ≠ 1.

(b) The GL(1) and central-character mechanisms. In the GL(1) model (PDF 108), and for classical X_1(N), diamond operators come from Frobenius classes through class field theory or the central character. Here G = PGL_n, so T_{λ,n} = 1 and det = ξ carries no diamond information. The p-part of Δ_Q is therefore not in the closed algebra generated by traces unless one assumes something more.

(c) A charitable reading of the authors' intent. Remark 9.5 (p. 417) says the real difficulty lies in "proving local-global compatibility, especially at v|p". So the authors think of local–global compatibility as part of the conjecture's content. But the stated clause at Q is only (2). The proof says "Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B" and gives no argument.

(d) Deriving it from clause (3). One could try to treat Q as additional R-primes with character twists and then decompose. That is not in the paper. It would also fail integrally: patching needs O/ϖ^n and O[Δ]-coefficients, where eigen-decomposition by O-valued characters is not available.

(e) The same step in §5. The paper's GL(2) proof needed exactly this input and said so. The proof of Lemma 5.6 says "assumption 3 above guarantees (by Hensel's Lemma) that the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces". On p. 380: "The image of S_N ... is contained in the image of R_∞ by Conjecture A, because it is given by the image of the diamond operators. T^an_{Q,1} therefore contains the diamond operators, and the p. 415 surjection R_{𝒮_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,𝔪} does not follow for Q ≠ ∅. issues.locator: §9.3, paragraph after Conjecture B, p. 415 (published version)
issues.printed: By dévissage, conditions 4 and 5 are satisfied if and only if they are satisfied for n = 1, e.g., with coefficients in the residue field k = O/ϖ.
issues.correction: "... are satisfied if and only if they are satisfied for m = 1, i.e., with coefficients in the residue field k = O/ϖ." The only change needed is n to m. "e.g." should arguably also read "i.e.", but that is stylistic.
issues.reason:
I checked the page image. On PDF p. 119, which is published p. 415 (§9.3, the last sentence of the paragraph after Conjecture B), the text reads "for n = 1". A 300 dpi zoom confirms the letter is n. The arXiv v2 text has the same sentence (cg-v2.txt l. 4604-4606), so this is not a typesetting defect and is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

Conjecture B (pp. 414-415) uses its letters consistently. n is the rank: r̄_m : G_F → GL_n(T^an_{Q,ψ}/m), the characteristic polynomial X^n − ..., and condition (1) "weights equal to [0,1,...,n−1]". The coefficient exponent in conditions (4)(a), (4)(b) and (5) is m: H^i_ψ(Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^m)_m, H^i_ψ(∂Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^m)_m, and H^*_ψ(Y, O/ϖ^m)_m → H^*_ψ(Y_0(Q), O/ϖ^m)_{m_Q}. Read literally, "n = 1" would mean GL_1, which makes no sense here. The phrase "with coefficients in the residue field k = O/ϖ" shows the exponent 1 is intended.

Elsewhere the paper sometimes uses n as a coefficient exponent too. For example, the proof of Lemma 9.6 on p. 416 uses O/ϖ^n while n = 2 is the rank. So the letters are loose in places, but the sentence explicitly refers to conditions 4 and 5, which are written with ϖ^m.

I redid the dévissage myself, and the claim is correct with m. Take the exact sequences 0 → O/ϖ^{m−1} → O/ϖ^m → O/ϖ → 0, where the first map is multiplication by ϖ. The long exact sequences in cohomology are Hecke-equivariant, and localization at m is exact. So by induction, vanishing for m = 1 gives vanishing for all m in (4)(a) and (4)(b). For (5), the maps lim_k ∏ Q_x(V_x)^{k!} come from Hecke operators on complexes, so they commute with the connecting maps. The five lemma then carries the m = 1 isomorphism to all m. The converse direction is trivial.

The candidate's correction and reason are accurate.

issues.locator: §9.3 (after Conjecture B), Remark 9.3, published p. 415 (PDF p. 119). arXiv v2 (p. 87, Remark 9.3) has the identical text, including the superscript q_0−1 in all three places. arXiv v1 has no Conjecture B or Remark 9.3 (it covers only Part 1, l0 = 1).
issues.printed: Remark 9.3 ... In the latter two cases (where (q0, l0) = (2, 2) and (2, 1) respectively), the key point is that the lattices in question satisfy the congruence subgroup property [77], which yields vanishing for both (H^1)_𝔪 and (by duality, considering both 𝔪 and 𝔪^*) (H_c^{q_0−1})_𝔪 where 𝔪 is a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal. On the other hand, the vanishing of (H_c^{q_0−1})_𝔪 also implies the vanishing of (H^{q_0−1})_𝔪 after localization at 𝔪, since the cohomology of the boundary vanishes after localization at 𝔪.
issues.correction: In all three places, replace the degree q_0−1 by q_0+l_0+1, which equals 2q_0+l_0−1 = d−1 = dim Y here because q_0 = 2. The text then reads "(by duality, considering both m and m^*) (H_c^{q_0+l_0+1})_m ... the vanishing of (H_c^{q_0+l_0+1})_m also implies the vanishing of (H^{q_0+l_0+1})_m". Concretely, this is H_c^5 and H^5 for GL(2)/F with F a quartic CM field, and H_c^4 and H^4 for GL(3)/Q. The candidate's proposed correction, d−1 = 2q_0+l_0−1, is the same thing and is right and minimal.
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered page and the transcription above matches it. §8.4 and §9 of the paper say that Y has real dimension d = 2q0+l0, and that Part (4)(a) of Conjecture B asks for H^i_𝔪 = 0 when i ∉ [q0, q0+l0]. By §8.4's formulas, GL(2) over a CM quartic field (r2 = 2) has l0 = 2 and d = 6, so q0 = 2. GL(3)/Q has l0 = 1 and d = 5, so q0 = 2. In both cases H^{q0−1} = H^1. Poincaré/Verdier duality (see the paper's own use of it in §9 and Remark 9.5) pairs H^i(Y,k)_{𝔪^*} with H_c^{d−i}(Y,k)_𝔪. So "by duality, considering both 𝔪 and 𝔪^*" turns the vanishing of H^1 given by the congruence subgroup property into the vanishing of H_c^{d−1}, not H_c^{q0−1} = H_c^1. The next sentence ("the vanishing of H_c^{q0−1} implies the vanishing of H^{q0−1}", because the boundary cohomology vanishes at 𝔪) is then circular as printed: H^{q0−1} = H^1 is exactly what the congruence subgroup property already gave.

The degree that actually needs this argument is never treated. For GL(2) over a CM quartic field, the range is [2,4] and d = 6. H^0_𝔪 = 0 because 𝔪 is non-Eisenstein. H^6 = 0 by virtual cohomological dimension: vcd = d − (Q-rank) = 6 − 1 = 5. But H^5 is not automatic, and it needs exactly the duality step with degree d−1 = 5 = q0+l0+1. For GL(3)/Q, vcd = 5 − 2 = 3, so H^4 happens to vanish anyway, but the argument as intended still concerns degree d−1 = 4. With the correction, the remark reads coherently: H^1_𝔪 = 0 (congruence subgroup property), so H_c^{d−1}_𝔪 = 0 (duality over 𝔪 and 𝔪^*), so H^{d−1}_𝔪 = 0 (boundary vanishing at 𝔪).

Each printed sentence is literally true: H_c^1_𝔪 ≅ H^1_𝔪 = 0 via the boundary sequence. The fault is the index, which makes the duality step misattributed and leaves the top degree out. The intended meaning (the Poincaré-dual degree of 1) is clear from "by duality", so I class it as an index misprint; "error" is also defensible, since the printed step fails to cover degree d−1. It sits in a remark supporting a conjecture, so nothing proved in the paper depends on it. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The paper sets up Y(K) for G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) in §9, and §8.4 says dim Y = 2q_0+l_0. For GL(2) over a quartic CM field (r_2 = 2) this gives l_0 = 2 and d = 6. For GL(3)/Q it gives l_0 = 1 and d = 5. So q_0 = 2 in both cases, as the remark says.

Part (4)(a) needs the localized cohomology to vanish outside [q_0, q_0+l_0]:
- GL(2)/F: degrees 0, 1, 5 and 6.
- GL(3)/Q: degrees 0, 1, 4 and 5.

H^0_m = 0 because m is non-Eisenstein. H^d = 0 because Y is non-compact. The congruence subgroup property gives H^1_m = 0 for every non-Eisenstein m, including m^*.

Poincaré duality is Hecke-equivariant up to replacing m by m^*: (H_c^{d−i})_m is dual to (H^i)_{m^*}. That is why the text says "considering both m and m^*". So from H^1 it gives vanishing of H_c^{d−1} = H_c^{q_0+l_0+1}, not of H_c^{q_0−1} = H_c^1. The boundary sequence then turns this into (H^{d−1})_m = 0.

As printed, q_0−1 = 1, so the remark fails in two ways:
- Duality is credited with giving H_c^1. H_c^1 does vanish, but through the boundary sequence, not through duality.
- The next sentence concludes (H^1)_m = 0, which was the starting point, so it is circular.
- Degree d−1 is never treated. This matters for GL(2)/F: the virtual cohomological dimension is 6 − 1 = 5 = d−1, so H^5 does not vanish for free. (For GL(3)/Q it is 5 − 2 = 3, so H^4 would vanish anyway.)

Defence considered: no convention in the paper shifts the indexing of H_c. Remark 9.5 uses the same duality, which reverses degrees between cohomology and compactly supported cohomology. No reading makes "q_0−1" the degree that duality produces. The only intended degree consistent with the words "by duality, m and m^*" and with the goal of (4)(a) is d−1 = q_0+l_0+1. The intended meaning is therefore clear from context. It is a wrong-index slip, the protocol's example of a misprint. It could also be called an error with affects = nothing, since the argument as printed does not close; the candidate chose that.

Consequences: Remark 9.3 is cited nowhere else in the paper. The §9 results (Theorem 9.19 etc.) assume Conjecture B outright. The later Ihara-type argument uses the congruence subgroup property of the S-arithmetic group PSL_2(O_F[1/x]) on its own, not this remark. The remark's claim, that (4)(a) can be checked in these cases, is true once the degree is corrected.

issues.locator: §9 (Conjecture B discussion), Remark 9.3, published p. 415 (PDF p. 119). arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2) has identical text, citing [BMS67]. arXiv v1 ("... I") has no such remark. Serre's 1970 SL_2 paper is not in the bibliography of either version; the only other Serre item nearby is [78], Arbres, amalgames, SL_2.
issues.printed: Remark 9.3 Part (4)(a) of Conjecture B may be verified directly in a number of small rank cases, in particular for GL(2)/F when F is CM field of degree either 2 or 4, or for GL(3)/Q. In the latter two cases (where (q_0, l_0) = (2, 2) and (2, 1) respectively), the key point is that the lattices in question satisfy the congruence subgroup property [77], which yields vanishing for both (H^1)_m and (by duality, considering both m and m^*) (H_c^{q_0-1})_m where m is a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal. [Bibliography] 77. Bass, H., Milnor, J., Serre, J.-P.: Solution of the congruence subgroup problem for SL_n (n ≥ 3) and Sp_2n (n ≥ 2). Inst. Hautes Études Sci. Publ. Math. 33, 59–137 (1967)
issues.correction: Cite Serre's paper as well: J.-P. Serre, "Le problème des groupes de congruence pour SL2", Ann. of Math. (2) 92 (1970), 489–527. Suggested wording: "...satisfy the congruence subgroup property ([77] for GL(3)/Q; Serre, Ann. of Math. 92 (1970) for GL(2)/F with F CM of degree 4)". Serre proves that the congruence kernel of SL2(O_S) is finite when |S| ≥ 2, that is, when O_F^× is infinite. For a CM quartic field the unit rank is r1+r2−1 = 1, so this applies. For a totally imaginary F the kernel is μ(F), which is finite but not trivial. So "congruence subgroup property" here has to mean a finite kernel. The proposed correction is right and minimal.
issues.reason: I rendered PDF p. 119 and read the text: "the latter two cases" are GL(2)/F with F CM of degree 4 ((q_0,l_0)=(2,2)) and GL(3)/Q ((2,1)), and the paper cites only [77] for both. [77] is Bass–Milnor–Serre, whose title and content restrict it to SL_n with n ≥ 3 and Sp_2n with n ≥ 2. Since Sp_2 = SL_2 is excluded, SL_2 is not covered. For the GL(2)/F case the lattice sits in G = SL_2 over F (the restriction of scalars of SL_2 from F), and no isogeny turns this into SL_n with n ≥ 3 or Sp_2n with n ≥ 2. I checked the attribution in the survey by Prasad–Rapinchuk, "Developments on the congruence subgroup problem after the work of Bass, Milnor and Serre" (arXiv:0809.1622), §2.3: "The results obtained in [3] exhibited two possibilities for C^S(G) for G = SL_n (n ⩾ 3) and Sp_2n (n ⩾ 2) ... Subsequently, it was shown in [49] that this description of C^S(G) remains valid for G = SL_2 if |S| > 1." Here [3] is BMS and [49] is Serre 1970. §5.6 of the same survey calls the SL_2 case with |S| > 1 "established first by Serre in [49]". BMS §15 only states the metaplectic conjecture for SL_2. For F a CM quartic field, S is the set of archimedean places, which are 2 complex places, so |S| = 2 and Dirichlet gives unit rank 1. Serre's theorem therefore applies and gives C ≅ μ_F. The mathematical claim in the remark is true, but the reference given does not prove it for one of the two cases it is cited for. That is an asserted step without adequate support, i.e. a citation gap. It sits in a heuristic remark and the statement is true, so nothing downstream is affected. The case for the paper is only partly sound. For GL(3)/Q the lattices are commensurable with SL3(Z), and [77] proves a trivial congruence kernel there, so the citation fits. For GL(2)/F with F a quartic CM field, the lattices are commensurable with SL2(O_F), or equivalently with arithmetic subgroups of SL2(C)^2. [77] cannot cover them. Its title and theorems are limited to SL_n with n ≥ 3 and Sp_2n with n ≥ 2, which excludes Sp_2 = SL2. The SL2 case was left open there and settled later by Serre (Ann. Math. 1970), who showed the kernel is finite exactly when |S| ≥ 2. The fact the remark asserts is true: F has 2 complex places, so |S| = 2 and CSP holds with kernel μ(F). The imaginary-quadratic case is correctly left out of "the latter two cases", since |S| = 1 there and CSP fails. So the mathematics is right, but half of its stated justification is missing. This matches the repo's precedent of recording a missing or wrong citation as "gap / nothing". It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Consequences: [77] is used only in this remark, nothing in the paper refers back to Remark 9.3, and the remark is a side comment on how plausible Conjecture B is. All later results in §9 assume Conjecture B as a hypothesis. Side note, not verified: for totally imaginary F the kernel μ(F) is nontrivial, so the "yields vanishing of (H^1)_m" step may need extra care when p divides |μ(F)|. The remark is informal ("may be verified directly"), and this candidate does not claim that.

I checked the rendered pages 407, 408, 412, 413, 414 and 415.
(i) In §9, G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) (p. 412). So g = diag(α,…,α) is trivial in G(A^∞), and T_{α,n} = T(1) = id. The normalised T_{λ,n} is therefore a scalar: N(λ)^{−n} as printed, or 1 with the §5 normalisation. The constant term of the characteristic polynomial in Conjecture B then makes det r_m(Frob_λ) a fixed power of N(λ). By Chebotarev, det r_m = ε^k with k fixed; k = n(n−1)/2 once the normalisation is repaired (X-K9-0, a separate issue).
(ii) Type S_Q requires "(2) it is of determinant ξ" (§8.5.2, p. 408). The local rings R_v, R_v^1, R_v^{χ_v} and D_v also fix the determinant as ξ.
(iii) §8.5 (p. 407) fixes ξ only as a continuous lift of det r̄ with ξ|_{I_v} = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for v | p and ξ|_{I_v} = 1 for v ∤ p. It then says "For example, we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}". Nothing in §9 or §9.5 specialises ξ; the only occurrences of ξ are in §8.5. So θ = ξε^{−n(n−1)/2} is unramified at every finite place, hence a character of the narrow class group, and θ ≡ 1 mod m. It can be non-trivial.
Concrete admissible data: F = Q(√−23) (h = 3), p = 3 > n = 2, where 3 is unramified and split, and O = Z_3[ζ_3]. Take θ a non-trivial character Cl(F) → μ_3 and ξ = εθ. This satisfies every condition of §8.5. Then det r_m = ε ≠ εθ = ξ in T_m^× whenever θ is non-trivial in T_m, for example when m supports characteristic-0 cohomology, as with π_0 in Theorem 5.16(8a). In that case r_m is not of type S_Q, so "It follows" fails.
The fix is harmless. Theorem 5.16(7) forces ξ = det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2} when Theorem 9.19 is applied. Alternatively, twisting by η restores a type-S_Q lift, and the surjection survives because the η(Frob_λ) are units.
This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It is also distinct from X-K9-0: after that correction the issue remains unless ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}. As an alternative classification, this is a missing hypothesis, which could be recorded as a gap. I checked all three passages against the page images (PDF pp. 111, 112, 118, 119).

(1) What the determinant of r_m is. In §9, G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) (p. 411). T_{α,n} is the Hecke operator for diag(α,…,α), which is trivial in PGL_n, so T_{α,n} = id. With the unnormalised operators, the constant term of the characteristic polynomial in Conjecture B gives det r_m(Frob_λ) = N(λ)^{n(n−1)/2} for all λ ∉ S_Q. Chebotarev then gives det r_m = ε^{n(n−1)/2}. This uses the correction of X-K9-0 / H-part2-17. With the printed 1/N(a)^k normalisation one gets ε^{n(n−3)/2}, which is a separate error. Either way, det r_m is a fixed power of ε and has nothing to do with ξ.

(2) What type S_Q requires. It requires det = ξ (condition (2), p. 408). §8.5 allows any ξ lifting det r̄ with the stated restrictions on inertia. Since r̄_m ≅ r̄ gives det r̄ = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}, the character θ = ξε^{−n(n−1)/2} is unramified at every finite place and trivial mod m_O. It is also trivial at real places, because p is odd. So θ is a character of Cl_F of p-power order. It can be non-trivial whenever p | h_F and ζ_p ∈ O. The paper forces ζ_p ∈ O as soon as R ≠ ∅, since the distinct χ_{v,i}/ψ_v factor through (k_v^×)^n/k_v^× into 1+m_O. Example: F = Q(√−23), h_F = 3, p = 3 > n = 2, 3 splits in F, O ∋ ζ_3, θ : Cl_F ↠ μ_3, ξ = εθ. Every §8.5 condition holds, but det r_m = ε ≠ ξ. So "It follows that r_m is of type S_Q" fails for this choice of ξ. If p ∤ h_F, ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2} is forced and the sentence is correct. Nothing in §9 fixes ξ.

(3) The defence, and why nothing downstream breaks. θ has p-power order and p > n, so θ^{1/n} exists, is unramified everywhere and is ≡ 1 mod m_O. The twist r_m ⊗ θ^{1/n} reduces to r̄ and has det ξ. At v|p it is still Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1], since the twist is unramified and within the FL range. At v ∈ R its inertial characteristic polynomials are unchanged. At v ∈ Q it is still of type D_v. So it is of type S_Q (resp. S_Q^χ). Its trace algebra equals that of r_m, because tr(r_m⊗θ^{1/n})(g) = θ^{1/n}(g)·tr r_m(g) with θ^{1/n}(g) ∈ O^×. So R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,m} still exists.

Where the sentence is used:
- §9.5, p. 426: "By Conjecture B, we have surjections R_S ↠ T_m and R_{S^χ} ↠ T_{χ,m}".
- Theorem 9.19 and its proof, p. 427, where R_{S_{Q_N}} acts on cohomology "by Conjecture B".
All of these survive if one uses the same fixed twist for every N and for both the 1- and χ-versions; the twist also commutes with the diamond and inertia data at Q. Theorem 5.16 assumes det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2} (hypothesis (7)), and r must be of type S, so ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2} there and the printed sentence is literally correct. Theorem 1.1 goes through 5.16.

So the paper's text is a genuine, harmless slip: the asserted step fails for some ξ that §8.5 allows. The candidate labels it a gap; 'error' fits PROTOCOL §18 slightly better, because the step is false rather than merely unproved. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.correction: The determinant of the printed matrix is (N(x)+1)^2 − T_x^2, which is −(T_x^2 − (1+N(x))^2). The follow-on sentence "T_x^2 − (1+N(x))^2 ∉ 𝔪" is still correct as written, because it is the same element up to a sign.
issues.reason: I recomputed it: det[[a,b],[b,a]] = a^2 − b^2. With a = N(x)+1 and b = T_x this gives (1+N(x))^2 − T_x^2. The paper prints T_x^2 − (1+N(x))^2, which is the negative, so this is a real sign slip. The matrix is taken exactly as printed, so no convention in the paper makes the stated sign right. The expression is used only once afterwards, to say it is not in 𝔪, and so φ^∨∘φ is invertible after localizing. That property does not depend on the sign. Mod 𝔪 we have T_x ≡ α+β and N(x) ≡ αβ ≡ 1, so the expression reduces to ±(1−α)(1−β)(1+α)(1+β). This is nonzero exactly when α, β ≢ ±1, which is the Taylor–Wiles condition. A search of the text finds the expression nowhere else. The 47 known bracket errors are unrelated. Minor note: the candidate's "printed" field writes the determinant as "T_x^2 − (1 + N(x))^2", which matches the page.

issues.locator: §9.3, proof of Lemma 9.6, published pp. 417–418 (PDF pp. 121–122), checked on the rendered pages. The arXiv v2 text is word for word the same (v2 p. 89, cg-v2.txt ll. 4689–4717). arXiv v1 has no amalgam or Lyndon argument: a grep finds neither word.
issues.printed: p. 417: "For convenience, let us also assume that x is trivial in the ray class group corresponding to the component group of Y (this is equivalent to imposing a further congruence condition on x, but is imposed only for notational convenience in the argument below). ... (Without the extra assumption on x, one would have to amalgamate different pairs of lattices Γ_i occurring in the decomposition of Y according to the action of the ray class group, cf. Sect. 4.1.4 of [6]. The argument would then proceed quite similarly, but it would require more notation)". p. 418: "We claim that this sequence is equivariant with respect to the Hecke operator U_{x^2}, which acts on H^*(G, O/ϖ^n) by 1. First, recall the definition of U_{x^2}. It is defined to be 1/N(x)^2 times the operator induced by taking the double coset operator for Γ^1_0(x) corresponding to the matrix: (π_x^2 0; 0 1). ... g := (π_x 0; 0 π_x^{-1}). With this normalization, the matrix g lies in G. In particular, the corresponding map on H^*(G, O/ϖ^n) is given by multiplication by the degree of this operator on Γ^1_0(x), which is N(x)^2, and thus (after normalizing) it follows that U_{x^2} acts by 1."
issues.correction:
The proof needs the following, all of which can be supplied by standard arguments.
(a) Realise the Lyndon sequence as the Ext_G(−, O/ϖ^n) sequence of 0 → C_1(T) → C_0(T) → Z → 0, where T is the Bruhat–Tits tree at x. Then U_{x^2} on H^*(Γ^1_0(x)) is induced by the G-endomorphism T_1 of C_1 ≅ Z[G/Γ^1_0(x)] that sends an edge to the N(x)^2 edges two steps from it. There is a unique G-endomorphism T_0 of C_0 with ∂T_1 = T_0∂: A(v) = v − N·S_1(v) + S_2(v) on one vertex type and B(w) = S_1(w) − N·w on the other. On the Γ^1-terms this is the 2×2 Hecke matrix [[T_x^2 − N, −N T_x],[T_x, −N]], i.e. U_x^2 on oldforms. Its augmentation is 1, so the sequence is equivariant and the un-normalised double coset acts on both H^*(G)-terms by 1. With the paper's 1/N(x)^2 normalisation, U_{x^2} therefore acts on H^*(G) by N(x)^{-2}, not by 1 as printed. This is harmless because N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, so U_{x^2} − N(x)^{-2} is a unit exactly when U_{x^2} − 1 is.
(b) For general x: the operator diag(ϖ_x, ϖ_x^{-1}) ∈ SL_2(F_x) preserves components, and the same tree argument applies to each component's S-arithmetic group. Its two vertex stabilisers are the Γ^1-lattices of the components paired by [x], as in [6, §4.1.4].
(c) Also needed: the Φ-invariants and T^an-localisation bookkeeping behind "repeat this argument for each lattice Γ_i".
issues.reason:
1. I rendered pp. 416–418 and transcribed the text above. The v2 text is the same, so this is not a bracket defect.

2. The proof asserts equivariance of the whole Lyndon/Mayer–Vietoris sequence, including the connecting map H^{i-1}(Γ^1_0(x)) → H^i(G). It never defines U_{x^2} on H^*(Γ^1)^2 or on H^*(G). Its only justification is that g ∈ G, so "the corresponding map on H^*(G) is multiplication by the degree N(x)^2". What this argument actually proves is U_{x^2}∘res^G_{Γ_0} = res^G_{Γ_0}. That is not a map in the sequence: the composite H^i(G) → H^i(Γ^1)^2 → H^i(Γ_0) is res − res = 0.

3. I checked from scratch which action the sequence really carries. G = Γ^1 *_{Γ^1_0} Γ^1 acts on the (q+1)-regular tree with quotient one edge. The sequence comes from 0 → Z[E] → Z[V] → Z → 0 via Ext_G(−, M), using Shapiro for compact induction. The Hecke operator T is the G-endomorphism of Z[E] described in the correction, and its image T(e) has q^2 terms. A G-equivariant lift T_V to Z[V] with T_V∂ = ∂T must be a finite combination of distance spheres. Solving the coefficient equations forces T_V(v0) = v0 − qS_1(v0) + S_2(v0) and T_V(v1) = −qv1 + S_1(v1). The lift is unique because G has no nonzero invariants in Z[V]. Using the other translation direction gives the mirror formulas. In both cases εT_V(v0) = 1 − q(q+1) + q(q+1) = 1 and εT_V(v1) = −q + (q+1) = 1. By naturality of connecting maps, δ∘T = δ, so T acts on H^*(G) by 1, not by N(x)^2.

4. A python check on tree balls for q = 2, 3, 4 confirms ∂T = T_V∂ and ε∘T_V = 1 (tree.py in my agent folder).

5. A degree-0 sanity check with trivial coefficients: T acts on H^0(Γ_0) by q^2. On H^0(Γ^1)^2 the lift gives the matrix [[1+q(q+1), −q(q+1)], [q+1, −q]], whose eigenvalues are 1 (on the diagonal, which is the image of H^0(G)) and q^2.

6. No other equivariant structure can give N(x)^2 on H^*(G) in general. It would need (N(x)^2 − 1)δ = 0, which fails for O/ϖ^m once m is large relative to the Taylor–Wiles level.

7. So the printed claim "U_{x^2} acts by 1" is literally wrong by the unit N(x)^{-2} ≡ 1 mod p, and the equivariance it rests on is asserted, not shown. The conclusion still holds, because only invertibility mod ϖ is used and α_x ≢ ±1.

8. The restriction to x trivial in the ray class group is acknowledged and the general case is waved at [6, §4.1.4]. I could not consult [6], which is cited as a Calegari–Venkatesh preprint.

Overall the candidate's description (equivariance asserted, not shown; the general case of x only sketched) is accurate. Lemma 9.6 itself is not in doubt. Defence first.
- The lemma is true, and the authors flag the argument as "implicit in … Chapter 4 of [6]".
- They explicitly reduce to x trivial in the ray class group and point to [6, §4.1.4] for the general case, which is indeed only notational (see (b)).
- The equivariance also holds. I checked the chain-level identity ∂T_1(e) = B(v_1) − A(v_0) by script on (N+1)-regular trees for N = 2, 3, 4, for both the forward and the backward double coset. It holds, with aug A = aug B = 1 and exactly N^2 edges in T_1(e).

The objection still stands, for two reasons.
1. The paper never defines the U_{x^2}-action on the middle term H^*(Γ^1)^2 and never proves that the maps of the sequence commute with it. The one justification it gives ("g ∈ G, so the map on H^*(G) is multiplication by the degree N(x)^2") computes [KgK]∘res^G_{Γ^1_0(x)}. That is not a map in the sequence: the composite H^*(G) → H^*(Γ^1)^2 → H^*(Γ^1_0(x)) is zero.
2. That justification also gives the wrong scalar. By naturality of the connecting map for the endomorphism (T_1, T_0, id_Z), δ∘[KgK] = δ. So on the image of δ the compatible scalar is 1 for the un-normalised operator, i.e. N(x)^{-2} for the paper's U_{x^2}. This differs from the printed 1 in O/ϖ^n whenever ϖ^n does not divide N(x)^2 − 1. It is harmless for the localisation, since N(x) ≡ 1 mod p.

So the key step is asserted without an adequate proof, and the stated result is not in doubt. The general-x case and the per-component and Φ bookkeeping are only sketched, but they are routine.

Consequences: Lemma 9.6 is cited nowhere else. Only Remark 9.8 discusses it. Theorems 9.19, 5.16 and 1.1 assume Conjecture B in full (including part 5) for each Q_N. The gap therefore affects only this proof.

The candidate's correction is right. I have made it concrete: the explicit T_0, and the scalar N(x)^{-2}. Separate items, not this one: the index slip H^{i−1}(G) → H^i(Γ^1)^2 in the displayed sequence (X-K9-15), and the normalisation issues (H-part2-17). This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.correction: lim_{k→∞}(U_x − β_x)^{k!} and lim_{k→∞}(U_x − α_x)^{k!}. These are the idempotents onto the α_x-part and the β_x-part of H^i(Y_0(x), O/ϖ^n)_m, matching the paper's own projectors: Conj. B(5) lim_{k→∞} ∏ Q_x(V_x)^{k!} (p. 415), P_x = lim(U_x − β_x)^{n!} (§7, p. 394), and e_α := lim Q(V)^{n!} (p. 422). Using a letter other than n also removes the clash with the fixed exponent in O/ϖ^n.
issues.reason: Put T = End(H^i(Y_0(x), O/ϖ^n)_m). This ring is finite, and T[U_x] = T_α × T_β. On the α-part, U_x − β_x is a unit u ≡ α_x − β_x mod the radical. In a finite ring the powers u^n are eventually periodic, and they converge only if u = 1. Since α_x − β_x is in general not ≡ 1, the printed operator limit does not exist, whereas u^{k!} → 1 and the operator is nilpotent on the β-part, so (U_x − β_x)^{k!} converges to the idempotent. Everywhere else the paper writes its projectors with a factorial (Conj. B(5), §7, §9.4.1, §9.5). One could instead read the expression like §7's direct limit lim_→ T^n M, which Lemma 7.3 says is a direct summand of M. That reading recovers the right module, but the printed notation (lim_{n→∞}, called 'projections') is the operator limit. Either way the intended meaning is clear and the isomorphism H^i(Y)^2_m ≅ H^i(Y_0(x))_m = (α-part) ⊕ (β-part) is unaffected. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The earlier verdict H-part2-25 (bound-variable clash in §9.5) concerns a different point.

issues.locator: §9.4 "An approach to Conjecture B part 5", first paragraph, published p. 419 (PDF p. 123). arXiv v2 has the same text in §9.2 (v2 PDF p. 90). arXiv v1 does not contain this section.
issues.printed: In this section, we present an informal approach to proving part 5 of Conjecture B under a stronger assumption that r̄ has enormous image, at least in the analogous case of GL(n) (from which it should be easy to deduce the corresponding claim for PGL, since manifolds for the former are circle bundles over manifolds for the latter, and so have highly related Hecke actions).
issues.correction: Replace "circle bundles" with "torus bundles". Each fibre of a GL(n) space over the corresponding PGL(n) space is a quotient of the GL(1) arithmetic manifold of §8.2, so up to finitely many components it is (S^1)^{r1+r2−1}, or (S^1)^{r1+r2−1} × R if the identity component A_∞^0 of the split central torus is not divided out. With A_∞^0 divided out, the fibres are circles only when r1+r2 = 2. For F = Q or F imaginary quadratic the fibres are finite: the two spaces agree up to components, as §5.5 already says. Without the A_∞^0 quotient the fibres are never circles. The point the authors need still holds: the fibres come from the centre, so the Hecke actions are closely related.
issues.reason:
Rendered p. 419; the printed text matches the quote. §9 treats an arbitrary number field F (G = Res_{F/Q}PGL(n), G_∞ = PGL_n(R)^{r1} × PGL_n(C)^{r2}). The GL(n) spaces are never defined in the paper, so the natural reading takes the paper's own GL(1) conventions from §8.2, p. 403: Y = F^×\A_F^×/UK_∞, with K_∞ the identity component of the maximal compact of (F⊗R)^×, and X_Q the further quotient by A_∞^0.

Compute the fibre of Y_GL → Y_PGL. It is F^×\A_F^× modulo (the level ∩ centre) and (K_∞^0 ∩ centre). At a real place, SO(n) ∩ scalars ⊂ {±1}. At a complex place, U(n) ∩ scalars = S^1. So the archimedean part is (R_{>0})^{r1+r2} up to finite index. Dividing by the diagonal R_{>0} gives R^{r1+r2-1}. Dirichlet's unit theorem (units of rank r1+r2-1) then turns this into a compact torus T^{r1+r2-1}, times a finite set. Without the R_{>0} quotient there is an extra R factor.

The paper's own §8.2 (p. 403) gets exactly this for GL(1): "the cokernel of the map O_F^× → R^{×r1} × C^{×r2}/K_∞, which is (S^1)^{r1+r2-1} × R … the components of X_Q consist simply of a product of circles".

Test cases:
- F = Q or F imaginary quadratic (r1+r2 = 1): the fibres are finite, so the GL spaces are finite covers (times R), not circle bundles.
- F totally real cubic: the fibres are 2-tori.
- The statement is literally true only when r1+r2 = 2.

A non-standard choice such as K_∞ = SU(n) at complex places changes the count, but it still does not give circles in general.

The intended point is correct: the GL spaces fibre over the PGL spaces with fibres that are compact abelian orbits of the centre, so their Hecke actions are closely related. The authors plainly know the right fibre (p. 403), so this is loose wording in an explicitly informal heuristic remark. One could also file it as a misprint whose intended meaning ("products of circles") is clear from §8.2. Nothing in the proofs or results depends on it. Printed text checked on the rendered page (PDF p. 123). The paper never defines GL(n) spaces in §9: Y(K) there is only for G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n). With any standard choice, GL_n(F)\GL_n(A_F)/K K_∞^0 (optionally also divided by A_∞^0) maps onto the PGL(n) space. The fibres are orbits of the centre Z(A) = A_F^×, i.e. quotients of F^×\A_F^×/U K_∞ (A_∞^0). The paper computes these itself in §8.2, p. 403. The fibres of Y_Q are "the connected components of the cokernel of O_F^× → R^{×r1} × C^{×r2}/K_∞, which is (S^1)^{r1+r2−1} × R. Passing to X_Q excises the factor of R." This follows from Dirichlet's unit theorem: Z(R)/(Z(R) ∩ K_∞^0 · R_{>0}) ≅ R^{r1+r2−1}, and the unit lattice has full rank there.

So the fibre dimension is r1+r2−1 (or r1+r2 without the R_{>0} quotient). It is 1 only for r1+r2 = 2, e.g. a real quadratic field or a cubic field with one complex place. The paper contradicts itself here. §5.5, p. 380, says: "When F = Q or an imaginary quadratic field, the associated locally symmetric spaces are very similar (the same up to components)". That is fibre dimension 0, not circle bundles, and imaginary quadratic F is the paper's main case.

Defence tried: §8.2 speaks of "a product of circles". Read loosely as "torus bundle", including the zero-dimensional case, the remark would be right for every F under the A_∞^0 convention. But "circle bundle" means S^1 fibres, and as printed the claim is false outside r1+r2 = 2. The intended meaning (torus fibres coming from the centre) can be recovered from §§5.5 and 8.2, so one could argue for "misprint". I kept "error" because a precise geometric claim is false as stated.

Consequences: the remark is a parenthetical in a section the authors call "informal". It only motivates working with GL(n) instead of PGL(n). Nothing later cites it. §9.4.2 is an informal sketch, and Theorem 9.19 and the other results assume Conjecture B outright. The Correction (Invent. Math. 227, 2022) only fixes brackets and does not mention this.

issues.reason: This is a genuine notation clash, confirmed on the page images (PDF pp. 123–128 = pp. 419–424). The Notation section fixes k = 𝒪/ϖ, and elsewhere the paper writes k_v for the residue field of F_v (§7; §9.1, "(k_v^×)^n"). Section 9.4.1 itself writes GL_n(𝒪_x/ϖ_x) for the local residue ring. Even so, from Cor. 9.13 on, §9.4 uses the bare letter k for 𝒪_x/ϖ_x, whose characteristic is ℓ ≠ p, while still using k for 𝒪/ϖ, whose characteristic is p. The two meanings sit in one phrase: "universal deformation over k of D(k) to k[k^×/k^{×q}]" and "k[G(k)]". Read with the paper's own convention k = 𝒪/ϖ, the statements are wrong. First, |k^×| = |k| − 1 is prime to p, so k^× ⊗ Z_p = 0 and q = 1. Cor. 9.13 and the display before it would then lose the tame p-part. I recomputed the local group: F_x^× ≅ Z × k_x^× × (1+ϖ_x𝒪_x), and the last factor is pro-ℓ, so the pro-p completion is Z_p ⊕ (k_x^× ⊗ Z_p). This group is cyclic of order the p-part of N(x) − 1, which is at least p. Second, GL_n(𝒪_x)/U(x) ≅ GL_n(𝒪_x/ϖ_x), not GL_n(𝒪/ϖ); the two residue fields have different characteristics. The intended meaning can be recovered, so this is a misprint and not a mathematical error. 'affects' = nothing is right. §9.4 is explicitly an "informal approach" to Conjecture B part 5. Definition 9.11 through Remark 9.18 are cited only inside §9.4 (9.4.2 uses Thm 9.16), and the main results assume Conjecture B rather than depending on §9.4. The candidate's correction is right in principle, but it lists only some of the affected places. Its suggested exponent m is itself already in use.

issues.locator: §9.4.1, proof of Lemma 9.12, p. 421 (arXiv v2, p. 91)
issues.printed: (§9.4.1, proof of Lemma 9.12, p. 421 = PDF p. 125; identical wording in arXiv v2 p. 91) "There is a natural map M → n-ind^G_B res^B_G(M) = ⊕_W n-ind^G_B M^w_B → n-ind^G_B M_B. Note that M and n-ind^G_B M_B are elements of 𝒞 of the same length, and all the irreducible constituents of n-ind^G_B M^w_B for w ≠ id are distinct from π. Thus, by comparing lengths, to prove that the composite of these maps is an isomorphism it suffices to prove that the first map is injective. If K denotes the kernel, then res^B_G(K) = 0. Yet this contradicts the assumption that M (and hence K) lies in 𝒞, since res^B_G(π) ≠ 0. □"
issues.correction: Delete the clause "and all the irreducible constituents of n-ind^G_B M^w_B for w ≠ id are distinct from π". It is false: for every w, each constituent of n-ind^G_B M^w_B is n-ind^G_B(χ^w) ≅ π. Then run the kernel argument on the composite g: M → n-ind^G_B M_B, not on the first map. By Frobenius reciprocity (res^B_G left adjoint to n-ind^G_B), g is adjoint to the projection res^B_G(M) → M^{id}_B = M_B. Let K' = ker g. By naturality, res(K') → res(M) → M_B is zero. res is exact and the decomposition into χ^w-parts is functorial, so res(K')^{id} ↪ M^{id}_B. Hence res(K')^{id} = 0. But K' ∈ 𝒞 has finite length. If K' ≠ 0 it contains a copy of π, and res(π)^{id} = χ ≠ 0, a contradiction. So K' = 0. Equivalently, g is nonzero on every irreducible subrepresentation π' ⊂ M, so ker g contains no irreducible and is 0. Since g is an injection between modules of the same length, it is an isomorphism. The minimal textual fix is to replace "the first map" by "the composite", "res^B_G(K) = 0" by "res^B_G(K)^{id} = 0" and "res^B_G(π) ≠ 0" by "res^B_G(π)^{id} ≠ 0", and to drop the false clause. Both candidates' repairs (C-K10-0 and H-part2-22) are correct. The statement of Lemma 9.12 is unchanged.
issues.reason:
I checked the page image at 220 dpi and the quoted text is exact; v2 has the same wording. The premise fails because each χ^w is χ with its entries permuted, and n-ind^G_B(χ^w) ≅ n-ind^G_B(χ) = π for every w ∈ W. I checked this in two ways. (a) By the paper's own Lemma 9.9: π is fixed by ρ̄ and equals n-ind(χ) for χ sending the uniformizers to the distinct eigenvalues, with no ordering specified. So every ordering χ^w gives the same π. (b) Directly: the Jacquet module of n-ind(χ^w) has constituents {χ^v : v ∈ W}, each exactly once. The χ^v are distinct on the uniformizers because the α_i are distinct, so the Jacquet module splits into generalized eigenspaces for D. Hence χ is a D-quotient, and Frobenius reciprocity gives a nonzero, hence surjective, map n-ind(χ^w) → π, with π irreducible by Lemma 9.9. Both Jacquet modules have dimension n!, so the kernel has zero Jacquet module. A nonzero subrepresentation of an induced representation cannot have zero Jacquet module, so the kernel is 0. By exactness of n-ind, every constituent of n-ind M^w_B is ≅ π. The inference the paper wants is: M has only π-constituents, so its projections to the w ≠ id summands vanish, so injectivity into ⊕ gives injectivity into the id factor. That inference needs the false premise, so the step is invalid as written. The repair above is just the paper's own kernel argument applied to the id-eigenspace, and I checked it step by step. One small point in the candidate's reasoning: what makes Frobenius reciprocity work is that χ (not χ^w) occurs as a direct-summand quotient of the Jacquet module of n-ind(χ^w). The conclusion is still correct. The lemma's statement is unaffected. Its later uses are Cor. 9.13 (the equivalence with R-modules) and the proof of Thm. 9.16 ("we may assume that M = n-ind^G_B M_B"), and both rely only on the true statement. §9.4 is also explicitly presented as an informal approach. This is not a bracket-typesetting issue. Defence attempted and it fails. Here χ^w is χ with its components permuted, so it sends the uniformizers to the same distinct eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_x).

(1) The paper's own Lemma 9.9 says rec(π) = ρ̄ iff π is "the irreducible unramified principal series n-ind(χ)" with χ sending each uniformizer to a distinct eigenvalue. No ordering is specified, so n-ind(χ^w) is that same π. Lemma 9.10 and Definition 9.11 also treat 𝒞 as a block with the single irreducible π.

(2) Directly: the normalized Jacquet module of n-ind(χ^w) has constituents χ^v (v ∈ W), each once. These are pairwise distinct on the uniformizers, so Ext^i vanishes between them (the paper says this itself) and the Jacquet module is a direct sum. So χ is a quotient, and Frobenius reciprocity gives a nonzero map n-ind(χ^w) → n-ind(χ). Both sides are irreducible (Lemma 9.9; with q ≡ 1 mod p the reducibility condition χ_i/χ_j = ν^{±1} reduces to χ_i = χ_j, which does not occur). So the map is an isomorphism. By exactness of n-ind, every constituent of n-ind M^w_B is ≅ π, for every w.

The inference the paper needs is this: M has only π-constituents, so its projections to the w ≠ id summands are zero, so injectivity into ⊕_W gives injectivity into the id-summand. That inference rests entirely on the false clause. Injectivity of M → ⊕_W n-ind M^w_B does not rule out a kernel of the id-projection. I found no charitable reading: "distinct from π" can only mean non-isomorphic, and no nearby statement supplies the missing step.

The paper's own tools repair the step: the same adjunction and kernel argument, restricted to the id-eigenspace. Length equality holds as the paper says: length_A(M_B) = length_G(M), and n-ind(χ) = π is irreducible. So the lemma is true.

Downstream uses: Lemma 9.12 is not cited by number. It is used implicitly in Cor. 9.13 (n-ind gives an equivalence with R-modules), in Lemma 9.14 ("Using this description of 𝒞"), and in the proof of Thm. 9.16 ("we may assume that M = n-ind^G_B M_B"). All of these need only the true statement, so no stated result is affected. §9.4 is also explicitly labelled an "informal approach". This is not one of the 47 bracket defects.

Side note: Def. 9.11's "associated to π" should read "associated to ρ̄". That is a separate slip and does not bear on this item.

issues.correction: In the display, the right-hand side should be (Z_p ⊕ lim_← k^×/k^{×p^m})^n, which is ≅ (Z_p × k^×⊗Z_p)^n ≅ (Z_p × Z/q)^n. In Cor. 9.13, 'below and and 𝒞' should read 'below and 𝒞'. For R, the only needed change is the known bracket fix A[X] → A⟦X⟧. Writing R = ⨂_{i=1}^n (A[T_i]/(T_i^q − 1) ⊗ A⟦X_i⟧), completed, i.e. A⟦(Z_p × Z/q)^n⟧, only makes the intended reading explicit. It does not fix an error. The printed R is correct if the big ⊗ is read as covering both factors, with each variable implicitly indexed by i. Using ⊗_A instead of ⊗_𝒪 changes nothing, because A = 𝒪/ϖ^k is a quotient of 𝒪. A[T]/(T^q − 1) is correctly a polynomial quotient, since it is the group ring A[Z/q].
issues.reason: I checked this against the setup at the start of §9.4.1 (p. 420). There, x is a prime with N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, so x ∤ p, and D ≅ (F_x^×)^n. For one factor, F_x^× ≅ Z × k_x^× × (1+m_x), and 1+m_x is pro-ℓ with ℓ ≠ p. So lim_m F_x^×/F_x^{×p^m} ≅ Z_p × (k_x^× ⊗ Z_p) ≅ Z_p × Z/q. The left side of the display explicitly carries the exponent n, so it is (Z_p × Z/q)^n, of Z_p-rank n. The right side as printed has rank 1, so the isomorphism is false as written. The large parentheses around the right side, with nothing after them, also point to a dropped exponent n. The doubled 'and' in the statement of Cor. 9.13 is a plain typo. Both slips appear identically in arXiv v2 p. 91. The part of the claim about R is weaker than stated. The candidate says the printed R has only one X, but the natural reading of ⨂_{i=1}^n A[T]/(T^q−1) ⊗_𝒪 A⟦X⟧ is the n-fold tensor product of the whole factor. That reading gives the completed group ring of (Z_p × Z/q)^n, which is correct. At most this is ambiguous notation, and it is not counted here as an error. The proof of Lemma 9.14 drops the n in the same way ('A[T]/(T^q−1)-modules', 'k[k^×/k^{×q}]'), consistent with loose notation rather than a mathematical mistake. None of the three slips is one of the 47 known bracket errors.

issues.locator: §9.4.1, proof of Lemma 9.14, p. 422 (PDF p. 126). arXiv v2 p. 92 has the same text.
issues.printed: p. 422 (PDF p. 126), proof of Lemma 9.14: "Since finitely generated injective A[T]/(T^q − 1)-modules are free, it follows that the image of an injective module has a filtration whose pieces are isomorphic to Φ := Ind_{B(k)}^{G(k)}(ψ), where ψ is the universal deformation over k of D(k) to k[k^×/k^{×q}]. Yet Φ is a direct summand of Ind_{B(k)}^{G(k)} k[D(k)] and thus of k[G(k)]; hence it is injective and acyclic."
issues.correction: ψ is the universal deformation, over k, of the trivial character of D(k_x) = (k_x^×)^n. It takes values in k[(k_x^×/k_x^{×q})^n] = k[D(k_x)/D(k_x)^q], which is the direct factor of k[D(k_x)] belonging to the p-part of D(k_x). Here k_x = O_x/ϖ_x and q = |k_x^× ⊗ Z_p|.
issues.reason: D(k) = (k^×)^n (printed in the same proof: "(k^×)^n = D(k) ⊂ B(k)"). The universal deformation ring of its trivial character over k is the group algebra of its maximal p-quotient, k[(k^×/k^{×q})^n], which is n-fold and matches R = ⊗_{i=1}^n A[T]/(T^q−1) ⊗ … of Cor. 9.13. The single factor matters for the proof. For a quotient D → D/H, the module k[D/H] = Ind_H^D k is projective (equivalently injective) over k[D] only when p ∤ |H|. With one factor k[k^×/k^{×q}] and n ≥ 2, H has order divisible by q^{n−1}. So Φ would not be a direct summand of Ind k[D(k)], and the conclusion 'hence it is injective' would fail. With the n-fold group algebra the argument works. The meaning is clear from Cor. 9.13 and from the parallel dropped exponent on p. 421 (H-part2-23 / X-K10-1). The H-part2-23 verdict called the dropped n in this proof 'loose notation'. I count it as a misprint because, read literally, it would break the injectivity step. The overload of k (residue field at x versus k = O/ϖ) is recorded separately in H-part2-24.

issues.locator: §9.4.1, Remark 9.15, p. 422 (published version)
issues.printed: Remark 9.15 Since the group U(x) is pro-p, the higher cohomology of U(x) vanishes. Hence, for any subgroup U(x) ⊂ Γ ⊂ G(O_x), by Hochschild–Serre there are identifications H^i(Γ, M) ≃ H^i(Γ/U(x), M^{U(x)}).  [published p. 422 = PDF p. 126, §9.4.1; arXiv v2 p. 92 has the identical wording "Since the group U(x) is pro-p, the higher cohomology of U(x) vanishes."]
issues.correction: Replace "pro-p" with "pro-ℓ, where ℓ ≠ p is the residue characteristic of x (so U(x) is pro-prime-to-p)". The phrase "the higher cohomology of U(x) vanishes" should say "with coefficients in any M ∈ 𝒞" (these are smooth, p-power-torsion A = O/ϖ^k-modules). Nothing else in the remark needs to change. Both candidates propose this correction. It is correct and minimal.
issues.reason:
Checked on the rendered page images (published PDF p. 126 = p. 422, and v2 p. 92): "pro-p" is printed as quoted, with no lost prime such as p′. Setup (§9.4.1, p. 421): x is a prime of F with N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, and U(x) ⊂ G(O_x) = GL_n(O_x) is the full congruence subgroup of level x. Let ℓ be the residue characteristic of x, so N(x) = ℓ^f. If ℓ = p, then N(x) ≡ 0 mod p, which contradicts N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, so ℓ ≠ p. U(x) = 1 + ϖ_x M_n(O_x) has successive quotients (1+ϖ^i M_n)/(1+ϖ^{i+1} M_n) ≅ M_n(O_x/x), which are elementary abelian ℓ-groups. So U(x) is pro-ℓ and not pro-p. The coefficient modules M lie in C, which consists of smooth modules over A = O/ϖ^k, so they are p-power torsion and ℓ acts invertibly. For a pro-ℓ group, H^i(U(x), M) = lim H^i(U(x)/V, M^V) is then 0 for i ≥ 1, which is the vanishing the remark needs. The stated reason would give the opposite: a nontrivial pro-p group U has H^1(U, F_p) = Hom(U, F_p) ≠ 0, and U(x) is infinite. So the sentence as printed is false, but the intended meaning (pro-prime-to-p) is clear from context and from the correct conclusion. That makes it a slip rather than a failed argument, so I class it as a misprint under PROTOCOL §18; "error" is also defensible, since "U(x) is pro-p" is a false statement. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, which the 2022 Correction lists and which concern only ⟦ ⟧. Only the stated reason is wrong. The conclusion (U(x)-cohomology vanishes, so Hochschild–Serre gives H^i(Γ,M) ≃ H^i(Γ/U(x), M^{U(x)})) is correct. So the later use of the remark still holds: identifying R^kF ≃ H^k(G(O_x),M) and R^kG ≃ e_α H^k(U_0(x),M) on p. 422, and hence Theorem 9.16 and §9.4.2. Two small comments on the candidate: its locator (§9.4.1, Remark 9.15, p. 422; same in v2) is correct. Its correction is right, though the letter ℓ is also used for the invariant l_0 elsewhere in the paper, so "pro-prime-to-p" may be clearer. Defence attempted and failed. In §9.4.1 (p. 421), p is the paper's fixed global prime: x is a prime of F with N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, π is a mod-p representation, and 𝒞 is the category of locally admissible G-modules over A := O/ϖ^k. There is no local convention under which p could mean the residue characteristic of x. U(x) is the full congruence subgroup of level x in G(O_x) = GL_n(O_x), so U(x) = 1 + ϖ_x M_n(O_x). Its successive quotients are ≅ M_n(O_x/x), which are elementary abelian ℓ-groups, where ℓ is the residue characteristic of x. Since N(x) = ℓ^f ≡ 1 mod p, we get ℓ ≠ p. So U(x) is infinite and pro-ℓ, and not pro-p. The stated reason would in fact give the opposite conclusion: a nontrivial pro-p group U has H^1(U, F_p) = Hom(U, F_p) ≠ 0.

The conclusion is nonetheless true for the right reason. Take M ∈ 𝒞, which is smooth and p-power torsion. Then H^i(U(x), M) = colim_V H^i(U(x)/V, M^V) over open normal V. Each U(x)/V is a finite ℓ-group, and |U(x)/V| acts invertibly on M, so this is 0 for i ≥ 1. U(x) is normal in G(O_x), hence in every Γ between U(x) and G(O_x), so Hochschild–Serre gives H^i(Γ, M) ≃ H^i(Γ/U(x), M^{U(x)}) as printed.

The slip may have come from the paragraph on p. 421, where "pro-p image" is correctly said of the deformation χ̃ restricted to D(O_x). Only the justifying adjective is wrong, and the intended meaning (pro-prime-to-p) is forced by the correct conclusion. So I class it as a misprint under PROTOCOL §18. "Error" is also defensible, since "U(x) is pro-p" is literally false; the candidates chose that label.

Consequences. Remark 9.15 is used on p. 422 to identify R^k𝓕(M) ≃ H^k(G(O_x), M) and R^k𝓖(M) ≃ e_α H^k(U_0(x), M). It is used again implicitly in Remark 9.18 (p. 424) for R^1𝓕(π) ≃ H^1(GL_n(k), π^{U(x)}) and R^1𝓖(π) ≃ e_α H^1(U_0(k), π^{U(x)}). Through these it feeds Theorem 9.16 and §9.4.2. All of these uses need only the vanishing of U(x)-cohomology on 𝒞, which holds. So no statement or proof is affected.
