issues.correction: State in Theorem 5.16 the hypotheses under which Theorem 9.19 is proved. (6) should read "If r is ramified at a prime x, then r|I_x is unipotent and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p", i.e. delete the proviso "if, furthermore, r̄ is unramified at x". (4) should read "r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big (in the sense of [3, Definition 2.5.1])". This is exactly what §8.5 (p. 406 bullet; R ⊇ ramification primes of r̄ with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p), Proposition 8.5 and §9.5 assume. The alternative is a separate argument for primes where r̄ is unipotently ramified and N(x) ≢ 1 mod p. In case (8a) that could be a solvable base change followed by descent, which is not "immediate". In case (8b) it is unavailable, since the authors themselves note 8b is not obviously preserved under base change. The candidate's proposed correction is right and essentially minimal.
issues.reason:
Checked from the page images. Theorem 9.19 is proved inside the §8.5/§9.5 setup. That setup explicitly assumes N(v) ≡ 1 mod p at every v ∤ p where r̄ ramifies. It also needs a set R that contains all primes where r̄ ramifies and has N(v) ≡ 1 mod p for each v ∈ R.

This congruence is actually used. Lemma 8.2, whose conclusion "Spec R^χ_loc is irreducible" is needed for Theorem 6.4, rests on [76, Lemma 3.3] and Taylor's [11, Prop. 3.1]. Those are Ihara-avoidance local computations in the setting q_v ≡ 1 mod p. The characters χ_{v,i} of p-power order that the rings R_v^χ need must also be nontrivial.

Theorem 5.16(6) imposes N(x) ≡ 1 mod p only where r is ramified and r̄ is not. Where r̄ is ramified, it asks nothing. Such cases exist. Take n=2 and E an elliptic curve with multiplicative reduction at x, p ∤ ord_x(Δ_E) and N(x) ≢ 1 mod p. By Tate-curve theory, r̄ = E[p] is ramified at x and r|I_x is unipotent, so (6) holds, but no R as in §8.5 can exist. So Theorem 9.19 does not apply, and the claim that Theorem 5.16 is "immediate" fails in this case.

This is not just a formality for n ≥ 3. Take n = 3, q = N(x) ≢ 1 mod p, and r̄|I_x unipotent of Jordan type (2,1), with Frobenius eigenvalues a, aq on the block and b ≡ aq² on the rest. Then there are unipotent lifts of type (2,1) and of type (3), so R_x^1[1/p] can have more than one component. Without the nontrivial χ_{x,i}, Ihara avoidance is not available, and nothing in the paper handles this. Hypothesis 8b does not exclude it, since r may still be non-minimally ramified at primes where r̄ ramifies.

Secondary point: (4) says only "r̄ is big" (CHT Def. 2.5.1 applies to subgroups), while Prop. 8.5 and §9.5 assume r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big. Bigness does not obviously pass to the normal subgroup of prime-to-p index: H^1(H, ad^0) = H^1(H', ad^0)^{H/H'} does not force H^1(H', ad^0) = 0. This part could be read as loose wording, and I did not build an explicit counterexample.

Theorem 1.1 is likely unaffected. In §10, Theorem 5.16 is applied over fields L chosen by Moret–Bailly, and there these extra conditions can be arranged. What is affected is Theorem 5.16 in the generality stated. Defence attempted, and it fails.

(a) Congruence condition. The whole proof of Theorem 9.19 lives in the §8.5 setting. There R must contain every prime where r̄ ramifies and have N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. The Hecke side (§9.1) uses Iwahori level at v ∈ R with characters ψ_v of Iw(v)/Iw_1(v) = (k_v^×)^n/k_v^× → 1+m_O, and these are trivial unless p | N(v)−1. Lemma 8.2, which gives irreducibility of Spec R^χ_loc for Taylor's trick, is proved via [11, Prop. 3.1], which assumes q_v ≡ 1 mod p.

Theorem 5.16(6) imposes the congruence only where r is ramified and r̄ is not. So it admits r̄ that is unipotently ramified at x with N(x) ≢ 1 mod p. Example: n = 2, E semistable with multiplicative reduction at x, p ∤ ord_x(Δ). Case (8b) makes this especially clear: r is then ramified only where r̄ is, so (6) imposes no congruence at all. Such x cannot lie in R, so Theorem 9.19 does not apply.

Putting x in R with trivial χ_x does not repair the argument when n ≥ 3. Example: n = 3, q̄ = N(x) mod p with q̄, q̄² ≠ 1, r̄|G_x with Frobenius eigenvalues ᾱ, q̄ᾱ, q̄²ᾱ and rank-1 monodromy. Unipotent lifts then lie on two distinct components of R^1_x[1/p], one with regular N and one with rank-1 N. Without Ihara avoidance, r and r_p(π_0) may lie on different components.

The condition in (6) mirrors the n = 2 condition of Part I, which is harmless there because the unipotent ring at a ramified r̄ is just the Steinberg component. For general n it is not.

(b) Bigness. CHT Definition 2.5.1 defines bigness of a subgroup of GL_n(k), so "r̄ is big" literally means r̄(G_F) is big. Prop. 8.5 and §9.5 need r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) to be big, and (3) does not bridge the gap. Computation (script h1.py in my scratch dir): take p = 7, n = 3, r̄ = Sym² ρ̄ with ρ̄(G_F) = GL_2(F_7), det ρ̄ = ε̄, and F linearly disjoint from Q(ζ_7).
- H^1(GL_2(F_7), ad^0 Sym²) = 0, so r̄(G_F) is big (the other conditions are easily checked).
- H^1(SL_2(F_7), ad^0 Sym²) has dimension 1, so r̄(G_{F(ζ_7)}) is not big.
- (3) still holds.
- r = Sym² of an elliptic curve's 7-adic representation satisfies (1), (2), (5) and (7).
Taken alone, (4) could be read charitably as a slip for the standard hypothesis. Together with (a), though, the claimed "immediate" deduction does not cover the stated generality.

Consequences: only Theorem 5.16 as stated is affected. Its only later use is the sketch in §10 (proof of Theorem 1.1, potential modularity and Sato–Tate). There the stronger hypotheses can be arranged: take p large and L linearly disjoint, so the image of G_{L(ζ_p)} contains Sym^{2n−1} SL_2(F_p), which is big. Then a further solvable base change, unramified at p, makes N(x) ≡ 1 mod p at the finitely many ramified primes, and the paper notes this preserves 8a. So Theorem 1.1 is unaffected, but Theorem 5.16 is proved only under the corrected hypotheses.

issues.reason: I rendered PDF pp. 126, 129 and 119 and checked them. The transcription is exact. (1) Q_N versus Q: §9.5 introduces only the sets Q_N ('For each integer N ≥ 1, let Q_N be a set of primes …'). Δ̃ is declared to be the Galois group of Y_1(Q_N) → Y_0(Q_N), and Δ_N = (Z/p^N)^q with q = |Q_N|. The Hecke projector in the display acts on the cohomology of Y_{Δ_M}(Q_N). So the Q in ∏_{x∈Q} can only be Q_N. The paper carried the generic Q over from Conjecture B, which is stated for an arbitrary Q, without adding the index. The proof of Theorem 9.19 on p. 427 keeps the indices correctly (Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M)). This is a dropped index with a clear intended meaning, so it is a misprint. (2) Variable clash: in lim_{n→∞} the n is bound inside explicit parentheses, and the result is the ordinary idempotent, independent of the outer n in O/ϖ^n. Conjecture B(5) on p. 415 writes the same operator as lim_{k→∞} ∏_{x∈Q} Q_x(V_x)^{k!} on H^*(Y, O/ϖ^m), which shows the intent. On p. 422, lim_→ Q(V)^{n!} can only mean the limit over the exponent, even though n is also the rank. Neither reuse produces a false or ambiguous statement. I agree with the earlier refutation of H-part2-25 on this point, so that part of the candidate is not a new mistake. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Nothing downstream changes.

issues.correction: The identity should read H^*_χ(Y_1(Q_N), O/ϖ^n)^∨_𝔪 ≃ H_{∗,χ^{-1}}(Y_1(Q_N), O/ϖ^n)_{𝔪^∗}, i.e. homology with coefficients in O(χ)^∨ = O(χ^{-1}). issues.reason:
Checked on the page images at PDF pp. 116, 129, 130 and 131, and at arXiv v2 p. 95.

1. The paper's definition (§9.1, p. 412) is H_{i,ψ}(Y_i(Q), O) := H_i(Y_i(Q), O(ψ)). Here a section of O(ψ) is an f on π^{-1}(U) with f(γu) = ψ(γ)f(u). So "H_{∗,χ}" means homology with coefficients in O(χ) itself, not in its dual.

2. Recomputation. Let A = O/ϖ^n, which is self-injective. Let C = C_*(Ỹ), a finite free Z[Γ]-complex (via Borel–Serre), and M the monodromy module. Then Hom_A(Hom_{Z[Γ]}(C, M), A) ≅ C ⊗_{Z[Γ]} Hom_A(M, A), and Hom_A(−, A) is exact. So H^i(Y, L)^∨ ≅ H_i(Y, L^∨) canonically. The transpose of T(g) is T(g^{−1}), which gives 𝔪 ↦ 𝔪^∗. Sections g with g(γu) = χ(γ)^{−1}g(u) pair with O(χ) into O, so O(χ)^∨ = O(χ^{−1}). This gives H^*_χ(..)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H_{∗,χ^{−1}}(..)_{𝔪^∗}. Equivalently, the printed right-hand side H_{∗,χ}(..)_{𝔪^∗} is (H^*_{χ^{−1}}(..)_𝔪)^∨.

3. The cited Conjecture B part (4) only covers vanishing outside degrees [q0, q0+l0] and vanishing of boundary cohomology. It cannot turn χ^{−1} into χ.

4. Is the printed isomorphism accidentally true? For n = 2, yes, though not for the reason given. Then χ_{v,2} = χ_{v,1}^{−1}, so χ^{−1} is the Weyl swap of χ. The Iwahori normaliser [[0,1],[ϖ_v,0]] identifies O(χ) with O(wχ) compatibly with Hecke operators away from R. For n ≥ 3 this fails in general. The normaliser only gives cyclic rotations, and a generic tuple of distinct p-power-order characters with trivial product has {χ_i^{−1}} ≠ {χ_i}. So the two sides involve different Bernstein components and inertial types at v: ∏(X−χ_{v,i}) versus ∏(X−χ_{v,i}^{−1}).

5. Where it is used. The proof of Theorem 9.19 (p. 427, first bullet) says the cohomology of D^2_N = D̃^χ_N/ϖ^N computes H^*_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_𝔪, and makes this an R_{S_χ}-module. As printed, D̃^χ_N computes instead the dual of H^*_{χ^{−1}}, which is naturally an R_{S_{χ^{−1}}}-module. So one step of the proof is wrong as printed. The fix is a pure relabelling.

6. The trivial-coefficient analogue on p. 425 is fine. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

On 'affects': I choose "the proof" rather than the candidate's "nothing", because a step of the proof of Theorem 9.19 literally depends on this false identification. No stated result changes: Theorem 9.19 concerns H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪 with trivial coefficients, the χ-side is auxiliary, and the argument survives the relabelling. I tried to defend the printed text, then checked the page images of PDF pp. 116, 117, 129, 130 and 131, and v2 p. 95.

(1) Definitions (p. 412). H_{i,ψ}(Y_i(Q),O) is defined as H_i(Y_i(Q), O(ψ)). Sections of O(ψ) satisfy f(γu) = ψ(γ)f(u). So the subscript χ on H_{∗,χ} means coefficients in O(χ) itself; no convention hides a dual. The pointwise product of an O(ψ)-section and an O(ψ')-section is constant on fibres exactly when ψψ' = 1, so O(χ)^∨ = O(χ^{-1}).

(2) Universal coefficients. A = O/ϖ^n is self-injective, and Hom_A(C_*(Ỹ) ⊗_Γ M, A) = Hom_Γ(C_*(Ỹ), Hom_A(M, A)). This gives H^i(Y, L)^∨ ≅ H_i(Y, L^∨), with T(g) dual to T(g^{-1}), which accounts for 𝔪 ↦ 𝔪^∗. Using Poincaré duality, as in Remark 9.5, still leaves the dual local system. Conjecture B(4) is about vanishing outside degrees [q0, q0+l0] and about the boundary. It cannot change χ^{-1} into χ.

(3) Strongest defence, which works only partly. H^*_χ ≅ H^*_{wχ} holds Hecke-equivariantly away from R for every Weyl permutation w, not just cyclic rotations. The reason is that the Iwahori intertwiners T_s satisfy T_s' T_s = ±q_v, which is a unit because v ∤ p; I checked this numerically for GL_2(F_5). So the printed identity is true whenever {χ_{v,i}^{-1}} = {χ_{v,i}} for every v ∈ R, and in particular always when n = 2, since χ_{v,1}χ_{v,2} = 1. This is not the reason the paper gives. In §8.5.1, however, χ_v is an arbitrary tuple of distinct characters with trivial product. For n ≥ 3 that generally fails the condition. For example, take n = 3, χ_v = (a, a^2, a^{-3}) with a of order p ≥ 5; then {a^{-1}, a^{-2}, a^3} ≠ {a, a^2, a^{-3}}.

(4) Why the printed identity fails in that case. The two sides are Hecke modules of different inertial types, ∏(X−χ_{v,i}) and ∏(X−χ_{v,i}^{-1}) (Conjecture B(3)), and strong multiplicity one separates their rational eigensystems. The printed right-hand side is really (H^*_{χ^{-1}})^∨_𝔪, which is naturally an R_{S^{χ^{-1}}}-module. There is also a semilinear isomorphism through an automorphism σ of O with σχ = χ^{-1}, but it is not O-linear, so it does not rescue the O-linear R^2_∞-structure that patching needs.

(5) Consequences. The only place the paper uses this passage is the proof of Theorem 9.19 (p. 427). There, D^2_N = D̃^χ_N/ϖ^N is said to compute H^*_χ(…)^∨_𝔪, and that identification is used to transport the R_{S^χ_{Q_N}}-action (and hence the R^2_∞ = R^χ_loc[[x]]-action). As printed, that step fails for general χ when n ≥ 3. After relabelling χ to χ^{-1} in the homology, everything goes through: the degree bounds, the minimal complex, and the mod-ϖ identification H^{l0} ≅ H^{l0}_χ, since χ ≡ 1 mod ϖ. Theorem 9.19 concerns H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪 with trivial coefficients, so no stated result changes.

(6) This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The trivial-coefficient analogue on p. 425 is correct.

On classification, I keep 'error' rather than 'misprint'. The subscript χ appears consistently in two displays (the D̃^χ_N definition and the note), and it comes with a justification that does not address the coefficients. So the intended meaning cannot be read off from context; the reader has to redo the duality. I choose 'the proof' rather than the candidate's 'nothing', because a step of the proof as written fails, even though the fix is a relabelling.

issues.printed: p. 426 (PDF p. 130), last bullet: "Let T = T^1 = T^2 be the complex with T^i = H^{i−l_0}(Y, O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪 and with all differentials d : T^i → T^{i+1} equal to 0." p. 427 (PDF p. 131), first bullet: "We introduced above perfect (homological) complexes of S_N-modules D̃_N and D̃^χ_N above; they are concentrated in degrees q_0, …, q_0 + l_0. We now regard these as cohomological complexes concentrated in degrees 0, …, l_0. Then we let D^1_N (resp. D^2_N) denote the perfect complex of S_N-modules D̃_N/ϖ^N (resp. D̃^χ_N/ϖ^N). Note that the cohomology of D^1_N (resp. D^2_N) computes H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_𝔪 (resp. H^*_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_𝔪), after a shift in degree by q_0. issues.correction: T^i = H^{q_0+l_0−i}(Y, O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪 for 0 ≤ i ≤ l_0, with zero differentials, so that T^{l_0} = H^{q_0}(Y, O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H/ϖ. Turning the homological complex D̃_N, which sits in degrees q_0, …, q_0+l_0, into a cohomological complex in degrees 0, …, l_0 means taking D^i = D̃_{q_0+l_0−i}. This is a reflection, not a shift by q_0. Hence H^i(D^1_N) ≅ H^{q_0+l_0−i}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_𝔪, and likewise for D^2_N with H_χ. The same slip occurs in the display at the bottom of p. 427 (also in v2). There, "H^{l_0}((D^1_M)^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ) = H^{l_0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^□ ≅ H^{l_0}_χ(…)^□" should read H^{q_0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^{∨,□}_𝔪 ≅ H^{q_0}_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^{∨,□}_𝔪.
issues.reason: I checked this against the page images at 250 dpi and against the paper's own requirements. (1) Theorem 6.3(3) (p. 344) requires T to live in degrees 0, …, l_0 with d = 0 and H^{l_0}(T) ≅ H/ϖ. Here H = H^{q_0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪. Conjecture B(4)(a) says localized cohomology vanishes outside degrees [q_0, q_0+l_0], so H^{q_0−1}(Y, K/O)_𝔪 = 0. With the long exact sequence for 0 → O/ϖ → K/O → K/O → 0 this gives H/ϖ ≅ H^{q_0}(Y, O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪. (2) As printed, T^i = H^{i−l_0}(…)^∨ is nonzero only when q_0 ≤ i−l_0 ≤ q_0+l_0, that is, for i between q_0+l_0 and q_0+2l_0. In the required range 0 ≤ i ≤ l_0 the degree i−l_0 runs from −l_0 to 0, where this cohomology vanishes (q_0 ≥ 1 for n ≥ 2). So the printed T is 0 in degrees 0, …, l_0. That contradicts both T^{l_0} ≅ H/ϖ ≠ 0 and D^i_N ⊗ k ≅ T, since D̃_N ⊗ k has zero differentials and homology H_c(Y, k) ≅ H^c(Y, k)^∨_𝔪. The printed formula also increases in i where it should decrease, so no reading of it works. (3) D̃_N is homological, with d: D_c → D_{c−1}. Re-indexing it cohomologically with increasing differentials forces i = const − c, so it cannot be a shift. The paper's own claim that condition (c) is clear needs H^{l_0}(D^1_N ⊗ O/ϖ^n) ≅ H/ϖ^n = H_{q_0}. So homological degree q_0, the cokernel end, must become cohomological degree l_0, the top degree, as Lemma 6.2 and Theorem 6.3(i) require. That gives i = q_0+l_0−c, exactly as the candidate says. A plain shift by q_0 would put H^{q_0+l_0} in degree l_0, which is wrong. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The candidate's quotation and locators are right (§9.5, proof of Theorem 9.19, p. 426 and p. 427; same in v2). The fix is purely notational: with the corrected T and indexing, every hypothesis of Proposition 6.6 and Theorem 6.3 holds as the authors intend, and nothing later uses the printed indexing. Theorem 9.19 and its consequences (Theorem 5.16) are unaffected, so 'affects: nothing' is right.

issues.correction: Add a condition to the choice. For each N, choose the surjections R^1_∞ = R^1_loc⟦x_1,…,x_g⟧ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}} and R^2_∞ = R^χ_loc⟦x_1,…,x_g⟧ ↠ R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}} so that their reductions mod ϖ agree. They must agree under the fixed N-independent isomorphism R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ (Lemma 8.2(2) with x_i ↦ x_i) and the isomorphism R^□_{S_{Q_N}}/ϖ ≅ R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}}/ϖ (the global rings agree mod ϖ, and the representatives agree mod ϖ). Such a choice exists. Take any surjection on side 1 as in Prop. 8.5(4); it is an R^1_loc-algebra map. On side 2, use the natural map R^χ_loc → R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}}, which reduces mod ϖ to the side-1 map. Send each x_i to any lift of the image of x_i mod ϖ. The resulting map is surjective mod ϖ, so it is surjective by complete Nakayama, since it is surjective on reduced cotangent spaces. Strictly, only equality of the induced actions on H^{l_0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M),O/ϖ)^□ is needed, and this choice is a sufficient way to get it. (Separately, the actions on H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M),…) should come from R_{S_{Q_M}} and R^i_∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_M}}; the printed index is Q_N, which is an index misprint.)
issues.reason:
Proposition 6.6 (p. 390) needs, for each M ≥ N, an isomorphism H^{l0}(D^1_M⊗S_N/ϖ) ⥲ H^{l0}(D^2_M⊗S_N/ϖ) that becomes an isomorphism of R^1_∞⊗_O S^□_N/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞⊗_O S^□_N/ϖ-modules. The ring identification is the fixed one from the first bullet, and it must work at every level for the patching to go through.

In the proof of Theorem 9.19, the R^i_∞-actions come from the chosen surjections R^i_∞ ↠ R^□. The paper makes the framings agree mod ϖ but puts no condition on these surjections: it just says "we can and do choose". It then states without argument that the isomorphisms are compatible with the R^i_∞-actions.

That statement fails for some choices the text allows. Take g ≥ 1, which is the usual case since q can be taken large. Let f^1, f^2 be a compatible pair, and change f^2 to x_1 ↦ f^2(x_1) + z_1^2. Since z_1^2 lies in m^2, the new map still hits generators of the cotangent space, so it is still a surjection as Proposition 8.5 provides. Here j = n^2|T|−1 ≥ 1. On H^{l0}(...)^□ ⊗ k = H⊗k[[z_1,…,z_j]], a nonzero free k[[z]]-module, the element z_1^2 acts injectively. So x_1 acts differently on the two sides by the nonzero operator z_1^2, and the required equivariance fails.

The other ingredients do match mod ϖ. The maps R^1_loc → R^□_{S_Q} and R^χ_loc → R^□_{S^χ_Q} both come from restricting the same mod-ϖ framed deformation. The Hecke/Galois actions on H(O/ϖ) ≅ H_χ(O/ϖ) agree by Carayol/Chebotarev. So the only missing condition is compatibility of the images of the x_i. The authors took this care for the framings ("agree modulo ϖ") but not for the surjections.

This is an omitted but necessary condition behind an asserted step, so it is a gap. It is easily repaired by the Nakayama argument above, and Theorem 9.19 stays true. Prop. 6.6 (p. 390) takes as input one fixed isomorphism R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ. It also needs, for each M ≥ N, isomorphisms H^{l_0}((D^1_M)^□⊗S_N/ϖ) ⥲ H^{l_0}((D^2_M)^□⊗S_N/ϖ) "of R^1_∞⊗S^□_N/ϖ ⥲ R^2_∞⊗S^□_N/ϖ-modules". In the proof of Thm 9.19, R^i_∞ acts on these groups only through the chosen surjections R^i_∞ ↠ R^□ followed by Conjecture B. The paper fixes the representatives so that they agree mod ϖ, but it puts no condition on the surjections: it says only "By Proposition 8.5, we can and do choose surjections". Prop. 8.5(4) says only that R^□ is a quotient of R_loc⟦x_1,…,x_g⟧, a non-canonical choice made separately on each side and for each N.

The R_loc part is compatible automatically, because the natural maps R^1_loc → R^□_S and R^χ_loc → R^□_{S^χ} agree mod ϖ. The images of the x_i are free. For example, swap the images of x_1 and x_2 on side 2 only, or add to one of them a non-zero element mod ϖ of the maximal ideal. Both give valid surjections, but then x_1 acts differently on the two sides, and the Hecke/z-module H^{l_0}(…)^□ does not generally make the two actions agree. So the claim "These isomorphisms are compatible with the actions of R^i_∞" does not follow from the choices as stated.

Defences tried:
- The "natural" isomorphism R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ cannot be adjusted per N to absorb the mismatch, because Prop. 6.6 fixes it independently of N.
- Nothing nearby in the paper supplies the condition. A search for "compatib" finds no such statement, and the Correction (Invent. Math. 227) is only about brackets.
- A charitable reader would read "we can and do choose" as meaning a compatible choice, and that choice is easy to make (see correction). So this is a small omitted condition plus an unjustified compatibility claim, not a false result.

The step matters. The compatibility is exactly what gives the R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ-module isomorphism H^{l_0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ ≅ H^{l_0}(P^2_∞)/ϖ on p. 428. That isomorphism, with [11, Lemma 2.2] and Lemma 8.2, gives near-faithfulness over R^1_∞, and then over R_S by Prop. 6.3(iv). Theorem 9.19 in turn gives Theorem 5.16 ("This theorem will follow immediately from Theorem 9.19") and hence Theorem 1.1. With the compatible choice described above, the proof goes through, so no stated result is affected.

On the candidate's correction: it is right and essentially minimal, except that "Only with this choice" overstates it. Agreement of the maps mod ϖ is sufficient, while what is necessary is only agreement of the induced actions.

issues.correction: H^{l_0}((D^1_M)^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ) = (e_{Q_M} H^{q_0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪)^□ →(∼) (e_{Q_M} H^{q_0}_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪)^□ = H^{l_0}((D^2_M)^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ). Here e_{Q_M} = lim_n (∏_{x∈Q_M} Q_x(V_x))^{n!} is the projector from the definition of D̃_M on p. 425. Equivalently, the middle terms are (e_{Q_M} H_{q_0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)_{𝔪*})^□ and its χ-version. So the degree l0 on Y should be q0, and the dual and the localization at 𝔪 are missing.
issues.reason:
1) Conventions. D̃_N is a homological complex of S_N-modules, built in §7.1 from singular chains (Lemmas 7.1–7.4). It lives in degrees q0..q0+l0, and on p. 425 H_i(D̃_N ⊗ S_M/ϖ^n) ≅ (projector) H_i(Y_{Δ_M}(Q_N), O/ϖ^n)_{𝔪*}. Section 6 needs a cohomological complex in degrees 0..l0 that resolves its top cohomology (Lemma 6.2; Theorem 6.3(i)). So the reindexing has to send homological degree q0+l0−i to cohomological degree i. Top cohomological degree l0 is then the lowest homological degree q0: H^{l0}(D ⊗ S_N/ϖ) = e H_{q0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)_𝔪 = e H^{q0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪.
2) The paper's own data force this. In the proof it sets H^1 = H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪. Theorem 6.3(3),(c) requires H^{l0}(T) ≅ H/ϖ and H^{l0}(D^1_N ⊗ O/ϖ^n) ≅ H^1/ϖ^n. With H^{q0−1}(Y, K/O)_𝔪 = 0, H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪/ϖ^n = H^{q0}(Y, O/ϖ^n)^∨_𝔪. The final line of the proof also reads off H^1 = H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪 from conclusion (iv).
3) The printed middle term H^{l0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^□ is literally cohomology of Y in degree l0, with no dual and no localization. In general l0 ≠ q0: for PGL_2 over a totally real field, l0 = 0 and q0 = [F:Q]; for PGL_3 over Q, l0 = 1 and q0 = 2. So the first and last equalities are false as printed. Even reading "after a shift in degree by q0" as a plain shift does not rescue it, because that would give degree q0+l0.
4) Why it is only a misprint. H^* and H^*_χ with O/ϖ coefficients agree in every degree, Hecke-equivariantly, because χ ≡ 1 mod ϖ and the primes in R are disjoint from Q_M. So the corrected isomorphism in degree q0 holds, and it is exactly the input Proposition 6.6 needs. With q0 in place of l0 the argument goes through unchanged. Theorem 9.19, and through it Theorem 5.16 and Theorem 1.1, are not affected.
5) The candidate's correction is right. Adding the ^□ and the Q_M-projector (the complex is D̃_M, built with Q = Q_M) matches the definition on p. 425. This is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. The same l0/q0 slip in T^i = H^{i−l0}(Y, O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪 on p. 426 (should be H^{q0+l0−i}) supports the diagnosis and may deserve its own item.

I checked this against the page image and against how the paper uses these objects.
(1) What the cohomology is: on p. 425, Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M) is the Δ_N-subcover of Y_1(Q_M) → Y_0(Q_M). Here Q_M is its own set of Taylor–Wiles primes, chosen separately for each M via Prop. 8.5. The display on p. 427 identifies H^{l0}((D^1_M)^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ) with H^{l0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^□, so this is level-Q_M cohomology.
(2) Conjecture B (§9.3) gives a surjection R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,𝔪} for the same Q as the level. It comes from a Galois representation r_𝔪 that is unramified outside S_Q and of type D_v at v ∈ Q. So Conjecture B makes R_{S_{Q_M}} act on the level-Q_M cohomology. It gives no action of R_{S_{Q_N}}: that ring classifies deformations unramified outside S ∪ Q_N, and Q_N and Q_M are different prime sets.
(3) As printed the statement is not even well defined. The text allows N = 0, but Q_N is only defined for N ≥ 1 ("For each integer N ≥ 1, let Q_N be a set of primes..."), so R_{S_{Q_0}} makes no sense.

Its ψ must be an R_∞-isomorphism with H/ϖ^N, where R_∞ acts via φ_M; condition (c) says the same. So the R_∞-action on H^*(D_M ⊗ S_N/ϖ^n) has to factor through the level-M surjection R^i_∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_M}}, which defines φ^i_M. The earlier patching arguments are consistent with this: p. ~2111 of the text says "via φ_N and the map R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,𝔪}" for level-Q_N modules.
This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and it is the same in v2.
A small fix to the candidate's transcription: the resp. surjection is printed as R^2_∞ ↠ R_{S^χ_{Q_N}}, without the □.
The candidate cites "Theorem 6.3(b)". Condition (b) itself only asks for an R_∞-action. The compatibility with φ_M comes from (c) (take the N = 0 case of (b)) and from how D_{M,N} is built in the proof, so the candidate's reasoning holds with that citation adjusted.

issues.reason: I rendered PDF pp. 132–133 and confirmed the text. The mismatch is real: the bullet assumes N_2 > n, while the next paragraph and condition (4) use N_2 > n + 1. The deeper problem is that "N_2 > n + 1" is copied from [76] = BLGHT II without changing its n. I checked a local copy of BLGHT II (cy2fin.pdf). Its Theorem 6.4 reads: "n is an even positive integer ... l + 1 = N_1N_2 ... Suppose that N_2 > n + 1" with "r : Gal(F̄/F) → GSp_n(Z_l)". So n there is the dimension of r. The proof then says "apply the results of section 4 with N = N_2". Section 4 starts: "Let N > n + 1 denote positive integers with n even and N odd", and by Lemma 4.1 the piece V_λ has rank n. So the candidate is right that the text is inconsistent, but wrong that the fix is N_2 > n + 1 and that nothing is affected. The repair is routine: N_2 can be taken as large as needed, since p, or A and p in the general case, are chosen freely via Moret–Bailly/Chebotarev. It is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. A side note: BLGHT also needs N_2 odd and prime to S, where S contains 2. CG only says "prime to the conductor of A", which is another imprecision in this sketch.

issues.correction:
The minimal repair is to the reduction sentence. Replace "it suffices ... to prove that for each n, there exists a p such that r is potentially modular" by: "it suffices to show that for each n there is a finite Galois extension L/K such that ρ and Sym^{2n−1}ρ are both modular over every L′ with K ⊂ L′ ⊂ L and L/L′ soluble."
- The simultaneous statement for {ρ, Sym^{2n−1}ρ} comes from the same argument, applying Moret–Bailly (Prop. 6.2 of [76]) to the product of the two moduli schemes. This is the device of HSBT Thm 3.2/4.1 with a finite set N, and of the remark after BLGHT II Thm 8.1.
- Modularity over soluble subfields follows from Arthur–Clozel cyclic descent (AC Thm 4.2, which holds over any number field). The right twist is fixed by the Galois representations attached to regular algebraic cuspidal π over arbitrary number fields ([7], [8]).
- HSBT's Brauer + Rankin–Selberg computation (Jacquet–Shalika, Shahidi, Gelbart–Jacquet) then works unchanged over any K.

Item (5) should also refer to the p-adic representations: r|G_L and the λ′-adic V_{λ′,t}, whose reductions are r̄|G_L and r̄′|G_L. The candidate's proposed correction is broadly right but is a to-do list rather than a minimal fix. It misses the need for simultaneity, and its point about the CM case is not an error.

I checked the page images for PDF pp. 132–133 and pp. 87–88 (Theorem 5.16). I also downloaded HSBT (Annals 171) and BLGHT (Taylor's cy2fin.pdf) and read the cited proofs.

(1) What the cited argument actually uses. HSBT Theorem 4.2's proof says: "Apply Theorem 4.1 with N = {2, m+1}. Let F′/F be as in the conclusion ... Then (A,i) × F_j is automorphic arising from ... π_j of GL_2(A_{F_j}), and Symm^m(A,i) × F_j is automorphic arising from ... Π_j of GL_{m+1}(A_{F_j})". It then uses the Rankin–Selberg product π_j × Π_j to get L(Sym^{m+1})L(Sym^{m−1}, s−1). HSBT Theorem 4.1 gives automorphy of all n ∈ N simultaneously over one Galois F′, and over "any intermediate field F′ ⊃ F″ ⊃ F with F′/F″ soluble", via CHT Lemma 4.3.2, which is for totally real fields. This is how HSBT get the even symmetric powers from odd-dimensional-rep (odd-m) potential automorphy.

(2) What CG reduce to. CG reduce only to "for each n, there exists a p such that r [= Sym^{2n−1}] is potentially modular". That is individual potential modularity, with p and the field depending on n. It says nothing about a common field for Sym^1 and Sym^{2n−1}, and nothing about soluble intermediate fields. Remark 10.1 confirms that even symmetric powers are not handled directly.

(3) The reduction is not just unexplained; the stated input is too weak for the cited route. Suppose each odd Sym^a is automorphic over its own field. Brauer induction plus Rankin–Selberg of Π_a with itself then gives only two kinds of fact: every odd Sym^a, and the products L(Sym^2)L(Sym^4)⋯L(Sym^{2a}). The measure (1 + c(χ_4 − χ_6))·μ_ST with c = 0.05 is positive (minimum density 0.9) and is not μ_ST, where χ_k = tr Sym^k. Yet I checked numerically that it gives mean 0 to every χ_odd, to χ_2, and to every sum Σ_{k≤a} χ_{2k} with a odd. So those facts cannot force Sato–Tate. The simultaneous version is needed, and the paper neither states nor proves it. Over an arbitrary K, the soluble descent HSBT rely on is also not available off the shelf. Neither point is addressed.

(4) Both points can be filled by standard means. BLGHT remark after Thm 8.1: "one simply chooses F′ so that the schemes ... simultaneously have F′ rational points". Descent works via Arthur–Clozel plus the Galois representations from Conjecture B. So the stated result is not in doubt, but the proof as written has a gap.

The candidate's reason overstates some things. The representations are stated. Item (5)'s r̄ notation is a slip. Theorem 5.16(6) asks for N(x) ≡ 1 mod p only where r ramifies and r̄ does not, which can be arranged. The CM dismissal is standard. Its core point about the Brauer/Sato–Tate reduction over arbitrary K is right, and (1)–(3) sharpen it. Potential modularity, part (1), is the n = 1 case and is not affected. Defence first.

**Points where the paper is standard practice, not wrong**
- **CM case.** "If A has CM, then the result is well known" copies BLGHT II Cor. 8.8 word for word ("If E is CM then the result is well known. If E is not CM it follows from the previous theorem as in the proof of 4.2 of [HSBT]"). CM Sato–Tate goes back to Hecke and Deuring. The separate cuspidality issue is candidate C-K10-4.
- **Arbitrary K.** "[81] is totally real" is not fatal. HSBT's descent step (CHT Lemma 4.3.2, BLGHT Lemma 1.3) is AC Thm 4.2 descent plus a twist fixed by attached Galois representations, and both exist over any number field.
- **Moret–Bailly.** BLGHT Prop. 6.2 is stated for an arbitrary number field and yields a Galois F′/F.
- **Construction details.** These can be carried out routinely:
  - put l′ in S2 using t ≡ 0, so that V_{λ′,t} is crystalline and l′ is unramified in L, as Thm 5.16 needs where BLGHT used the ordinary Thm 2.3;
  - choose M cyclic, so automorphic induction over L exists;
  - kill the auxiliary ramification at q locally while staying linearly disjoint, so bigness survives;
  - get condition (6) and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p by a soluble base change unramified at p (the remark after Thm 5.16).
- **Item (5).** It loosely names residual representations, but the next sentence makes clear that the λ′-adic V and the λ-adic Sym^{2n−1}(A) are meant.

**What is genuinely missing**
I checked HSBT (Annals text, Thms 4.1–4.2). Thm 4.1: "There is a Galois totally real field F′/F such that for any n ∈ N and any intermediate field F′ ⊃ F′′ ⊃ F with F′/F′′ soluble, Symm^{n−1} A is automorphic over F′′." The proof of Thm 4.2 then says "Apply Theorem 4.1 with N = {2, m+1}". So it needs Sym^1 and Sym^m modular over one common Galois field, and over all its soluble subfields, for the Rankin–Selberg identity L(Sym^{m+1})L(Sym^{m−1}) = ∏ L(σ_j×π_j⊗χ_j)^{a_j}.

CG's reduction, "for each n ... r is potentially modular", treats each n separately. On that route, separate information does not suffice:
- Using only Sym^{2n−1} over its own field, Rankin–Selberg π_j×π_j^∨ controls only sums of consecutive even powers: χ_2, then χ_4+χ_6, then χ_8+χ_10, and so on.
- The measure μ(1+ε(χ_4−χ_6)) satisfies every one of those constraints, so they do not pin down the Sato–Tate measure.

So the step "it suffices" is asserted with a citation whose proof uses a stronger input that CG never states. The candidate's own descent point is real but routine.

**Consequences**
§10 is the last section, and nothing later uses it (Remark 10.1 only). Theorem 1.1 (conditional on Conjecture B) is not in doubt, since every repair is standard. Hence affects = the proof. Related slips in the same sketch are recorded separately: the N_2 bound (H-part2-32) and the p/q swap (H-part2-31).

The special-case argument for A then runs at p, with the auxiliary prime l, and never uses a 'mod-q representation' of A. The final step applies Theorem 5.16 at p to r = Sym^{2n−1}ρ_{E,p} over L′, as its hypotheses in (1) indicate. Its hypothesis (8)(a) (p. 383) needs an automorphic π_0 with good reduction at p whose p-adic representation reduces to Sym^{2n−1}ρ̄_{E,p}. Nothing supplies one, because A is tied to E only mod q.
(b) Reading 2: transfer through E[q] ≃ A[q] and apply 5.16 at q. Then (1) is at the wrong prime, and so are 'unramified at p' and 'at the prime at p'. Theorem 5.16 needs the prime to be unramified in the base field (p. 382), and nothing makes L′ unramified at q.
(c) q is not a power of p: (2) and (3) treat q as a second prime.
So no faithful reading makes the printed hypotheses support the printed final step.

Why it is a misprint. The intended argument is clear and standard (as in BLGHT II §6), and either relabelling makes every step work. Take the minimal fix. By Proposition 6.2 of [76] applied to the twisted modular curve X_{E[p]} ('twists of a modular curve'), pick A with A[p] ≅ E[p] which is special at q. The special case then gives Sym^{2n−1}(A) automorphic over some L′ unramified at p. Moret–Bailly can impose splitting at p. So Sym^{2n−1}ρ_{A,p}|_{G_{L′}} is an automorphic lift of Sym^{2n−1}ρ̄_{E,p}|_{G_{L′}} with good reduction at p, since A has good reduction at p by (2). That is (8)(a) for Theorem 5.16 at p, and the other hypotheses come from (1) and are preserved over L′. X-K10-14's side remark is also right: if A were special at p and E[p] ≅ A[p], then E would already be special at p over L and A would be pointless. That confirms the congruence prime and the special prime must differ.

Consequences. The passage is the last step of the paper's final proof. Nothing later uses it (Remark 10.1 and the references follow). The statement of Theorem 1.1, which is conditional on Conjecture B, is unaffected. The printed proof fails as written: its final application of Theorem 5.16 lacks its residual-modularity input. It is restored by relabelling alone, so kind = misprint (H-part2-31 said error) and affects = the proof (X-K10-14 said nothing). 'Nothing' is arguable, since the mathematics as intended is right. I chose 'the proof' because the slip swaps the logical roles of the two primes across three hypotheses, rather than being a local typo in one symbol.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 7.1, p.41 (choice of η_v at finite places) (arXiv v2; published Annals version not collated)
issues.printed: "At each non-archimedean place v of K, we set η_v := min{1, |t₁(t₁ − 1)|_v, |t₂(t₂ − 1)|_v}. … (µ_{t_i,v}, m_{F,η,v})_v = (µ_{t_i,v}, [F]_v)_v for this choice of η, because the potentials for µ_{t_i,v} are constant on disks of radius η_v."
issues.correction: At places v | 2 take η_v := |2|_v · min{1, |t₁(t₁ − 1)|_v, |t₂(t₂ − 1)|_v}. The claim is then true: in the potentially good range the support of µ_{t,v} is a type II point of diameter |Δ_t|_v^{1/6} = |2|_v^{2/3}|t(t − 1)|_v^{1/3} ≥ |2|_v min{1, |t(t − 1)|_v}, and in the bad-reduction ranges of Proposition 3.5 smaller radii are harmless. (7.5) grows by Σ_{v|2} r_v log 2 = log 2, which is divided by 2|F| and absorbed into C(ε).
issues.reason: The claim fails at v | 2 when |t_i(t_i − 1)|_v = 1. There η_v = 1, but µ_{t_i,v} is a point mass at ζ_{a,R} with R < 1. Indeed λ_{t,v}(0) = λ_{t,v}(ζ_{0,1}) = 0 and f_t(ζ_{0,1}) = ζ_{0,1/|4|}, so the support lies in a residue class of ζ_{0,1} other than that of 0. For x ∈ D(a,R), λ(ζ_{x,1}) − λ(x) = log(1/R) > 0, so the non-archimedean term of Proposition 7.3 is positive, not 0. Counterexample: take ω a primitive cube root of 1 and t₁ ≠ t₂ the roots of t² − (6ω² − 4)t − (3ω − 4) = 0 (discriminant 48ω(1 − ω) ≠ 0). Then ψ₃(ω, t_i) = 0, so x = ω ∈ π(E_{t₁}[3]) ∩ π(E_{t₂}[3]) ⊆ F. Also t₁t₂ = 4 − 3ω and (t₁ − 1)(t₂ − 1) = 15 + 3ω are 2-adic units, so |t_i(t_i − 1)|_v = 1 and η_v = 1. The reduction is supersingular (|j(t_i)|_v ≤ |2|^8), so the 3-torsion reduces to non-identity points and x ∈ D(a_i, R_i). The bound therefore acquires a positive term that is not divided by |F|, which would break the small-height case of Theorem 8.1. With the corrected η_v the equality holds and all later statements stand.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 1.4, p.36 (arXiv v3; published Annals version not collated)
issues.printed: "By the Northcott property and Torelli's Theorem, there are up-to Q̄-isomophism only finitely many C_Q̄'s … such that h(ι([Jac(C_Q̄)])) < c1. By applying Raynaud's result on the Manin–Mumford Conjecture to each one of these finitely many curves separately, we obtain Theorem 1.4."
issues.correction: For each of the finitely many curves C a bound for #((C − P₀) ∩ Jac(C)_tors) uniform in P₀ ∈ C(ℚ̄) is needed, because Theorem 1.4 quantifies over all P₀. For g ≥ 3 it follows from Raynaud's theorem for the surface C − C ⊆ Jac(C): its torsion lies in finitely many points and elliptic torsion cosets, and a coset t + E pulls back to a curve in C × C with no component C × {P₀}, so each P₀ meets it in boundedly many points. For g = 2, C − C = Jac(C), and a uniform Manin–Mumford for the translates C − P₀ is required, e.g. Kühne's later uniform Manin–Mumford theorem (arXiv:2101.10272), which proves Theorem 1.4 without the dependence on d.
issues.reason: Raynaud's theorem gives, for each embedding C − P₀ ⊆ Jac(C), a finite set, with no control of its size as P₀ varies over the infinitely many points of C(ℚ̄). The statement is true, but the displayed step does not prove it.

issues.printed: "Remark. It is also possible to give an upper bound for ℓ_A. For example, Eichler [17] gave a general argument that yields for the modular group that ℓ_A < c log ε_D for an explicit c."
issues.correction: No bound ℓ_A ≪ log ε_D holds uniformly. ℓ_A can be about √D while log ε_D is about log D. Eichler's argument bounds the word length of the geometric code of the closed geodesic, which is a different quantity from ℓ_A.
issues.reason: Take a odd with a² + 4 squarefree, for example a = 13 or 101 (D = 173 or 10205 = 5·13·157). Then D = a² + 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8) is a fundamental discriminant, and a² + 4 is squarefree for a positive proportion of a. For the principal class, (a + √D)/2 has regular continued fraction [a; a, a, …]. A regular partial quotient a in an odd position becomes a run of a − 1 twos in the minus continued fraction, so the reduced period is ((a + 2, 2, …, 2)) with a − 1 twos, and ℓ_A = a. Meanwhile ε_D = ((a + √D)/2)² = (a² + 2 + a√D)/2, so log ε_D ≈ 2 log a, and ℓ_A / log ε_D → ∞. A direct computation for a = 5, 7, 13, 21, 51, 101, 201, 401 gives ℓ_A = a. In each case the product of the reduced w over the period equals ε_D, as in (6.3), which confirms that ℓ_A is the paper's quantity. The remark is not used elsewhere in the paper.
issues.known: Partly: P. Humphries and A. C. Nordentoft, "Sparse equidistribution of geometric invariants of real quadratic fields", arXiv 2211.05890v2 (28 August 2025), Remark 3.22, observe that Eichler's argument bounds the geometric code of the geodesic and not ℓ_A (the arithmetic code), so the remark is unsupported. They do not show that the bound fails. The counterexample family here is new.

issues.correction: State (6.6) for the unit vector u = φ/‖φ‖: Weyl(u, χ) ≪_ε r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}. It follows from Theorem 4 and [12, Theorem 5] together with the Rankin–Selberg size of ‖φ‖ for the normalization a(1) = 1. It is also what the proof of Theorem 2 uses, since c(φ)⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ = ⟨f, u⟩u.
issues.reason: The forms φ are normalized by a(1) = 1 in (5.7), p.962, and the Shimura relation in Theorem 4 forces this too. [12, Theorem 5] (Duke 1988, p.85, read on the page image) bounds the coefficients of a spectral weight-1/2 form with eigenvalue 1/4 + t² by |λ|^A ch(πt/2)|n|^{−2/7+ε}. Here t = r/2, so Theorem 4 gives |Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ)| ≪ r^C cosh²(πr/4)|D|^{3/4−2/7+ε}. That bound has an exponential factor, which (6.6) omits. The factor cannot simply be dropped. For a(1) = 1, Rankin–Selberg unfolding gives ⟨φ, φ⟩ ≍ L(1, sym²φ)/cosh(πr), so ⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ is about e^{πr/2} times the unit vector u. As printed, (6.6) would therefore make the Weyl integrals of u exponentially small in r, which the cited results do not give. For u the two exponentials cancel: Weyl(u, χ) = ‖φ‖ Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) ≪ L(1, sym²φ)^{1/2} r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}, and L(1, sym²φ) ≪ r^ε. The coefficient bound "c(φ) ≪ |r|^{−A}" used for Theorem 2 on p.969 holds for u, so Theorem 2 stands. Noted by the extraction ("The spectral norm gate").

issues.locator: Published p. 106, the last display of the introduction; compare §7, p. 148
issues.printed: An irreducible flat connection (E,∇) with torsion determinant L is called cohomologically rigid, if [(E,∇)] is a reduced isolated point of M_dR(X,L,r). This is equivalent to vanishing of  H¹_dR(X,(End(E),∇)) = 0,  and hence explains the nomenclature.

("equivalent to vanishing of … = 0" is also one "vanishing" too many.)
issues.reason: M_dR(X,L,r) is the moduli of connections with the determinant fixed, so its Zariski tangent space at an irreducible point is H¹_dR(X,End⁰(E,∇)) — which is exactly what p. 148 says. In characteristic zero the trace splitting gives End(E) = End⁰(E) ⊕ O_X as flat bundles, so H¹_dR(X,(End(E),∇)) = H¹_dR(X,End⁰(E,∇)) ⊕ H¹_dR(X,(O_X,d)) and the second summand is H¹(X,C), of dimension b₁(X). For every X with b₁(X) > 0 — every curve of positive genus, and every variety the paper is really about — the printed condition therefore holds for no connection at all, and the notion it defines would be empty. Read on the rendered page: the display carries an underlined "End" with no superscript.

The invariant that is canonical is the one the proof has just built: the characteristic polynomial of the Morita-reduced Higgs sheaf π′_*F, which is independent of the splitting because F is unique up to unique isomorphism. Theorem 2.17 should require of M that this reduced invariant equal a, rather than only that M be supported on Z′_a with π′_*M of characteristic polynomial a^{p^d}; the descent of a should be deduced from that canonicity, not from uniqueness of p^d-th roots.

Witness for the two printed claims (r=2): let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, Z′ an elliptic curve over k with a nowhere-vanishing ω ∈ H⁰(Z′,Ω¹), and S = Spec k[ε]/(ε²). issues.locator: Definition 5.2, published p. 139, together with Lemma 5.6 and its proof, p. 141
issues.printed: One denotes by Def_ϱ: Art_F → Sets the functor sending a finite-dimensional commutative local F-algebra A to the set of isomorphism classes of continuous representations ϱ′: Γ→GL(r,A), such that there exists a finite field extension F′/F, an F-morphism A→F′, and an isomorphism (ϱ′)_{F′}≃ϱ_{F′}. We say that ϱ is rigid, if Def_ϱ is corepresented by B∈Art_F. … [Lemma 5.6, proof:] This shows that Def_ϱ̂(F_q) is represented by the formal scheme which is the formal completion of M_B(X/C,det(ϱ),r)⊗_Z F_p at the point [ϱ].
issues.correction: Def_ϱ must be the fixed-determinant deformation functor — the same convention as everywhere else in the paper — namely the isomorphism classes of continuous ϱ′ with det ϱ′ = det ϱ. Otherwise Definition 5.2 does not define the notion Lemma 5.6 and Theorem 5.4 use.
issues.reason: As literally defined the functor is the unrestricted one, and it is never corepresented by an Artinian algebra once b₁(X) > 0. Twisting ϱ′ = ϱ⊗χ by a continuous character χ: Γ → 1+m_A is a deformation of ϱ for every A ∈ Art_F, and for p > r distinct characters give non-isomorphic twists (an isomorphism ϱ⊗χ ≅ ϱ forces χ^r = 1 on determinants, and 1+m_A is a p-group). The character functor A ↦ Hom_cont(Γ,1+m_A) is corepresented by the completed group algebra F_q[[Γ^ab ⊗ Z_p]] ≅ F_q[[x_1,…,x_b]] with b = b₁(X), so it acts freely on Def_ϱ and forces the hull of Def_ϱ to have dimension at least b₁(X). For X a curve of genus g ⩾ 1 no absolutely irreducible ϱ would then be rigid, and Lemma 5.6 — whose right-hand side is the completion of the moduli space M_B(X/C,det(ϱ),r) with the determinant fixed — would be false. With the fixed-determinant reading both statements are correct and this is plainly what is meant.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition A.2, published p. 154, lines 12–14
issues.printed: On the other hand, m^*θ−r^*θ ∈ Ker(H⁰((Z′_a)_p, Ω¹_{(Z′_a)_p/Spec k[t]/(t−1)^p}) → H⁰(Z′_a, Ω¹_{Z′_a})). Thus, m^*θ−r^*θ has support in Z′_p ↪ T^*Z ×_k G′_m, where Z′ ↪ T^*Z′ is the zero-section.
issues.correction: The support assertion does not follow and is false as stated. What has to be established is that the class φ(m^*θ−r^*θ) is pulled back from a neighbourhood of the zero section on which D_{Z′} splits — a Brauer-class computation, not a support statement. The symbol Z′_p also has to be disambiguated: Remark A.1 defines V_n = V ×_k Spec k[t]/(t−1)^n, a thickening in the group direction, whereas the appeal to [OV, Corollary 2.9] in the last line needs the infinitesimal neighbourhood of the zero section inside T^*Z′. ("T^*Z ×_k G′_m" is a misprint for T^*Z′ ×_k G_m.)
issues.reason: m is the conic action, so m^*θ = tθ and r^*θ = θ and hence m^*θ − r^*θ = (t−1)θ. Writing ε = t−1, which satisfies ε^p = 0 on (Z′_a)_p, and θ = ξ dx in local coordinates, the section is εξ dx. It does lie in the displayed kernel, because it dies at ε = 0; but it is non-zero at every point where ξ is invertible and ε^{p−1} ≠ 0, so its support is the closure of the locus where θ ≠ 0, not a thickening of the zero-section {ξ = 0}. The two thickenings occurring in the step — the p-th neighbourhood in the t-direction and a neighbourhood of the zero section in the fibre direction — are different schemes. Proposition A.2 carries Theorem A.4, Remark A.5 and Corollary A.7; the appendix is itself presented as an alternative route to Theorem 1.4, which §§2–7 prove independently, and Question A.8 records that its scope is deliberately limited.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 6.1, published p. 146, lines 3–5
issues.printed: Since there are infinitely many prime numbers p such that there exists a good closed point s∈S (Lemma 5.11), we conclude that the Kodaira–Spencer class vanishes everywhere on X_S.
issues.correction: Apply Lemma 5.11 after inverting a non-zero coefficient of gr(∇_S) — equivalently, after shrinking S — which its own proof allows, since the finitely generated ring R₁ ⊂ C chosen there may be enlarged at will and Cassels's theorem then sends the adjoined inverse to a p-adic unit. Infinitude of residue characteristics on its own does not give the density the deduction needs.
issues.reason: The good points of Lemma 5.11(c) are closed points of S of pairwise distinct residue characteristics, and such a family need not meet every non-empty open subset of a positive-dimensional arithmetic base: in Spec Z[t] the closed points (p,t), p prime, realise every residue characteristic and all lie in V(t), where the non-zero section t vanishes. The vanishing of a section at all of them therefore does not make it zero. What is true, and is what the proof needs, is this: gr(∇_S) is a section of a coherent sheaf on the integral scheme X_S, so it is non-zero if and only if it is non-zero on the generic fibre; if gr(∇_C) ≠ 0 there is a non-empty open V ⊂ S over which it is non-zero, and a good point inside V contradicts the vanishing established for every good s. The rest of the proof is unaffected: on the reduced fibre X_s the identity gr(∇_s) = ω·id together with nilpotency does force ω = 0.

issues.locator: Remark 2.16(a) and (b), published pp. 116–117
issues.printed: (a) The vector space of degree-r sections in H⁰(Z′, Sym^• Ω¹_{Z′}[λ]) is isomorphic to A_{Z′,r}(k). … (b) For a∈A_{Z′,r}(S) we define the spectral cover Z′_a to be the closed subscheme of T^*Z′×_kS defined by the sheaf of ideals generated by the section θ^r+a₂θ^{r−2}+…+(−1)^r a_r in (π′×_k Id)_*O_{T^*Z′×_kS} = (Sym^• T_{Z′})⊗_k O_S.
issues.correction: In (a): the space of *monic* degree-r sections whose λ^{r−1}-coefficient vanishes — an affine space over A_{Z′,r}(k) — or, kept linear, the degree-r sections whose λ^r- and λ^{r−1}-coefficients both vanish. In (b): that section lives in H⁰(T^*Z′×_kS, (π′×Id)^* Sym^r Ω¹_{Z′}), as the display on p. 117 correctly states, and for dim Z′ > 1 the ideal is the one generated by its components.
issues.reason: A degree-r section of Sym^• Ω¹_{Z′}[λ] is ⨁_{i=0}^{r} H⁰(Z′,Sym^i Ω¹_{Z′})·λ^{r−i}, which contains the i = 0 summand k·λ^r and the i = 1 summand H⁰(Z′,Ω¹_{Z′}); (2.5) defines A_{Z′,r} as ⨁_{i=2}^{r}, the paper having just noted that "the definition above omits the i=1 term, since our Higgs fields are trace-free by assumption". The two spaces are therefore never equal: for Z′ = P¹ one has H⁰(Sym^iΩ¹) = 0 for all i ⩾ 1, so A_{Z′,r}(k) = 0 while the degree-r sections are k·λ^r ≠ 0. Part (b) itself uses the corrected description, its element being monic with no λ^{r−1} term. This is the remark the authors introduce with "Since it is central to our approach, we give a more detailed description", which is why the imprecision is worth recording rather than passing over.

issues.locator: §8.1, proof of Theorem 8.4, p. 299
issues.printed: "A general X = Ω^∞E may be replaced by its Postnikov truncation τ_{≤2p−2}X, which splits as a product of Eilenberg–MacLane spaces, up to homotopy equivalence of loop spaces. Indeed, the deloop Ω^∞ΣE can have non-vanishing homotopy in degrees ∗ ≥ 2 only, and the shortest possible k-invariant is 𝒫^1 : K(Z/p, 2) → K(Z/p, 2p). Hence τ_{≤2p−2}X splits as a product of Eilenberg–MacLane spaces, and this splitting respects the H-space structure."
issues.correction: The loop-space (H-space) splitting of τ_{≤2p−2}X can fail. The reduction to Eilenberg–MacLane spaces needs another argument, e.g. treat the single possible 𝒫^1-extension between π_1 and π_{2p−2} directly, or truncate at 2p − 3 and handle degree 2p − 2 separately.
issues.reason: The k-invariant 𝒫^1 : K(Z/p, 2) → K(Z/p, 2p) of the deloop connects π_2(Ω^∞ΣE) = π_1(X) to π_{2p−1}(Ω^∞ΣE) = π_{2p−2}(X), inside the range of the truncation. For E = ΣS^∧_p (p odd), α_1 ∈ π_{2p−3}(S) is detected by 𝒫^1, so τ_{≤2p−1}QS² has non-trivial k-invariant 𝒫^1ι_2 = ι_2^p, and τ_{≤2p−2}QS¹ is not a product of Eilenberg–MacLane loop spaces. The conclusion of Theorem 8.4 is not contradicted in this example: the Hurewicz image of α_1 survives in the indecomposables. But the argument as written does not prove it, and Lemma 8.5 needs an H-space splitting.

Iterating Lemma 26 with ε₀ as in the proof of (3.25) gives log log(λz)_n ≥ log(γ(λ).f(z))_n − 2ε₀ for all λ ∈ Λ′. So M(z, a) ≥ N(f(z), a − 2ε₀) ≥ ½ min_∆ h · e^{β(a−2ε₀)} for large a, since h > 0 is continuous on the compact ∆ (Theorems 13 and 37). Hence c⋆(z) > 0, and then c > 0 in Theorem 3.
issues.reason: Proposition 30 only proves that a_L converges and that its limits are bounded. Neither Lemma 29 nor Proposition 30 bounds c⋆ below. Baragar's estimate (log R)^{β+o(1)} does not exclude c = 0 either, since it allows, say, (log R)^β/log log R. Theorem 3 asserts c > 0, and the constant is Σ over base points of (log z_n⁽⁰⁾)^β c_∞(z⁽⁰⁾), so positivity needs this missing step. The step is routine with the paper's own lemmas.

issues.locator: §9, p. 30 (arXiv v1); checked on the page image
issues.printed: “This looks like a D_3 root system; however, the Weyl-invariant quadratic form in this case is q(s_1, s_2, s_3) = s_1² + s_2² + s_3³ − ¼(s_1 + s_2 + s_3)² rather than the usual dot product, and with this form, we have a realization of the C_3 root system with simple roots α_1 = (0, 1, −1), α_2 = (1, −1, 0), α_3 = (0, 2, 2).”
issues.correction: On the space of characters (s_1, s_2, s_3), where the paper has just written the Weyl action, the invariant form is s_1² + s_2² + s_3² + (s_1 + s_2 + s_3)², and the simple roots are (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1), of type C_3. The printed form, with s_3² for the misprinted s_3³, is the invariant form on the dual space of cocharacters (u_1, u_2, u_3). There the vectors (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (0, 2, 2) are the images 2α^∨/q(α^∨) of the simple roots, and α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1).
issues.reason: The paper's reflection for α_3 is r_3(s) = (s_1 + s_2 + s_3, −s_3, −s_2), which is s − ⟨s, α_3^∨⟩α_3 with α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1) and α_3 = (−1, 1, 1). The computation gives q(r_3 s) − q(s) = (5/4)((s_1 + s_2 + s_3)² − s_1²) ≠ 0, so q is not invariant on characters. A form a|s|² + b(Σs)² is invariant under r_1, r_2, r_3 exactly when a = b. Its inverse matrix I − J/4 gives the printed q on cocharacters. With the roots (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1) and the printed coroots, the Cartan matrix is [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 2, −1], [0, −2, 2]], of type C_3. All this was checked by computation in exact arithmetic. The positive chamber stated next, Re s_1 > Re s_2 > |Re s_3|, is correct, and nothing later uses q.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 6.1, §6.2 (p = 3) and §6.3 (p = 2), p.21 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: "So assume 9|k, in which case (3,0,0) is a non-singular solution modulo 9 and so lifts to solutions modulo 3ⁿ, n ≥ 2." … "So assume k ≡ 1 (mod 4) and we find the non-singular solution (1,0,0) modulo 4 … This then lifts to higher powers of 2."
issues.correction: The two lifts exist only in part of the stated classes: every x ≡ (3,0,0) mod 9 has M(x) ≡ 9 mod 27, and every x ≡ (1,0,0) mod 4 has M(x) ≡ 1 mod 8. Complete the argument with further points. For p = 2 and k ≡ 5 mod 8, use (x₁, 0, 2) with x₁² = k − 4 ≡ 1 mod 8, a 2-adic square. For p = 3, use (3,0,0) when k ≡ 9 mod 27; when k ≡ 18 mod 27, use (3y, 3, 0) with y² = (k − 9)/9 ≡ 1 mod 3; when 27 | k, use (3, 3, x₃) with x₃ a root of x₃² − 9x₃ + 18 − k, whose discriminant 9 + 4k = 9(1 + 4k/9) is a 3-adic square. Each is an exact ℤ_p-point, since the required square roots exist in ℤ₂, resp. ℤ₃.
issues.reason: The gradient of M at (3,0,0) is 6 and at (1,0,0) it is 2, so the lifting needs M(a) ≡ k modulo 27, resp. 8 (Hensel's lemma in the form ‖F(a)‖ < ‖F′(a)‖²). A direct check confirms the two failing classes, k ≡ 18 mod 27 and k ≡ 5 mod 8 (e.g. k = 18, 5). Counting solutions modulo 3⁴ and 2⁶ confirms that Proposition 6.1 itself holds in every admissible class.

issues.printed: "V₃(w) = [[1, 0], [−x₂, −1]] w, so that we write V₁V₃(w) = Aw + b, with A = [[−1 − x₂², −x₂], [−x₂, −1]] … Now, if x₂ ≠ 0, then A has infinite order and Aⁿ − I is invertible … the orbit V₁V₃(p) is infinite if k ≠ 4 … For k = 4, we use instead p = (−1, 2, 0) … and the argument above gives an infinite orbit"
issues.correction: V₃ acts on w = (x₁, x₃) by [[1, 0], [x₂, −1]], so A = [[x₂² − 1, −x₂], [x₂, −1]] with trace x₂² − 2. A has infinite order only for |x₂| ≥ 2, and Aⁿ − I is invertible only for |x₂| ≥ 3, as the paper itself finds for U₂ in §5.2.3. Run the argument with planes x₂ = c, |c| ≥ 3. To show Zariski density for every k, use the points (−t² + k − 4, −t² + t + k − 4, 2) of the parametric family, whose x₂ = −t² + t + k − 4 is unbounded, instead of the single base point (k − 4, k − 4, 2).
issues.reason: x₃ ↦ x₁x₂ − x₃ is linear in w with matrix [[1, 0], [x₂, −1]]. With the correct A the base point p = (k − 4, k − 4, 2) has x₂ = ±1 for k = 5, 3, where A has order 3 and (A² + A + I)b = 0. Its V₁V₃-orbit then has exactly 3 points (checked for k = 3, 5), so the claim "the orbit V₁V₃(p) is infinite if k ≠ 4" fails. For k = 4 and (−1, 2, 0), A is parabolic and Aⁿ − I is singular; the orbit is nevertheless infinite (checked). The density statement for U₁ survives with the repair.

By Nakayama IĀ = (f′_{j+1}, …, f′_m)Ā, so (f′_{j+1}) + (f′_{j+2}, …, f′_m)² has the radical of IĀ, which lies in no associated prime of Ā because IĀ contains a non-zero-divisor; Kaplansky's Theorem 124 then gives f″. Since f″ ∈ I² ⊆ (t)², the new generators keep the form (5.4) and minimality. Theorem 5.6 is true.
issues.reason: When h < m the first h minimal generators need not generate I up to radical. Example: P = O[[t1,t2]], I = (t1(ϖ+t2), ϖt2(ϖ+t2), t1t2), a minimal generating set of the form (5.4) with d = (1, 2, ∞). issues.locator: Theorem G, Introduction p. 7 (and footnote 1), and the sentence before Conjecture A, p. 60
issues.printed: p. 7: “When F is a CM field and ℓ is sufficiently large, Conjecture A is known by [45, Theorem 1.3]. … Theorem G. … For ℓ > 20, there exists an integer µ ≥ 1 …” Footnote 1: “The precise bound is given in [45, (1.2)], in our situation, ℓ > 20 is sufficient if [F : Q] = 2.” p. 60: “part (ii) is known for sufficiently large ℓ; see [45, Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.3].”
issues.correction: [45, Theorem 1.3] gives ρ_m only modulo an ideal I with I^4 = 0, so it does not give Conjecture A(ii). The nilpotent-free result, whose bound is (1.2), is [45, Theorem 1.4 = Theorem 5.13]; it assumes ℓ unramified in F and a strictly regular weight (λ_{τ,1} > λ_{τ,2} for every τ), whereas the complexes C_K of §13 have trivial coefficients (λ = 0). So the cited results do not supply Conjecture A(ii) for C_K; Theorem G should also assume Conjecture A(ii) (and ℓ unramified in F), or cite a result covering trivial weight.
issues.reason: For n = 2 and F imaginary quadratic, the left side of [45, (1.2)] is 16 + 3(a_1 − a_2) + (b_1 − b_2) for λ_τ̃ = (a_1, a_2), λ_τ̃c = (b_1, b_2); its minimum over regular weights is 20, at λ = ((1,0),(1,0)), which is the footnote's ℓ > 20. At λ = 0 the Lan–Suh vanishing behind [45, Thm 5.10] fails already in degree 0. Also ℓ = 23 with F = Q(√−23) meets ℓ > 20 but is ramified in F. Theorem G as stated therefore rests on an input the citation does not provide; its other inputs (Conjectures C, D via Theorem 13.12) need only ℓ > 3.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 3.1, induction step, p. 29 (published); same in arXiv v2
issues.printed: "Now let r > 1. Then Z = ⋃_{i=1}^{r−1} Y_i is a divisor with normal crossings on X which fulfills all the assumptions of the theorem, and the same is true for Z_r = Y_r ∩ Z = ⋃_{i=1}^{r−1}(Y_r ∩ Y_i) on Y_r."
issues.correction: State and prove Theorem 3.1 for smooth divisors Y_i that are not necessarily irreducible (or connected), and discard empty intersections. The base case r = 1 works verbatim: for d = 1, Y is a finite set of closed points with separable residue fields, and 0 → C → ⊕_x Ind_{K(x)}^K Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ → Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ → 0 stays exact on G_K-coinvariants because H_1(G, Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ) = 0 for finite G. Z_r is non-empty when d ≥ 2, because X ∖ Y_1 is affine and Y_r is proper of positive dimension, so Y_r meets Y_1. When d = 1 the right-hand column is trivially exact.
issues.reason: The theorem assumes the Y_i are smooth irreducible divisors, and the base case r = 1, d = 1 uses 'the unique point x ∈ Y'. The divisors Y_r ∩ Y_i on Y_r are smooth but in general reducible, and can be empty. For example, on a surface two smooth curves meeting transversally in two points have Y_r ∩ Y_i equal to two points. So the induction applies the theorem outside its stated hypotheses. The argument itself never uses irreducibility beyond the base case, which extends as stated.

At the auxiliary split primes in Proposition3.7 choose a split torus in one factor and an anisotropic torus in the other; prove this stronger property survives the twist.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.1, p.9 (published version)
issues.printed: "Let t_i := Σ_{v|w_i} x_v. Then since |x_{v_{i,j}} − x_{v_{i,j′}}| ≤ 2, we have x_{v_{i,j}} = t_i/k_i + O_k(1). We have Σ_i t_i = 0, since u, α_r, and α_s all have norm 1. Thus Σ_{i,j} max(x_{v_{i,j}}, 0) = Σ_i t_i + O_k(1) = O_k(1)."
issues.correction: Normalise the α_i first. Their relative norms η_i = Nm_{L/K}(α_i) are units of K, since the ideal (α_i) has trivial relative norm. Pigeonhole the α_i by the class of η_i in O_K^*/(O_K^*)^d, which has at most d^{[K:ℚ]} = O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) classes. Within one class, η_i = η₀e_i^d with e_i ∈ O_K^*; replace α_i by α_i/e_i, which leaves the ideal unchanged. Then Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s) = 1, so every t_i = log|Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s)|_{w_i} vanishes, and the stated height bound follows. The loss is a factor O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) in N + 1, so (2.1) is unchanged.
issues.reason: The boxes control only PUL(α_i), i.e. the differences of coordinates within each block, because P drops the block sums t_i. Units u ∈ O* = ker(Nm_{L/K}) have t_i = 0, but an arbitrary generator α_i of ℘_i^{ℓa_i}℘̄_i^{−ℓb_i}℘₀^{−ℓa₀}℘̄₀^{ℓb₀} has t_i(α_i) = log|Nm_{L/K}(α_i)|_{w_i}, the logarithm of a unit of K, which need not be bounded. "Norm 1" in the absolute sense gives only Σ_i t_i = 0. The step Σ max(x_v, 0) = Σ_i t_i + O(1) needs each t_i = O(1) (for example t₁ = T, t₂ = −T gives Σ max ≈ T). So the claimed bound on H(uα_r/α_s) is not justified as written, though the repair costs only a constant depending on [L : ℚ].

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 4.1, p. 404
issues.printed: "By the discussion and Lemma 31.32.4(3) in [Stacks, Tag 01OF] and Lemma 29.38.2 in [Tag 01VL], we know that O_X̃(−E) = O_X̃(1) is π-relatively ample."
issues.correction: Replace the boundary divisor E by the exceptional Cartier divisor D = V(I·O_X̃) of the (normalized) blow-up. D is supported on E but in general has multiplicities aσ ≥ 1, given by the polarization function of the admissible decomposition. Then O(−D) ⊗ π*L^k is ample, and Theorem 4.1 holds with L̃_k(−D). In Proposition 4.2 take ℓ0 ≥ n0·k·max aσ, so that g^{ℓ0}, which vanishes to order ≥ ℓ0 along every boundary component, gives a section twisted by −n0k′D.
issues.reason: The Stacks lemma gives O(1) = I·O_X̃ = O(−D) for the exceptional divisor of the ideal I of AMRT IV Thm. 2.2, not for the reduced boundary E. On a Hirzebruch cusp resolution (d = 2), −E is not π-ample whenever some boundary curve has self-intersection −2, since (−E)·Eσ = bσ − 2 = 0. The conclusion survives with D in place of E.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 8.2.1, p.59
issues.printed: "We may further assume that L^♭ + ⟨x⟩ is integral and has a basis (e′_1, …, e′_n) such that val(e′_i) = a′_i. Let L′^♭ = ⟨e′_1, …, e′_{n−1}⟩. Then we have Int_{L^♭,V}(x) = Int_{L′^♭,V}(x′), and ∂Den_{L^♭,V}(x) = ∂Den_{L′^♭,V}(x′), where x′ = e′_n."
issues.correction: Replace the two claimed equalities by the equality of differences: with φ = Int_{L^♭,V} − ∂Den_{L^♭,V} and φ′ = Int_{L′^♭,V} − ∂Den_{L′^♭,V}, Theorem 6.1.3 cancels the horizontal parts, so φ(x) = Int(L^♭ + ⟨x⟩) − ∂Den(L^♭ + ⟨x⟩) = Int(L′^♭ + ⟨x′⟩) − ∂Den(L′^♭ + ⟨x′⟩) = φ′(x′). The induction hypothesis φ′ = 0 then gives φ(x) = 0 for x ∉ M(L^♭), which is all the rest of the proof uses.
issues.reason: Only the full functions Int_{L^♭}(x) = Int(L^♭ + ⟨x⟩) and ∂Den_{L^♭}(x) depend on the lattice L^♭ + ⟨x⟩ alone. Their horizontal and vertical parts depend on the hyperplane L^♭_F. By Definition 6.1.2, ∂Den_{L^♭,H}(x) and ∂Den_{L′^♭,H}(x′) are sums over integral L″ ⊇ L^♭ + ⟨x⟩ = L′^♭ + ⟨x′⟩ with the different conditions t(L″ ∩ L^♭_F) ≤ 1 and t(L″ ∩ L′^♭_F) ≤ 1; geometrically, Z(L^♭)_H ≠ Z(L′^♭)_H. So the two stated equalities do not follow from what precedes them. The step is repaired in one line and the theorem stands.

Then the automorphism g̃ of N (see §4.4, 4.5) carries ^𝕃Z(L′) to ^𝕃Z(L). In particular, Int(L) only depends on the isometry class of L."
issues.correction: A lift g̃ ∈ J(F) of g ∈ SO(V)(F) has spinor norm η(g̃) = sn(g) in F^×/(F^×)², so η(g̃) = 1 forces sn(g) = 1. What the argument needs is only val η(g̃) = 0, since g̃ carries RZ^{(ℓ)}_G to RZ^{(ℓ + val η(g̃))}_G (§4.5) and N = RZ^{(0)}_G; that is available exactly when some isometry carrying L′ to L has spinor norm of even valuation, which the remark does not establish.
issues.reason: There are isometric pairs for which every isometry has spinor norm of odd valuation. Take m even and ε = −1: for m even and U unimodular, ϵ(ϖU) = χ(U), so V^−_m ≅ ϖ·H^−_{m,F}. Write H^−_m = M ⊥ ⟨w⟩ with M self-dual of rank n = m − 1, and let L ⊆ V be M with the scaled form, so that all its fundamental invariants are 1 and val(w) = 1. An element of SO(V)(F) stabilizing L preserves L_F and the line L^⊥_F, hence is a product of an even number of reflections in vectors of L or of L^⊥_F (for p odd the orthogonal group of a unimodular lattice is generated by the reflections in its vectors of unit norm, O'Meara 92:4); each such reflection has spinor norm of valuation 1, so the stabilizer has spinor norms of even valuation. Since V is isotropic, sn : SO(V)(F) → F^×/(F^×)² is surjective; choosing h with val sn(h) odd and L′ = hL gives isometric lattices such that every g ∈ SO(V)(F) with gL′ = L has val sn(g) odd. Remark 4.11.5 is the invariance input for Lemma 9.2.2 (i) (the O(W)(F)-invariance of Int^⊥_{L^♭,V}), hence for Proposition 9.2.3 and Theorem 9.3.2. The conclusion is presumably true — Theorem 4.15.1 asserts it, and for m = 4, ε = −1 it follows from Terstiege's explicit formulas (Remark 4.15.2) — and an automorphism of RZ_G outside J(F) shifting the components would supply it; but no such argument is given here, and this extraction did not settle it.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.3, Proposition 5.2, Theorems 5.7 and 5.8, pp.25–31
issues.printed: Proposition 5.2: "Let m ∈ Z_{>0} such that Z(m) ≠ ∅; and if b is odd, we further assume that for a fixed D, √(m/D) ∈ Z, as in Theorem 2.4." Lemma 5.3 likewise, with the proof "we conclude by [BK03, Theorem 4.11, (4.73), (4.74)], since both d_0 and k are independent of m." But: "Theorem 5.7. For every m representable by (L, Q) …" and "Theorem 5.8. For every positive integer m, we have the following bounds …", proved from Proposition 5.2.
issues.correction: For b odd and m/D not a square, add this to the proof of Lemma 5.3. In [BK03, Thm. 4.11(ii)] (r odd), the m-dependence through d_0 = d_0(m) enters as log|4m/D_0²| − 2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ). By the functional equation of L(s, χ_{D_0}), this is log m + 2L′(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2)/L(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2) + O(1): the log|D_0| terms cancel. The logarithmic derivative at κ − 1/2 ≥ 2 is bounded by |ζ′/ζ(2)|, and the χ_{d_0}-factors of σ_m(s) are bounded uniformly as in the proof of Proposition 5.2. So Lemma 5.3 (with O(1) uniform in m) and Proposition 5.2 hold for every m with Z(m) ≠ ∅. That is what Theorems 5.7–5.8 assert, and what Proposition 6.4 and Lemma 7.6 use.
issues.reason:
Theorem 5.8 is proved from equation (3.1), Proposition 3.2 and Proposition 5.2, so for b odd its proof covers only m ∈ D·(Q^×)². It is then applied to arbitrary integers:
- in Proposition 6.4 to M = Q(λ) for a difference λ of two lattice vectors ("Theorem 5.8(i) implies X^{b/2} ≪ −log|Q(λ_x)| ≪ A(M) ≪ M^{b/2} log M");
- in Lemma 7.6 to m = a_1(n)², a square but not in general D times a square.
Both feed Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 7.1, hence the main theorem for every odd b ≥ 3. For b even, d = (−1)^{r/2}det(L) does not depend on m and there is no gap. BK03 Theorem 4.11 was read in arXiv:math/0204100v2 (p.27): its r-odd formula contains log|4m/D_0²| and −2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ).

issues.locator: §7.3, construction of μ, p.43
issues.printed: "We define the a_i as follows: suppose that a_n ≠ 0; we define a_i = 0 for n + 1 ≤ i ≤ e^{e^{p^n}}, and we then define a_i = 1 for i = ⌈e^{e^{p^n}}⌉. This implies that Σ_{i≤n} a_ip^i ≡ μ mod p^N with N ≥ e^{e^{p^n}} – that is, there is an integer x_n of size O(p^n) that approximates μ mod p^N, with N double-exponential in the size of x_n. … the lattice Λ created this way must also have property 2."
issues.correction: Make the gaps double-exponential in the discriminant rather than in x_n: after a_n ≠ 0, set a_i = 0 for n < i < exp(exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)})) with C depending only on L (so that exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)}) exceeds the discriminant of L_n below). Then property (2) of Lemma 7.11 holds with L_n = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j}, and the example stands.
issues.reason: Property (2) of Lemma 7.11 needs N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}}, where D_i is the discriminant of the approximating sublattice L_i. Here L_i = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j : 1 ≤ j ≤ c}, with e_j, f_j orthogonal and Q positive definite. So D_i ≍ Π_j (Q(e_j) + x_n²Q(f_j)) ≥ x_n^{2c} ≥ p^{2cn}, because a_n ≠ 0 forces x_n ≥ p^n. The printed choice gives only N ≈ e^{e^{p^n}}, which is far below e^{e^{D_i}}, so the proof of Lemma 7.11 (m_i < e^{D_i} and (Y_Λ.Z(m_i)) > N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}} > e^{m_i}) does not apply. "Double-exponential in the size of x_n" is not double-exponential in D_i ≍ x_n^{2c}. The example is illustrative and not used for the main results.

issues.locator: Proposition 14, pp.725–727, and Remark 16, p.727, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 709–744 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 814976ee…f40a); also footnote 4, p.712
issues.printed: Proposition 14: close CM points of the same type with the same projection to X(1)×X(1) lie on a low-degree Hecke curve, stated for Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points alike. Remark 16: "Hecke curves do not pass through anti-Heegner CM points. Thus, …" anti-Heegner CM points repel. Footnote 4: the 2-to-1 ambiguity of [BT13] "can be rectified by using the stronger repulsion statement found in Proposition 14."
issues.correction: Proposition 14 holds for Heegner CM points (CM⁺) only, with Lemma 15 applied with h₀ = 1 (erratum Proposition 2.1). Close anti-Heegner CM points lie on low-degree conjugate Hecke curves instead. The first clause of Remark 16 (Hecke curves contain no anti-Heegner points) is true; its repulsion claim is false.
issues.reason: The real-analytic involution conjugating the second factor preserves the hyperbolic metric and swaps Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points, so anti-Heegner points cannot all repel. In general no h₀ ∈ SL₂(Z) reduces to the non-identity coset of the stabilizer H in its normalizer, which is where the proof fails (erratum §§1–2). The appeal in footnote 4 therefore rests on the withdrawn part; the main theorems hold by the corrected argument of the erratum.

issues.locator: §4, the paragraph after Corollary 15 on parabolic curves, v3 p.11 (published p.141), in arXiv 2108.13397v3 (15 September 2023, the final author version; PDF SHA-256 e23989fb…b722); published page numbers are those the extraction recorded from the open-access publisher PDF (SHA-256 77c20bc7…e148), which could not be re-fetched here
issues.printed: "We say that a curve X is parabolic if it has genus 0 and the degree of X̄ ∖ X is at most 2. If X is proper of genus 0, then there is a unique Galois section, and it is geometric if and only if X = P¹. If X is parabolic affine, every Galois section of X is cuspidal (the only non-trivial case is settled by [Sch15, Theorem A]). Because of this, we can always assume that X is non-parabolic."
issues.correction: The sentence is false as stated. What the later reductions need is a statement about the t-birationally liftable (or birationally liftable) sections of a parabolic affine X, which have to be treated directly, including the case where X̄ ∖ X is a single point of degree 2. The reductions to non-parabolic X rest on this: "We may assume that X is non-parabolic" in the proof of Lemma 16, and "it is immediate to check that t-b.l. sections are quasi-t-b.l." after Definition 18, where the identity map is not available for parabolic X.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let k = Q and X = P¹_Q ∖ V(T² − 2). Then X is affine, of genus 0, with boundary a single point of degree 2, so it is parabolic. The paper defines a Galois section to be cuspidal if it is associated with a k-rational point of X̄ ∖ X (§1). The boundary has no Q-rational point, so X has no cuspidal sections. But 0 ∈ X(Q), so X has a geometric section. Schmidt's theorem concerns the existence of rational points and splitting; it does not make a degree-2 boundary point rational. The paper's Theorems A–C are not claimed to fail here, only this justification of the reduction. Noted by the extraction (item 77, with the reduction gap in items 81, 96 and 112).

If x ∈ X, then for opens U containing x the section ι_U(s) is the geometric section at x, which is not in the cuspidal packet P_{U,x}. issues.printed: "(ii) The number of supersingular points in X₀(N)(F_{p²}) that correspond to supersingular elliptic curves over F_{p²} with the Frobenius trace a_{p²} = 2p or −2p and the j-invariant different from 0 and 1728 is at least µ(⌊(p−1)/12⌋ − 3/2 + (−3/p) + ½(−1/p)). In particular, there is a supersingular point with a_{p²} = 2p or −2p in X₀(N)(F_{p²}) over X(1)(F_{p²})∖{0,1728} that is unramified for π if p ≡ 1 mod 12 or p ≥ 31."

issues.reason: The conclusion needs the lower bound to exceed the number of ramification points, which (i) bounds by µ/6. At p = 47: ⌊46/12⌋ = 3, (−3/47) = −1 (47 ≡ 2 mod 3) and (−1/47) = −1 (47 ≡ 3 mod 4), so the bound is µ(3 − 3/2 − 1 − 1/2) = 0 < µ/6. A computation over all primes 31 ≤ p ≤ 400 finds 47 as the only failure, and beyond that the floor term dominates. The main theorem is unaffected: Lemma 5.2(iii) covers p = 47, and Rubin's own verification (Remark 2.3) covers small p. Found by the review REV-PAPER-BURUNGALE-KOBAYASHI-OTA-21.

issues.correction: The count of geometric branches over k-points needs an extra term for the non-rational branches through rational singular points. For a geometrically integral curve C with normalization of genus g and arithmetic genus p_a, one has Σ_{x∈C(k)} #ν^{−1}(x) ≤ #C̃(k) + 2 Σ_x δ_x ≤ q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g). The constant q + 4q^{1/2} + 3 in Theorem 9.1 and in Theorems 1.5, 1.7, 10.1 and Corollaries 1.11, 1.14, 1.15, obtained from Lemma 3.15 in (9.8), is not established by the v2 argument.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let D ⊂ P² over k = F_3 be the projective closure of y² = x²(x − 1). It is geometrically integral (r = 1) with normalization P¹, parametrized by x = t² + 1, y = t(t² + 1), so g_g = 0 and the right side is q + 1 = 4. D(F_3) consists of (0,0), (1,0), (2,1), (2,2) and the point at infinity. The origin is an ordinary node with tangent cone y² + x² = 0. Since −1 is not a square in F_3, its two branches t = ±i are defined only over F_9. The left side is therefore 2 + 4 = 6 > 4. The proof's flaw: Lemma 3.17 correctly relates the product of Z*_{D,k}(ζT) over ζ ∈ μ_d to the zeta functions of the C̃_j over k′. But the zeros and poles of Z*_{D,k} cannot be read off from that product. Here Z*_{D,k}(T) = (1 + T)/((1 − T)²(1 − qT)), and the extra factor (1 + T)/(1 − T) disappears under T ↦ −T. The bound with q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g) follows from Weil's bound for C̃ together with b_x ≤ δ_x + 1 ≤ 2δ_x at singular points, and it is attained in the example. The general reducible, weighted sum in (9.8) needs the analogous count, including intersections of Frobenius-conjugate components. Noted by the extraction (gap G1, items bad-branch-bound and global-sum-source), which checked the page image.

Proof: "In the setting of the proposition, the primitive embedding of Λ into Λ_2d corresponds to a tuple (V, W, γ, t)."
issues.correction: Assume Λ is a primitive sublattice of Λ_2d. In the proof of Theorem 2.10, choose the lattice Λ containing v, w with v² = 2, v·w = 1 to be primitive. For example, in Λ_2d = ⟨2d⟩ ⊕ U with basis h, e, f, take the span of v = e + f and w = kh + e. It is primitive, since (x, y, z) ↦ (z, y − z) retracts it, and its Gram matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2dk²]] is positive definite.
issues.reason: The proof starts from a primitive embedding Λ ⊂ Λ_2d, which the statement does not provide, and the statement fails for non-primitive Λ. In Λ_2 = ⟨2⟩ ⊕ U, the sublattice Λ generated by 2h and 2(e + f) has Gram matrix diag(8, 8). Take m = 1, which satisfies (i) and (ii) for every N, a, b. A primitive embedding of Λ into Λ_2 would give a 2-dimensional subspace of Λ_2/2Λ_2 = F_2³ on which the half-norm Q(x, y, z) = x² + yz vanishes, since Λ has all half-norms even. The nonzero zeros of Q are (0,0,1), (0,1,0) and (1,1,1), and each pairwise sum has Q = 1, so no such plane exists. Noted by the extraction (items 38–41), which also gave the primitive choice above.

issues.correction: Frac(k[x][[t]]) is a proper subfield of k(x)((t)). The erratum says this but gives the witness Σ_{n≥1} t^n/x^n, which lies in Frac(k[x][[t]]). A valid witness is Σ_{n≥1} t^n/x^{n!}.

The recursion c_n = (a_n − Σ_{i≥1} b_i c_{n−i})/b_0 gives ord_x(c_n) ≥ −m(n + 1). Every element of Frac(k[x][[t]]) therefore has x-poles growing at most linearly in n, while Σ t^n/x^{n!} has poles of order n!.
